title: fix(server): capture legal multi-request prefill CUDA graph batches
author: nvpohanh
body:
[by Codex]

## Motivation

When `--context-length` is smaller than a prefill CUDA-graph capture bucket, the old capture path creates one synthetic request with `seq_len=num_tokens`. That exceeds the per-request context limit and can cause the #21112 illegal-memory-access failure during graph warm-up.

Clamping the aggregate prefill token ceiling to `context_length` avoids that crash, but unnecessarily disables graph replay for legal multi-request prefills whose total token count exceeds one request's context length.

## Design

This PR fixes the capture shape rather than applying a per-request cap to an aggregate-token setting:

- Resolve legal prefill capture buckets once in `ModelRunner.init_prefill_cuda_graph()` and write the filtered list back to `cuda_graph_config.prefill.bs` before constructing the runner.
- Keep every backend's capture buckets expressed in aggregate tokens and cap them at `context_length * max_capture_requests`: request-pool size for `tc_piecewise`/`breakable`, or the resolved fixed request-slot count for `full`.
- During capture, partition a bucket of `num_tokens` into the fewest synthetic requests such that every request has `seq_len <= context_length`.
- For `full`, preserve its fixed request-axis contract by padding any unused request slots with zero-length sentinels after the context-bounded synthetic requests.
- If filtering leaves no legal bucket, log the backend, context length, and request-pool capacity and fall back to eager prefill.
- Remove the earlier ServerArgs-time `context_length * max_running_requests` calculation because `max_running_requests` is not always resolved at that stage.
- For DeepSeek's MHA prefill path under BCG, register and select the existing `attn_mha` companion on CUDA as well as HIP. This ensures the captured attention op receives MHA head metadata instead of the same-layer-id `attn_mqa` metadata.

This preserves graph coverage for multi-request prefills while keeping every synthetic request within the per-request context bound.

## Validation

- `git diff --check`
- `python -m py_compile` on all five changed Python files
- Black check in `lmsysorg/sglang:dev-cu13`: all five changed files left unchanged

## 4xGB200 DSR1 NVFP4 verification

Passed on four NVIDIA GB200 GPUs at commit `aec6c63161` using a staged DeepSeek-R1-0528 ModelOpt NVFP4 checkpoint:

- TP4, FlashInfer attention, `context_length=2048`, `max_running_requests=8`, `chunked_prefill_size=4096`, decode CUDA graphs disabled, and FlashInfer autotuning disabled.
- Prefill graph configuration: `backend=breakable`, `bs=[4096]`. The only capture bucket is therefore larger than one request's context and is constructed as two legal synthetic requests.
- All four ranks completed `Capture target prefill CUDA graph` for 4,096 tokens in about 20.9 seconds; capture used about 1.41 GiB per GPU.
- The server reached readiness. A two-prompt `/generate` request returned four completion tokens for each prompt; server-reported prompt lengths were 1,301 and 1,301 tokens (2,602 aggregate, greater than the 2,048-token per-request context).
- Both runtime prefills logged `cuda graph: True`.
- AIHub Slurm step `4272943.2` completed with exit code `0:0`.

## Earlier H100 verification

Passed on one H100 80GB at commit `e689f496ba`:

- `Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct` with `--context-length 2048 --mem-fraction-static 0.7 --attention-backend flashinfer --cuda-graph-backend-prefill tc_piecewise`.
- Piecewise prefill CUDA-graph capture completed across every configured bucket through 8,192 aggregate tokens (`4 * context_length`).
- The server reached readiness and completed its startup `/generate` request successfully.

## Related

- Fixes the capture-shape issue underlying #21112 / #22516.
- Follow-up to the discussion in #30206.

title: [CPU] add fused_qk_gemma_norm and refactor norm kernel implementation
author: mingfeima
body:
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->

## Motivation

CPU norm kernels in sgl-kernel (L2Norm, RMSNorm, Gemma variants, LayerNorm, gated RMSNorm, and fused add paths) were implemented as separate, largely duplicated loops. Each kernel reimplemented the same reduce → scale → (weight / bias / gate) logic with slightly different tensor layouts and stride handling.

This PR refactors those kernels into a single trait-based framework. The goal is to:

- Reduce maintenance cost when adding or changing norm variants (notably Gemma / QK-style RMSNorm)
- Unify 2D / 3D / 4D input handling in one code path
- Keep the existing public `torch.ops.sgl_kernel.*_cpu` APIs unchanged
- Improve performance on AVX512 via a BF16 fast path and faster approximate exp for `SiLU`
- Add `fused_qk_gemma_norm` for Qwen3.5

## Modifications

Core refactor (sgl-kernel/csrc/cpu/norm.cpp)
Introduce shared infrastructure:

- NormParams: normalizes 2D / 3D / 4D inputs into a logical [B, H, T, D] layout with stride-aware input indexing and contiguous output
- NormMode + NormTraits: compile-time flags for weight, bias, shift, mean, and gate; shared apply_* helpers
- NormReduceGeneric: generic vectorized reduce + apply path for all modes
- NormReduce<M, BFloat16, D> (AVX512): specialized fast path for BF16 when D ∈ {32, 64, 128, 256, 512}

Migrate all existing CPU norm ops onto the unified framework:

- l2norm_cpu
- rmsnorm_cpu, fused_add_rmsnorm_cpu

title: Optimize LongCat-Flash router GEMM with the HPC-Ops bf16xfp32 kernel
author: BBuf
body:
## Motivation

Optimize the LongCat-Flash router GEMM (bf16 activations x fp32 router weight) with the `gemm_bf16xfp32` kernel from [HPC-Ops](https://github.com/Tencent/hpc-ops): the fp32 weight is decomposed once into two cached bf16 halves (`w = w_high + w_low / 256`) and the kernel computes both bf16 GEMMs fused, preserving fp32-weight accuracy while running on bf16 tensor cores.

Originally this PR carried an in-tree port of the kernel; now that the image builds HPC-Ops in (#31390), it consumes `hpc.gemm_bf16xfp32` directly per the discussion with the Hunyuan team — future kernel-side updates (e.g. their H200 tuning) land by bumping the pinned hpc commit, with no re-porting.

## Modifications

- `sglang/jit_kernel/dsv4/gemm.py`: the accelerated branch of `linear_bf16_fp32` calls `hpc.gemm_bf16xfp32` (weight split + split-K flag workspace cached on the weight tensor; guarded on hpc availability + Hopper + shape constraints, cublas fp32 fallback otherwise).
- `LongcatFlashRouter` dispatches through it for the benchmarked (hidden_size, num_experts) shapes with a per-shape min-M guard; unbenchmarked shapes / router_bias keep the original path. Opt-in globally via `SGLANG_OPT_BF16_FP32_GEMM_ALGO=hpc`.
- Dropped the previously inlined sm90 kernel source and JIT wrapper.

## Accuracy

- `test/registered/gemm/test_linear_bf16_fp32_hpc.py`: hpc path vs fp32 reference on both LongCat router shapes (rtol 0.08 / atol 0.01, upstream tolerance), min-M dispatch, weight-split cache reuse — passes on H200.
- `test/registered/unit/models/test_longcat_flash_router_hpc_gemm.py` (CPU): router dispatch logic.
- `7 passed, 6 subtests passed` on H200.

## Performance (H200)

`hpc.gemm_bf16xfp32` vs the current fp32 GEMM path (`x.float() @ w.t()`), LongCat router shapes:

| shape | m | HPC (us) | fp32 mm (us) | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| k=6144, n=768 | 64 | 15.5 | 35.6 | 2.31x |
| k=6144, n=768 | 512 | 38.4 | 120.4 | 3.14x |
| k=6144, n=768 | 8192 | 430.0 | 1661.1 | 3.86x |
| k=3072, n=384 | 64 | 14.8 | 23.1 | 1.56x |
| k=3072, n=384 | 512 | 20.7 | 44.1 | 2.13x |
| k=3072, n=384 | 8192 | 113.1 | 487.8 | 4.31x |

(The router GEMM is one small slice of the forward; e2e effect is correspondingly modest — this keeps the fp32-weight routing numerics while removing the fp32-GEMM cost.)

## Model-level validation (LongCat-Flash-Lite-FP8, H200 TP1)

A/B against origin/main (identical hardware, one GPU each on the same box; greedy smoke outputs match token-for-token):

GSM8K (1319 questions, parallel 128):

| | GSM8K accuracy | Invalid |
|---|---|---|
| main | 0.798 | 0.000 |
| **this PR** | **0.802** | 0.001 |

`bench_one_batch_server` (input 1024 / output 128):

| bs | metric | main | this PR | delta |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | input tok/s | 15190 | 15613 | **+2.8%** |
| 16 | input tok/s | 68588 | 71021 | **+3.5%** |
| 64 | input tok/s | 62175 | 65509 | **+5.4%** |
| 1 | output tok/s | 242.4 | 244.8 | +1.0% |
| 16 | output tok/s | 2111.2 | 2104.7 | -0.3% |
| 64 | output tok/s | 5569.1 | 5549.5 | -0.4% |

Reading the numbers: the router GEMM's M is the token count, so **prefill** (m = 1024 x bs, far above the per-shape min-M guard) rides the HPC-Ops kernel and gains **+2.8~5.4%** end-to-end input throughput; **decode** at bs <= 64 sits below the Lite guard (min_m = 128) and intentionally keeps the cublas path, hence parity there. Accuracy is unchanged (an earlier 200-question A/B of the bit-equivalent in-tree port showed the same picture: 0.80 -> 0.82).

Requires HPC-Ops in the environment (built into the image by #31390); without it every path falls back to the existing cublas fp32 GEMM, so nothing changes for other users.

title: [Spec] Add DSpark: confidence-scheduled speculative decoding
author: sglang-bot
body:
DSpark speculative decoding — semi-autoregressive block drafting + confidence-scheduled, variable-length verify.

## Follow-up work (separate PRs)

Kept out of this PR to limit its footprint; planned as follow-ups after it lands:

- The `num_tokens_per_bs` family (runners / graph runners / spec helpers) is misnamed — the value is per request, not per batch. Renaming it to `num_tokens_per_req` is mechanical (~240 internal occurrences).
- The fa3 backend rewrites `speculative_num_draft_tokens` in place for draft workers; it should keep the server-args value verbatim and read a derived `num_tokens_per_req` field instead.
- The per-algorithm hooks in `speculative_hook.py` duplicate the shared num_steps/topk forcing and spec batching defaults across algorithms.
- The DSpark Triton kernels live outside the `sglang.kernels` ops layout; migrating them waits on untangling their `ScheduleBatch` coupling.
- The dsv4 backend carries algorithm-keyed instance state: the draft-block attention support and the `needs_cpu_seq_lens` opt-out are keyed on flags fixed at construction. These are the only instance-keyed modes in the attention layer, where every other speculative path dispatches on per-batch data (spec input types, ragged layouts) or capability methods.
- The decode cuda-graph runner drives ragged verify as a parallel token-bucket-keyed mode beside the bs-keyed graphs, with its own capture/admission paths. Unifying the two keyings — uniform verify windows as the special case of token keying — would remove the duplicated capture machinery, but re-keys every algorithm's replay path and needs its own performance validation.
- The final shape of the shared draft-worker construction layer (`draft_worker_common`, shared with DFLASH) is undecided: a stateless builder module as today, or a shared block-draft worker base class owning the common identity/lifecycle code; the module name should follow whichever outcome.
- Hand-built DSpark draft batches leave `can_run_dp_cuda_graph` unset, and the dp-attention sync gate ANDs it into graph admission, so the dense-draft block never replays cuda graphs under dp attention. Whether that conservatism is required (the draft forward is attention-TP-local) or a missed graph path needs GPU validation.
- The confidence-relay staging (device-to-host confidence transfer for the scheduler) lives in the shared overlap-utils module while its only producer and consumer are DSpark components, and the planner imports its constants back from there; it also allocates its CUDA buffers lazily on first use. Relocating it into the DSpark component package (with construction-time allocation) would shrink the shared-file footprint.
- The dsv4 attention-metadata builders (causal expansion, page-table/positions) were rewritten as triton kernels serving every dsv4 path, speculative or not. Triton-vs-torch parity is CI-covered; a dedicated performance validation of the non-speculative dsv4 paths on the new builders is still to be done.
- The `SGLANG_DSPARK_*` environment variables sit inside the generic test-and-debug block (plus one under spec config) instead of a dedicated section, and three boolean perf toggles (`FAST_KERNEL`, `FAST_SAMPLING`, `FP32_LM_HEAD`) carry no verb category token, unlike the sibling `OPT_*` entries. Renaming becomes an alias-deprecation exercise once released, so the regrouping and renames should happen soon after landing.

title: [AMD] Fix GLM-5.2 MTP Quark excludes
author: wangjiaxin99
body:
Co-author: @Raiden-Makoto 

## Summary

This PR fixes GLM-5.2 MXFP4 MTP/NextN loading with Quark quantization.

GLM-5.2 uses `GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM`, but its draft/MTP path currently reuses the DeepSeek NextN implementation. Quark records MTP excluded weights under the checkpoint prefix `model.layers.78.*`, while SGLang builds the draft runtime modules under `model.*`, `model.decoder.*`, and the fused MoE prefix `model.decoder.mlp.experts`.

Because of this prefix and granularity mismatch, Quark `exclude_layers` can fail to match bf16 MTP weights. Some MTP modules may then be incorrectly built as MXFP4 parameters, causing shape mismatches when loading bf16 weights.

This issue matches the MTP prefix mismatch described in Wafer's GLM-5.2 AMD writeup: https://www.wafer.ai/blog/glm52-amd.

## What Changed

- Added a GLM-specific NextN class: `GlmMoeDsaForCausalLMNextN`.
- Routed GLM DSA draft models from `GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM` to `GlmMoeDsaForCausalLMNextN` instead of `DeepseekV3ForCausalLMNextN`.
- Extracted DeepSeek NextN quant-config handling into `_resolve_nextn_quant_config()` so GLM can override the behavior cleanly.
- Expanded Quark `exclude_layers` at runtime for GLM-5.2 MTP:
  - `model.layers.78.eh_proj` -> `model.eh_proj`
  - `model.layers.78.enorm` -> `model.enorm`
  - `model.layers.78.hnorm` -> `model.hnorm`
  - `model.layers.78.shared_head.norm` -> `model.shared_head.norm`
  - decoder block weights -> `model.decoder.*`
  - routed expert leaf excludes also add the coarse fused-MoE prefix `model.decoder.mlp.experts`

This keeps mixed quantization behavior: excluded MTP modules remain bf16, while non-excluded draft modules can still use their Quark quant config.

## Why This Is Needed

The existing DeepSeek NextN mapper only handles:

```text
model.layers.61 -> model.decoder
```

GLM-5.2 MTP uses:

```text
model.layers.78
```

Also, the fused routed experts module is queried by SGLang using the coarse runtime prefix:

```text
model.decoder.mlp.experts
```

but Quark may record expanded leaf names such as:

```text
model.layers.78.mlp.experts.0.gate_proj
model.layers.78.mlp.experts.0.up_proj
model.layers.78.mlp.experts.0.down_proj
```

Mapping only the leaf names is not enough, because the fused MoE module checks the coarse module prefix. This PR adds the runtime names that SGLang actually queries.

## Validation

Tested with GLM-5.2 MXFP4 on 4 AMD GPUs.

Without MTP:

```text
Output throughput: 49.15 tok/s
Mean TPOT:         19.58 ms
Mean E2E latency:  30515.29 ms
```

With MTP:

```text
Output throughput: 180.70 tok/s
Mean TPOT:         4.75 ms
Mean E2E latency:  8297.65 ms
Accept length:     5.94
```

Observed improvement:

```text
Output throughput: ~3.68x higher
TPOT:              ~4.12x lower
E2E latency:       ~3.68x lower
```

TTFT remains roughly unchanged, which is expected because MTP primarily accelerates the decode phase rather than prefill.

## Test Commands

Server without MTP:

```bash
HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3 sglang serve \
  --model-path amd/GLM-5.2-MXFP4 \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 30000
```

Server with MTP:

```bash
HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3 sglang serve \
  --model-path amd/GLM-5.2-MXFP4 \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
  --speculative-algorithm EAGLE \
  --speculative-num-steps 5 \
  --speculative-eagle-topk 1 \
  --speculative-num-draft-tokens 6 \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 30001
```

Benchmark command:

```bash
python -m sglang.bench_serving \
  --backend sglang \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port <PORT> \
  --model amd/GLM-5.2-MXFP4 \
  --tokenizer amd/GLM-5.2-MXFP4 \
  --dataset-name random \
  --random-input-len 10000 \
  --random-output-len 1500 \
  --random-range-ratio 1.0 \
  --num-prompts 8 \
  --request-rate inf \
  --max-concurrency 1 \
  --warmup-requests 1
```

## Reference

Wafer GLM-5.2 AMD performance writeup:

https://www.wafer.ai/blog/glm52-amd

## Related Work

Part of the generic DeepSeek NextN quant-config handling overlaps with the earlier fix proposed in #29781. This PR builds on that direction and extends it for GLM-5.2 by adding `GlmMoeDsaForCausalLMNextN`, GLM-specific runtime prefix remapping, fused MoE exclude handling, and `layer_quant_config` key remapping.

The ROCm draft-depth `cuda_runtime.h` guard mentioned in the Wafer writeup was already addressed by #29373.

title: [AMD] [MORI-EP] Skip LocalExpertCount kernel in decode graph when not recording
author: rbrugaro-amd
body: ## Motivation `_should_record_expert_distribution()` in the mori EP token dispatcher returned `True` whenever the CUDA stream was capturing. This baked mori's `LocalExpertCountKernel` (and its buffer memsets) into the decode CUDA graph for **every** run — including normal serving with no expert-distribution recorder configured. The kernel then replayed on every decode step, producing a `local_expert_count` that nothing consumes when recording is off (the recorder hook is inactive), i.e. dead work in the decode hot path. This affects any MoE model served via the mori EP all-to-all backend with CUDA graphs enabled. ## Modifications Gate the capture-time path on whether an expert-distribution recorder is actually configured (non-Noop) instead of on `is_current_stream_capturing()` alone: - No recorder configured (common serving path) + capturing → **skip** the count kernel. - A configured (non-Noop) recorder, even before `start_record()` → still bake the machinery in at capture time, so `start_record()` works when called after graph capture (the recorder's own `_on_hook` continues to gate the actual gather on recording/capturing). - Actively recording → unchanged. Single-file change: `python/sglang/srt/layers/moe/token_dispatcher/moriep.py` (+19/−2). Because the two recording paths (configured-but-not-yet-recording, and actively-recording) are left untouched, there is no expert-distribution recording regression: an EPLB `stat_approx` record run (`expert_distribution_recorder_mode=stat_approx` + `/start_expert_distribution_record` → traffic → `/dump_expert_distribution_record`) still produces non-empty per-layer expert counts, and its gsm8k accuracy is unchanged (0.975). ## Accuracy Tests 8×MI355X, DeepSeek-R1 MXFP4, mori EP (tp8/ep8/dp8, DP attention, aiter, full decode CUDA graph). Post-patch, no recorder: ```bash python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path \ --tp-size 8 --ep-size 8 --dp-size 8 --enable-dp-attention --moe-a2a-backend mori \ --trust-remote-code --load-balance-method round_robin --moe-dense-tp-size 1 \ --enable-dp-lm-head --mem-fraction-static 0.7 --chunked-prefill-size 1024 \ --max-running-requests 128 --context-length 4096 --max-total-tokens 32768 \ --attention-backend aiter --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 32 --deepep-mode normal # (env: SGLANG_USE_AITER=1 SGLANG_MORI_DISPATCH_DTYPE=bf16 # SGLANG_MORI_NUM_MAX_DISPATCH_TOKENS_PER_RANK=128 MORI_SHMEM_MODE=ISOLATION) python -m sglang.test.few_shot_gsm8k --num-shots 5 --num-questions 200 --parallel 128 \ --host http://127.0.0.1 --port 30000 ``` ``` Accuracy: 0.965 Invalid: 0.000 ``` ## Speed Tests and Profiling Decode-dominant `bench_serving` A/B (baseline vs patched), same server config, same settings, back-to-back, `random` input 256 / output 1024, seed 42, 8 warmup, `num-prompts = 8 × concurrency`: ```bash python -m sglang.bench_serving --backend sglang --host 127.0.0.1 --port 30000 \ --dataset-name random --random-input-len 256 --random-output-len 1024 \ --random-range-ratio 1.0 --num-prompts $((C*8)) --max-concurrency $C \ --warmup-requests 8 --seed 42 # C in {16, 32, 64} ``` | concurrency | Median TPOT (ms) baseline → patched | Output tput (tok/s) baseline → patched | |---|---|---| | 16 | 19.78 → 19.56 (**−1.1%**) | 793.79 → 802.86 (**+1.1%**) | | 32 | 21.20 → 20.98 (**−1.0%**) | 1473.77 → 1490.12 (**+1.1%**) | | 64 | 23.25 → 22.85 (**−1.7%**) | 2631.25 → 2683.34 (**+2.0%**) | Median ITL moves the same way (−1.1%…−1.2%). ~1–2% TPOT / output-throughput improvement, increasing with decode concurrency — consistent in direction at every point, as expected from removing one small per-MoE-layer-per-decode-step kernel from the decode graph. Decode batch was capped at 32 (`--cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 32`); the uplift ceiling is likely a bit higher at larger decode batches, where the kernel would have replayed more per step. --- ### CI States Latest PR Test (Base): :x: [Run #28825048244](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/28825048244) Latest PR Test (Extra): :x: [Run #28825048081](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/28825048081)

title: [HiCache] Support packed and sidecar draft caches for MTP/EAGLE/DSpark
author: 1e4ves
body:
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->

## Motivation

HiCache must restore every cache state required by speculative decoding, not only the target model KV cache.

MTP/EAGLE draft models may keep KV, DSA indexer, or SWA state in separate device pools. If HiCache restores only the target pools, the prefix can report a cache hit while the draft-side state is missing or uses a different slot mapping. This can reduce speculative acceptance after an L2/L3 replay.

This PR adds two draft-cache integration paths so each draft topology can reuse the appropriate target cache index space.

## Design

| Path | Models/topology | Host-pool layout | Transfer semantics |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Packed** | Standard NextN MTP/EAGLE, including DeepSeek-V3.2, GLM-5.x, DeepSeek-V4, MiMo-V2.5; also DeepSeek-V4 DSpark | Draft KV/indexer/SWA buffers are appended as tail layers of the matching target host pool | Target and draft share the same host slots and are moved by the same HiCache operation |
| **Sidecar** | Standalone EAGLE/EAGLE3, DFlash, and non-DeepSeek-V4 DSpark | Separate `DRAFT`, `DRAFT_INDEXER`, or `DRAFT_SWA` host-pool entries are created only for non-empty draft state | Sidecars derive indices from target KV or SWA and are attached to the same L2/L3 operation |

The sidecar host pool uses the same slot count as its source target host pool, keeping target and draft host indices one-to-one. Draft SWA follows target SWA trailing-page semantics; draft full KV and DSA indexer follow target KV indices.

Inkling HiCache MTP is intentionally not supported by this PR.

## Modifications

- Add a HiCache draft plan that selects packed or sidecar mode before building the tree cache.
- Keep the existing packed MTP path for compatible NextN models and DeepSeek-V4 DSpark.
- Pack draft KV, DSA indexer, and SWA buffers into the corresponding target host pools.
- Add dynamic sidecar registration for non-packed draft pools:
  - `DRAFT <- KV`
  - `DRAFT_INDEXER <- KV`
  - `DRAFT_SWA <- SWA`
- Transfer registered sidecars together with their source pool for L2 and storage-backed L3 operations, including Mooncake.


## L3 replay validation
Tested the PR against main@39537885961c using the same 200 ShareGPT prompts:
- 128 output tokens per request
- Cold run → flush device cache → L3 replay


### DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731   (Dspark)
Version | Cold accept length / rate | Replay accept length / rate
-- | -- | --
upstream/main | 3.317 / 46.77% | 2.660 / 33.57%
This PR | 3.285 / 46.12% | 3.323 / 46.86%


### DeepSeek-V4-Flash

Version| Cold accept length / rate | Replay accept length / rate
-- | -- | --
upstream/main | 2.506 / 50.19% | 2.060 / 35.38%
this PR | 2.510 / 50.36% | 2.515 / 50.51%


## accuracy validation

### GSM8K — DeepSeek-V4-Flash-FP8

| Metric | Result |
| --- | ---: |
| Accuracy | **97.0%** (194/200) |
| Cached tokens | **137,728** |
| Cache hit ratio | **62.1%** |

### GSM8K — DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731

| Metric | Result |
| --- | ---: |
| Accuracy | **97.5%** (195/200) |
| Cached tokens | **125,184** |
| Cache hit ratio | **62.3%** |

title: [Mamba] Support speculative decoding with extra_buffer_lazy
author: YAMY1234
body:
## Motivation

`extra_buffer_lazy` (#27118) reduces each running request's mamba checkpoint footprint from 2 slots to 1, but was guarded off for speculative decoding ("Follow-up: Support MTP"). This PR implements that follow-up. The freed slots matter because the mamba pool is shared: whatever the running requests do not pin becomes extra RadixCache capacity for cached checkpoints (quantified below).

## Modifications

Non-spec lazy allocates the second slot and swaps the write pointer right at the boundary — each decode step advances exactly 1 token, so the boundary is known at prepare time. Under MTP a verify step advances 1..num_draft_tokens accepted tokens and a crossing is only known after verify, so the swap is deferred: prepare a spare slot first, swap only once the crossing is confirmed.

- `ScheduleBatch.mamba_lazy_spec_prepare` (scheduler phase, before each verify):
  - when the next boundary is reachable this step (within 2×num_draft_tokens), make sure the spare slot exists, without touching `mamba_next_track_idx` — the slot may end up never written;
  - record this step's write target on the batch; by result-processing time the request's pointer may already have moved under overlap, so it has to be recorded now.
- Post-verify state commit: unchanged — the existing mask-gated scatter writes the crossing state into the spare slot on a real crossing, and writes nothing otherwise (the spare slot is kept and reused next step).
- `_mamba_lazy_spec_update` (result processing, accept counts now known):
  - running, crossed into the spare slot → promote it: free the old checkpoint, repoint `mamba_next_track_idx`;
  - running, crossed with no spare slot available → the state was written in place into the checkpoint slot; bookkeeping only;
  - finishing → donate the checkpoint slot only if no scatter has written it (this step's in-place fallback) or may still write it (an in-flight verify with no spare slot inside the crossing window); otherwise skip the RadixCache insert.
- Allocation failures no longer evict (applied to the non-spec boundary prealloc as well): a transient slot is not worth a cached checkpoint — restoring the old evict-on-failure behavior collapses the reuse hit rate back to the extra_buffer column in the benchmark below. On failure the boundary is simply not tracked.
- Slot ownership is unchanged: allocation, holding, free and donation stay request-owned (the existing ping-pong buffer); the batch carries only a read-only per-iteration write plan.
- `extra_buffer_lazy` still rejects DFLASH/DSPARK (their verify bypasses `prepare_mamba_track_for_verify`) and PD disaggregation (the decode-side pool is not wired for lazy).

## Accuracy Tests

Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct, NEXTN (steps=3, topk=1, draft=4), TP4. "Pool" is the mamba state pool (`--max-mamba-cache-size`), shared by running requests and cached checkpoints.

| Config | GSM8K (200q) | decode-cache KL | prefill-cache KL | accept len |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| lazy | 0.960 | 0.000214 | 0.000334 | 2.400 |
| extra_buffer (baseline) | 0.965 | 0.000229 | 0.000334 | 2.356 |
| lazy, small pool (68 slots / 16 concurrent reqs) | 0.965 | n/a* | n/a* | 2.426 |
| lazy, every spare-slot allocation forced to fail | 0.960 | n/a* | n/a* | 2.426 |

KL compares logprobs of a cache-hit generation against a no-cache recompute (existing KL kit). *With the small pool, every cached entry is evicted before the kit's second turn (0/32 hits, identical for the extra_buffer baseline), so there is nothing to compare — the first two rows carry the KL evidence.

**Checkpoint-boundary finish test.** The risky corner of this feature is a request finishing right at a checkpoint boundary while the overlapped next verify may still write its checkpoint slot — a stale write landing after the slot enters the RadixCache would silently corrupt it. Setup: prompt of 500 tokens, checkpoint interval 64 (checkpoints at 448, 512, ..., 768, 832, ...); requests are forced (exact `max_new_tokens`) to finish at chosen offsets around the boundary at 832, then we generate a 32-token continuation from the finished sequence twice — reusing the cache vs after flushing it — and compare. The "exhausted" rows force every spare-slot allocation to fail during the test, emulating a pool with no free slot at any boundary (worst case). `cached_tokens` of the continuation reveals which checkpoint the finished request left in the cache:

| finish position | mamba pool | checkpoint served to the continuation | greedy tokens | max \|Δlogprob\| |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| −2..+2 around the boundary | has free slots | **768** — the previous safe checkpoint; the just-written 832 slot is deliberately not cached (the in-flight verify could still write it) | 32/32 identical | 3.7e-4 |
| −2..+2 around the boundary | exhausted | **448** — no safe decode-phase checkpoint exists, so the insert is skipped and only the last in-prompt checkpoint remains | 32/32 identical | 3.6e-4 |
| +16 / +32 past the boundary | has free slots | **832** — the crossing was confirmed while still running; the checkpoint advanced normally | 32/32 identical | 2.0e-4 |
| +16 / +32 past the boundary | exhausted | **832** — written in place as the fallback; safe to cache because the crossing was already settled | 32/32 identical | 2.0e-4 |

The logprob diff is the per-token log-ratio between the two runs — numerical-noise level throughout. The same grid with MTP off also passes, all token-identical (28 cells in total).

## Speed Tests and Profiling

What lazy buys is memory. RadixCache reuse benchmark: 48 independent conversations × 3 turns; on turns 2–3 we report the fraction of the prompt served from cache (`cached_tokens / prompt_tokens`); `max_running_requests=16` for both strategies.

| mamba pool | extra_buffer_lazy | lazy + evict-on-failure | extra_buffer |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| unconstrained (1024 slots) | 0.9677 | — | 0.9677 |
| constrained (96 slots) | **0.106–0.147** (3 runs) | 0.0161 | 0.0161 |

With an unconstrained pool the strategies are identical. Under a constrained pool, lazy's 16 running requests pin 32 slots instead of 48, leaving 64 vs 48 slots for cached checkpoints — about 7–9× higher reuse in this setup. The middle column keeps lazy but restores the old evict-on-allocation-failure behavior: the evictions consume exactly the capacity lazy freed, collapsing reuse back to the extra_buffer level — which is why this PR removes the evict (a temporary slot is never worth a cached checkpoint). Accept length is unchanged in every configuration (2.36–2.43, including forced allocation failure): checkpoint tracking never touches the sampling path.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).
- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).
- [ ] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations).
- [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed).
- [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance).

title: [DSA] Integrate Q8KV8 FP8 Sparse MLA Prefill into the DSA Backend (DeepSeek-V3.2)
author: JackChuang
body:
## Summary
This PR integrates the SM90 Q8KV8 FP8 sparse-MLA prefill kernel from PR-1 (#25751) into SGLang's **DSA prefill backend** (`dsa_backend.py`), so DeepSeek-V3.2 serving runs **native FP8 query × FP8 KV** sparse attention during prefill end-to-end. It is opt-in via `--dsa-prefill-backend flashmla_sparse_q8` (the `--nsa-prefill-backend` alias still works; requires `fp8_e4m3` KV; the bf16 baseline remains `flashmla_sparse`), and adds the concurrency/correctness fixes the kernel needed under real multi-rank load. Decode is unchanged (`flashmla_kv`).

- **Performance:** beats the bf16 (`flashmla_sparse`) baseline on every shape — single-request **+4.6–7.7%** (peak +7.7% @16k), saturated throughput **+1.8–2.7%** (H200, TP8/EP8/DP8, both arms fp8 KV; medians over repeated A/B rounds).
- **Accuracy:** **q8 matches q16 across 3.6k–65k context** — identical 1319-question unseen gsm8k at every rung, per-rung **|Δ| ≤ 0.004** (pooled −0.002, negligible); both arms flat at **0.95–0.96** with no context-length degradation. On **LongBench-v2** (thinking-ON, unique 10k–147k-token documents — the kernel-heaviest workload): **0.602 vs 0.616, a gap within the protocol's sampling noise (Δ −0.014 ± 0.015)**.

## Motivation

PR-1 (#25751) delivered the Q8KV8 kernel as a standalone, independently reviewable block. Running sparse-MLA prefill as native FP8 — rather than dequantizing the fp8 KV back to bf16 and using the bf16 kernel — avoids a paged-fp8→bf16 round-trip, halves KV-side memory traffic, and unlocks FP8 tensor-core throughput, turning PR-1's kernel speedup into an end-to-end serving win.

## Context

Part of roadmap #25746. PR-1 (#25751) = the standalone SM90 kernel + unit tests + microbenchmark. This PR adds, on top of that kernel: the **DSA-backend integration** (`dsa_backend.py`); **additional kernel-correctness coverage** (concurrency/correctness fixes that only surfaced under real DP8 end-to-end load); and **end-to-end accuracy + performance validation** supplementing PR-1's kernel-level microbenchmark/tests.

## Modifications

| file | role |
|---|---|
| `dsa_backend.py` | integration + `flashmla_sparse_q8` routing (`_forward_flashmla_sparse_q8kv8`), dispatch, RAGGED gate, startup validation + decode guard |
| `triton_ops/cache_ops.py` (re-exported via `utils.py`) | fused Triton q-prep: concat(q_nope, q_rope) + bf16→fp8 cast (`concat_and_cast_q_fp8_pad`) |
| `dsa/dequant_k_cache.py` | fused gather + dequant + requant of paged fp8 KV (`gather_dequant_requant_fp8_paged`; no fp8→bf16→fp8 round-trip) |
| `server_args.py` | `flashmla_sparse_q8` in `DSA_CHOICES` |
| `kernel.cuh` | concurrency/correctness fixes on the PR-1 kernel (race, deadlock, stale-P, masked-softmax, proxy fence) |
| `test/registered/jit/…_sm90.py` | +6 e2e-discovered corner-case gates folded into the PR-1 unit tests (21 = 15 + 6) |

**Key points:**
- **Explicit backend selection:** `--dsa-prefill-backend flashmla_sparse_q8` is a first-class DSA prefill impl (no hidden env; `--nsa-prefill-backend` is a deprecated alias); `flashmla_sparse` keeps the bf16 path. Always FP8 + SM90-only, both validated at startup with explicit errors (fail-fast); rejected as a `--dsa-decode-backend` (prefill-only).
- **Native FP8 KV (no round-trip):** the paged fp8 KV is gathered, dequantized per-group, and re-quantized per-tensor in one fused kernel. Identity per-tensor scales — a raw bf16→fp8 cast is accurate on real DeepSeek-V3 magnitudes, so no dynamic rescaling.
- **Fused FP8 q-prep:** concat q_nope/q_rope and cast bf16→fp8 in one pass — worth **~+3.5% c=1 throughput / ~+1.7% saturated** end-to-end vs a separate concat + cast (measured at il=16k and 32k). The Triton kernel supports power-of-two head counts only (guarded at the call site, with a generic concat + cast fallback; DeepSeek's 128 heads and all its TP splits qualify).
- **Correctness fixes from e2e:** full-topk dispatch (−1 sentinels clamped to distinct zero pad rows ⇒ uniform control flow across DP ranks — a data-dependent loop bound had deadlocked the cross-rank collective at long context), plus a `fence.proxy.async` determinism fix (orders the V-transpose STSM writes before the consumer WGMMA reads).

## Usage

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path <DeepSeek-V3.2> \
  --dsa-prefill-backend flashmla_sparse_q8 \   # native FP8 sparse prefill (this PR)
  --dsa-decode-backend flashmla_kv \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 \
  --tp-size 8 --ep-size 8 --dp-size 8 --enable-dp-attention --trust-remote-code
```

`flashmla_sparse_q8` is always FP8 (requires `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3`) and SM90-only — both asserted at startup. For the bf16 baseline use `--dsa-prefill-backend flashmla_sparse` (the only change needed to A/B). Prompts whose prefill context ≤ `index_topk` (2048) take the dense one-shot path, where both backends are identical.

## Experimental Results

### Performance (H200, TP8/EP8/DP8, both arms fp8 KV)

q8 wins every rung of all four tables below: at the default chunked-prefill size (32768), single-request latency **+4.6–7.7%** (peak +7.7% @ il=16k) and saturated throughput **+1.8–2.7%**; at the secondary chunk size (16384), single-request **+2.6–6.9%** and saturated **+1.6–2.7%** (il ≤ 2k excluded: dense path, both arms identical). The edge is largest at low load and shrinks toward saturation — profiling shows an overlap/makespan effect (un-overlapped per-layer all-reduces at c=1 amplify a small compute saving), not a compute-share effect. Numbers are medians over repeated A/B rounds; each row's Δ varies by only ≈ 0.3% across rounds, so the deltas sit well outside run-to-run noise. All settings are upstream defaults.

| 120k (c16) | 20,601 | 20,260 | +1.7% | 69,148 ms | 70,379 ms | +1.7% |
| 160k (c16) | 19,240 | 18,731 | +2.7% | 98,132 ms | 101,094 ms | +2.9% |

**Where the advantage comes from (profile decomposition).** Both arms serve the identical il=64k workload (c=1 and c=16) while sglang's built-in torch profiler captures a full 8-rank trace per arm (`/start_profile` → bench → `/stop_profile`); GPU kernel time is bucketed by kernel name and averaged across ranks. Δ = q16 − q8 = GPU-busy time q8 saves per rank over the capture window:

| Δ = q16 − q8 (mean per-rank GPU-busy, ms) @ il=64k | c=1 (latency) | c=16 (saturated) |
|---|--:|--:|
| attention prefill kernel (direct delta; q8 kernel −10.9%) | +154 | +564 |
| indexer / topk | +76 | +89 |
| **NCCL (barrier amplification)** | **+1,876** | +1,046 |
| q-prep / cast | +26 | +146 |
| MoE / GEMM / other | +23 | +116 |
| **total** | **+2,156 (+6.4% of q16 busy)** | **+1,962 (+2.4%)** |

The totals independently match the end-to-end tables (+6.4% ↔ the 64k c=1 ΔTTFT +6.4%; +2.4% ↔ saturated +2.5%). Reading: at saturation the win converges to the direct kernel delta; at c=1 the per-layer all-reduces are un-overlapped and stall on the slowest rank, so q8 reaching each barrier sooner turns a 154 ms kernel saving into 1,876 ms less collective spin — an **overlap/makespan** effect, which is why the single-request advantage (+5–8%) exceeds the saturated one (+2–3%).

### Correctness

sglang-standard pytest `tests/test_sparse_mla_q8kv8_prefill_sm90.py` — **21/21 passed**. The PR-1 suite plus 6 new corner-case gates that real e2e serving exposed:

| Group | Cases | Coverage |
|---|--:|---|
| Original PR-1 suite | 15 | correctness (d_qk 512/576), sink/topk_length, corner shapes, precision, buffer ownership |
| NEW — masked −1-sentinel | 2 | few-valid rows (ctx < topk) vs a −inf fp32 reference; cos 0.9998 |
| NEW — s_q envelope | 3 | s_q 2048/4096/6144 first-band NaN watch; cos 0.9999 |
| NEW — large S_KV | 1 | S_KV=65536 / large gathered index; cos 0.9999 |

### Accuracy

#### gsm8k

End-to-end, both arms fp8 KV, chunk32768, greedy decoding (temperature 0), uniform methodology — context length is the only variable.

**One methodology, one variable.** Every row is the SAME test: gsm8k, **all 1319 test questions, identical at every rung, all unseen** (few-shot examples come from the gsm8k *train* split, so no evaluated question's answer ever appears in the prompt); completion API, temperature 0, same stop strings and scoring. The **only variable is context length** (the few-shot count). Accuracy = fraction correct (higher = better); Δ = q8 − q16 (negative = q8 lower); σ = same-config run-to-run standard deviation.

| context (tokens) | method | q8 | q16 | Δ (q8−q16) | σ (q8 / q16) |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 3.6k (3,574) | 20-shot | 0.956 | 0.958 | −0.002 | 0.001 / 0.001 |
| 6.9k (6,943) | 40-shot | 0.952 | 0.955 | −0.004 | 0.002 / 0.001 |
| 13k (13,466) | 80-shot | 0.956 | 0.958 | −0.002 | 0.001 / 0.000 |
| 20k (20,074) | 120-shot | 0.955 | 0.954 | +0.000 | 0.003 / 0.004 |
| 26k (26,383) | 160-shot | 0.958 | 0.958 | +0.000 | 0.002 / 0.004 |
| 40k (40,364) | 240-shot | 0.955 | 0.958 | −0.003 | 0.001 / 0.003 |
| 65k (65,375) | 390-shot | 0.955 | 0.958 | −0.003 | 0.002 / 0.001 |

**q8 matches q16 across 3.6k–65k context**: per-rung **|Δ| ≤ 0.004** (all within the σ ≈ 0.001–0.004 run-to-run noise floor), pooled Δ = **−0.002** — a very small quantization cost in the expected direction, negligible in magnitude. Both arms are flat at **0.95–0.96 with no context-length degradation**.

Note: few-shot examples are drawn from the *train* split (lm-eval convention; one-line variant of the stock gsm8k bench, script archived) so every evaluated question is unseen at every rung.

#### LongBench-v2

End-to-end, both arms fp8 KV, chunk32768; thinking-ON at the official protocol — temperature 0.6 / top-p 0.95, max-tokens 16,384 (sampling is required for long CoT and keeps absolutes leaderboard-comparable; the single-run sampling noise floor is ≈ ±0.027 at N=334, so we report means over repeated runs); harness = sglang's built-in `run_eval --eval-name longbench_v2`.

The adversarial accuracy test for a sparse-*prefill* kernel is one where every request runs a full sparse prefill over a long, *unique* context — no shared prefix, no dense-path dilution — and the answer depends on that prefill being right. LongBench-v2 is exactly that: after the 2,300–147,000-token filter, all 334 scored four-way multiple-choice questions (exact letter-match scoring, no judge) carry a unique 10k–147k-token document (median 51k), so each request invokes the kernel under test **183–2,196 times** (prefill chunks × 61 MLA layers), and the up-to-16k-token thinking chain then amplifies any prefill numerics into the final answer.

| arm | mean score | σ |
|---|--:|--:|
| q8 (`flashmla_sparse_q8`) | **0.602** | 0.012 |
| q16 (`flashmla_sparse`) | **0.616** | 0.023 |

Δ = **−0.014 ± 0.015 (SE of the mean difference) — within the protocol's sampling noise** (< 1σ; same-config repeat runs spread by up to 0.045, more than the mean gap itself): no measurable fp8 accuracy cost on the workload with maximal kernel exposure. Both arms were measured on the exact submitted revision.

## Known Upstream Issue (not introduced by this PR)

- **DSA fused top-k v2 (paged) crashes with an illegal memory access on ~160k-token prefill** — affects `flashmla_sparse` and `flashmla_sparse_q8` identically (shared indexer/top-k path, upstream of both prefill kernels); il ≤ 120k is unaffected. Workaround: `SGLANG_OPT_USE_TOPK_V2=0` — with it the il = 160k benches pass and reproduce the table's deltas. Tracked upstream: **<ISSUE LINK — TBD>**.

070826 update: Seems like the 'DSA fused top-k v2' issue is solved by #30512 

## Next
- Will release GLM5.2 support and optimization soon, (perf gain upto 2x~4x compared to dpsk-v3.2).
- I also noticed if I optimize the e2e shared path, q8 kernel path can also bring more performance gain. So those optimization will be release along with the next GLM5.2 PR to further improve the dpsk-v3.2's  performance.

- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).

- [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance).

title: [hicache]: add  mamba_io_kernel
author: jojoakm
body:
## Motivation

SGLang's HiCache supports Mamba models (e.g., Qwen-Next), but the Mamba state transfer between host and device previously relied on `direct` I/O backend only (pure DMA). This PR introduces a dedicated JIT-compiled CUDA kernel for Mamba KV cache transfer, providing a `kernel` I/O backend option that uses cache-bypass loads/stores with software pipelining for efficient PCIe transfer. The block-cooperative design achieves up to **14x speedup** over the existing MLA kernel at low concurrency.

## Modifications

**New files:**
- `python/sglang/jit_kernel/csrc/kvcacheio/transfer_mamba.cuh` — CUDA kernel implementation with two kernels:
  - `transfer_mamba_load_kernel`: page_first → layer_first (per-layer load)
  - `transfer_mamba_backup_kernel`: layer_first → page_first (all-layer backup)
  - Uses `load_nc`/`store_nc` (cache-bypass) instructions with double buffering to maximize outstanding PCIe transactions
- `python/sglang/jit_kernel/transfer_mamba.py` — Python JIT wrapper exposing `transfer_kv_mamba_pf_lf` and `transfer_kv_mamba_lf_pf`

**Modified file:**
- `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/memory_pool_host.py` — `MambaPoolHost` integration:
  - Relaxed layout restriction: now supports both `page_first` and `page_first_direct` (was `page_first_direct` only)
  - Removed `io_backend='direct'` restriction on `load_to_device_per_layer` and `backup_from_device_all_layer`
  - Set `can_use_write_back_jit = True` so `HostPoolGroup`'s AND logic keeps indices on CPU for MLA staged kernel; Mamba's own path uses `.to(cuda)` to move indices when needed
  - Load/backup paths now route to `transfer_kv_mamba_pf_lf` / `transfer_kv_mamba_lf_pf` when `io_backend='kernel'`

## Accuracy Tests

Tested with Qwen-Next model (tp=4) using HiCache with `--hicache-write-policy write_through` and `--hicache-io-backend kernel`. Model outputs verified consistent with `direct` backend across multiple concurrency levels (1, 4, 8, 12, 16, 64, 256).

## Speed Tests and Profiling

**Micro-benchmark: Mamba JIT kernel vs MLA kernel (page_first src, H2D)**

| items | item_size | total | mamba (ms) | mla (ms) | m/a | mamba_bw | mla_bw |
|-------|-----------|-------|-----------|---------|-----|---------|-------|
| 4 | 512KB | 20MB | 0.53 | 6.47 | 12.3x | 39.7 GB/s | 3.2 GB/s |
| 16 | 512KB | 80MB | 1.97 | 7.13 | 3.6x | 42.6 GB/s | 11.8 GB/s |
| 64 | 512KB | 320MB | 8.08 | 7.61 | 0.9x | 41.6 GB/s | 44.1 GB/s |
| 256 | 512KB | 1280MB | 33.9 | 31.1 | 0.9x | 39.5 GB/s | 43.1 GB/s |
| 4 | 1MB | 40MB | 0.99 | 13.9 | 14.0x | 42.2 GB/s | 3.0 GB/s |
| 16 | 1MB | 160MB | 3.88 | 14.3 | 3.7x | 43.2 GB/s | 11.8 GB/s |
| 64 | 1MB | 640MB | 16.4 | 15.4 | 0.9x | 40.9 GB/s | 43.6 GB/s |
| 256 | 1MB | 2560MB | 65.6 | 62.3 | 1.0x | 40.9 GB/s | 43.1 GB/s |
| 4 | 2MB | 80MB | 1.93 | 27.9 | 14.5x | 43.5 GB/s | 3.0 GB/s |
| 16 | 2MB | 320MB | 7.73 | 28.4 | 3.7x | 43.4 GB/s | 11.8 GB/s |
| 64 | 2MB | 1280MB | 32.3 | 31.1 | 1.0x | 41.6 GB/s | 43.1 GB/s |

At low concurrency (4 items), the Mamba kernel achieves **12-14x speedup** over the MLA kernel (~43 GB/s vs ~3 GB/s), because the block-cooperative design engages all 32 warps per item while the MLA kernel's flat warp-to-item mapping leaves most warps idle. At high concurrency (64+ items), both saturate PCIe bandwidth (~41-44 GB/s) and the gap disappears.

**End-to-end benchmark (H20, tp=4, Qwen-Next, input=4096, output=128)**

| Concurrency | Backend | Mean TTFT (ms) | Mean ITL (ms) | Throughput (req/s) |
|-------------|---------|---------------|--------------|-------------------|
| 1 | kernel | 219 | 4.7 | 1.21 |
| 1 | direct | 213 | 4.8 | 1.20 |
| 16 | kernel | 1288 | 13.0 | 5.41 |
| 16 | direct | 1215 | 11.9 | 5.84 |
| 256 | kernel | 14727 | 151 | 7.51 |
| 256 | direct | 14843 | 151 | 7.49 |

End-to-end performance is comparable between `kernel` and `direct` backends, as prefill computation dominates TTFT and dilutes the transfer speed advantage.

- [ ] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).

title: [MoE Backend] Add HPC-Ops FP8 MoE runner backend
author: BBuf
body:
## Motivation

Add a new opt-in MoE runner backend `hpc_ops` wrapping the monolithic FP8 fused-MoE kernels from [HPC-Ops](https://github.com/Tencent/hpc-ops), the production-grade operator library for LLM inference from the Tencent Hunyuan AI Infra team.

This is the second half of the first-phase HPC-Ops <-> SGLang integration discussed with the Hunyuan team (attention backend: #30540).

Enable with:

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507-FP8 \
  --moe-runner-backend hpc_ops
```

> [!NOTE]
> The HPC-Ops kernels run on any sm90+ GPU, but they are currently **tuned primarily for H20**. On other hardware (H100/H200/B200, ...) the speedup may be limited or absent — the H200 numbers below reflect exactly that. Further kernel-side tuning for non-H20 GPUs is planned as follow-up work with the Hunyuan team, and the backend stays strictly opt-in so default paths are unaffected.

## Modifications

- New `python/sglang/srt/layers/moe/moe_runner/hpc_ops.py`: a fused-func runner backend (same shape as flashinfer_trtllm / cutlass) with two paths:
  - **Blockwise FP8** (128x128 weight blocks + dynamic per-token-group-128 activations, e.g. Qwen3-FP8 / Hy3-FP8 checkpoints) → `hpc.fuse_moe_blockwise`.
  - **Per-tensor FP8** with static activation scales → `hpc.fuse_moe` (per-expert dequant alphas `w_scale * a_scale`, inverse a2 scale for the activation requant — same wiring as the flashinfer CUTLASS per-tensor path).
  - Both kernels fuse gather → grouped gate_up GEMM → SiLU-and-mul (+ FP8 requant) → grouped down GEMM → weighted top-k reduce in one call.
- `Fp8MoEMethod`: precompute the HPC-Ops scale layouts once at `process_weights_after_loading` (the kernel wants `[E, N/128, K/128]` fp32 dequant scales with the K dim padded to a multiple of 4) and build `HpcOpsMoeQuantInfo` in `apply`.
- The kernels consume **global** top-k expert ids together with `rank_ep` / `num_expert_total`, so `hpc_ops` is added to `skip_local_expert_mapping` in the standard dispatcher — contiguous-partition EP works without the local-expert remap.
- Enum/choices/registry wiring + a numerical unit test (`test/registered/moe/test_hpc_ops_moe.py`, skipped when HPC-Ops is not installed or on pre-sm90 GPUs).

Constraints checked with clear errors: gated SiLU only, no fused shared experts, no `apply_router_weight_on_input` / `no_combine` / swiglu clamp, hidden dims 128-aligned, bf16 hidden states.

## Kernel-level correctness (H200)

Three-way comparison on Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 MoE shapes (E=128, topk=8, hidden=2048, inter=768) with properly blockwise-quantized random weights, including **unsorted** top-k ids (SGLang router order; upstream HPC-Ops tests only cover sorted ids):

| comparison | cosine | max_rel |
|---|---|---|
| triton fused_experts vs fp32-exact | 0.99974 | 0.024 |
| **hpc_ops vs fp32-exact** | **0.99974** | 0.024 |
| hpc_ops vs triton | 0.99993 | 0.013 |

i.e. the hpc_ops path is exactly as faithful to fp32 math as the triton reference. Unit test result on H200: `2 passed, 6 subtests passed` (blockwise + per-tensor, tokens ∈ {7, 64, 512}).

## Validation on Qwen3 (Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507-FP8, H200 TP1) — blockwise FP8 path

### Accuracy

`benchmark/gsm8k/bench_sglang.py --num-questions 1319 --parallel 128`:

| MoE runner backend | GSM8K accuracy | Invalid |
|---|---|---|
| auto (deep_gemm) | 0.940 | 0.000 |
| triton | 0.937 | 0.000 |
| **hpc_ops** | **0.944** | 0.000 |

### Performance

MoE-layer kernel latency, hpc_ops vs triton fused_experts (Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 decode shapes, us):

| tokens | HPC-Ops | Triton | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 89.9 | 356.4 | 3.96x |
| 8 | 85.9 | 361.8 | 4.21x |
| 32 | 148.9 | 366.8 | 2.46x |
| 128 | 182.4 | 279.8 | 1.53x |
| 512 | 206.0 | 278.3 | 1.35x |
| 1024 | 241.9 | 279.7 | 1.16x |
| 2048 | 460.9 | 411.7 | 0.89x |
| 4096 | 677.6 | 733.0 | 1.08x |

e2e `sglang.bench_one_batch_server` (input 1024 / output 128, output tok/s):

| bs | auto (deep_gemm) | triton | hpc_ops |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 269.7 | 255.4 | 269.6 |
| 16 | 2070 | 2083 | **2126** |
| 64 | 5786 | 5795 | 5788 |

The large kernel-level wins over triton in the small-batch regime translate to parity-to-+2.7% e2e against the deep_gemm default on this model (MoE GEMMs are one slice of the forward); the backend stays strictly opt-in.

## Validation on Hunyuan v3 (tencent/Hy3-FP8, H200 TP4) — per-tensor FP8 path

HPC-Ops was released together with the Hunyuan v3 model; `tencent/Hy3-FP8` is a per-tensor FP8 checkpoint with static activation scales, so this run exercises the `hpc.fuse_moe` per-tensor path end-to-end (192 experts, topk 8, shared expert as a separate MLP). Launch:

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model tencent/Hy3-FP8 --tp 4 --dtype bfloat16 --kv-cache-dtype bfloat16 \
  --moe-runner-backend hpc_ops --trust-remote-code
```

GSM8K (1319 questions):

| MoE runner backend | GSM8K accuracy | Invalid |
|---|---|---|
| default (auto) | 0.942 | 0.000 |
| **hpc_ops** | **0.942** | 0.000 |

`bench_one_batch_server` (input 1024 / output 128):

| bs | metric | default (auto) | hpc_ops | delta |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | input tok/s | 17693 | 18180 | +2.8% |
| 1 | output tok/s | 141.3 | 135.4 | -4.2% |
| 16 | input tok/s | 33521 | 29329 | -12.5% |
| 16 | output tok/s | 950.5 | **1010.1** | **+6.3%** |
| 64 | input tok/s | 33635 | 29229 | -13.1% |
| 64 | output tok/s | 2544.3 | **2700.1** | **+6.1%** |

Decode throughput improves ~6% at bs 16/64 (the per-tensor fused kernel is strongest in the small/medium-M regime); large-M prefill chunks are slower, matching the kernel latency curve — a mixed prefill/decode deployment can also combine this with `--decode-attention-backend`-style per-phase selection later.

## Test

- `test/registered/moe/test_hpc_ops_moe.py` passes on H200 (skips cleanly without HPC-Ops installed, so CI is unaffected).
- e2e GSM8K + perf as above.

title: [AMD] Enable Fast Triton Sparse MLA backend
author: clintg6
body:
# Fast Triton Sparse MLA Kernels for DSA (Prefill + Decode)

## Summary

This adds `triton` as an explicit DSA prefill/decode backend:

```bash
--dsa-prefill-backend triton
--dsa-decode-backend triton
```

The new backend provides pure Triton sparse MLA kernels for the fp8 DSA path on ROCm, validated on MI355X (gfx950) and MI300X (gfx942). It replaces the previous Triton prefill env-var gate, SGLANG_DSA_TRITON_PREFILL, with a faster kernel exposed through the normal backend option and adds a fast Triton kernel for the decode path.

## What Changed

- Adds `triton` to `DSA_CHOICES` for `--dsa-prefill-backend` and `--dsa-decode-backend`.
- Adds startup validation in both server-args paths so Triton DSA is only used with `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3`.
- Adds standalone Triton prefill and decode dispatch branches in `dsa_backend.py`.
- Ensures HIP Triton DSA uses the raw MLA KV layout (`512 nope + 64 rope`) instead of the scaled fp8 layout used by other non ROCm backends.
- Extends the gfx950 fused-rope skip path to include Triton, matching the TileLang/AITER raw-layout flow.

## Kernel Notes

- Prefill uses a split-dim 4x128 implementation for the 512-wide nope dimension, plus the 64-wide rope tail.
- Prefill can split topk work across CTAs and reduce partial online-softmax state in Triton.
- Decode uses an adaptive split-K path with a fused single-pass fast path when `kv_splits == 1`.
- Kernels use `exp2` with `sm_scale * LOG2E` prescaling.

The kernels consume raw fp8 MLA KV cache layout on HIP. They are not intended for NVIDIA's scaled fp8 KV layout.

## Validation

- GSM8K 400-question validated: TileLang and Triton both produced 95.5% accuracy with 0% invalid answers. Accuracy also verified on gfx942
- Isolated prefill microbench on MI355X/GLM-5.2 shape (`H=16`, `D_V=512`, `D_TAIL=64`, `topk=2048`) showed about 10% speedup for the split-dim prefill kernel versus the earlier 512-wide-dot Triton env gated kernel, with cosine similarity 1.00000.
- End-to-end GLM-5.1-MXFP4 serving on TP4 MI355X (`ISL=8192`, `OSL=1024`) showed Triton improving throughput by roughly 3-5% versus TileLang in the measured concurrency range.
- Performance improvement is seen across all concurrencies, TPs, and for short and long context.

## Performance

End-to-end GLM-5.1-MXFP4 serving on TP4 MI355X, concurrency 2:

| Backend | Total tok/s | Output tok/s | Mean TTFT (ms) | Mean TPOT (ms) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| TileLang | 1,005 | 112 | 834 | 17.1 |
| Triton | 1,044 | 116 | 701 | 16.6 |
| Improvement | +3.9% | +3.6% | -16.0% | -2.9% |

## Changed Files

- `python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/dsa/triton_sparse_mla.py`: updates the Triton prefill implementation with split-dim and split-K paths.
- `python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/dsa/triton_sparse_mla_decode.py`: adds the Triton decode implementation.
- `python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/dsa_backend.py`: adds Triton prefill/decode dispatch and removes the old env-var-gated prefill path.
- `python/sglang/srt/server_args.py`: exposes `triton` as a DSA backend choice.
- `python/sglang/srt/arg_groups/overrides.py`: validates Triton DSA override combinations against fp8 KV cache requirements.

title: [NVIDIA] Add flashinfer MNNVL backend for allreduce only
author: wenscarl
body:
## Motivation

SGLang already supports **fused** allreduce via FlashInfer (`kARResidualRMSNorm`: allreduce + residual + RMSNorm in one kernel) for DeepSeek-V3/V4 models. However, not every allreduce site can use the fused path — `RowParallelLinear`, attention output fallback, and MoE TP fallback all perform **pure (non-fused)** allreduce that currently always falls back to NCCL/custom-allreduce even when the FlashInfer mnnvl/trtllm workspace is already initialized and available.

This PR routes those pure allreduce calls through FlashInfer `AllReduceFusionPattern.kAllReduce`, reusing the existing workspace with no extra memory cost.

## Changes

### `flashinfer_comm_fusion.py` — new `flashinfer_allreduce()`
Wraps `AllReduceFusionPattern.kAllReduce` for pure TP allreduce. Returns `None` on any of:
- FlashInfer unavailable or `_flashinfer_comm` not initialized
- Input is not 2D contiguous (e.g. 3D vocab embedding output — graceful NCCL fallback)
- Workspace not initialized or buffer too small

### `parallel_state.py` — dispatch hook + group tagging
- `_tag_groups_for_flashinfer_pure_allreduce()`: stamps a `_fi_workspace_hint` attribute (`"attn_tp"` / `"moe_tp"` / `"moe_ep"`) on `_TP`, `_ATTN_TP`, `_MOE_TP`, `_MOE_EP` group coordinators after `initialize_model_parallel()`.
- `GroupCoordinator.all_reduce()`: checks `_fi_workspace_hint` and dispatches to `flashinfer_allreduce()` before the existing `ca_comm`/`pymscclpp`/NCCL chain. Falls back transparently if `flashinfer_allreduce()` returns `None`.

### `server_args.py` — new flag
`--enable-flashinfer-pure-allreduce` (`resolvable=True` so post-process passes can set it).

### `model_runner.py` — wiring
Calls `set_flashinfer_pure_all_reduce()` and `_tag_groups_for_flashinfer_pure_allreduce()` alongside the existing `set_custom_all_reduce` / `set_mscclpp_all_reduce` setup.

### `overrides.py` — auto-enable for DeepSeek-V3/V4
- Added `DeepseekV4ForCausalLM` to `_FLASHINFER_ALLREDUCE_FUSION_ARCHS`.
- New `_FLASHINFER_PURE_ALLREDUCE_ARCHS` frozenset (`DeepseekV3ForCausalLM`, `DeepseekV32ForCausalLM`, `DeepseekV4ForCausalLM`).
- `_flashinfer_allreduce_fusion_auto_enable` now also sets `enable_flashinfer_pure_allreduce=True` for archs in `_FLASHINFER_PURE_ALLREDUCE_ARCHS` — users running DeepSeek-V3/V4 no longer need to pass `--flashinfer-allreduce-fusion-backend` or `--enable-flashinfer-pure-allreduce` manually.
- `_enforce_disable_allreduce_fusion` now also clears `enable_flashinfer_pure_allreduce` when the fused backend is force-disabled.

### `test_flashinfer_pure_allreduce.py` — unit tests
5 unit tests using `_FakeFlashInferComm` covering: correctness (`output == input × world_size`), 1D/3D shape guard, non-contiguous guard, unavailable flag, uninitialized workspace.


## Performance and Accuracy
Benchmarked DeepSeek V4 Flash on Blackwell with `sglang.benchmark.one_batch`, using TP=4 and sweeping batch sizes.

Command:

```bash
python3 -m sglang.benchmark.one_batch \
  --model-path deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash \
  --tp-size 4 \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --batch-size 1 2 4 8 16 32 64 \
  --input-len 512 \
  --output-len 128 \
  --run-name ds_v4_flash_decode_bs_sweep \
  --disable-flashinfer-autotune \
  --result-filename ds_v4_flash_decode_bs_sweep.jsonl \
  --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_mxfp4
  ```
| BS | Old decode tok/s | PR decode tok/s | Decode delta | Old decode lat | PR decode lat | Old overall tok/s | PR overall tok/s |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 147.51 | 157.69 | +6.9% | 6.78 ms | 6.34 ms | 539.58 | 624.73 |
| 2 | 285.43 | 304.95 | +6.8% | 7.01 ms | 6.56 ms | 1,014.16 | 1,185.12 |
| 4 | 535.28 | 569.52 | +6.4% | 7.47 ms | 7.02 ms | 1,959.97 | 2,269.91 |
| 8 | 1,071.14 | 1,103.58 | +3.0% | 7.47 ms | 7.25 ms | 2,863.78 | 4,586.34 |
| 16 | 1,966.24 | 2,016.57 | +2.6% | 8.14 ms | 7.93 ms | 8,205.76 | 8,482.90 |
| 32 | 3,510.57 | 3,616.18 | +3.0% | 9.12 ms | 8.85 ms | 14,871.86 | 15,267.53 |
| 64 | 6,247.72 | 6,157.77 | -1.4% | 10.24 ms | 10.39 ms | 24,242.08 | 23,916.24 |


Accuracy:
```
python3 benchmark/gsm8k/bench_sglang.py \
  --num-shots 8 \
  --num-questions 1316 \
  --parallel 1316
```

Without this PR:
```
Accuracy: 0.958
Invalid: 0.000
Latency: 95.622 s
Output throughput: 1312.239 token/s
```
With this PR:
```
Accuracy: 0.958

Latency: 107.229 s
Output throughput: 1158.934 token/s
``

title: :sparkles: [llm][npu][quant] Add W8A8 MXFP8 quantization for Qwen3 MoE on Ascend NPU
author: TallMessiWu
body:
# Summary

Adds **W8A8 MXFP8** quantization (8-bit weights + 8-bit activations, block_size = 32) for Qwen3 / Qwen3.5 **MoE** (FusedMoE) LLM models on Ascend NPU, continuing the NPU quantization work tracked in #21584. Both **online** (`--quantization mxfp8`) and **offline** (msmodelslim, flagless — selected by the checkpoint's `quant_model_description.json`) paths are supported and share the same fused-experts kernel. Requires Ascend A5 (Ascend 950) — the fused MoE MX kernels (`npu_grouped_matmul_swiglu_quant_v2`, `npu_dynamic_mx_quant`) are A5-only.

> #23795 (dense W4A4) has landed and this branch is merged up to `main`, so the diff is now the MoE MXFP8 delta only. It reuses the merged dense MXFP8 infrastructure — `NPUMXFP8LinearMethod`, the `Fp8Config` NPU dispatch, and `ModelSlimMXFP8Scheme` (from #22352).

**Online quantization (`--quantization mxfp8`)**

- On the **Ascend NPU** backend, `Fp8Config.get_quant_method()` dispatches FusedMoE layers to the new `NPUMXFP8OnlineMoEMethod` (the `isinstance(layer, FusedMoE)` branch, mirroring the existing dense `NPUMXFP8LinearMethod` linear branch). It subclasses `UnquantizedFusedMoEMethod` and overrides only `create_moe_runner`, to attach the MXFP8 per-gmm kernels — weight creation, weight post-processing and the forward pass are the unquantized Ascend ones. On GPU the `FusedMoE` branch is untouched.
- BF16/FP16 expert weights `w13`/`w2` are quantised once at load via `npu_dynamic_mx_quant(dst_type = torch_npu.float8_e4m3fn)` — a 3D `[E, N, K]` input is accepted directly (no per-expert loop) — into `float8_e4m3fn` weights + UE8M0 (`float8_e8m0fnu`) block scales, kept as **non-contiguous transpose views**.
- Forward: on the `ascend_tp` dispatcher, `npu_moe_init_routing_v2` with **`quant_mode=3`** (count `group_list`) — the per-token MXFP8 activation quant is fused directly into routing, so the same kernel launch emits the sorted `float8_e4m3fn` payload *and* its `float8_e8m0fnu` block scale, saving a separate `npu_dynamic_mx_quant` pass — → **gmm1** `npu_grouped_matmul_swiglu_quant_v2` (gate_up + swiglu + requant fused, **cumulative** `group_list`) → **gmm2** `npu_grouped_matmul` (**count** `group_list` + explicit `group_list_type`). The UE8M0 scale dtypes are passed explicitly; the e4m3 `x`/`weight` dtypes are left implicit. DeepEP has no MXFP8 dispatch dtype, so on that path the dispatcher keeps sending BF16 and gmm1 quantizes the hidden states itself via `npu_dynamic_mx_quant` before the fused kernel — both dispatchers reach gmm1 with the same input. Only the `ascend_tp` path is validated end-to-end on A5.
- **Fused-routing quant optimization:** the fused `quant_mode=3` scale comes back flat (`[N, K/32]`) instead of the pair-split `[N, K/64, 2]` layout gmm1 expects, so `_normalize_mxfp_scale` reshapes it before use. Verified via a standalone probe script (`npu_moe_init_routing_v2(quant_mode=3)` vs. the two-step `quant_mode=-1` + `npu_dynamic_mx_quant` reference) to be byte-identical (cos = 1.0) on Ascend A5 + torch_npu 2.10.0.post2, then confirmed end-to-end on the online and offline launch scripts — so this fused path is the only routing-quant implementation kept (no runtime toggle, no two-step fallback branch).

**Offline quantization (msmodelslim pre-quantized weights, flagless)**

- `W8A8_MXFP8` MoE checkpoints are detected from `quant_model_description.json` and handled by the new `ModelSlimMXFP8MoEScheme`, which registers `float8_e4m3fn` expert weights + `uint8` (E8M0, exponent + 127) block scales and delegates weight post-processing + forward to the **same** `NPUMXFP8MoEMethod` kernel (offline branch: reshape `[E, N, K/32] → [E, N, K/64, 2]` + transpose, no re-quant).
- **Router gate:** msmodelslim also quantises `mlp.gate` (`W8A8_MXFP8`). The gate is a `ReplicatedLinear`, so its quantization is now **description-driven** — for the offline `modelslim` path the gate receives the quant config and is dequantised correctly via `ModelSlimMXFP8Scheme`; the online path keeps it in BF16 (unchanged). Previously the fp8 gate was cast to BF16 **without** its block scale, scrambling the router and producing garbage output; this is the fix that makes the offline path usable.

# Benchmark Results

Validated end-to-end on Ascend A5 hardware (Qwen3-30B-A3B). Both W8A8 MXFP8 modes (online and offline msmodelslim) are compared against the BF16 baseline.

## Performance

Both paths ship the FRACTAL_NZ expert-weight layout (review item 8). Against BF16, online and offline W8A8 MXFP8 deliver **~+44% throughput** and **~-30% TPOT / E2E latency**; the two modes are within noise of each other.

| Metric | BF16 (avg) | Online W8A8 (avg) | vs BF16 | Offline W8A8 (avg) | vs BF16 |
|--------|-----------|-------------------|---------|--------------------|---------|
| **Request Throughput (req/s)** | 3.03 | 4.37 | **↑ +44.2%** | 4.35 | **↑ +43.6%** |
| **Input Token Throughput (tok/s)** | 1191.70 | 1719.21 | **↑ +44.3%** | 1709.32 | **↑ +43.4%** |
| **Output Token Throughput (tok/s)** | 640.99 | 924.73 | **↑ +44.3%** | 919.41 | **↑ +43.4%** |
| **Total Token Throughput (tok/s)** | 1832.69 | 2643.95 | **↑ +44.3%** | 2628.72 | **↑ +43.4%** |
| **Mean E2E Latency (ms)** | 10101.74 | 7004.54 | **↓ -30.7%** | 7043.46 | **↓ -30.3%** |
| **Median E2E Latency (ms)** | 7159.17 | 4950.51 | **↓ -30.9%** | 4986.98 | **↓ -30.3%** |
| **P99 E2E Latency (ms)** | 38648.60 | 26909.35 | **↓ -30.4%** | 27005.87 | **↓ -30.1%** |
| **Mean TTFT (ms)** | 168.29 | 134.96 | **↓ -19.8%** | 136.54 | **↓ -18.9%** |
| **Median TTFT (ms)** | 153.14 | 133.13 | **↓ -13.1%** | 136.12 | **↓ -11.1%** |
| **P99 TTFT (ms)** | 1204.71\* | 231.07 | **↓ -80.8%** | 227.01 | **↓ -81.2%** |
| **Mean TPOT (ms)** | 47.44 | 32.79 | **↓ -30.9%** | 32.96 | **↓ -30.5%** |
| **Median TPOT (ms)** | 46.91 | 33.20 | **↓ -29.2%** | 33.24 | **↓ -29.1%** |
| **P99 TPOT (ms)** | 80.22 | 49.60 | **↓ -38.2%** | 49.81 | **↓ -37.9%** |
| **Mean ITL (ms)** | 47.44 | 32.81 | **↓ -30.8%** | 32.98 | **↓ -30.5%** |

> Improvement = `(quantized - bf16)/bf16` for throughput and `(bf16 - quantized)/bf16` for latency; positive values are a performance gain.
>
> \* The BF16 P99 TTFT is skewed by a single outlier run (3100.86 ms); the other two BF16 runs were 263.73 and 249.55 ms. Every quantized configuration is consistently low and stable here.

### FRACTAL_NZ weight layout (review item 8)

ND vs NZ on the same benchmark, everything else equal:

| Metric | Online: ND → NZ | Offline: ND → NZ |
|--------|----------------|-----------------|
| **Total Token Throughput (tok/s)** | 2592.53 → 2643.95 (**+2.0%**) | 2552.76 → 2628.72 (**+3.0%**) |
| **Mean E2E Latency (ms)** | 7146.17 → 7004.54 (**-2.0%**) | 7259.02 → 7043.46 (**-3.0%**) |
| **Mean TTFT (ms)** | 144.32 → 134.96 (**-6.5%**) | 145.93 → 136.54 (**-6.4%**) |
| **P99 TPOT (ms)** | 51.58 → 49.60 (**-3.8%**) | 52.73 → 49.81 (**-5.5%**) |

Not the ~10% the int paths saw, but consistent across both modes, so NZ is what this PR
ships. A standalone kernel probe on the same box (gmm1 + gmm2 only, 128 experts) measured
+1.4% on decode-shaped and +3.8% on prefill-shaped inputs against a 0.2-0.3% noise floor,
matching the end-to-end delta.

Two things worth recording, since neither is obvious from the int8 precedent:

- **The cast must precede the transpose.** `npu_grouped_matmul_swiglu_quant_v2` asserts
  that weight and weight_scale carry the same transpose flag (`CheckMXTranspose`), and
  `npu_format_cast` returns a physically retiled, non-transposed tensor — so casting the
  already-transposed view fails outright with `transpositions are true/false`. The int8 MoE
  methods transpose first, but they carry no MX scale to keep in sync; the dense W4A8 path
  already uses the order adopted here.
- **Contiguous weights are not the answer.** Making weight and scale both contiguous is
  numerically correct but measurably slower (-6.2% decode at 128 experts), so the
  transpose views stay. A small-expert-count microbenchmark inverts this conclusion
  entirely (E=4 rates contiguous 58% *faster*), which is why the numbers above come from
  the real 128-expert shape.

## Accuracy (GSM8K)

Validated on Ascend A5 hardware (Qwen3-30B-A3B), three runs each. Both W8A8 MXFP8 modes stay within run-to-run noise of the BF16 baseline.

| Run | BF16 | Online W8A8 | Offline W8A8 |
|-----|------|-------------|--------------|
| Run 1 | 95.68 | 95.53 | 95.68 |
| Run 2 | 95.91 | 95.98 | 95.91 |
| Run 3 | 96.13 | 96.29 | 95.75 |
| **Average** | **95.91** | **95.93** | **95.78** |
| **vs BF16** | — | **↑ +0.03** | **↓ -0.13** |

> GSM8K accuracy (%); `vs BF16` is the average-over-average delta in percentage points.
> Both deltas are smaller than the 0.45 pp spread of the BF16 baseline's own three runs.

# Style / consistency with the merged NPU quant PRs (#22352, #23650, #23795)

- All NPU ops go through `torch.ops.npu.*`; **no top-level `import torch_npu`**, no `current_platform` guards (module stays importable on CUDA/CPU/AMD/XPU CI).
- **Online** returns the method directly from `Fp8Config.get_quant_method` (mirrors dense `NPUMXFP8LinearMethod`). **Offline** subclasses `ModelSlimMoEScheme` and delegates weight post-processing / forward to a `self.kernel` (`NPUMXFP8MoEMethod`), registered in `get_moe_scheme`'s `moe_quant_schemes` list — the same pattern as the int8 / W4A4 / W4A8 MoE schemes.
- MoE weight + scale are kept as **non-contiguous transpose views** (`.transpose(1, 2)` with no `.contiguous()`), with the expert weight cast to **FRACTAL_NZ before** that transpose; gmm1 uses the fused `npu_grouped_matmul_swiglu_quant_v2`; the `group_list` count↔cumulative conversion is explicit (gmm1 cumulative, gmm2 count).

# Files Changed

**New**

| File | Change |
| ---- | ------ |
| `srt/layers/quantization/modelslim/schemes/modelslim_mxfp8_moe.py` | offline `ModelSlimMXFP8MoEScheme` for `W8A8_MXFP8` MoE checkpoints |

**Modified**

| File | Change |
| ---- | ------ |
| `srt/hardware_backend/npu/quantization/moe_methods.py` | add the per-gmm kernel `NPUMXFP8MoEMethod` (online + offline `process_weights_after_loading`, `apply_fused_gmm1_swiglu` for w13, `apply` for w2); cast the expert weights to FRACTAL_NZ ahead of the transpose |
| `srt/hardware_backend/npu/utils.py` | `_is_nz_aligned`: add the fp8 branch — e4m3 is single-byte, so it shares int8's column rule. It previously fell through to the catch-all `True`, which no caller exercised (the packed-FP4 callers return early via `customize_dtype`, and dense MXFP8 never format-casts) |
| `srt/hardware_backend/npu/quantization/online_moe_methods.py` (new) | `NPUMXFP8OnlineMoEMethod(UnquantizedFusedMoEMethod)`, the `--quantization mxfp8` entry point |
| `srt/hardware_backend/npu/moe/matmul.py` | add `GroupedMatmulSwigluQuant`, the reusable wrapper around `npu_grouped_matmul_swiglu_quant_v2` |
| `srt/hardware_backend/npu/moe/hidden_states_quant.py` → `quant.py` | rename + teach `HiddenStatesDynamicQuant` the `float8_e4m3fn` (`npu_dynamic_mx_quant`) dtype |
| `srt/layers/quantization/unquant.py` | drop the hardcoded `dispatcher_output_dtype: "bf16"` that clobbered the value the NPU kernel had just set (it duplicated `NPUUnquantMoEMethod`) |
| `srt/layers/moe/moe_runner/ascend.py` | stop rejecting DeepEP at runner construction |
| `srt/layers/quantization/fp8.py` | dispatch FusedMoE layers to `NPUMXFP8OnlineMoEMethod` under `is_npu() and use_mxfp8` |
| `srt/arg_groups/overrides.py` | skip the `mxfp8` → `flashinfer_trtllm` runner-backend override on NPU, so the backend stays `auto` and resolves to Ascend (it also gates FusedMoE's w1/w3 shard swap) |
| `srt/layers/quantization/modelslim/modelslim.py` | add `("W8A8_MXFP8", ModelSlimMXFP8MoEScheme)` to `get_moe_scheme`'s `moe_quant_schemes` |
| `srt/layers/quantization/modelslim/schemes/__init__.py` | export `ModelSlimMXFP8MoEScheme` |
| `srt/models/qwen3_moe.py` | make the router `gate` quant **description-driven** (offline modelslim only) so a quantised `mlp.gate` loads/dequantises correctly instead of being cast to BF16 without its scale |
| `docs_new/docs/advanced_features/quantization.mdx`, `docs_new/docs/hardware-platforms/ascend-npus/ascend_npu_quantization.mdx` | document MXFP8 MoE (Ascend support row + online/offline prose + router-gate note) |

# Status

**WIP / Draft.** Online (`--quantization mxfp8`) and offline (msmodelslim) MoE MXFP8 are both **validated end-to-end on Ascend A5** (see Performance above). GSM8K accuracy is within run-to-run noise of the BF16 baseline (see Accuracy above).

@OrangeRedeng's review is addressed. It was first applied as a single refactor commit (`6bd7056`), which garbled generation on A5 in a way that could not be bisected, so that commit was dropped and the review was redone one item at a time, each verified on A5 before the next:

| # | Item | Commit |
| - | ---- | ------ |
| 6 | offline checkpoints load flagless, drop `--quantization` from the docs | `9efe9998d` |
| 7 | rename `hidden_states_quant.py` → `quant.py`, teach it mxfp8 | `efe50dfa3` |
| 2, 5 | `GroupedMatmulSwigluQuant` wrapper + pick the matmul by `weight_prefix` | `2d06d61a5` |
| 1 | stop rejecting DeepEP; gmm1 quantizes when the dispatcher sends bf16 | `1efd2ca35` |
| 3, 4 | inherit `UnquantizedFusedMoEMethod`, rename to `NPUMXFP8OnlineMoEMethod` | `ea24f248d` |
| 8 | `npu_format_cast` (NZ) | `d419aa41f` |

Re-validating the baseline first also surfaced three regressions from the preceding `main` merge, in which upstream restructured the NPU MoE layer (`fused_moe_method_npu.py` deleted, `moe_methods.py` / `moe_runner/ascend.py` / `npu/moe/*.py` added) and this PR's implementation was re-ported onto the new layout. None are review-related:

| Commit | Regression |
| ------ | ---------- |
| `e9b36bb5d` | the e8m0 block-scale dtype was resolved off `torch` instead of `torch_npu`; the grouped matmuls reject torch's dtype object, so every gmm1 died |
| `9ac21f5ff` | `--quantization mxfp8` forced `moe_runner_backend` to `flashinfer_trtllm` unconditionally, including on NPU. Beyond picking a runner that does not exist there, that flag also drives FusedMoE's w1/w3 shard swap and a 128-alignment round-up — and once item 3 above makes this method inherit `UnquantizedFusedMoEMethod`, it matches the shard-swap list, loading every expert with gate and up exchanged. Silent degenerate output; this is what garbled the big-bang refactor |
| `969087364` | `ModelSlimMoEMethod.apply` reads `{w13,w2}_weight_offset` unconditionally; MXFP8 is a pure scale format with no zero point, so the offline scheme never created one |

# Related Issues

Part of #21584 (MXFP8/MXFP4 support on Ascend NPU for Qwen3 LLM). Builds on merged #23795 (dense W4A4) and #22352 (dense W8A8 MXFP8 — provides the dense linear MXFP8 method + `Fp8Config` NPU dispatch + `ModelSlimMXFP8Scheme` this MoE work reuses).
