title: [Diffusion][Kernel] Fuse Wan2.2 NVFP4 bias + GELU on Blackwell
author: BBuf
body:
## Motivation Wan2.2 ModelOpt NVFP4 MLPs currently execute the `fc_in` hot path as three separate operations: ```text NVFP4 GEMM -> BF16 bias add -> tanh GELU ``` On GB300, the bias add and GELU are memory-bound and account for a meaningful part of denoising time. This PR fuses the last two operations while preserving the eager half-precision rounding boundary. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["DenoisingStage._maybe_toggle_quality_fusions"] --> B{"request quality"} B -->|"lossless"| C["unmount_nvfp4_bias_gelu
reference path"] B -->|"high"| D["mount_nvfp4_bias_gelu
eligible Wan NVFP4 sites only"]:::changed D --> E["ColumnParallelLinear.forward
NVFP4 GEMM returns output and deferred bias"]:::changed E --> F["bias_gelu_tanh
fused BF16/FP16 bias add plus tanh GELU"]:::changed C --> G["NVFP4 GEMM with bias
then native GELU"] F --> H["fc_out"] G --> H L["Legend: dashed border = added or modified"]:::changed classDef changed stroke-dasharray:5 5,stroke-width:2px; ``` The request-scoped quality gate only defers `fc_in` bias when the live linear method is `ModelOptFp4LinearMethod`. Unquantized checkpoint-excluded linears and the default `quality=lossless` path remain unchanged. ## Modifications - Add a lightweight JIT CUDA bias + approximate-GELU kernel with: - FP16/BF16 support; - 16-byte vectors before Blackwell and 32-byte vectors on Blackwell; - occupancy-capped persistent launch geometry; - PDL wait/trigger support; - an explicit half-precision rounding boundary after the bias add. - Add a request-scoped Wan NVFP4 fusion site and integrate it with the existing diffusion `quality=high` lifecycle. - Add registered H100 and B200 kernel tests, a registered kernel benchmark, and Wan mount/unmount plus excluded-linear regression tests. ## Accuracy Tests Hardware: NVIDIA GB300 (compute capability 10.3). - 11 focused GPU tests pass on the rebased PR: ```bash python3 -m pytest -q \ test/registered/kernels/ops/elementwise/test_bias_gelu.py \ python/sglang/multimodal_gen/test/unit/test_wan_gelu_mlp.py # 11 passed ``` - The fused kernel is bit-exact with `F.gelu(input + bias, approximate="tanh")` for FP16 and BF16, including the production `(1, 4096, 13824)` shape. - Main A/B and PR A/B `quality=high` MP4 files are byte-identical. A direct 81-frame comparison gives: | Accuracy metric | Main vs PR | | --- | ---: | | Decoded frames | 81 | | Mean / worst-frame SSIM | `1.000000 / 1.000000` | | Mean / worst-frame PSNR | `inf / inf` | | Maximum decoded-pixel difference | `0 / 255` | | LPIPS | `0` (identical decoded frames) | | MP4 SHA256, main | `d68d70a1cc7efc04bc6c5fbcf985d2f9f7b41edc4e54a23497541bbf821cd961` | | MP4 SHA256, PR | `d68d70a1cc7efc04bc6c5fbcf985d2f9f7b41edc4e54a23497541bbf821cd961` | The following comparison shows frames 1, 41, and 81 from the exact artifacts used for the metrics (same prompt, seed, shape, steps, guidance, and GPU): ![Wan2.2 NVFP4 main versus PR generated-frame comparison](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BBuf/sglang/pr-assets-37075/pr-assets/37075/wan22-nvfp4-main-vs-pr.png) - Candidate `quality=lossless` is byte-identical to the unmodified lossless baseline: `d75f78b4264618a0b8e170cd8d2649f18434787baee27374052dc4867b8205e5`. - Existing `quality=high` versus `quality=lossless`, measured over all 81 decoded frames: mean/worst SSIM `0.986642 / 0.983460`, mean/worst PSNR `41.092099 / 39.520000 dB`. ## Speed Tests and Profiling End-to-end workload: - Model: `nvidia/Wan2.2-T2V-A14B-Diffusers-NVFP4` - Snapshot: `ac69f2655787c3af65e1756d001303cd4a4daa46` - GB300, one GPU, eager native SGLang, synchronized stage profiling - 832x480, 81 frames, 40 steps, guidance 4, seed 42 - Prompt: `A cat and a dog baking a cake together in a kitchen.` - Performance base: `89816a21a1b5e9cf1f21dc407256e73905151ecc` | Run | Denoise | End-to-end | Peak reserved | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Baseline A | 71.726712 s | 72.719473 s | 55.580 GiB | | Candidate A | 69.585341 s | 70.579956 s | 55.580 GiB | | Candidate B | 69.607537 s | 70.602064 s | 55.580 GiB | | Baseline B | 71.748749 s | 72.746630 s | 55.580 GiB | Mean improvement: - Denoise: `71.737731 s -> 69.596439 s`, **2.984889% faster**. - End-to-end: `72.733052 s -> 70.591010 s`, **2.945073% faster**. - Paired denoise improvements: `2.985458%` and `2.984320%`. - Peak reserved memory is unchanged. Five profiled denoise timesteps after warmup: | Metric | Baseline | Candidate | | --- | ---: | ---: | | CUDA time | 11,316.079 ms | 11,005.284 ms | | CUDA events | 22,688 | 22,282 | | BF16 add | 1,553.063 ms | 1,138.976 ms | | Native GELU | 218.014 ms | 36.028 ms | | Fused bias + GELU | 0 ms | 207.587 ms | The targeted add + GELU chain decreases from `1,771.077 ms` to `1,382.591 ms` (`388.486 ms` saved). FP4 GEMM and attention kernel counts remain stable. The registered microbenchmark was repeated on GB300 after rebasing onto `032fe91bf1`: | Rows x hidden | JIT | PyTorch add + GELU | Speedup | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 32760 x 5120 | 171.9725 us | 498.9286 us | 2.90x | | 32760 x 13824 | 457.6064 us | 1338.7175 us | 2.93x | ## Checklist - [x] Format code with pre-commit (all applicable hooks pass). - [x] Add unit tests (registered H100/B200 kernel coverage and Wan integration coverage). - [x] Update documentation (N/A: no new public option or user-facing behavior). - [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results. - [x] Follow the SGLang code style guidance. --- ### CI States Latest PR Test (Base): :white_check_mark: [Run #33283700621](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/33283700621) Latest PR Test (Extra): :white_check_mark: [Run #33317400114](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/33317400114) Latest PR Test (AMD ROCm 7.2): :x: [Run #33283700582](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/33283700582)

title: [Kernel] Add tuned LFM2.5 Triton MoE configs on B300
author: BBuf
body:
## Motivation

LFM2.5-8B-A1B uses two BF16 Triton MoE GEMMs on B300 (`SM103`):

- gate/up projection: `E=32, N=3584, K=2048, topk=4`
- down projection: `E=32, N=2048, K=1792, topk=1`

The generic Triton path previously fell back to heuristic schedules for this
model/device pair. A shape-specific KDA kernel improved over that fallback, but a
separately tuned generic Triton baseline was faster for medium/large token counts
and high-concurrency serving. Therefore this PR has been converted to a
**config-only** change, following the same conclusion as #37159.

## Changes

Add B300 (`NVIDIA_B300_SXM6_AC`) Triton 3.7.1 configs for LFM2.5:

- gate/up config with 8 tuned M buckets
- down config with 8 tuned M buckets
- TMA enabled in every selected config

There is no custom kernel, dispatch branch, or model-specific runtime code in the
final diff.

## Tuning setup

Hardware: NVIDIA B300 SXM6 AC (`SM103`). Software: CUDA 13.0, PyTorch
2.13.0+cu130, Triton 3.7.1.

The tuner ran on PR base `771e613d96de0ee89631bc308a2525aaeae9f13e`, where
the former KDA dispatch did not exist:

- 100 deterministic `E=32, topk=4` routing samples
- M grid: `1, 8, 32, 256, 1024, 2048, 4096, 16384`
- 240 focused configs per M
- `BLOCK_M`: 16/32/64/128/256
- schedules covering `BLOCK_N` 32/64/128/256, `BLOCK_K` 64/128,
  4/8 warps, 3/4/6 stages, and group sizes 1/8/16/32
- both gate/up and down TMA variants tested

The runtime uses nearest-M selection between the tuned buckets. Gate/up and down
configs use the same `BLOCK_SIZE_M` at each bucket, as required by the shared
expert-row alignment.

## Kernel results

The table compares the tuned generic Triton configs in this PR with the removed
KDA candidate. Times are microseconds per CUDA-Graph replayed gate/up + down pair.
A negative final-column value means tuned Triton is faster.

| M | Tuned Triton total (us) | KDA total (us) | Tuned vs KDA |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 20.017 | 20.660 | -3.11% |
| 2 | 32.027 | 31.309 | +2.29% |
| 4 | 52.441 | 55.971 | -6.31% |
| 8 | 75.484 | 79.210 | -4.70% |
| 16 | 101.460 | 98.284 | +3.23% |
| 32 | 110.967 | 111.268 | -0.27% |
| 64 | 113.710 | 137.305 | -17.18% |
| 128 | 121.576 | 138.931 | -12.49% |
| 256 | 131.048 | 140.796 | -6.92% |
| 512 | 147.158 | 168.365 | -12.60% |
| 1024 | 167.568 | 244.532 | -31.47% |
| 2048 | 238.466 | 328.062 | -27.31% |
| 4096 | 413.532 | 551.839 | -25.06% |
| 16384 | 1242.570 | 1974.426 | -37.07% |

KDA has two small wins at M=2 and M=16 and is effectively tied at M=32. Tuned
Triton is consistently faster from M=64 onward. At M=4096, KDA's specialized
gate/up kernel is 3.4% faster, but its down projection is much slower, so the
combined path still loses by 25.06%.

## LFM2.5-8B-A1B serving results

Two TP1 servers were benchmarked concurrently. GPU assignments were then swapped
and the full matrix repeated. Each assignment used seeds 1001/1002/1003. Results
pair the same physical GPU and use the geometric mean of GPU0/GPU1 ratios to
remove multiplicative card-to-card bias.

- concurrency: `1, 4, 16, 32, 64`
- decode: input 1, output 256, `max(16, 4 * concurrency)` prompts
- mixed: input 1024, output 256, `max(8, 2 * concurrency)` prompts
- fixed lengths with `--random-range-ratio 1.0`
- cache flushed before each trial

Positive throughput means tuned Triton is faster. Positive ITL means KDA has
higher (worse) ITL.

| Workload | Concurrency | Tuned throughput advantage | KDA ITL penalty |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| decode 1/256 | 1 | +0.38% | +0.44% |
| decode 1/256 | 4 | -0.78% | -0.36% |
| decode 1/256 | 16 | +0.67% | +0.73% |
| decode 1/256 | 32 | -0.56% | -0.38% |
| decode 1/256 | 64 | **+6.36%** | **+6.29%** |
| mixed 1024/256 | 1 | +1.06% | +1.20% |
| mixed 1024/256 | 4 | +1.94% | +1.45% |
| mixed 1024/256 | 16 | +1.86% | +1.07% |
| mixed 1024/256 | 32 | +1.31% | -0.14% |
| mixed 1024/256 | 64 | **+10.20%** | **+8.56%** |

Decode through concurrency 32 is effectively tied (all throughput differences
within 0.8%). The tuned configs win clearly at concurrency 64 and win every mixed
throughput point after GPU crossover correction.

## Correctness and validation

- Tuned generic Triton and the former KDA candidate matched exactly (`rtol=0`,
  `atol=0`) for both projections at M =
  `2, 4, 8, 16, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 4096, 16384` (22 cases).
- Completed 60 paired serving runs plus two additional concurrency-16 sanity
  runs, including the GPU0/GPU1 crossover.
- Both JSON files parse successfully, contain the expected 8 M buckets, enable
  TMA in every bucket, and keep gate/up and down `BLOCK_SIZE_M` aligned.
- `git diff --check` passes; the final PR diff contains only the two config files.

## Conclusion

The initial KDA work identified a real missing-config problem, but the custom
kernel is not the best fix after tuning the existing Triton path. The final PR
keeps the useful artifact—the tuned generic Triton configs—and removes 951 lines
of custom kernel, dispatch, and test code.

## Checklist

- [x] Tune generic Triton on the PR base, including gate/up and down TMA.
- [x] Compare 14 kernel token counts.
- [x] Validate exact output across decode and prefill shapes.
- [x] Compare concurrency 1/4/16/32/64 with three seeds and GPU crossover.
- [x] Convert the final diff to config-only.

title: [XPU] Qwen3.8-flash-next enablement
author: Xia-Weiwen
body:
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->

## Motivation

Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (generic model support merged into `main` via #37500)
introduces several architectural features new to SGLang — a sparse-attention
indexer (QSA), HyperConnection (gated multi-stream residual mixing), a
PLE/N-gram auxiliary embedding, and MTP/NEXTN speculative decoding on top of
a hybrid linear+full attention backbone. This work enables the model
end-to-end on the XPU backend, since the current implementation of these
new features assumes CUDA in several places.

## Plan

Staged enablement:
1. **Functionality ready** (this PR) — model runs E2E on XPU without errors, exercising every new feature at least once, using existing portable (Triton/torch) kernels where a custom SYCL kernel isn't required.
2. **Acceptable performance** (future) — remove the worst algorithmic bottlenecks (unbatched ops, Python-loop fallbacks) without necessarily writing new SYCL kernels.
3. **Peak performance** (future) — write/optimize dedicated SYCL kernels in sgl-kernel-xpu for any remaining hot paths.

This PR covers Stage 1.

## Current Status

Stage 1 (functional E2E correctness) is complete. Per-component implementation status:

| Component | Status | Implementation on XPU |
|---|---|---|
| QSA sparse-attention indexer | Fixed a real OOB gather bug in compressed-KV update (`update_key_state_and_compress`), plus added a `forward_xpu` dispatch | Reuses the existing device-generic Triton/torch fallback path (same code CUDA falls back to when its fast custom kernel isn't applicable); underlying dense attention math uses sgl-kernel-xpu's existing FMHA SYCL kernel |
| HyperConnection (gated residual mixing) | Fixed hardcoded `cuda` device selection | Pure torch-native, no custom kernel needed |
| PLE / N-gram embedding | Works out of the box, no changes needed | Pure torch embedding lookup + all-reduce |
| MTP / NEXTN speculative decoding | Fixed 4 device-portability bugs: hardcoded CUDA device in the Mamba state pool, hardcoded CUDA sync calls, a missing kernel arg in the GDN Triton wrapper, and an int64-overflow bug when packing XPU pointers into scatter-kernel metadata | Uses existing Triton GDN kernel and Triton-based Mamba-state-scatter kernel; no new SYCL kernel required |
| MoE (routed + shared experts) | Verified working | Existing sgl-kernel-xpu `moe_align_block_size` SYCL kernel |
| Vision encoder | Verified working | Existing sgl-kernel-xpu non-paged-prefill FMHA SYCL kernel |

Stage 2 (performance tuning) has not started yet.

Re-verified (all scenarios above, BF16 + FP8, 1×B60 + TP=4) after rebasing
onto `main` on two machines. One new requirement surfaced by the rebase:
QSA's forced `page_size=64` conflicts with the mamba radix-cache's
`no_buffer` strategy, and `extra_buffer` is currently unsupported on XPU
(`supports_mamba_cache_extra_buffer()` hardcodes `False` for XPU regardless
of model) — so `--disable-radix-cache` is required on XPU for this model
until that gap is addressed (tracked in `docs/KNOWN_ISSUES.md`).

## Upstream PRs to Track

- **#37500** — "Squash-merge Qwen 3.8 Flash Next integration into main":
  **merged** 2026-09-08. Supersedes #36497 (below); this is now our base.
- ~~#36497~~ — "Introduce Qwen 3.8 Flash Next": **superseded/closed** by
  #37500. Kept here for history only.
- **#36601** — "[AMD] Support Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on ROCm": parallel
  per-vendor enablement PR. Useful reference for how device-specific
  speculative-decoding/graph-replay code is layered on top of the generic
  model support.
- **#36644** — "[Qwen3.8] Fix FP8 KV cache support in QSA": still open; QSA
  correctness fix worth checking once XPU FP8 KV-cache support is tackled.
- **#36651** — "[Qwen3.8] Add PD state transfer for Flash Next": **merged**,
  inherited via the `main` rebase. Adds prefill/decode-disaggregation
  transfer of QSA/PLE recurrent state — out of scope for this PR, but
  required reference for a future XPU PD-disaggregation effort.
- **#38346** — "Fix QSA compress-group OOB gather clamp": **merged**,
  inherited via the `main` rebase. Superseded our own hand-rolled clamp in
  `qsa_indexer.py`; we removed our duplicate and kept upstream's fix.
- **#35051** — "Fix XPU USM pointer overflow via uint64 ptr tables":
  **merged**, inherited via the `main` rebase. Superseded our own
  `_signed_i64()` workaround in `mamba_state_scatter_triton.py`, which we
  removed since it became actively incompatible with upstream's fix.
- **sgl-kernel-xpu #341** — "[MoE] Add Xe2 FP8 W8A16 grouped GEMM support":
  adds a real, Xe2-native FP8 MoE kernel to sgl-kernel-xpu (dispatches FP8
  weights × BF16 activations internally, since Xe2/BMG has no native FP8×FP8
  MMA; reports 1.18x-2.15x speedup vs. the evaluated W8A8 path). This is the
  long-term/performant fix for XPU FP8 MoE, complementary to the Stage-1
  generic-Triton-fallback stopgap already implemented in this branch (see
  `docs/KNOWN_ISSUES.md`). **Merged** on 2026-09-04.

### Design precedents (already merged, informational only)

Not dependencies — these are past XPU-enablement PRs for earlier
Qwen-family models, useful as coding-pattern references for Stage 2/3
kernel work (e.g. adding a fused sgl-kernel-xpu kernel, following the same
structure):

- #33354 — fused GDN kernel from sgl-kernel-xpu for Qwen3.5
- #32227
- #35775
- #24390

- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).
- [ ] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations).

- [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance).

1. Ping Merge Oncalls to start the process. See the [PR Merge Process](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/.github/MAINTAINER.md#pull-request-merge-process).

4. After green CI and required approvals, ask Merge Oncalls or people with Write permission to merge the PR.

title: [AMD][DSV4] feat: enable fp8 two-pool unified_kv on gfx950
author: amd-danli103
body:
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->
## Motivation

<!-- Describe the purpose and goals of this pull request. -->
Under `unified_kv`, DSv4 keeps KV in bf16 across the full latent — `qk_nope_head_dim` 448 plus `qk_rope_head_dim` 64, **1024 B per token per layer**. The nope half actually does not need that precision. Storing nope as fp8 with per-tile E8M0 scales while leaving rope in bf16 cuts the row to **640 B** (512 B of fp8 nope at a fixed stride, plus the same 128 B of bf16 rope), which measures out at **1.51× the KV capacity at identical memory** on gfx950. At fixed HBM more tokens stay resident, so longer contexts and higher concurrency fit on the same node.

Off by default behind `SGLANG_DSV4_UNIFIED_KV_FP8`; it requires gfx950 and implies `is_unified_kv_triton()`. Other architectures warn and fall back to bf16, so nothing on the existing path changes.

## Modifications

<!-- Detail the changes made in this pull request. -->
Two pools instead of one, then every writer and reader of the pool:
- **layout / sizing** — nope is a 512 B fp8 row (448 values + inline e8m0 scales, padded so the stride stays a power of two); rope stays 128 B of bf16. PD disaggregation and HiCache offload are refused for now because both assume one pool per layer.
- **writers** — SWA scatter, fused QK norm+RoPE store, compressor norm+rope store, and the packed ring store used by prefill and target-verify.
- **readers** — decode through aiter's `mla_a8w8` v4 nm asm kernel; prefill through aiter's opus kernel.
- **decode overhead** — drop a `masked_fill_` on empty segments the builders cannot produce, cache `qo_indptr` (it only depends on the token count), skip a `kv.contiguous()` the group-quant kernel does not need (it already takes the row stride), and cap `num_kv_splits` to 4 above 40 tokens where aiter's occupancy heuristic over-splits.

Everything stays behind `SGLANG_DSV4_UNIFIED_KV_FP8` (default off) plus the gfx95 gate. The DSv4 unified_kv path is ROCm-only; the only common-code touch is one new `elif` in the JIT norm+rope-store template, existing branches unchanged.

## What this buys: KV capacity

Four configurations, each a pair of servers with byte-identical CLI differing only in the env switch. Taken on this rebase (`ec07b65ed6 `):

| config | `available_bytes` | bf16 `full_token` | fp8 `full_token` | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TP8 | 135.59 GB | 16,126,208 | 24,223,744 | **1.5021×** |
| TP8 + MTP | 132.97 GB | 15,417,344 | 23,161,088 | **1.5023×** |
| TP8 + DP8 | 119.85 GB | 14,399,488 | 21,605,120 | **1.5004×** |
| TP8 + DP8 + MTP | 115.35 GB | 13,612,288 | 20,424,448 | **1.5004×** |

`available_bytes` matches exactly within every pair, which it has to — otherwise a weight-footprint difference would land in the ratio. `bytes_per_full_token` goes 8918.00 → 5945.00 in the no-MTP cells and 9064.20 → 6042.46 in the MTP cells: **0.6666× in all four**, not the row's 0.625, because the indexer term in `_get_bytes_per_full_token` does not scale with the KV row width — it was already fp8 with its own scales.
A fifth pair at a different `mem-fraction` on the previous stack gave 14,211,840 → 21,451,520 (**1.5094×**), so the ratio is not an artefact of one memory setting.

## Accuracy Tests

<!-- If this pull request affects model outputs (e.g., changes to the kernel or model forward code), provide accuracy test results. -->
GSM8K, all 1319 questions, paired runs differing only in the fp8 switch, all four cells on this rebase, on top of #37140's rebuilt AOT. Prefix caching on. No regression observed.

| DP | MTP | fp8 | bf16 |
|---|---|---|---|
| off | off | 0.949 | 0.940 |
| off | EAGLE | 0.948 | 0.945 |
| 8 | off | 0.947 | 0.952 |
| 8 | EAGLE | 0.946 | 0.947 |

## Speed Tests and Profiling

<!-- If this pull request impacts inference speed, provide benchmarking and profiling results. -->
Same machine, MI355X, radix cache off. The first four tables are TP=8; the last is DP=8 + dp-attention. Two servers, byte-identical CLI within each table, differing only in `SGLANG_DSV4_UNIFIED_KV_FP8`. 
`ttt ratio` is fp8 ttt / bf16 ttt (higher is better). The trade is a small decode cost for 1.50× `full_token`.

**ISL/OSL: 8k /1k (no MTP)**
| conc | bf16 ttt | fp8 ttt | ttt ratio | bf16 TTFT | fp8 TTFT | bf16 ITL | fp8 ITL |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | 4837 | 4470 | 0.924 | 1472 | 1486 | 12.57 | 13.75 |
| 16 | 7377 | 7146 | 0.969 | 2806 | 2827 | 14.79 | 15.39 |
| 32 | 11035 | 10800 | 0.979 | 5176 | 5204 | 16.77 | 17.29 |
| 48 | 13050 | 12855 | 0.985 | 7564 | 7615 | 19.09 | 19.50 |

**ISL/OSL: 8k /1k (MTP, accept length 2.13–3.04, against 2.00–3.04 for bf16)**
| conc | bf16 ttt | fp8 ttt | ttt ratio | bf16 TTFT | fp8 TTFT | bf16 ITL | fp8 ITL |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | 6115 | 5850 | 0.957 | 1716 | 644 | 9.29 | 9.77 |
| 16 | 10417 | 10261 | 0.985 | 639 | 362 | 8.11 | 8.32 |
| 32 | 14255 | 13967 | 0.980 | 665 | 630 | 9.94 | 10.28 |
| 48 | 16115 | 15749 | 0.977 | 673 | 681 | 11.73 | 12.20 |

**ISL/OSL: 68k/200 (no MTP)**
| conc | bf16 ttt | fp8 ttt | ttt ratio | bf16 TTFT | fp8 TTFT | bf16 ITL | fp8 ITL |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 20064 | 19665 | 0.980 | 7165 | 7245 | 12.65 | 13.50 |
| 16 | 23071 | 22798 | 0.988 | 23901 | 24119 | 15.20 | 16.00 |
| 48 | 24009 | 23792 | 0.991 | 68289 | 68906 | 20.03 | 20.42 |

**ISL/OSL: 68k/200 (MTP, accept length 2.40 / 2.84 / 2.95 against 2.25 / 2.84 / 2.95 for bf16)**
| conc | bf16 ttt | fp8 ttt | ttt ratio | bf16 TTFT | fp8 TTFT | bf16 ITL | fp8 ITL |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 20426 | 20468 | 1.002 | 3514 | 5841 | 8.95 | 6.45 |
| 16 | 22930 | 22676 | 0.989 | 9244 | 12048 | 8.52 | 8.71 |
| 48 | 23502 | 23233 | 0.989 | 17511 | 14785 | 12.58 | 13.17 |

**ISL/OSL: 8k /1k, TP8/DP8 Attn(no MTP)** 
| conc | bf16 ttt | fp8 ttt | ttt ratio | bf16 TTFT | fp8 TTFT | bf16 ITL | fp8 ITL |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 64 | 15383 | 15321 | 0.996 | 7730 | 7702 | 24.29 | 24.52 |
| 128 | 21912 | 21916 | 1.000 | 13622 | 13552 | 27.64 | 27.73 |

The cell to flag is **8192/1024 at c=8** under TP=8: 7.6% less throughput, ITL +1.18 ms. That is the worst of the 14 TP=8 cells; everything else there is within 4.3%, and every cell at concurrency ≥ 16 is within 3.2%. 

The leftover gap is the decode reader, not anything this PR still owns. fp8 goes through aiter's `mla_a8w8` asm kernel, which is tuned for 64 q heads; TP=8 leaves 16 local heads, so it is occupancy-bound — it loads *less* per row (640 B vs 1024 B) and is still slower. The DP=8 table above shows the gap falls into noise. A Triton rewrite was measured and was slower at every shape, so it was dropped. Closing the TP=8 gap needs an `mla_a8w8` variant for 16 q heads on the aiter side; that is a separate PR.

## Reproducing this
One branch, one env variable, two commands, no code edits to switch arms. Taken on MI355X, ROCm 7.2, TP=8, DeepSeek-V4-Pro.

**1. Rebuild `sgl_kernel`** — needed for #37140's AOT half, if your image is earlier than #37140, you need to rebuild as so, otherwise 6 related tests would fail.
```
cd python/sglang/kernels/aot
cp pyproject_rocm.toml pyproject.toml
AMDGPU_TARGET=gfx950 MAX_JOBS=$(nproc) python3 setup_rocm.py build_ext --inplace
cd -
export PYTHONPATH=$PWD/python/sglang/kernels/aot/python:$PWD/python
```
AMDGPU_TARGET is not optional — `setup_rocm.py` defaults to gfx942, which keeps the software cast.
**2. Start a server.** This is the CLI the accuracy matrix was taken on. The two arms differ only in the last export.
```bash
export SGLANG_DEFAULT_THINKING=1
export SGLANG_DSV4_REASONING_EFFORT=high
export SGLANG_USE_ROCM700A=0
export SGLANG_HACK_FLASHMLA_BACKEND=unified_kv_triton
export AITER_BF16_FP8_MOE_BOUND=0
export SGLANG_OPT_USE_AITER_BATCHED_GEMM=1
export SGLANG_OPT_UNIFIED_CACHE_FREE_OUT_OF_WINDOW_SLOTS=1
export SGLANG_TIMEOUT_KEEP_ALIVE=900
export SGLANG_DSV4_UNIFIED_KV_FP8=1      # the fp8 arm adds exactly this line

python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path <DeepSeek-V4-Pro> --served-model-name deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8888 --trust-remote-code \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 --attention-backend dsv4 --page-size 256 \
  --swa-full-tokens-ratio 0.10 --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 \
  --enforce-shared-experts-fusion \
  --tool-call-parser deepseekv4 --reasoning-parser deepseek-v4 \
  --chunked-prefill-size 8192 --mem-fraction-static 0.89 \
  --max-running-requests 64 --cuda-graph-max-bs 64 \
  --speculative-algorithm EAGLE --speculative-num-steps 3 \
  --speculative-eagle-topk 1 --speculative-num-draft-tokens 4 \
  --watchdog-timeout 3600
```

**3. For the capacity number** the server need not finish starting — the sizing line comes before CUDA-graph capture, and `unified_fp8=True` is the only reliable confirmation that the switch took effect, since `is_unified_kv_fp8()` also requires gfx95 and `is_unified_kv_triton()`.

```
DSV4 memory calculation: unified=True, unified_fp8=True, bytes_per_full_token=6042.46, available_bytes=132.97 GB, ..., full_token=23161088
```

**4. For accuracy**, once the server is ready:

```bash
python3 benchmark/gsm8k/bench_sglang.py --num-questions 1319 --parallel 256 --port 8888
```

**5. Unit tests**, single GPU.

```bash
HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python3 -m pytest $(git diff --name-only origin/main..HEAD -- test/) -q
```
## Follow-up
1. For SPD, we support MTP in this initial version, DSpark is further supported in #38901.
2. HiCache is further supported in #37778, many thanks to @1am9trash .
3. PD is now supported in #39166.
4. HiSparse would be supported soon.
5. PCP is supported in #39923, many thanks to @AMD-yanfeiwang .

title: [Feature] Add Aaronson-Gumbel text watermarking
author: JustinTong0323
body:
## Motivation

Some deployments need a machine-readable signal that text was generated by an AI system, including provenance workflows and transparency obligations such as [Article 50 of the EU AI Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng). This PR adds opt-in text watermarking to sampled generation without adding tokens or changing default serving behavior.

## What this PR adds

- Keyed Aaronson-Gumbel sampling over the post-penalty, grammar-masked, top-k/top-p/min-p distribution, with model-free Gamma-test detection from token IDs.
- Returned logprobs reflect the pre-watermark target distribution (the sampler computes them from the unforced distribution when `return_logprob` is set, matching the speculative-decode semantic).
- Server configuration through `--enable-watermark` plus one `--watermark-config` JSON object, given as a file path or inline (`key`, `key_b`, `context_window`, `mixing_probability`, `max_probability`, `default_enabled`, `enforce_all`), with explicit opt-in, default-on, and enforce-all policy modes and secret redaction.
- Per-request enablement, keys, and context windows, including mixed watermarked and unwatermarked batches.
- Opt-in dual-key selection with a deterministic per-context coin and matching detector views; single-key behavior is unchanged when key B is absent.
- Verified normal decode plus NGRAM, EAGLE, EAGLE3, and NEXTN, including TP2/TP4 and DP2/TP2 normal/NEXTN service gates.
- An in-tree `WatermarkDetector` that also works as a copied package without SGLang or PyTorch, plus a reference HTTP detection server that uses the same `--watermark-config`.
- Repeated-context loop prevention, greedy bypass, fused normal/speculative state kernels, and a host-gated path that launches no watermark kernels for fully disabled batches.
- Fail-closed admission for unsupported modes, including DFLASH/DSPARK, pipeline-parallel speculation, rejection-sampling speculation, beam search, PD disaggregation, custom logit processors, and non-CUDA devices.

## Performance and evidence

Relative results are within-engine ON/OFF comparisons. Finite-top-k and speculative rows use random 1,024/512 requests, c8, temperature 0.8, top-p 0.95, top-k 20, 10 warmups, 100 measured requests, and three repetitions unless noted.

| Workload | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Qwen3-8B, GSM8K-100 (sgl-eval) | 95-97% accuracy / 100% stop across normal decode (B200), NGRAM with `--disable-overlap-schedule` (H200), and EAGLE3; detection ON p=`1.09e-20` to `4.18e-27`, OFF p=`0.325-0.995`; greedy stopped safely in every gate |
| Qwen3-8B H200, no spec, finite top-k, c1 / c8 | Output throughput `+0.13% / +0.02%` (run-to-run noise) |
| Qwen3-8B GB300, no spec, unlimited top-k, c8 | `224.88 → 212.84` output tok/s per stream (`−5.35%`) |
| Qwen3.5-9B GB300 TP2, NEXTN 3/1/4 | TPOT `2.246 → 2.451 ms` (`+9.17%`); final-head same-pair spot check `+8.92%` |
| Capability enabled, fully disabled EAGLE3 traffic | TPOT `2.465 → 2.469 ms` versus merge-base (`+0.14%`) |
| Dual key versus single key, GB300 | Output throughput `−0.21%` c1 / `−1.50%` c8, within repetition variance |
| Speculative accept length | `2.759 → 2.783` (`+0.85%`) |

The DP2/TP2 gate used Qwen3-8B on two H200 GPUs: GSM8K-100 was 95% with 100% stop, both ranks detected at p=`1.84e-23`, disabled controls were p=`0.358`, repeated one-rank-idle batches remained healthy, and a DP2/TP2 NEXTN smoke detected at p=`2.14e-36` on both ranks.

## Cross-engine reference

Compare each engine's within-engine ON/OFF delta rather than absolute throughput.

| Workload | SGLang | vLLM nightly |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen3.5-9B MTP, TP2 GB300, c8, top-k 20 | TPOT `+9.17%`; accept length `+0.85%` | `dual_key_gumbel`: TPOT `+14.24%`; accept length `+0.72%` |
| Qwen3-8B H200, no spec, top-k 20, c1 / c8 | Output throughput `+0.13% / +0.02%` | Plain Gumbel: `−1.70% / −2.11%` |

## Limitations

- Temperature 0 carries no signal. Short or low-entropy spans are weaker, and `max_probability` trades signal for ordinary sampling at low-entropy positions.
- Paraphrase and translation erase the signal; edits reduce the number of usable contexts.
- Murmur32 is a keyed, non-cryptographic mix. Key holders can both detect and forge; inline `--watermark-config` JSON is process-visible, and core dumps may contain in-memory keys.
- Unlimited top-k requires a full-vocabulary sort and measured `−2.8%` to `−7.2%` per-stream throughput; finite `top_k=20` was within noise. Unlimited-top-k speculative verification uses the slower tensor path.
- Watermarking stops after `min(4,096, per-request token-pool capacity)` admitted contexts. Runtime uses 32-bit context-hash admission while the detector deduplicates exact tuples; rare collisions and conservative sibling suppression only dilute signal.
- Speculative cost and acceptance are model- and workload-dependent, especially for top-k-1 draft chains, although the public NEXTN/EAGLE3 measurements above preserved acceptance.

The in-tree [`watermarking/README.md`](https://github.com/JustinTong0323/sglang/blob/watermark/python/sglang/srt/sampling/watermarking/README.md) is the design reference. Evaluation results remain in **Performance and evidence** and **Cross-engine reference** above. Configuration, request semantics, the normative detector contract, standalone use, and the compatibility matrix are in the [`text_watermarking.mdx` operator guide](https://github.com/JustinTong0323/sglang/blob/watermark/docs/docs/advanced_features/text_watermarking.mdx).

Co-authored-by: Nihar Patel <nihpat95@gmail.com>

## Test plan

CUDA selector/state parity suites, OpenAI endpoint e2e, the Rust `wire.rs` schema test, registry entries in `test_parity.py` and `test_model_overrides.py`, full changed-file pre-commit/taxonomy checks, and public-model GSM8K/detection/greedy/speculative/TP/DP service gates.

title: [ROCm] Make DSA indexer top-k exact with cooperative selection
author: jiejingzhangamd
body:
## Summary

- add a ROCm-specific cooperative top-k implementation for the three DSA indexer entry points
- use an fp32 coarse histogram, exact radix tie refinement, and an overflow rescan
- split long rows across blocks when a low batch size would otherwise leave the GPU underutilized
- preserve the raw, paged, and ragged interfaces and guard launches to the score device
- keep the CUDA implementation unchanged; ROCm tracks the native `topk.hip` source and does not hipify `topk.cu`

## Motivation

The previous ROCm path used `topk.hip` generated by hipifying `topk.cu`. Its fp16 coarse key can collapse a large part of a real indexer row into one bucket, and overflowing the candidate buffer can silently drop valid winners. On captured GLM-5.2 logits, selected-value recall fell as low as 0.53.

The new native HIP kernel keeps the selection exact by refining the full fp32 key and rescanning the row when the tie buffer overflows. It reaches 1.0 selected-value recall against `torch.topk` on the same inputs.

## Performance vs. the original `topk.hip`

Baseline `old generated` is the original ROCm `topk.hip` produced from `topk.cu`, rebuilt from xiaobochen-amd/sglang `main` at [`92562f066`](https://github.com/xiaobochen-amd/sglang/commit/92562f0660b1c05d2de5b823e8b471be8def44cd). `new native` is the tracked `topk.hip` in this PR. Measurements are on MI355X (gfx950), graph replay, width 131,072, 100,500 live positions, top-k 2,048, page size 1. Times are microseconds per call; lower is better.

```
distribution  batch   old generated   new native   speedup
tiny              1            95.2         31.6      3.02x
tiny              2            95.5         30.0      3.18x
tiny              4            95.6         31.2      3.06x
tiny              8            96.0         31.4      3.06x
tiny             14            95.8         32.7      2.93x
tiny             32            96.3         36.9      2.61x
tiny             64            98.4         48.1      2.04x
tiny            128           119.9         58.5      2.05x
tiny            256           121.9         62.7      1.94x

diffuse           1            54.3         31.6      1.72x
diffuse           2            55.1         30.9      1.78x
diffuse           4            55.5         31.5      1.76x
diffuse           8            56.7         31.7      1.79x
diffuse          14            56.4         33.1      1.70x
diffuse          32            56.3         36.6      1.54x
diffuse          64            77.3         49.4      1.56x
diffuse         128            96.7         59.1      1.64x
diffuse         256           103.4         63.2      1.64x

clustered         1           160.9        102.2      1.57x
clustered         2           161.6        101.0      1.60x
clustered         4           161.8        102.1      1.59x
clustered         8           162.1        103.4      1.57x
clustered        14           162.0        104.9      1.54x
clustered        32           162.7        111.4      1.46x
clustered        64           162.6        122.9      1.32x
clustered       128           185.9        169.0      1.10x
clustered       256           186.9        174.2      1.07x
```

On captured GLM-5.2 decode shapes, row splitting gives a further 2.1-2.8x speedup over the original generated kernel.

## Comparison with `topk_v2`

This is a same-run comparison against the current JIT [`topk_v2.cuh`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/python/sglang/kernels/jit/csrc/deepseek_v4/topk_v2.cuh) on MI355X (gfx950). Both kernels use graph replay, width 131,072, 100,500 live positions, top-k 2,048, and page size 1. Times are microseconds per call; lower is better.

### GLM-5 ROCm shape and score distribution

The synthetic sweep uses a GLM-5 long-context decode-like shape: float32 scores `[B, 131072]`, live length 100,500, top-k 2,048, and a page-size-1 transform, with `B` swept from 1 to 256. Separate logits captured from an actual GLM-5.2-MXFP4 ROCm decode had 20 score rows per call and live context up to 134,849 tokens.

The real captured scores were approximately 0.04-180, not tiny `1e-16` values. They were nevertheless highly concentrated under the fp16 coarse key: an 8-bit fp16 key populated only 4-126 bins, and the largest bin held 6%-88% of a row. Whether the top-2,048 boundary landed inside that dominant bin varied by call.

The sweep distributions should therefore be read as follows:

- `diffuse`: broad random control; less concentrated than captured GLM-5 logits.
- `tiny`: scale-invariance stress (`1e-16 * randn`); not the literal GLM-5 value range.
- `clustered`: single-bin-style overflow stress; more concentrated than typical captures.

Real GLM-5 lies between `diffuse` and the synthetic `clustered` case in coarse-bin concentration. The actual captures are the reason candidate-buffer overflow must remain exact, while `tiny` separately verifies that fp16 conversion cannot erase score ordering.

```
distribution  batch   native topk.hip   topk_v2
tiny              1              31.5       73.1
tiny              2              30.1       73.2
tiny              4              30.8       73.1
tiny              8              30.9       73.2
tiny             14              32.5       73.2
tiny             32              37.1       73.3
tiny             64              48.8       73.3
tiny            128              58.7       74.6
tiny            256              63.2       76.1

diffuse           1              31.9       34.2
diffuse           2              31.0       34.2
diffuse           4              31.3       34.5
diffuse           8              31.6       34.5
diffuse          14              33.1       34.7
diffuse          32              36.6       35.1
diffuse          64              49.5       38.1
diffuse         128              59.2       39.6
diffuse         256              62.9       46.5

clustered         1             102.2      109.2
clustered         2             101.0      109.4
clustered         4             102.2      109.5
clustered         8             103.1      109.6
clustered        14             105.1      109.6
clustered        32             111.1      109.6
clustered        64             122.9      109.9
clustered       128             168.9      110.6
clustered       256             174.5      111.0
```

For tiny scores, the native HIP kernel is 1.20-2.43x faster. On diffuse scores it is 1.05-1.10x faster through batch 14, while `topk_v2` becomes 1.04-1.49x faster from batch 32 onward. For shorter diffuse rows (4K-65K live positions), `topk_v2` is 1.24-2.96x faster because its register and one-block streaming paths avoid the native kernel's row-split launch overhead.

Correctness is not equivalent. `topk_v2` uses an fp16 coarse histogram and caps the threshold-bin candidate buffer at 2,048 without an overflow rescan. Selected-value multiset recall against `torch.topk` at batch 1 is:

```
distribution   native topk.hip   topk_v2
tiny                    1.0000     0.0420
diffuse                 1.0000     1.0000
clustered               1.0000     0.0220
```

Therefore the apparent `topk_v2` advantage on high-batch clustered inputs is not a valid like-for-like speedup: it does not return the exact top-k on that distribution. The native HIP kernel rescans the row when the candidate buffer overflows and remains exact.

## Test plan

- [x] ROCm `sgl-kernel` build for gfx950 using the tracked native `topk.hip`
- [x] `pytest python/sglang/kernels/aot/tests/test_topk.py -q` - 161 passed
- [x] pre-commit checks on all changed files
- [x] mixed-device launch and rejection coverage
- [x] both one-block and row-split paths

title: [Perf] diffusion: Accumulate chunked LoRA merges with addmm
author: Levius-Fubuki
body:
## Purpose

The 2D diffusion LoRA merge path currently materializes `B @ A` for every chunk and then launches a separate in-place add. At the configured 32 MiB chunk limit, this creates a large temporary allocation and an additional kernel launch.

This PR:

- uses `Tensor.addmm_` to accumulate each 2D LoRA product directly into the base weight;
- preserves the existing chunk-size and scaling policies, including ordered multi-adapter accumulation;
- adds coverage for FP32/FP16/BF16, contiguous and transposed non-contiguous tensors, negative strength, `alpha / rank` scaling, and forced multi-chunk execution;
- checks in a standalone CUDA microbenchmark that validates numerical parity before measuring latency and peak allocation.

This does not change LoRA loading, merge precision policy, stacked/greater-than-2D fallback behavior, non-tensor handling, or model-specific behavior. It uses a standard PyTorch matrix primitive with no device or compute-capability branch, consistent with the torch-native LoRA optimization merged in #20562.

## Test Plan

### LoRA regression tests

python -m pytest -q \
  python/sglang/multimodal_gen/test/unit/test_lora_inference_mode.py \

  python/sglang/multimodal_gen/test/unit/test_fused_lora_compose.py \

```

```

### RTX 4090 operator benchmark

  --warmups 50 --repetitions 500 \
  --output /tmp/lora-merge-addmm.csv \
  --profile-output /tmp/lora-merge-addmm-profiler.txt
```

Hardware/software: NVIDIA RTX 4090 (SM89), driver 595.71.05, CUDA 13.0, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130. No configuration changes.

Each of 30 dtype/shape/rank cases ran seven alternating-order rounds. The table shows representative paired medians; latency is in microseconds and allocation is the extra PyTorch peak during one merge.

| Dtype | Shape | Rank | Scale | Old / New (us) | Speedup | Old / New allocation | Max abs diff |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| BF16 | 320x320 | 4 | 1.0 | 29.805 / 20.484 | 1.455x | 0.20 / 0 MiB | 0 |
| BF16 | 4096x4096 | 32 | -0.5 | 42.408 / 21.207 | 2.000x | 32 / 0 MiB | 1.53e-5 |
| BF16 | 12288x4096 | 64 | 1.0 | 428.542 / 225.182 | 1.903x | 64 / 0 MiB | 3.05e-5 |
| FP16 | 4096x4096 | 32 | -0.5 | 42.899 / 21.074 | 2.036x | 32 / 0 MiB | 3.81e-6 |
| FP32 | 1280x1280 | 8 | 1.0 | 29.098 / 23.919 | 1.217x | 6.25 / 0 MiB | 9.31e-10 |
| FP32 | 12288x4096 | 4 | 0.25 | 1284.776 / 484.248 | 2.653x | 64 / 0 MiB | 4.66e-10 |

Across all 30 cases:

- geometric-mean speedup: `1.695x`
- minimum case speedup: `1.217x`
- maximum case speedup: `2.653x`
- regressed cases: `0/30`
- candidate extra peak allocation: `0` bytes in every case
- maximum old/new difference: BF16 `3.05e-5`, FP16 `3.81e-6`, FP32 `9.31e-10`

The profiler changes the hot-path operator sequence from `matmul/mm + add_` to `addmm_`.

`torch.compile`, CUDA Graph replay, and concurrency scaling are not applicable: this helper is decorated with `@torch.no_grad()` and runs while loading or merging adapters, outside the compiled model forward and serving request path. The claim is limited to merge latency and temporary allocation, not end-to-end generation throughput.

title: [AMD][DSv4] Fuse the DSv4 FP4 indexer prefill-schedule preamble into one kernel
author: heachary
body: ## Motivation The FP4 indexer (#37353) builds its persistent-grid schedule with a torch-op preamble that runs once per C4 layer. Every op touches only a few hundred elements, so the whole block is launch latency bound. On a DeepSeek-V4-Pro 128k/1k conc-64 DP8TP8 MTP trace (MI355X) that is **33 dispatches and 146 us per layer per step.** These 33 kernels can be fused into a single kernel. ## Trace results ### Before ### After The trace shows all 33 kernels being fused into a single kernel. ## Summary of changes Adds `python/sglang/kernels/ops/attention/dsv4/fp4_indexer_schedule_hip.py`, which collapses the preamble into a single Triton kernel. Everything it computes is a reduction or a scan over the row count; the only real dependency is that AITER's `_prefill_cta_info_kernel` needs the finished prefix sums, so the schedule now costs two dispatches instead of 33. - **Split-factor search.** AITER picks the smallest `s` with `sum_i ceil(chunks_i / s) <= P` by materialising an `[s_max, T]` tensor and extracting the first feasible index arithmetically (~18 of the 27 ops). That sum is monotonically non-increasing in `s`, so a binary search over `s` returns the identical answer in registers, with no intermediate tensor. - **Page-table pad** is one kernel that writes every output element, so the destination no longer needs pre-zeroing. - **`row_to_batch` / `local_starts`** are emitted in-kernel â sglang always schedules one row per query token over its whole window. - **Pinned `cta_info`** lets the logits kernel skip its `-inf` pre-fill, the same way the existing workspace path already does: the length-aware top-k only reads `[0, c4_seq_len)`, which is always covered by a CTA. - Rows past `MAX_FUSED_ROWS` (one row per lane) keep AITER's preamble â a prefill that wide is compute-bound and does not care about ~30 extra launches. No new flags; active whenever `--enable-deepseek-v4-fp4-indexer` is on (HIP). ## Accuracy GSM8k (1319 questions, DP8TP8 + MTP + FP4 indexer): 0.940 / 0.920 before, 0.948 / 0.931 after. ## Performance ### Fixed length isl/osl = 8k1k, conc=4/64, mtp=on, image = lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:v0.5.18-rocm720-mi35x-20260902 | Concurrency | Output Throughput â baseline (tok/s) | Output Throughput â fusions (tok/s) | Delta | |---|---|---|---| | 4 | 311.66 | 359.43 | +15.3% | | 64 | 2592.46 | 2677.55 | +3.3% | The launch latency bound kernels are a fixed cost and the benefits of fusing them are more pronounced at lower latencies. ### Agent-X conc64, mtp=on, image = lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:v0.5.18-rocm720-mi35x-20260902 | Config | Throughput per GPU (tok/s) | p50 ITL (ms) | Mean accept length | Decode step (ms) | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | baseline | 20295 | 32.36 | 2.48 | 85.0 | | fp4_indexer_fusion | 20752 | 31.27 | 2.49 | 82.5 | ~3% improvement in decode step time --- ### CI States Latest PR Test (Base): :hourglass_flowing_sand: [Run #33844863732](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/33844863732) Latest PR Test (Extra): :x: [Run #33844863368](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/33844863368) Latest PR Test (AMD ROCm 7.2): :hourglass_flowing_sand: [Run #33844863663](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/33844863663)

title: [HiSparse] Add speculative decoding support with multi-step KV cache swapping
author: huangtingwei9988
body:
## Prerequisite

- Kernel implementation #32162 provides the multi-step gather/commit swap kernel, including cross-step miss deduplication, extra-page lookup, scratch-space management, cache commit, and device-location resolution. This PR focuses on integrating that kernel into the SGLang serving path.

## Motivation

This PR adds end-to-end HiSparse support for multi-step speculative decoding, currently targeting linear EAGLE/MTP decoding with multiple draft tokens. It integrates the multi-step swap kernel from #32162 into the HiSparse coordinator and speculative-decoding lifecycle, covering logical target-slot reservation, per-layer scratch and cache state, verify preparation, accepted-token commit, host backup, and request cleanup. Draft KV remains in its logical GPU address space instead of reusing the HiSparse target KV physical mapping, while the target KV continues to use HiSparse host/device placement. The PR also preserves speculative state when requests transition through HiSparse staging and, for Mooncake PD serving, carries separate target host/physical page indices and draft logical-device page indices. Together, these changes make HiSparse compatible with multi-step speculative decoding without falling back to sequential per-step LRU swapping.


## Accuracy Tests

- Model: GLM-5.2-W4AFP8
- Serving topology: 1P1D, TP8/DP8 with DP Attention
- KV cache: FP8
- Speculative decoding: EAGLE, 3 steps, top-k 1, 4 draft tokens
- CUDA Graph: enabled
- HiSparse: top-k 2048, 4096-slot device buffer, host/device ratio 4
- The only A/B variable was whether HiSparse was enabled.

|---|---:|---:|---:|
| GSM8K 20-shot (200 samples) | 195/200 (97.50%) | 192/200 (96.00%) | +1.50 pp |
| GPQA-Diamond (198 samples) | 180/198 (90.91%) | 182/198 (91.92%) | -1.01 pp |

title: [ROCm][DSV4] Enable breakable CUDA graph prefill
author: AMD-yanfeiwang
body:
## Summary

Enable breakable CUDA graph (BCG) prefill for the ROCm DeepSeek-V4 HIP radix backend.

## Changes

- Add captured-metadata support for HIP radix prefill capture and replay.
- Refresh attention, unified-KV, indexer, compressor, and FP4 workspace metadata in place.
- Preserve the existing CUDA memory-pressure guard while allowing explicit HIP BCG selection.
- Keep ROCm DSV4 mixed prefill/decode batches eager under DP attention; pure TP and other backends retain their existing replay policy.
- Pass host-proven `repeat_interleave(output_size=...)` and `extend_start_loc` metadata to avoid implicit GPU-to-host scalar synchronizations.
- Add focused coverage for capture/replay metadata, DP admission, address stability, underfilled buckets, and the no-D2H guard.

BCG remains opt-in through `--cuda-graph-backend-prefill breakable`.

### Validation

| Item | Configuration |
|---|---|
| Source | Current head `6c62e78486` |
| Hardware | 8 x MI355X, TP8 + DP8 attention, DP LM head |
| Image | `lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:v0.5.19-rocm724-mi35x-20260905` (`sha256:1951b978...121115d`) |
| Runtime | `unified_kv_triton`, full decode graphs, no speculative decoding |
| Comparison | Same node/image/source; only prefill backend differs (`disabled` vs `breakable`) |
| Method | 3 repeats per arm/point, seeds 42/43/44, `2 * concurrency` requests, exact token gates |

#### Performance

| Workload | C | Eager output tok/s | BCG output tok/s | Delta | Paired median | BCG graph-token share |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `1024 -> 1024` | 4 | 247.587 | 250.037 | +0.990% | +1.108% | 80.556% |
| `1024 -> 1024` | 8 | 485.620 | 483.977 | -0.338% | -0.482% | 12.500% |
| `1024 -> 1024` | 16* | 861.178 | 867.745 | +0.763% | +0.007% | 4.380% |
| `1024 -> 1024` | 32 | 1,548.698 | 1,532.551 | -1.043% | -0.557% | 2.326% |
| `1024 -> 1024` | 64 | 2,606.849 | 2,649.817 | +1.648% | +0.427% | 1.205% |
| `8192 -> 1024` | 32 | 1,262.841 | 1,245.668 | -1.360% | -0.119% | 19.718% |
| `8192 -> 1024` | 128 | 2,613.743 | 2,649.922 | +1.384% | +0.053% | 5.412% |

\* C16 uses the stable follow-up (eager/BCG CV `0.677% / 0.577%`); the first pass had 7.709% eager CV and was excluded from interpretation.

| Signal | Result |
|---|---|
| Highest-admission point (1K, C4) | TTFT `282.634 -> 188.345 ms` (-33.361%); output throughput +0.990% |
| Stable C16 follow-up | Output +0.763%, but same-seed paired median +0.007%: throughput-neutral |
| Production-like 8K | C32/C128 paired medians -0.119% / +0.053%: throughput-neutral |
| Admission policy | Zero graph records with running decode requests; DP-attention `MIXED` remains eager |
| Ready-state memory | BCG +0.943 GiB/GPU versus eager |
| Recommendation | Keep BCG opt-in; no material aggregate throughput regression or broad throughput-win claim |

#### Isolated prefill latency (earlier-image controls)

Pure-TP8 controls on `1e8531972` with the `20260904` image isolate graph replay from DP `MIXED` traffic:

| `1024 -> 64`, C1 (10 repeats) | Eager | BCG | Delta |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Output throughput | 74.817 tok/s | 81.987 tok/s | +9.584% |
| TTFT | 146.219 ms | 73.194 ms | -49.942% |
| E2E | 850.839 ms | 777.850 ms | -8.579% |

With receive coalescing and `[1K, 2K, 4K, 8K]` buckets, graph-token admission reached 100%:

| Workload / metric | C1 | C4 | C8 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `1024 -> 64` output-throughput delta | +8.935% | +0.346% | -0.534% |
| `1024 -> 1` request-throughput delta | +74.298% | +1.167% | +0.440% |
| `1024 -> 1` TTFT (eager -> BCG) | 164.864 -> 92.969 ms | 196.895 -> 194.525 ms | 320.755 -> 321.345 ms |

#### Correctness

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| Focused tests | 20 tests + 2 subtests passed |
| Primary performance samples | 42/42 completed exact request/input/output totals |
| Cold/warm all-rank parity | 64/64 eager/BCG pairs: exact 64-token completion, text, and token IDs across DP0-DP7 |
| Server health | 3/3 lifecycles exited 0; no post-ready HTTP 500, traceback, runtime error, or OOM |

### AgentX validation: DSpark + HiCache, eager vs breakable prefill CUDA graph

#### Requirements

- **Depends on #39007.** It adds `record_stream_for_v2_verify` / `record_stream_each` to the DSpark verify path; without it the target-verify tensors are not stream-lifetime-safe.
- **ROCm requires `SGLANG_ENABLE_WAR_BARRIER=1`.** The scheduler sets `_war_barrier_enabled = is_cuda() or SGLANG_ENABLE_WAR_BARRIER`, and `is_cuda()` is False on ROCm builds (`torch.version.cuda is None`), so the WAR barrier is on by default on NVIDIA but **off by default on ROCm**. It must be set explicitly on MI355X.

#### Setup

1× MI355X TP8, DeepSeek-V4 DSpark (66-shard), SGLang `v0.5.19-rocm724-mi35x-20260913`. AgentX `inferencex-agentx-mvp`, dataset `semianalysis_cc_traces_weka_062126`, 3600 s/point, seed 42, HiCache ratio 2.75, `mem-fraction-static` 0.85.
Controlled variable: `--cuda-graph-backend-prefill disabled|breakable`.

#### Throughput (breakable vs disabled)

| Concurrency | Output tok/s (eager → BCG) | Δ | Requests |

| 32 | **-2.98%** (p=0.018) | **-2.56%** (p<0.001) | **-5.02%** (p<0.001) |
| 48 | **-10.15%** (p<0.001) | **-4.02%** (p<0.001) | **-9.76%** (p<0.001) |


#### Prefill CUDA graph activity

| Concurrency | eager | breakable |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 16 | 0 | 709 |
| 32 | 0 | 1058 |
| 48 | 0 | 1243 |

## References

- #27833: generic ROCm BCG support.
- #27380: ROCm DSV4 unified-KV backend.

title: [AMD] Enable GLM DSA prefill top-k to the v2 kernel
author: EricKing626
body: ## Motivation **Add a packed-row top-k kernel to the DSA top-k v2 family and route GLM-5.x prefill through it. The prefill top-k kernel drops ~66% per launch; at ISL 70000 / OSL 300 that is +4.9% token throughput per GPU, −3.5% median TPOT and −4.8% median TTFT (geomean over concurrency 4-64); GSM8k 0.937 against 0.935 on the baseline.** PR #36684 and PR #36851 brought the v2 fused top-k to GLM-5.x on ROCm, but only decode ever reached it; prefill stayed on the legacy fused transform, which gathers the wide `page_size=1` table. The blocker was addressing, not math. The paged v2 entry assumes each row starts at column 0 of its own score row and owns one page-table row. DSA extend breaks both: all requests share one packed score buffer, so a row starts at some column in the middle, and every row of a request reads the same page-table row. Two lookup tables fix that, with no copy of the score buffer and no per-row page table, which at 327K context would be hundreds of MB per forward. The layout gets its own kernel because prefill row lengths vary within a launch: the level (register-2 / register-4 / streaming) has to be chosen per row at runtime, which the paged kernel, sized once off `max_seq_len`, cannot do. The packed entry also needs no `topk_v2_plan`, no cluster path and no compile-time level. ## Modifications **`topk_v2.cuh`** -- add `TopKPackedParams` and `topk_packed_kernel` next to `topk_ragged_kernel`, plus the `TopKKernel::transform_packed` host entry. Addressing, against the paged layout: | | paged entry (decode layout) | `transform_packed` (extend layout) | | --- | --- | --- | | score window of row `i` | `scores[i, :seq_lens[i]]` | `scores[i, row_starts[i] : row_starts[i] + seq_lens[i]]` | | page-table row | `page_tables[i]` | `page_tables[row_to_batch[i]]`, identity when `row_to_batch` is null | `row_starts` is required, `row_to_batch` optional. Shifting the score pointer keeps the selected index row-local, so the output path is untouched; the page-table row count must match the score row count only when `row_to_batch` is absent. Vector loads need the read base on a 4-float boundary, so the kernel rounds `row_starts[i]` down and masks the <= 3 columns ahead of the window in place. The level is then picked from the widened length, which keeps a row of exactly 8192 with a 3-column residue out of the register-2 implementation. Kernel, host entry and wrapper registration are behind `USE_ROCM`: only the ROCm DSA prefill emits this layout, and CUDA gets the same fusion from the ragged path. **`dsv4/topk.py`** -- register the `topk_transform_packed` wrapper when `is_hip_runtime()`, and add `topk_transform_packed_v2(scores, seq_lens, page_tables, out_page_indices, page_size, *, row_starts, row_to_batch=None)`. **`dsa/dsa_topk_backend.py`** -- route packed PAGED extend to `_topk_transform_v2_packed`, passing `ks` as `row_starts`. The row -> request map arrives whole-forward as `token_to_batch_idx` or per row-chunk as `batch_idx_list`, and both take this path: since #36960 capped the MQA-logits budget at aiter's 2 GiB `buffer_store` limit, a 70K prefill splits its rows on every forward but a request's first chunk, so routing only the whole-forward shape left 126 of 147 launches in a 70K trace on the legacy kernel (fixed by a6d769e). Two shapes fall back, checked in the dispatch so they do not trip the helper's asserts: a row stride that is not a multiple of 4, which the vectorized load needs and which an extend stride -- the batch's total KV length -- only satisfies by luck, and a `batch_idx_list` that is not a per-row tensor. The decode condition is left byte-identical, because `dsa_drop_wide_page_table` keys off exactly that condition. **`test_topk_v2.py`** -- `test_topk_v2_packed_rows` packs several requests into one score buffer, each with its own page-table permutation so a row/request mix-up cannot pass, and checks a row-local `torch.topk` reference; `test_topk_v2_packed_level_boundary` covers rows of exactly 8192 and 16384 with a 1-3 column masked residue, the case that overflows a register implementation if the level is picked from the un-widened length. ## Accuracy Tests GSM8k, 8x MI355X (gfx950), GLM-5.2-MXFP4, TP=4, non-MTP: ``` $ python3 benchmark/gsm8k/bench_sglang.py --port 8000 --num-questions 1200 --parallel 1200 baseline: Accuracy: 0.935 Invalid: 0.000 this PR: Accuracy: 0.937 Invalid: 0.000 ``` `test/registered/kernels/ops/attention/test_topk_v2.py` on gfx950: `300 passed`, including the 12 new packed cases. GSM8k prefills in one chunk, so the chunked route is covered separately: four concurrent ~78K-token prompts, three embedded access codes each, retrieved 12/12 with no cross-request leakage. Rows in those forwards span several requests, which is what `row_to_batch` addresses. ## Speed Tests and Profiling Baseline is main as merged (top-k v2 on, prefill still legacy); this PR is the prefill routing on top of it. Same build, same flags, non-MTP, 8x MI355X, TP4, `--max-running-requests 8`. **Kernel-level** -- prefill now launches `topk_packed_kernel`, which this series ran as `sglang::topk_main_kernel` up to 4bbbd19, while the packed addressing still lived in `TopKPagedParams`. It replaces `coop_topk_kernel`, the name ROCm traces show for the legacy transform since #37591 replaced the hipified source with a native one (`topk_transform_prefill_kernel` on CUDA), which is gone from the traces entirely. ISL 70000 / OSL 300 at concurrency 4, TP rank 0, same seed, grouped by launch grid (one block per score row): | grid.x | baseline | this PR | Δ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 16384 | 896.8 µs/launch | 319.7 µs/launch | **−64.3%** | | 16383 | 1972.3 µs/launch | 649.1 µs/launch | **−67.1%** | | 10922 | 1679.8 µs/launch | 568.6 µs/launch | **−66.2%** | | 8191 | 1644.5 µs/launch | 570.5 µs/launch | **−65.3%** | | 5462 | 955.1 µs/launch | 315.4 µs/launch | **−67.0%** | Per rank over the profiled window (4 extend steps): 185.3 ms → 63.8 ms of top-k, against 2.8 s of extend kernel time. **End-to-end** -- ISL 70000 / OSL 300. Geomeans are over the per-config ratios. | conc | Interactivity (tok/s/user) | Token TPUT per GPU (tok/s) | Δ TPUT | Median TTFT (ms) | Median TPOT (ms) | Median ITL (ms) | | --- | --- | --- | ---: | --- | --- | --- | | 4 | 29.34 → 30.35 | 4573.4 → 4761.6 | +4.1% | 3276 → 3128 | 34.08 → 32.95 | 10.63 → 10.52 | | 8 | 14.13 → 15.08 | 4938.7 → 5139.9 | +4.1% | 5774 → 5646 | 70.77 → 66.33 | 12.28 → 12.24 | | 16 | 12.44 → 13.08 | 5064.3 → 5296.6 | +4.6% | 27576 → 26563 | 80.38 → 76.43 | 12.21 → 11.99 | | 32 | 12.94 → 13.06 | 5004.1 → 5301.0 | +5.9% | 79535 → 74147 | 77.25 → 76.57 | 12.20 → 12.30 | | 64 | 12.72 → 13.00 | 4996.4 → 5297.1 | +6.0% | 181367 → 169622 | 78.60 → 76.91 | 12.11 → 12.01 | | **geomean** | **+3.7%** | | **+4.9%** | **−4.8%** | **−3.5%** | not claimed | Interactivity is `1000 / median TPOT`; Token TPUT per GPU is `(input + output) tok/s / 4` for one TP4 server. Concurrency above 8 exceeds the admission cap, so TTFT there is mostly queueing time. That sweep was measured on a branch based before #36960, so its prefill never split the MQA logits. Concurrency 4 was re-measured on current main with the final kernel and the chunked route, two runs per arm, and reproduces it: token TPUT per GPU 4491.4 / 4491.9 → 4733.1 / 4729.0 (**+5.3%** against the better baseline run), median TTFT 3302 / 3037 → 2846 / 2852 ms, median TPOT 37.65 / 34.75 → 33.35 / 33.38 ms, median E2E 14234 / 14240 → 13559 / 13565 ms. Reproduce: ```bash export SGLANG_ROCM_FUSED_DECODE_MLA=0 export ROCM_QUICK_REDUCE_QUANTIZATION=INT4 # FP4 model # On ROCm the DeepSeek-DSA hook leaves top-k v2 off unless it is set explicitly # (arg_groups/model_hook.py), and this path is unreachable without it. export SGLANG_OPT_USE_TOPK_V2=1 python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model GLM-5.2-MXFP4 \ --tp 4 --trust-remote-code --tool-call-parser glm47 --reasoning-parser glm45 \ --mem-fraction-static 0.85 --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 \ --disable-radix-cache --chunked-prefill-size 16384 \ --dsa-prefill-backend triton --dsa-decode-backend triton \ --enable-aiter-allreduce-fusion --tokenizer-worker-num 8 \ --max-running-requests 8 python3 -m sglang.bench_serving --backend sglang --dataset-name random \ --random-input-len 70000 --random-output-len 300 --random-range-ratio 0.8 \ --max-concurrency $CONC --num-prompts $((5 * CONC)) ``` ## Checklist - [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit). - [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests). - [x] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations). - [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed). - [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance). ## Review and Merge Process 1. title: [Perf] Vectorize alloc_extend_naive to remove the per-request Python loop
author: alexnails
body:
# Vectorize `alloc_extend_naive`

## The contract

For each request `i`, `alloc_extend_naive` fills `out_indices[start_pos[i] : end_pos[i]]`
(the request's extend span) with up to three consecutive runs of KV-cache slot
indices:

1. **Finish the current partial page** — up to `num1` tokens, continuing directly
   after `last_loc[i]` (i.e. `last_loc[i] + 1, last_loc[i] + 2, ...`). This only
   exists if `prefix_lens[i]` isn't already page-aligned.
2. **Whole new pages** — `num2` tokens (a multiple of `page_size`), each new page's
   slots taken in order from `free_pages`.
3. **Start of one final new page** — `num3` tokens, the remainder from the last
   page this request touches.

`num1 + num2 + num3 == extend_lens[i]` always, and each phase is skipped when its
count is 0. This rewrite computes exactly this, with no behavioral change — it
just computes every request's phases in parallel instead of in a Python loop.

## Phase-by-phase mapping (loop -> vectorized)

The old loop, per request `i`:

```python
num1 = min(seq_lens[i], ceil(prefix_lens[i])) - prefix_lens[i]
if num1: out_indices[start_pos[i]:start_pos[i]+num1] = last_loc[i] + 1 + arange(num1)
if prefix_lens[i] + num1 == seq_lens[i]: continue
num2 = (floor(seq_lens[i]) - ceil(prefix_lens[i]))
if num2: out_indices[...] = free_pages[start_new_pages[i]:end_new_pages[i]-need_page[i]] * page_size + arange(page_size) broadcast
if prefix_lens[i] + num1 + num2 == seq_lens[i]: continue
num3 = seq_lens[i] - floor(seq_lens[i])
if num3: out_indices[end_pos[i]-num3:end_pos[i]] = free_pages[end_new_pages[i]-1] * page_size + arange(num3)
```
(`ceil(x) = ceil_div(x, page_size) * page_size`, `floor(x) = (x // page_size) * page_size`.)

The new code computes, once, for the whole batch:

- `num1 = clamp(seq_lens, max=ceil_prefix) - prefix_lens` — identical formula,
  vectorized (`min` -> `torch.clamp(..., max=...)`).
- `done_after_1 = (prefix_lens + num1) == seq_lens` — this is exactly the loop's
  first `if ... == seq_lens[i]: continue` condition, computed for every request
  instead of tested per-iteration.
- `num2 = where(done_after_1, 0, floor_seq - ceil_prefix)`,
  `num3 = where(done_after_1, 0, seq_lens - floor_seq)` — identical formulas to
  the loop's `num2`/`num3`, but masked to 0 whenever the loop would have hit
  `continue` before computing them (so a request that finishes in phase 1 never
  contributes phantom phase-2/3 tokens or page demand — this is what makes
  `pages_per_req` below match the loop's actual page consumption, not the
  unconditional `num_new_pages` formula the loop computes up front but only
  partially uses).
- `pages_per_req = num2 // page_size + (num3 > 0)`, then
  `start_new_pages`/`end_new_pages` via cumsum — same role as the loop's
  `start_new_pages[i]`/`end_new_pages[i] - need_page[i]` (for phase 2) and
  `end_new_pages[i] - 1` (for phase 3); page assignment order across the whole
  batch is unchanged because it derives from the same running total of pages
  consumed so far, now computed once as a cumsum instead of incrementally by
  the loop.

Then, per **output slot** `j` (not per request):

- `owner = torch.searchsorted(end_pos, j, right=True)` maps slot `j` to its
  owning request `i` — `end_pos` is the exclusive-cumsum of `extend_lens`, so
  this is precisely "which request's `[start_pos[i], end_pos[i])` range contains
  `j`". `local = j - start_pos[owner]` is the offset within that request's
  extend, i.e. the loop variable that ranges implicitly over
  `pos_in_page[:numK]` / `arange(numK)` inside each `if numK:` block.
- `is_phase1 = local < num1_g`, `is_phase2 = ~is_phase1 & (local < num1_g + num2_g)`,
  else phase 3 — this is exactly which of the three loop branches slot `j`
  would have landed in.
- `val_phase1 = last_loc_g + 1 + local` — identical to the loop's phase-1 RHS.
- `val_phase2 = free_pages[start_new_pages_g + (local - num1_g) // page_size] * page_size + (local - num1_g) % page_size`
  — the loop's phase-2 RHS was `(free_pages[start:end].view(-1,1) + pos_in_page.view(1,-1)).view(-1)`,
  i.e. page `(local - num1) // page_size` of the slice, offset `(local - num1) % page_size`
  within it. Same page, same offset, computed directly instead of via a 2D
  broadcast + reshape.
- `val_phase3 = free_pages[end_new_pages_g - 1] * page_size + (local - num1_g - num2_g)`
  — identical to the loop's phase-3 RHS (`free_pages[end_new_pages[i]-1]`, offset
  `local` within the final page, which is `rel3` here since `num1+num2` tokens
  were already consumed).
- `out_indices = where(is_phase1, val_phase1, where(is_phase2, val_phase2, val_phase3))`
  selects the one formula that actually applies, per slot — this replaces the
  loop's `if numK:`/`continue` control flow with a per-slot select.

## Edge cases preserved

- **Zero-length extends** (`extend_lens[i] == 0`): contributes no slots to `j`
  (its `[start_pos[i], end_pos[i])` range is empty), exactly as the old loop's
  body would do nothing meaningful for it (there are no output indices to write).
- **Prefix exactly on a page boundary** (`prefix_lens[i] % page_size == 0`):
  `ceil_prefix == prefix_lens[i]`, so `num1 = 0` and phase 1 is skipped for
  every slot of that request — same as the loop never entering its `if num1:`
  block.
- **`num1 == 0`**: `is_phase1` is `False` for all of that request's slots;
  `val_phase1` is still computed (torch.where doesn't short-circuit) but never
  selected.
- **`num2 == 0`**: `is_phase2` is `False` for all of that request's slots
  (`num1_g + num2_g == num1_g`); `val_phase2` is still computed but never
  selected.
- **Tight free-page pool** (`free_pages` sized to exactly `num_new_pages.sum()`):
  `page_idx2`/`page_idx3` land exactly in `[0, free_pages.numel()-1]` for every
  slot whose phase actually needs a page, by construction of `start_new_pages`/
  `end_new_pages` as a running cumsum over the same total.

## Two bugs this surfaced, and why the fix is a host-side shape guard

`torch.where` evaluates **both** branches for every element — unlike the loop's
`if num2:` / `if num3:`, which never touch `free_pages` at all when a phase is
absent for a given request. So `val_phase2`/`val_phase3` are computed for every
slot regardless of whether that phase is ever selected there, which means the
index expressions feeding `free_pages[...]` must be valid for *every* slot, not
just the ones where the branch is live.

A 20,000-case randomized differential test against the original loop (see
below) initially crashed with `IndexError: index is out of bounds for dimension
with size 0`. The generator explicitly includes the shapes that produce this:
every request's extend fitting entirely inside its already-partially-used page
(so `pages_per_req.sum() == 0` and, for a tight pool, `free_pages` is empty),
the same shape mixed with requests that do need real pages in the same batch,
and `page_size=1` with an empty pool. Root-caused to two instances of the same
defect:

- `page_idx2` was clamped only on the upper bound (`max=free_pages.numel()-1`),
  which is `-1` when `free_pages` is empty, and `free_pages[-1]` on an empty
  tensor raises.
- `page_idx3`, which the fix was first modeled on by analogy, had the *identical*
  defect in the other direction (`min=0`, no upper bound) — and reproducing it
  in isolation confirmed indexing an empty `free_pages` at index `0` raises just
  as much as at index `-1`. **No amount of clamping rescues an index into a
  zero-length tensor** — there is no valid index into an empty array.

The actual fix is a host-side shape guard:

```python
if free_pages.numel() == 0:
    out_indices.copy_(last_loc_g + 1 + local)
    return
```

`free_pages.numel()` is static shape metadata, not a value read off the tensor's
data — reading it costs no host<->device sync on any backend, so this doesn't
reintroduce the kind of stall the rewrite is trying to remove. The guard is
correct because **`free_pages.numel() == 0` at this call site can only mean
every request in the batch needs zero new pages** (verified below, not
assumed), in which case every output slot is phase 1 by construction and no
`free_pages` read is needed. `page_idx2`/`page_idx3` are also now defensively
`min`/`max`-clamped to `[0, free_pages.numel()-1]` for the surviving (non-empty)
path — this is a no-op for well-formed inputs (the cumsum construction already
keeps them in range), it just closes the same class of gap if that ever stops
holding.

**Verifying the invariant, not assuming it.** Both real callers of
`alloc_extend_naive` guard the call:

- `python/sglang/srt/hardware_backend/npu/allocator_npu.py` (`alloc_extend`):
  `if num_new_pages_item > len(self.free_pages): return None` before calling
  `alloc_extend_naive` with `self.free_pages` unchanged.
- `tools/sglang-simulator/.../mem_cache_allocator.py` (`_alloc_extend_cpu`):
  same pattern, `if num_new_pages > len(self.free_pages): return None`.

So by the time either caller reaches `alloc_extend_naive`, `free_pages.numel() >=
num_new_pages.sum()` always holds; `free_pages.numel() == 0` therefore implies
`num_new_pages.sum() == 0`. If a caller ever violated that contract instead
(passed a `free_pages` smaller than actually needed), **the original loop is
already broken for that input too** — confirmed directly: passing a
genuinely-too-small `free_pages` to the original raises `RuntimeError: The
expanded size of the tensor (16) must match the existing size (0)` from the
phase-2 slice-assignment shape mismatch. The new code fails differently (either
via the shape guard's now-safe path, if the whole-batch-zero case doesn't apply,
or via the same class of crash the clamps guard against), but it does not
silently produce wrong output for contract-violating input — it was never a
supported input for the old implementation either, and this PR does not try to
make it one.

## Measured speedup (CPU, `torch.set_num_threads(1)`)

| bs   | page_size=1 | page_size=16 | page_size=64 | page_size=128 |
|-----:|------------:|-------------:|-------------:|--------------:|
| 1    | 0.86x       | 1.15x        | 1.13x        | 0.94x         |
| 8    | 3.42x       | 5.20x        | 4.46x        | 4.47x         |
| 64   | 9.14x       | 12.61x       | 12.20x       | 12.89x        |
| 256  | 12.00x      | 17.24x       | 14.73x       | 16.00x        |
| 1024 | 11.52x      | 15.40x       | 13.85x       | 13.40x        |

At `bs=1` both implementations take roughly 40-55us/call and the two are within
measurement noise of each other; across repeated runs the vectorized version
came out mildly *slower* for `page_size` in `{1, 128}` (0.84x-0.94x) and mildly
*faster* for `{16, 64}` (1.09x-1.15x). Reporting this honestly rather than
rounding it into a win: there is no consistent speedup at `bs=1`, and for two of
the four page sizes tested it's a small regression. The benefit is entirely a
function of batch size — vectorizing a loop that only ever ran once doesn't pay
for the extra tensor ops it replaces it with, but by `bs=8` it's already a clear
win everywhere, growing to 9-17x by `bs=64` and beyond.

The speedup also depends strongly on **extend length**, not batch size alone,
because the two implementations scale differently: the old loop's cost is
O(batch) Python dispatch and is nearly independent of how many tokens each
request extends by, while the vectorized version's cost scales with the total
token count. Same page_size=16, varying the per-request extend length:

| extend length per request | bs=64 | bs=1024 |
|---------------------------|------:|--------:|
| 1-8 tokens (decode-like)  | 20.3x | 109.5x  |
| 32-64 tokens              | 24.5x |  47.9x  |
| 256-512 tokens (prefill-like) | 5.5x | 4.9x |

So "how much faster" has no single answer: ~5x on long prefill extends, ~100x
on large decode-shaped batches. The table above happens to sit in the middle of
that range. Quoting one headline number in either direction would misrepresent
it.

## No tests added

This PR adds no test file and modifies no test file, per the task's explicit
instruction. Exactness was instead verified out-of-band: a throwaway
randomized differential script (not part of this PR, not committed) ran
**20,000 cases** comparing `torch.equal(out_indices_old, out_indices_new)`
against the original loop implementation (copied verbatim from
`origin/main:python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/allocator/paged.py`), covering batch
sizes 1-256, page sizes `{1, 4, 16, 64, 128}`, prefix lengths including 0 and
exact multiples of `page_size`, extend lengths including 0, free-page pools
both tight (sized to exactly the demand) and slack, and — added explicitly
after the bugs above surfaced, not left to chance — the all-zero-new-pages
shape, a mixed batch of zero- and real-page requests, and `page_size=1` with an
empty pool. **0 mismatches, 0 crashes**, across all 20,000 cases, after the two
fixes described above.
