title: [AMD] Add opt-in MiniMax-M3 TP4 indexer context partitioning
author: ThomasNing
body:
## Motivation

Under TP4, MiniMax-M3's four index-query heads are split across ranks while the index-K cache is replicated. Each rank scans the full index cache for its head. This PR adds an opt-in decode path that partitions the block reads across those four ranks and scores all heads while each K tile is resident.

The measured benefit is in the **indexer chain**, including communication: at batch 32 / 128K context, latency falls from 109.84 to 41.63 µs (62.1% lower latency, 2.64× speedup). Short contexts and small batches regress, so the feature defaults off. Full-model serving gains have not been measured.

## Modifications

- Add `SGLANG_MINIMAX_M3_INDEXER_CP=1`, default `0`, for gfx950 TP4 ordinary decode with attention CP/DP size 1, four index heads, four main KV heads, dimension 128, 128-token blocks, max scoring, and top-k 16. Unsupported run configurations log a reason and retain the existing path.
- Gather existing post-RoPE queries through the attention TP communicator, then let rank `r` read blocks `r, r+4, r+8, ...` for all four heads. The cache remains replicated; this reduces read traffic, not cache capacity.
- Use Triton kernels for shard scoring, local top-16 selection per head, and final merging. Keeping 16 candidates on every shard preserves global top-16 even when all winners belong to one shard. Initial/recent block priorities and native ROCm score/ID ordering are preserved.
- Exchange packed score/ID keys through SGLang's communicator, using AITER custom all-gather when supported and the existing fallback otherwise. Keys use FP32 **bitcast views for copying**, without numeric conversion. Warm both collective paths before graph capture; merge directly from the received layout.
- Keep the implementation in two new modules with small backend/dispatch changes. Existing top-k reuse is checked first. Prefill, index-value layers, model projections, checkpoint loading, and main sparse attention retain their existing paths.
- Add a manual four-rank correctness/timing harness, reproduction instructions, and all raw timing samples under `test/manual/minimax_m3/indexer_cp/`.

The initial scope excludes speculation, TBO, HiSparse, FP8 queries, and dense sparse decode. There is no automatic batch/context crossover policy. It does not require a main-attention backend change.

## Accuracy Tests

Completed on four MI355X / gfx950 GPUs:

- **8/8 cases passed on all ranks:** BF16 and FP8 E4M3 index caches × random scores, ties, winners concentrated on one shard, and mixed lengths.
- Exact selected-ID comparisons against native SGLang and an independent FP32 PyTorch reference, including empty rows and partial blocks.
- Changed sequence lengths after graph capture, including short, partial-block, and empty rows; replay matched both references.
- All **17 timing shapes** additionally passed native-versus-CP selected-ID parity in eager execution and graph replay.
- Repository pre-commit hooks passed for all changed files. The scorer, runtime helper, and benchmark script are byte-identical to the files used for the successful GPU run.

**Validation still outstanding:** runtime feature-gate/backend dispatch through a loaded server, full-model accuracy, serving TPS/TTFT/TPOT, and measurements with the fallback collective. The harness directly invokes the indexer helper. The shape gate also accepts FP16 queries and other FP8 cache variants, which were not covered by this run.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Four MI355X GPUs, BF16 queries, FP8 E4M3 index cache, AITER custom gather available. Both gathers are included; projections and main attention are excluded. Eight indexer calls per HIP graph, 100 replays per round, seven rounds alternating baseline/CP order. Each sample uses the slowest rank; reported values are the median of seven samples.

Inputs/cache are repeatedly reused and warm, without an L2 flush or rotating-layer protocol. These are microbenchmark results and cannot be interpreted as model throughput gains.

| Context | Batch | Native TP (µs) | CP (µs) | CP latency change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 8K | 1 | 9.40 | 15.40 | +63.8% |
| 8K | 8 | 7.72 | 18.32 | +137.3% |
| 8K | 32 | 12.12 | 19.58 | +61.5% |
| 32K | 16 | 20.80 | 20.04 | -3.7% |
| 32K | 32 | 30.41 | 24.38 | -19.8% |
| 128K | 1 | 12.71 | 15.93 | +25.4% |
| 128K | 8 | 32.85 | 24.02 | -26.9% |
| 128K | 16 | 51.71 | 32.08 | -38.0% |
| 128K | 32 | 109.84 | 41.63 | -62.1% |
| One 128K row, remaining 1K | 16 | 40.76 | 27.82 | -31.7% |
| One 128K row, remaining 1K | 32 | 68.89 | 34.62 | -49.7% |

Negative latency change is an improvement. All tested 8K shapes and batches 1–2 at 128K regress. The small 32K/batch-16 gain needs independent repetition. The README contains the complete 17-shape table, runtime versions, source hashes, and the reproduction command; `results-gfx950.json` contains every round.

## Checklist

- [x] Format changed files with repository pre-commit hooks.
- [x] Add reproducible four-rank correctness and speed checks (manual GPU harness).
- [x] Document enablement, supported configurations, results, and limitations.
- [x] Provide indexer-level accuracy and speed measurements, including regressions.
- [ ] Validate full-model accuracy and serving performance with CP off/on.
- [ ] Integrate the multi-GPU checks into registered CI.

title: [ROCm] Use the fused MLA absorb + RoPE + KV-write kernel for decode-sized forward modes only
author: jiaryang
body:
## Motivation

On gfx950, `fused_fp8_bmm_rope_cat_and_cache_mla` (#38340) replaces the absorbed q BMM and the
RoPE / cat / KV-write kernel with one launch. At decode and verify sizes this is a clear win, because
neither separate kernel fills the CUs. At prefill shapes (8k tokens x 4) the two separately tuned
kernels are faster. This PR keeps the fused kernel for decode-sized forward modes and uses the
two-kernel path that main already has for EXTEND, MIXED and SPLIT_PREFILL.

## Modifications

- In `forward_absorb_rocm_prepare()` (`forward_mla_rocm.py`), the fused kernel is now also gated on
  `not forward_mode.is_extend_or_draft_extend_or_mixed()`. That is false for EXTEND, MIXED and
  SPLIT_PREFILL, so DECODE, TARGET_VERIFY and DRAFT_EXTEND_V2 keep the fused kernel. `is_extend()` is
  not used because it includes TARGET_VERIFY, which is extend-shaped but decode-sized.

No new numerical path: the prefill modes take the same two-kernel path main uses whenever the fused
kernel is not selected. CUDA graphs are captured for DECODE and TARGET_VERIFY only, so the captured
graphs still contain the fused kernel.

## Accuracy Tests

`amd/GLM-5.2-MXFP4`, MI355X TP4, GSM8K 5-shot, 3 runs:

| | main | this PR |
|---|---:|---:|
| no MTP | 0.938 | 0.929 |
| MTP (EAGLE) | 0.932 | 0.936 |

## Speed Tests and Profiling

title: [Feat] [AMD] moe: Add native GLM MXFP4 Triton Gluon backend
author: jiejingzhangamd
body:
## Motivation GLM-5.2/5.3 decode on MI355X spends a material part of each step in the MoE layer. The existing runner boundary receives already-materialized top-k IDs and weights, so a model-specific kernel cannot optimize across router projection, top-k, route sorting, expert scheduling, activation quantization, routed experts, and the shared expert. This PR adds an **explicit, strict, whole-layer Triton Gluon MoE backend** for the audited GLM Quark MXFP4 contract. Its main optimization is not a standalone faster top-k operation: the selected routes directly become the expert schedule, removing the generic `topk_ids -> moe_sorting -> expert GEMM` handoff. The backend is opt-in and fail-closed. `auto` never selects it, unsupported contracts raise before execution, and a requested Gluon path never silently falls back to AITER or another MoE runner. ## Modifications ### 1. What this adds - `gluon` as a `MoeRunnerBackend` choice. - A reusable whole-layer `GluonMoeBackend` interface with model-specific binding, eager weight preparation, execution, and output ABI validation. - A GLM-5.2/5.3 implementation for serialized Quark W4A4 MXFP4 target experts and the audited BF16 NextN expert layout on gfx950. - Shape-family kernels for decode, speculative verification, and prefill, including continuous TP4/EP1 and TP8/EP1 coverage through a 32K prefill chunk. - TP/EP-aware shared-expert handling and reuse of SGLang's existing post-expert collective/finalization path. Enable the target and speculative paths explicitly: ```bash --moe-runner-backend gluon \ --speculative-moe-runner-backend gluon ``` ### 2. Kernel design The optimized layer owns this model-specific sequence: ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph A["Current SGLang + AITER boundary"] A0["BF16 hidden states"] --> A1["router GEMM"] A1 --> A2["M x 256 logits"] A2 --> A3["biased sigmoid top-8"] A3 --> A4["dense IDs + weights"] A4 --> A5["generic moe_sorting
count, bucket, pad, publish metadata"] A5 --> A6["quantize + GEMM1 + activation + GEMM2"] A6 --> A7["shared expert + add"] end subgraph G["GLM Triton Gluon whole-layer path"] G0["BF16 hidden states"] --> G1["router projection + input quant work
co-scheduled in one launch grid"] G1 --> G2["fixed 256-expert sigmoid top-8"] G2 --> G3{"active-token family"} G3 -->|"tiny M"| G4["selection/expert CTAs share a launch;
expert CTAs recompute the needed route rank"] G3 -->|"medium M"| G5["selection directly emits expert tickets,
sorted routes, and job descriptors"] G3 -->|"large M"| G6["chunk histogram + prefix/scatter
and bucketed grouped projections"] G4 --> G7["MXFP4 experts + shared expert"] G5 --> G7 G6 --> G7 end ``` Important details: - **Tiny M:** the router uses split-K CDNA4 MFMA work to expose enough CTAs on MI355X. Selection is compile-time specialized for 256 experts/top-8. The up-projection launch consumes the selected route directly instead of waiting for a generic sort. - **Medium M:** top-k appends routes directly to expert buckets and publishes the descriptors consumed by the expert projection. - **Large M:** chunked counting, prefix/scatter, and bucketed projections cover prefill shapes. The 32K family splits large routed-partial/code buffers so every gfx950 buffer address remains below the 4-GiB window. - **Quantization:** router projection and activation quantization are independent CTAs in the same launch grid; this removes a host launch and lets both work classes occupy the device together. They are not incorrectly described as a single CTA reading the input once. - **Shared expert:** TP/EP1 target execution consumes SGLang's normal appended shared-expert representation (257 experts). EP and NextN keep the native shared expert and add it before SGLang's existing collective. The isolated measurements below show that standalone top-k is approximately tied with AITER. The useful difference is the producer/consumer boundary: ```text AITER: router -> top-k metadata -> generic MoE sort -> expert work Gluon: router/quant -> top-k becomes the expert schedule -> expert work ``` ### rocprofiler-sdk kernel decomposition To separate GPU work from Python/dispatcher/launch overhead, the full TP8/EP1 MoE call was profiled at PR HEAD `317b7156d` with rocprofiler-sdk 1.1.0 (`--kernel-trace --marker-trace --stats`). Each AITER and Gluon arm was enclosed in its own ROCTx range and repeated 100 times on MI355X. `GPU active` below is the sum of device kernel durations per call. `GPU span` is from the first kernel start to the final kernel end under tracing; its parenthesized component is time between kernels and is profiler-sensitive. The `full MoE` column retains the low-overhead HIP-event result from the table above rather than treating traced wall time as application latency. | M | Path | Kernels / layer | GPU active | Traced GPU span (inter-kernel gaps) | Full MoE, low-overhead | |---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | AITER | 15 | 60.82 us | 649.17 us (587.41 us) | 574.97 us | | 1 | Gluon | 4 | 13.47 us | 70.76 us (57.44 us) | 99.42 us | | 16 | AITER | 14 | 95.57 us | 611.47 us (516.93 us) | 543.89 us | | 16 | Gluon | 3 | 39.05 us | 63.12 us (24.06 us) | 94.34 us | | 32 | AITER | 15 | 119.22 us | 657.49 us (537.73 us) | 706.99 us | | 32 | Gluon | 5 | 64.30 us | 104.74 us (40.52 us) | 159.48 us | The exact AITER device-time decomposition is: | AITER stage | M=1 | M=16 | M=32 | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Router matmul, including BF16-to-FP32 cast where present | 2.69 us | 6.39 us | 7.78 us | | Biased grouped top-k | 4.06 us | 4.96 us | 4.89 us | | Generic route metadata sort/pad | 6.25 us | 9.72 us | 14.06 us | | Routed input quantization + scatter | 2.76 us | 4.25 us | 4.68 us | | Routed gate/up GEMM + SiLU/multiply | 18.11 us | 27.87 us | 36.77 us | | Routed activation quantization + scatter | 2.67 us | 3.02 us | 3.81 us | | Routed down GEMM | 3.82 us | 14.42 us | 19.68 us | | Shared input quantization | 2.15 us | 2.88 us | 3.34 us | | Shared gate/up GEMM, including split-K reduce | 7.90 us | 6.26 us | 7.04 us | | Shared SiLU + multiply | 3.75 us | 8.15 us | 9.15 us | | Shared activation quantization | 1.51 us | 1.96 us | 2.18 us | | Shared down GEMM | 3.43 us | 3.40 us | 3.47 us | | Routed + shared final add | 1.73 us | 2.27 us | 2.37 us | | **Total GPU active** | **60.82 us** | **95.57 us** | **119.22 us** | Gluon performs the same logical work with fused shape-specific stages: | Gluon kernel/stage | M=1 | M=16 | M=32 | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Router GEMM + routed/shared input quantization | 2.48 us | 3.25 us | 3.60 us | | Top-k scheduling + routed/shared gate/up GEMM | 5.18 us | - | - | | Top-k scheduling + routed/shared gate/up + activation quantization | - | 23.91 us | - | | Top-k to expert-job schedule | - | - | 4.61 us | | Routed/shared gate/up GEMM + activation quantization | - | - | 33.80 us | | Activation + quantization | 2.52 us | - | - | | Routed/shared down GEMM + weighted reduction | 3.30 us | 11.89 us | - | | Routed/shared down GEMM | - | - | 18.10 us | | Weighted route reduction + shared add | - | - | 4.19 us | | **Total GPU active** | **13.47 us** | **39.05 us** | **64.30 us** | This changes the interpretation of the earlier isolated timings. At `M=1`, the Gluon `_router_linear` device body is **not** slower: it takes `2.48 us` while also quantizing routed and shared inputs, versus `2.69 us` for AITER's router-only GEMM. The earlier `17-18 us` versus `8-9 us` result measured the complete launch boundary, so it exposed launcher/dispatcher latency rather than slower router arithmetic. The current small-M optimization target should therefore not be the `2.48 us` router body in isolation. ### 3. SGLang integration, isolation, and support matrix The integration sits above `MoeRunnerCore`, because that interface starts after routing has already been computed. The runtime flow is: ```text explicit Gluon selection -> validate quant/model/runtime contract -> bind GLM backend -> prepare packed weights after checkpoint load and before CUDA graph capture -> dispatch by TP/EP, target/NextN, and active M -> validate rank-local output tensor ABI -> existing SGLang _finalize_normal_output / post_experts_all_reduce ``` Isolation from other paths: - `auto` never selects Gluon; AITER, Triton, FlashInfer, MegaMoE, DeepEP, CPU, and other models retain their existing behavior. - GLM modules and Gluon kernels are imported lazily only after explicit selection. - Binding validates `model_type`, hidden/intermediate dimensions, 256 routed experts, sigmoid normalized top-8, quant ABI, gfx950, TP/EP-local shapes, shared-expert state, stream mode, A2A, EPLB, MoE DP, and routed scaling. - Quark layout preparation is owned by the selected backend; Gluon does not construct a dummy AITER runner. - Unsupported M/topology/model/quant combinations raise an actionable error. There is no native/AITER fallback from the Gluon backend. Current audited matrix: | Total TP | EP | Rank-local routed experts | Rank-local intermediate | Target/NextN M coverage | |---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 4 | 1 | 256 | 512 | 1..32768 | | 4 | 4 | 64 | 2048 | 1..16768 | | 8 | 1 | 256 | 256 | 1..32768 | | 8 | 2 | 128 | 512 | 1..16768 | | 8 | 4 | 64 | 1024 | 1..16768 | | 8 | 8 | 32 | 2048 | 1..16768 | Current model scope: - GLM-5.2/5.3 `glm_moe_dsa` target with serialized Quark W4A4 MXFP4 experts. - GLM NextN/EAGLE draft with the exact audited BF16 expert ABI. This is intentionally not a generic Gluon MoE claim. Future fixed-topology MoEs can reuse the backend boundary, but each model still needs its own strict validator, weight-layout adapter, routing semantics, kernel family, correctness comparison, and performance evidence. The most direct next extension is another GLM-family Quark MXFP4 shape; unrelated models should not be enabled by relaxing the current checks. ## Accuracy Tests ### 4. Kernel correctness - Low-M old/new Gluon schedule comparison at M=1..8: exact bitwise match. - Router/top-k isolation at M=1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128: - identical dense logits: top-8 ID match fraction `1.0`; - maximum top-k weight difference `<= 5.96e-8`; - production split-logit selector vs. dense selector: IDs match `1.0`, weights exactly equal. - EP2/EP4/EP8 compact kernels vs. rank-masked AITER at M=65,96,192,255: - all outputs finite; - relative L2 ranges: `0.004556-0.004568` (EP2), `0.004146-0.004172` (EP4), `0.003849-0.003886` (EP8); - maximum absolute error `<= 9.77e-4`. - Large-M TP8/EP1 Gluon vs. AITER at M=128..32768: relative L2 `1.81%-2.33%`, consistent with different MXFP4 quantization/accumulation order. ### 5. End-to-end correctness Current integration was exercised on GLM-5.2-MXFP4 with EAGLE/NextN, FP8 KV cache, DSA Triton attention, and CUDA graphs: | Topology / arm | Result | |---|---| | TP4/EP4, AITER vs. Gluon | 8/8 exact response texts and 8/8 exact output-token ID sequences | | TP4/EP1, AITER vs. Gluon default shared fusion | 8/8 exact texts and token IDs | | TP4/EP1, AITER vs. Gluon with `--disable-shared-experts-fusion` | 8/8 exact texts and token IDs | Logs confirm the intended shared policy on every rank (EP target/NextN native; EP1 target fused and NextN native) and contain no fallback, skipped Gluon dispatch, assertion, runtime exception, memory access fault, or GPU fault. Strict AgentX functional canaries using the InferenceX workload configuration also completed for TP8/EP2, EP4, and EP8 with target and draft Gluon enabled: 16 backend reports per topology, zero skipped dispatches, zero request/benchmark errors, and no fallback. ### 6. GSM8K **Score: `0.9437` (94.37%, 1,240/1,314 correct).** The full run completed without request errors in 896.44 s at 146.98 output tok/s. This is above the existing 0.92 MI35x GSM8K accuracy threshold used by SGLang's GLM MXFP4 accuracy coverage. Configuration: - full 1,314-question GSM8K test set, 5-shot completion prompt; - GLM-5.2-MXFP4, TP4/EP1, target + NextN Gluon; - EAGLE `3/4/1`, FP8 KV cache, Triton DSA, CUDA graph; - `--chunked-prefill-size 32768`, 256 client threads, temperature 0, maximum 512 output tokens; - strict backend: no fallback. This run also covers the TP4/EP1 large-prefill family. An initial run exposed a real coverage boundary at `M=16802`; the implementation was extended to the full 32K chunk instead of reducing the prefill chunk or hiding the shape behind a fallback. A separate strict request with exactly 32,768 prompt tokens then completed successfully (`prompt_tokens=32768`, one generated token, 8.49 s E2E) with no runtime/GPU error or fallback. ### 7. Test inventory Latest local validation on MI355X: - `72 passed` across: - `test/registered/unit/models/test_gluon_moe_backend.py` - `test/registered/unit/spec/test_draft_construction_isolation.py` - `test/registered/unit/layers/moe/test_fused_shared_expert_scaling.py` - `test/registered/unit/models/test_glm_nextn_moe_ptpc.py` - Continuous dispatch tests enumerate every integer M in each supported range and assert strict rejection immediately outside the audited ranges. - Official Ruff error selection (`F401,F821,F823,UP037`): pass. - Ruff format check over all 25 changed Python files: pass. - `git diff --check`: pass. - Full repository CI: pending; this PR is intentionally opened as Draft. ## Speed Tests and Profiling ### Microbenchmark method - AMD Instinct MI355X, one rank of TP8/EP1 unless stated otherwise. - AITER `acf8fdf9307431ece8ee275971c41cb3d1a7020b`. - PyTorch `2.9.1+rocm7.2.0.git7e1940d4`, Triton `3.8.0`. - 20 warmups, 200 timed repetitions, alternating arm order, HIP-event medians. - The AITER baseline includes SGLang's real small-M sorting patch and native shared-expert work. - Measurements were collected on equivalent pre-rebase kernel revisions; the rebased integration and 32K TP4 adapter were subsequently correctness-tested as described above. #### Route preparation decomposition (microseconds) | M | AITER router + top-k + sort | Gluon router + quant + select/schedule | Speedup | |---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | 62.16 | 32.94 | 1.89x | | 8 | 62.86 | 31.96 | 1.97x | | 16 | 61.48 | 31.90 | 1.93x | | 32 | 200.78 | 47.40 | 4.24x | | 64 | 190.74 | 52.58 | 3.63x | | 128 | 175.76 | 47.06 | 3.73x | At M=1..16, AITER's standalone router is about 2x faster and standalone top-k is approximately tied. The net win comes from eliminating the generic `moe_sorting`/handoff, which costs about 38-50 us by itself. At M>=32, Gluon also has the faster router schedule. #### Complete rank-local MoE layer (microseconds) | M | AITER | Gluon | Speedup | |---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | 574.97 | 99.42 | 5.78x | | 8 | 578.35 | 85.32 | 6.78x | | 16 | 543.89 | 94.34 | 5.77x | | 32 | 706.99 | 159.48 | 4.43x | | 64 | 670.25 | 172.78 | 3.88x | | 128 | 674.65 | 203.26 | 3.32x | A later M=1 fusion removed the standalone activation-quant launch and improved the Gluon arm from `100.80 us / 4 launches` to `81.94 us / 3 launches` (`-18.71%`, exact bitwise output). The shared MTP M=6 schedule improved its isolated layer from `121.44 us / 5 launches` to `85.86 us / 3 launches` (`-29.30%`). #### Large-M complete layer | M | Gluon | AITER | Speedup | Latency reduction | |---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 128 | 0.153 ms | 0.510 ms | 3.33x | 69.9% | | 1024 | 0.224 ms | 0.563 ms | 2.52x | 60.3% | | 8192 | 0.789 ms | 1.941 ms | 2.46x | 59.4% | | 16384 | 1.370 ms | 3.600 ms | 2.63x | 61.9% | | 32768 | 2.711 ms | 7.042 ms | 2.60x | 61.5% | rocprof confirms that the savings are not only CPU launch timing: | M | AITER launches / GPU-active time | Gluon launches / GPU-active time | |---:|---:|---:| | 1 | 15 / 60.82 us | 4 / 13.47 us (later optimized to 3 launches) | | 16 | 14 / 95.57 us | 3 / 39.05 us | | 32 | 15 / 119.22 us | 5 / 64.30 us | ### AgentX end-to-end performance TP8/EP1, GLM-5.2-MXFP4, MTP `3/4/1`, strict target+draft Gluon, 32K chunk, two-node forward/reverse A/B: Con / MTP | P90 ITV | vs 09/24 baseline | tput/chip | succ request -- | -- | -- | -- | -- C1 3/4/1 | 316.970 | +22.98% | 2338.423 | 258 C1 5/6/1 | 295.403 | +14.62% | 2304.512 | 256 C2 3/4/1 | 243.293 | +29.63% | 2555.224 | 434 C2 5/6/1 | 175.893 | -6.28% | 2419.022 | 409 ## Checklist - [x] Format changed code with Ruff and run the repository's official Ruff error selection. - [x] Add focused unit tests for backend selection, model/quant/topology contracts, shared experts, weight preparation, dispatch coverage, and strict rejection. - [x] Document the design, integration boundary, supported matrix, accuracy, and performance in this PR description. - [x] Provide kernel microbenchmarks, rocprof decomposition, end-to-end performance, and accuracy results. - [x] Follow the SGLang code-style guidance for the changed Python files. - [ ] Run full upstream CI and resolve reviewer feedback. - [ ] Re-run the MTP 5/6/1 C=1 end-to-end arm before marking ready for review. --- ### CI States Latest PR Test (Base): :white_check_mark: [Run #41178229235](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/41178229235) Latest PR Test (Extra): :x: [Run #41178229265](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/41178229265) Latest PR Test (AMD ROCm 10): :x: [Run #41178229381](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/41178229381) > [!TIP] > Base CI only covers the core cases, and its workload may not exercise your change. title: [diffusion] kernels: stop specializing on per-request sequence lengths
author: mickqian
body:
## Motivation

Triton compiles one variant of a kernel per class of each integer argument it specializes: divisible by 16, equal to 1, or neither. Sequence lengths and row counts change with the resolution, the prompt and the input image, so a request whose sizes fall into a class the server's warmup did not hit compiles kernels on the spot.

Qwen-Image-Edit shows it on the nightly's first request. The server warmup conditions on a square image, giving 8192 tokens; the nightly's 1024×704 input gives a count not divisible by 16. With a cold Triton cache (a fresh machine or container), that first request spent 1.95 s in its first denoising step against 0.34 s for later steps. The Triton cache shows what compiled during that request: the select-0/1 LayerNorm modulation kernel, its residual variant and the LayerNorm-modulate kernel, each a second variant whose TTIR signature differs from the warmup's only in `seq_len` and `stride_i_b` losing `tt.divisibility = 16`.

## Modifications

The per-request sizes of these kernels go into `do_not_specialize`:

| Kernel | Arguments |
| --- | --- |
| `_fused_layernorm_scale_shift_gate_select01_kernel`, `_fused_residual_layernorm_scale_shift_gate_select01_kernel` | `seq_len`, `stride_i_b` |
| `_fused_scale_shift_4d_kernel` | `seq_len`, `num_frames`, `frame_seqlen` |
| `fuse_scale_shift_kernel_blc_opt` | `B`, `L` |
| `_layernorm_modulate_kernel` | `seq_len`, `n_rows` |
| `_qk_ln_head_kernel` | `n_rows` |
| `_temb_table_slices_kernel` | `rows` |
| `_pack_qkv_destination_major_kernel` | `rows` |
| `_cat_pad_cl3d_kernel` (Wan VAE) | `T`, `H`, `W`, `out_t`, `out_h`, `out_w` |
| `_dup_up3d_add_kernel` (Wan VAE) | `out_t`, `out_h`, `t_offset` |

Each of these arguments only feeds a row index or a row mask, while the loads and stores vectorize along the hidden dimension (the channels, for the VAE kernels), whose size and strides stay specialized. The arithmetic is unchanged and outputs are bit-identical. `mrope.py` and `vision_rope.py` already do the same for their sequence lengths.

The Wan VAE kernels keep more of their arguments specialized: the channel count, the element total and the strides, which the channel vectorization relies on, and the per-layer padding and cache length, whose constant folding is worth 1.5% of the cat/pad kernel's time. In the channels-first traversal of the DupUp3D kernel the output width is the contiguous dimension, so it stays specialized too. With channels a multiple of 16, those arguments stay in one class at every resolution.

## Accuracy Tests

- New `test/registered/kernels/ops/diffusion/test_shape_specialization.py`: each launch runs at a length divisible by 16, then at 57 and at 1 (frames only, for the VAE kernels), and a `triton.knobs.runtime.jit_post_compile_hook` asserts that the last two compile nothing. All 11 cases fail on main and pass with this change.
- The existing tests of these kernels pass unchanged (`test_modulate.py`, `test_layernorm_modulate.py`, `test_layout.py`, `test_wan_temb_table_slices.py`), including the bitwise cat/pad, DupUp3D and chunked causal-conv tests.
- Specialized and unspecialized variants give `torch.equal` outputs on the same inputs.

## Speed Tests

H200, `triton.testing.do_bench`, production-like shapes at one length divisible by 16 and one not:

| Launch | Shape (the two lengths) | main | This PR |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| select-0/1 LN modulation | 8192 / 8152 tokens × 3072 | 51.2 / 51.0 µs | 51.3 / 50.8 µs |
| residual select-0/1 | 8192 / 8152 tokens × 3072 | 80.6 / 80.4 µs | 80.6 / 80.7 µs |
| `fuse_scale_shift_kernel` (3D) | 8192 / 8152 tokens × 3072 | 43.9 / 43.6 µs | 43.6 / 43.3 µs |
| `fuse_scale_shift_kernel` (4D) | 21 frames × 1568 / 1561 tokens × 5120 | 255.8 / 254.8 µs | 256.0 / 254.7 µs |
| LayerNorm-modulate | 4096 / 4081 tokens × 4096 | 37.9 / 38.0 µs | 38.0 / 37.8 µs |
| per-head q/k LayerNorm | 4096 / 4081 tokens × 32 heads × 128 | 61.2 / 61.3 µs | 53.9 / 53.9 µs |
| Wan temb table slices | 1568 / 1561 tokens × 5120 | 79.7 / 79.3 µs | 79.7 / 79.3 µs |
| Ulysses QKV pack | 16384 / 16377 rows × 24 heads × 128 | 148.8 / 149.1 µs | 148.8 / 148.9 µs |
| Wan cat/pad | 256 ch × 4 × 180 × 320 / 256 ch × 1 × 181 × 321 | 131.5 / 68.7 µs | 131.5 / 68.7 µs |
| Wan DupUp3D add | 512→256 ch, 2 × 90 × 160 / 1 × 91 × 161 | 133.2 / 70.7 µs | 133.1 / 71.0 µs |

The LayerNorm-modulate, q/k and Wan VAE rows come from both variants interleaved in one process: separate runs of the LayerNorm-modulate kernel drifted by up to 3.5% between processes, which the interleaved run does not show. The per-head q/k LayerNorm runs 12% faster unspecialized; every other kernel is within ±1%.

End to end, nightly harness with an empty Triton cache:

| Case | main: first / measured / extra | This PR: first / measured / extra |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `qwen_image_edit_2511` | 16.38 / 14.35 / **+2.03 s** | 14.76 / 14.39 / **+0.38 s** |
| `flux1_dev_t2i_1024` | 4.37 / 4.19 / +0.18 s | 4.40 / 4.20 / +0.20 s |
| `zimage_turbo_t2i_1024` | 0.90 / 0.69 / +0.20 s | 0.94 / 0.70 / +0.25 s |
| `wan22_ti2v_5b_720p` | 53.83 / 53.15 / **+0.68 s** | 53.32 / 53.19 / **+0.14 s** |

On main, 1.63 s of Qwen-Image-Edit's extra is its first denoising step and 0.64 s of Wan's is its first VAE decode, which recompiles 11 layout-kernel variants at 1280×720. With this PR the first denoising step is as fast as the rest, and Wan's first decode is 0.17 s slower than later ones instead of 0.64 s; Wan compiles 22 Triton variants instead of 45. FLUX.1 and Z-Image have nothing to recompile; their first-request extra sits in the output path, and most of it is the perf dump the harness requests (#41711). Measured requests are unchanged. (The Wan row comes from a second run of the harness with the final VAE change.)

title: [ROCm] GLM-5.2 decode path: decode-shaped MoE/MLA tiles, split speculative softmax, and bf16 GEMM routing
author: jiejingzhangamd
body:
> Resubmission of #40358 under @jiejingzhangamd. The original commit authorship and patch series are preserved; commit SHAs were rewritten by the requested rebase onto `05817a40c98a09021945f894b8200911df8e1ec6`.

## Motivation

Four changes on the GLM-5.2 decode path on gfx950, found by profiling a
GLM-5.2-MXFP4 TP8/EP1 server at 104k context. They are all the same shape: at
decode batch sizes these kernels leave a 256-CU part mostly idle, and none of
them is made faster by doing less arithmetic.

- two of them launch a handful of workgroups because the tile or the reduction
  was sized for a regime decode never enters;
- one spends more time in launch overhead than in work;
- one lands on torch because a tuned table keyed on `(N, K)` has no entry for
  the shape and does not fall back to a neighbour.

Together they are **+5.7%** end to end on that configuration.

## Modifications

**`moe`: fold the padded-row fill into the shared-expert append kernel.**
`_post_process_topk_ids` bracketed the aiter shared-expert append with two
separate fills over the padded region -- one for the routed ids, one for the
weights -- three launches for a shape whose total work is a couple of
microseconds, once per MoE layer per step. The append kernel already writes
every one of those elements, so it fills the padded region itself. The id fold
requires EPLB remap off, since it relies on `pad_fill_id = 0` commuting with
`remap(0) = 0`; the weight fold additionally excludes the per-rank shared-slot
kernel, which has no shared-slot weights to zero. Where either precondition
does not hold, the separate fills run exactly as before.

**`mla`: size the absorb BMM tiles for decode.** aiter's config table has no
entry for the MLA absorb shapes, so decode falls into a bucket tuned for square
GEMMs (`BLOCK_SIZE_M=64, BLOCK_SIZE_N=256`). The grid is
`(heads, cdiv(M, BM) * cdiv(N, BN))`, so at 16 heads per rank and `N <= 512`
that launches 16-32 workgroups on a 256-CU part: starved of workgroups, not of
bandwidth or flops. This sizes the tile so the grid covers the machine and then
stops -- it does not keep splitting, because the kernel quantizes its own A tile
per token group, so every extra workgroup repeats that work (at M=200/N=512 an
unbounded split is 3.7x slower than the starved table entry).

**`spec`: split the vocab-wide speculative softmax across CTAs.** Speculative
sampling reduces across the vocabulary at every draft step and at verify. torch
reduces each row with one block, so at the row counts speculation actually runs
(1 to 32) a 154880-wide row occupies a handful of blocks, and it is read three
times. `temperature_softmax()` splits each row across CTAs -- partial
max+sumexp, an online-softmax merge, then normalize -- and folds the temperature
divide into the first pass, which drops the separate pass that materialized
`logits / temperatures`. It hands the call back to torch above the row count
where one block per row already fills the GPU, so callers use it
unconditionally.

`fast_sample`'s argmax gets the same treatment by routing it to the existing
`row_argmax()`, which already lands this optimization for the dspark accept
path. No second implementation is added: a split argmax written for this path
is 4.7-42% faster below 32 rows but 3x *slower* above it, where it fell back to
torch, and those are the verify row counts at higher concurrency.

**`linear`: route the bf16 decode shapes aiter's tuned table misses.** The aiter
tuned GEMM keys its table on `(N, K)` and does not fall back to a neighbour, so
a shape the table never saw lands on torch. A decode step hits one of those 79
times -- the MLA q up-projection, `(2048, 2048)` -- where torch runs at 8.4 us
against a 1.05 us weight-bandwidth roofline while aiter's own Triton a16w16
kernel does it in 5.0 us. What is missing is the routing, not a kernel.

The gate is `K` rather than a list of shapes: a list keyed on `(N, K)` is what
makes the aiter table miss these shapes to begin with, and a different tensor
parallel split moves every `N`. It is also bounded in the row count, because
what torch is slow at is the weight-bandwidth-bound regime decode lives in and a
prefill chunk is its opposite -- a 32768-token chunk is 1.25-1.44x *slower* on
the Triton kernel, so prefill must not be routed. `lm_head`, `(19360, 6144)`, is
1.33x slower there and stays where it was.

## Accuracy Tests

Every change is either bit-identical by construction or checked against a
reference before any timing.

| change | property | how it is checked |
|---|---|---|
| moe padded fill | bit-identical | the append kernel already writes those elements; folded only where the preconditions above hold |
| mla absorb tiles | bit-identical | same kernel, different tile; compared at every admitted M |
| `temperature_softmax` | fp32-accurate | vs a float64 reference, not vs torch, which is not ground truth at this width |
| `row_argmax` routing | bit-identical | vs `torch.argmax`, including the sampled index and the `gather` that consumes it |
| linear routing | bit-identical at M=1 | max rel diff 1.7e-4 at M=6, with the error against a float64 reference *equal* to torch's -- not accuracy traded for speed |

`temperature_softmax` against float64, MI355X, vocab 154880:

```
rows      this PR       torch       row sum deviation
   1     3.42e-11    3.42e-11                7.44e-08
   2     2.67e-11    3.27e-11                6.07e-08
   6     2.42e-09    2.89e-09                3.62e-08
  12     3.47e-10    3.47e-10                8.26e-08
  32     3.34e-09    3.34e-09                1.44e-07
  48     1.30e-09    1.30e-09                9.04e-08
  84     2.89e-09    2.89e-09                1.29e-07
```

`row_argmax` matches `torch.argmax` exactly at all seven row counts, and returns
the lowest index on an all-tied row, which ROCm's argmax does not guarantee
(#26358).

A GLM-5.2-MXFP4 TP8 server on an fp8 KV cache comes up and serves correctly with
`--dsa-decode-backend triton`, checked against prompts with verifiable answers
on both arms of every end-to-end run below.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

### Kernel level

`benchmark/kernels/bench_bf16_linear_routing.py` ships with this PR and needs no
server or model weights. It runs both arms in one process and interleaves them
ABBA, so the clock drift that moves kernels this small by ~10% lands on both;
the figure reported is the ratio's spread, not either arm's.

The speculative reductions, MI355X, vocab 154880, fp32, under CUDA graph replay
(the path decode runs on), us/call:

```
rows |  softmax: torch     PR    speedup  spread |  argmax: torch     PR    speedup  spread
   1 |           52.37   6.03      8.7x   23.36% |          12.00   4.61      2.6x    2.34%
   2 |           53.62   6.45      8.3x    0.79% |          34.48   4.71      7.3x    7.93%
   6 |           55.92   7.88      7.1x    0.45% |          34.65   5.24      6.6x    1.15%
  12 |           58.31   9.75      6.0x    1.51% |          34.04   5.75      5.9x    0.95%
  32 |           65.09  20.78      3.1x    0.75% |          33.98   8.70      3.9x    0.90%
  48 |           76.94  76.75      1.0x    0.29% |          36.97  11.19      3.3x    0.67%
  84 |           94.13  94.13      1.0x    0.22% |          45.80  12.28      3.7x    0.65%
```

Rows 48 and 84 in the softmax column are it handing the call back to torch above
its row limit: the harness measuring one implementation against itself, which is
the control for the rest of the column. The 23% spread at one row is the ratio's
own spread over six interleaved rounds on a 6 us kernel; every other point is
under 2%.

In eager the launch cost is not amortized and the softmax win shrinks to
1.1-1.4x; this is a graph-replay optimization and the docstrings say so.

The other two, from their own commits: the MoE append fold is 4.74 -> 1.61 us at
one row and flat in the row count, because what it removes is two launches
rather than work; the MLA `w_vc` absorb (N=256, K=512) goes from 18.1 to 3.6 us
at M=48, and `w_kc` from 12.9 to 3.1.

### End to end

Steady-state decode throughput per user, median over a 150 s window at
concurrency 1 and 2, geometric mean of the two. Base and patched arms were
interleaved across the session rather than run back to back, so linear drift
lands on both:

```
GLM-5.2-MXFP4 · TP8/EP1 · concurrency 1 and 2 · fp8 KV · 104k context
EAGLE 5/6 · --dsa-decode-backend triton · hierarchical cache off

                    vs base     read-to-read spread
base                      =     0.59%  (three reads)
three kernels        +3.94%     0.14%  (two reads)
+ linear routing     +5.67%     0.05%  (two reads)

geometric mean is over the two concurrencies; separately, at +linear routing
  concurrency 1     +4.95%
  concurrency 2     +6.39%
```

The effect is about ten times the baseline's own read-to-read spread. Within it,
the absorb tile accounts for +0.85% and the linear routing for +1.66%; the
softmax and the MoE fold make up the rest.

A trace replay of the same model (aiperf, 1800 s), one read per arm, covering
the three kernel changes only -- it was taken before the linear routing existed:

```
GLM-5.2-MXFP4 · TP8/EP1 · concurrency 1 · fp8 KV · 104k context
EAGLE 5/6 · --dsa-decode-backend triton · hierarchical cache off

per-user throughput, p90     +3.55%
per-GPU total throughput     +1.62%
```

Both arms completed the same number of profiled requests with no dropped
errors, so neither figure comes from a shortened or partly failed run.

Two harnesses with different workloads and different statistics -- a median over
a fixed-shape load and a p90 over a trace replay -- agree on the magnitude for
the part they both cover.

### What this does not claim

Neither figure is a position on a published curve. Both are paired A/B deltas on
one configuration, taken with hierarchical cache off, so they are not comparable
to a leaderboard point.

The end-to-end numbers were taken with the local split argmax described above
rather than with `row_argmax`; the difference between the two is ~1.5 us of a
12.6 ms decode step at these batch sizes, so the tables were not re-taken. The
trace-replay arms are one read each, so drift is not bracketed there; only the
first harness has repeat reads (0.59% on the base side) to bound its own noise.

title: [DSA] Q8KV8 FP8 Sparse Prefill on GLM-5.3-Flash with BF16 KV Cache
author: JackChuang
body:
> Part of the SM90 Q8KV8 FP8 sparse-attention roadmap #25746. > Throughout, **q8** = `--dsa-prefill-backend flashmla_sparse_q8` and **base** = `--dsa-prefill-backend tilelang`. Both configurations run the same bf16 KV cache and the same `--dsa-decode-backend tilelang`; only the prefill backend differs. **One-line summary:** `flashmla_sparse_q8` now serves GLM-5.3-Flash on Hopper (SM90): per DSA layer the sparse prefill is 1.53-1.72x faster than tilelang, which on a prefill-dominated workload is +11.16% to +12.44% total token throughput at 3.5k-120k input and 8.37% to 10.97% lower single-request TTFT at 8k-120k at TP4/EP4 (+5.82% to +12.06% and 6.06% to 11.28% lower at TP8/EP8), with no gsm8k few-shot count (1319 questions each) where q8 scores lower than base. ## TL;DR - **Before this PR, GLM-5.3-Flash could not use `flashmla_sparse_q8` at all.** Launching with it on H200 failed at backend construction (fp8-KV-only guard); relaxing that alone still fails on the KPool tail guard, the 2051-wide KPool top-k (kernel needs a multiple of 128), and zero-length RoPE in the Triton q-prep kernel. - **Per DSA layer (single H200, real backend code paths; 11 of this model's 45 layers are DSA):** at TP4's 16 local heads, q8 sparse prefill is **1.53-1.72x faster** than tilelang across 8k-131k context (1.53-1.72x at TP8's 8 local heads; 1.79-1.98x at 64 local heads). - **End to end** on a **prefill-dominated** workload (random dataset, 3.5k-120k input, **1-token outputs**), with the same server flags at both sizes: at **TP4/EP4**, total token throughput is **+11.16% to +12.44%** and single-request **TTFT is 8.37% to 10.97% lower at 8k-120k**; at **TP8/EP8** the same rows give **+5.82% to +12.06%** and **6.06% to 11.28% lower**. At 3.5k the TTFT difference is small and varies between runs, so it is not claimed. - **Accuracy:** gsm8k at four few-shot counts (5-120 shots, all 1319 questions at every count): **no shot count where q8 scores lower than base** after subtracting the server-to-server offset measured at 5 shots, where both run the identical dense path. LongBench-v2 (336 questions, every request on the sparse prefill path): **−0.003**, against a single-run noise of about ±0.027. - **Cost:** this PR adds one int32 buffer per attention backend (one per GPU here) to pad the 2051-wide top-k to the 2176 the kernel needs, at most `--chunked-prefill-size` rows (71.3 MB at 8192); no new flags or environment variables. ## Motivation On Hopper, GLM-5.3-Flash (`Glm5NextForConditionalGeneration`) runs with a bf16 KV cache (`--kv-cache-dtype auto` resolves to bfloat16 on SM90), so its DSA prefill computes in BF16. On SM90, FP8 doubles the peak tensor-core throughput of BF16 and halves the bytes moved per operand; that is why this series added an FP8 sparse prefill, `--dsa-prefill-backend flashmla_sparse_q8`, for DeepSeek-V3.2 (#30514) and extended it to GLM-5.2 (#31888). That backend could not run on GLM-5.3-Flash at all, because three properties of the model each block it: 1. **bf16 KV cache.** The q8 backend accepted only an `fp8_e4m3` KV cache, but this model is served from a bf16 cache on Hopper. 2. **NoPE MLA** (`qk_rope_head_dim=0`). The fused fp8 q-prep Triton kernel builds `tl.arange(0, ROPE)` and fails to compile at ROPE=0, as does the KV concat-cast kernel behind the opt-in `SGLANG_ENABLE_DSA_Q8KV8_KV_CAT_FUSION`. 3. **KPool top-k** (`index_kpool=4`). The KPool indexer appends up to `index_kpool - 1` tail tokens to every top-k row, so rows are `index_topk + index_kpool - 1 = 2051` wide, but the kernel walks top-k in pairs of 64-wide blocks and needs `topk % 128 == 0`, and the KPool tail guard did not admit q8. ## Modifications None of the three needs a change to the SM90 attention kernel: `d_qk=512` is already one of its two supported widths (512 and 576), `d_v=512` and `h_kv=1` match, and padding the local heads to 64 (from 16 at TP4 or 8 at TP8) already satisfies its contract. The fixes sit around the kernel: 1. **bf16 KV cache** (`dsa_backend.py`, `dequant_k_cache.py`). The q8 kernel only needs q and KV in fp8 at call time, so the validator now accepts a bf16 pool, q8 extend batches take the RAGGED top-k transform whatever the pool dtype, and prefix rows are gathered by slot and cast to fp8 per call (`gather_cast_kv_fp8_pad_paged`: on NoPE rows one vectorized Triton kernel that also zeroes the pad band, otherwise the existing MLA gather; bit-identical to the non-prefix cast). This mirrors an existing path in the opposite direction: `flashmla_sparse` already dequantizes an fp8 cache to bf16 on a prefix hit (`dequantize_k_cache_paged`). 2. **NoPE MLA** (`cache_ops.py`, `dequant_k_cache.py`). Both Triton kernels skip the rope segment behind a static `if ROPE > 0:`, so output with ROPE>0 is byte-identical to before. 3. **KPool top-k** (`dsa_backend.py`, `dsa_backend_kpool.py`). Top-k is padded with -1 to 2176 (output-invariant), and the KPool tail guard admits q8 prefill over a bf16 pool; an fp8 pool keeps the guard, since gathering packed fp8 rows through KPool tail columns is untested. Also included: - **Guards** (`dsa_backend.py`). At launch, q8 prefill rejects `--enable-mixed-chunk`, HiSparse, an fp8 dtype whose pool is not stored packed, and (not supported yet) an fp8 pool on a NoPE model; these previously failed mid-forward. At run time, a non-RAGGED q8 batch that carries top-k indices raises instead of silently running the bf16 kernel. - **Memory.** The q8 kernel needs a top-k width that is a multiple of 128, so the 2051-wide KPool top-k is padded with -1 to 2176 (fix 3 above). tilelang pads the same rows to 2112 (a multiple of its 64-column blocks) with a new tensor on every DSA layer call; this PR instead keeps the padded ids in one `(rows, 2176)` int32 buffer per attention backend that runs q8 prefill (one per GPU here), at most `--chunked-prefill-size` rows (71.3 MB at 8192). It is filled with -1 once and reused across DSA layers and forward passes; each call copies in only the 2051 real columns. - **Docs** (separate commits). The GLM-5.3-Flash docs page (`GLM-5.3-Flash.mdx` and its config) gains a Hopper `BF16 + Q8 sparse prefill` option, listed after `BF16 + TileLang` so the Hopper default does not change, with its own empty benchmark entries so it does not show the BF16 + TileLang numbers; `attention_backend.mdx` drops the stale `requires --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3`. - **Unchanged.** The SM90 kernel and its wrapper; fp8-KV behaviour for DeepSeek-V3.2 / GLM-5.2 apart from the launch-time checks above; DeepSeek-V4; every other DSA prefill and decode backend. ## Usage ```bash sglang serve --model-path zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash --tp-size 8 --ep-size 8 \ --moe-a2a-backend megamoe --moe-runner-backend deep_gemm --kv-cache-dtype bfloat16 \ --dsa-prefill-backend flashmla_sparse_q8 --dsa-decode-backend tilelang \ --mem-fraction-static 0.70 --disable-overlap-schedule --disable-shared-experts-fusion \ --max-running-requests 32 --max-prefill-tokens 8192 --chunked-prefill-size 8192 \ --context-length 131072 --cuda-graph-backend-prefill disabled ``` Opt-in only: without `--dsa-prefill-backend flashmla_sparse_q8`, no default and no other backend changes. **Hardware scope.** SM90 only (the kernel is SM90-gated). **Short prefills.** Batches whose longest KV length is at most `SGLANG_DSA_PREFILL_DENSE_ATTN_KV_LEN_THRESHOLD` (2048 by default) can take the dense MHA path instead, where both backends are identical. The decision is made per batch and has further conditions (for example, the batch's total KV length must fit the MHA chunk capacity), so under concurrency short requests can still reach the sparse path. ## Experimental Results **Setup.** All numbers are from H200 GPUs. Both sizes run the server flags in Usage, so the two sizes compare directly (`--context-length 131072` covers the 120k-input rows), and base differs only in `--dsa-prefill-backend tilelang`: - **TP4/EP4** on 4 GPUs: `--tp-size 4 --ep-size 4`. - **TP8/EP8** on 8 GPUs: `--tp-size 8 --ep-size 8`. Software: torch 2.13.0 (CUDA 13.0), FlashInfer 0.7.0.post1, sglang-kernel 0.4.8, Triton 3.7.1. The workload uses **1-token outputs**, so the throughput rows are prefill-dominated. Each version runs first in half of the repetitions, both servers restart every time, and the improvement averages the two orders. The accuracy runs used different server flags, the same for base and q8 (TP4 without expert parallelism, the default MoE backends, `--mem-fraction-static 0.80`, the default `--max-prefill-tokens`, overlap scheduling and shared-experts fusion on; LongBench-v2 also `--context-length 180224` and `--reasoning-parser glm45`), an earlier software image and an earlier revision of this PR's code.
Benchmark commands ```bash python3 -m sglang.benchmark.serving --backend sglang-oai-chat --dataset-name random \ --random-range-ratio 1.0 --seed 5 --flush-cache \ --random-input-len --random-output-len 1 --num-prompts

--max-concurrency # throughput: c = 64/64/64/32/16/8 for N = 3.5k/8k/16k/32k/64k/120k, P = 4c # TTFT: c = 1, P = 8 for 3.5k-16k and 4 for 32k-120k # N is in tokens (3.5k = 3,500). With 1-token outputs no request stays running after # its prefill, so --max-running-requests 32 does not limit these runs. ```

### Performance Benchmark **Per DSA layer** (single H200; times only the sparse prefill attention call, through the real backend code paths with synthetic indices and values; `do_bench` median per call; q8 time includes top-k padding, fp8 q-prep and the bf16 prefix gather-cast; speedup = tilelang / q8, higher = this PR better; ms columns at 16 heads; the 32k and 64k kv_len rows are omitted and fall in between): | s_q | kv_len | tilelang (ms) | q8 (ms) | speedup, 16 heads (TP4) | 8 heads (TP8) | 64 heads | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | 4096 | 8192 | 3.07 | 1.79 | 1.72x | 1.72x | 1.98x | | 4096 | 131072 | 3.06 | 2.00 | 1.53x | 1.53x | 1.79x | | 8192 | 8192 | 5.99 | 3.48 | 1.72x | 1.72x | 1.98x | | 8192 | 131072 | 6.01 | 3.87 | 1.55x | 1.55x | 1.79x | All columns come from one run on this PR's final code with the software listed in Setup. q8 pads the local heads to 64 and tilelang pads them to 16, so 8 and 16 heads cost the same in each backend; at 64 heads (all of the model's heads on one GPU) tilelang's work grows while q8's does not. Only 11 of the model's 45 layers are DSA (the other 34 are KDA linear-attention layers, which this PR does not touch), so the end-to-end gain is much smaller than the per-layer gain. **End to end** (improvement of q8 over tilelang, + = this PR better; for TTFT, the percentage by which it is lower): | input | throughput, TP4/EP4 | throughput, TP8/EP8 | TTFT, TP4/EP4 | TTFT, TP8/EP8 | |---|---|---|---|---| | 3.5k | +11.70% | +5.82% | +0.86% | +1.91% | | 8k | +12.07% | +8.33% | +9.31% | +6.06% | | 16k | +12.18% | +10.88% | +9.60% | +7.63% | | 32k | +12.44% | +11.21% | +10.17% | +8.94% | | 64k | +11.16% | +12.06% | +10.97% | +11.28% | | 120k | +11.24% | +11.65% | +8.37% | +10.92% | Spread across repetitions (1σ): throughput ±0.07-1.18 percentage points at TP4/EP4, and at TP8/EP8 ±0.32-1.42 from 8k up and ±3.15 at 3.5k; TTFT at 8k-120k ±0.23-0.49 at TP4/EP4 up to 64k, ±3.40 at 120k, and ±0.26-2.78 at TP8/EP8. Three entries (TP8/EP8 throughput at 3.5k, TP4/EP4 throughput at 32k and TTFT at 120k) include one repetition well away from the other three; with the median of the repetitions instead of the mean, the ranges are +11.12% to +12.21% (TP4/EP4) and +4.60% to +12.03% (TP8/EP8) for throughput, and 9.34% to 10.90% and 6.64% to 11.10% lower TTFT at 8k-120k. At 3.5k the TTFT difference is small (+0.86% ±3.27 at TP4/EP4, +1.91% ±1.47 at TP8/EP8) and varies between runs, so the TTFT claim covers 8k-120k only. **Absolute numbers by configuration** (medians, base → q8; the improvement above averages the two run orders, so it is not the ratio of these medians): | input | throughput, TP4/EP4 (tok/s) | throughput, TP8/EP8 (tok/s) | TTFT, TP4/EP4 (ms) | TTFT, TP8/EP8 (ms) | |---|---|---|---|---| | 3.5k | 32,118 → 35,885 | 40,914 → 42,795 | 193 → 192 | 196 → 192.5 | | 8k | 31,531 → 35,355 | 39,888 → 43,172 | 274.5 → 248.5 | 226 → 211 | | 16k | 31,044 → 34,835 | 39,191 → 43,364 | 560 → 506 | 452.5 → 415.5 | | 32k | 30,722 → 34,450 | 38,528 → 42,953 | 1,120 → 1,006 | 906.5 → 824 | | 64k | 30,200 → 33,588 | 37,524 → 42,065 | 2,142.5 → 1,907 | 1,718.5 → 1,526 | | 120k | 29,344 → 32,611 | 35,986 → 40,167 | 4,109 → 3,699 | 3,334.5 → 2,967 | Divided by GPU count, TP4/EP4's q8 throughput is 1.60-1.68x TP8/EP8's, while TP8/EP8's q8 single-request TTFT is 15-20% lower from 8k up. Two TP4/EP4 servers were not run side by side on 8 GPUs, and TP8/EP8's larger KV capacity matters more with longer outputs. **Where the time goes** (TP8/EP8, torch profiler, kernel time per GPU, averaged over the 8 GPUs and taking the median over server sessions, on a short separate test with 16,000-token requests rather than the benchmark rows): the sparse MLA prefill is 30.7% of tilelang's total kernel time, and this PR's kernel runs it 1.72x faster (256.1 → 149.0 ms), which alone cuts the total by 12.8%. The q8 preparation it adds (top-k padding, fp8 q-prep and the bf16 prefix gather-cast, 3.6 ms) costs 0.4%, the tensor concatenation that only the tilelang path runs (8.6 ms) saves 1.0%, and the fused MoE kernel (`deep_gemm` mega-MoE, which also carries the expert-parallel exchange) grows by 2.8% (190.1 → 213.5 ms). The total kernel time falls 10.6% (834.4 → 745.8 ms). ### Correctness and Accuracy Tests The accuracy runs used TP4 without expert parallelism (flags under Setup) and an earlier revision of this PR's code. This PR's later changes (where the padded top-k ids are stored, message text, launch-time checks, a pad-buffer width check that is a no-op at this model's top-k width, and the vectorized gather with bit-identical output) do not touch the numerics. **gsm8k** (all 1319 test questions at every shot count, few-shot examples from the train split, temperature 0, completion API, 2 repetitions; σ is the spread across them): | K (shots) | ~context | base mean (sigma) | q8 mean (sigma) | raw delta | delta vs control | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 5 | 0.8k | 0.9223 (0.0016) | 0.9166 (0.0011) | -0.0057 | *control* | | 20 | 3.3k | 0.8537 (0.0096) | 0.8575 (0.0032) | +0.0038 | +0.0095 | | 60 | 10k | 0.6740 (0.0161) | 0.6820 (0.0038) | +0.0080 | +0.0136 | | 120 | 20k | 0.3082 (0.0059) | 0.3048 (0.0086) | -0.0034 | +0.0023 | K=5 stays below the 2048-token dense threshold, where both configurations take the identical MHA path, so its −0.0057 is a pure server-to-server offset; the last column subtracts it. No shot count shows q8 scoring lower than base. The largest difference, q8 0.0136 higher at K=60, varies widely between the two repetitions (+0.0224 and +0.0049), so no gain is claimed. Both configurations score lower at longer contexts (0.92 at K=5, 0.31 at K=120), partly because of the completion API (on a separate base server with the same flags, K=120 scores 0.566 with the chat API and 0.324 with the completion API), so only the differences are claimed. **Kernel engagement and numerics.** A profiler capture on the LongBench-v2 q8 server shows 132 q8 kernel calls. For gsm8k, a separate profiled run at 4k and 16k context on an earlier commit shows 44 in q8 and none in base; the sweep itself was not profiled. q and KV are cast to fp8_e4m3 with scalar-1.0 scales; the largest magnitude seen in real GLM-5.3-Flash prefills is 13.9 (q; KV at most 5.2), 32x below the ±448 limit, so no rescaling is needed. **LongBench-v2**, where every prompt is longer than 2,048 tokens, so every request takes the sparse prefill path (thinking on, temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max-tokens 16,384, the 2,300-147,000-token subset selected with GLM-5.3-Flash's tokenizer, 336 questions, exact letter match; 2 repetitions): | statistic | base | q8 | delta | |---|---|---|---| | score (max-tokens 16,384) | 0.601 (σ 0.004) | 0.598 (σ 0.025) | **−0.003** | | answered by both, same repetition | 0.714 | 0.714 | **+0.000** | | truncated (no answer emitted) | 15.0% | 14.7% | — | No way of scoring shows a difference beyond about ±0.027, the binomial standard error of one run's score at 336 questions (−0.002 on the 255 questions answered in all four runs). About 15% of responses reach the 16,384-token cap while still reasoning and count as wrong in both configurations, so the claim is the difference, not the absolute score. ## Tests - `test/registered/unit/layers/attention/test_dsa_q8kv8_bf16_prefill_routing.py` (CPU, 24 cases): which top-k layout each prefill backend, KV dtype and batch type gets; which configurations q8 accepts and which it rejects at launch; the top-k padding and its buffer reuse; and the KPool tail guard for bf16 and fp8 pools. - `test/registered/kernels/ops/attention/test_q8kv8_dsa_nope_bf16_prefill.py` (1 GPU, 16 cases): the fp8 q-prep, KV cast and bf16 prefix gather kernels, with and without a rope part, match a plain torch cast byte for byte; and the q8 path on this model's shape (NoPE, bf16 pool, 2051-wide top-k) gives the same output with and without a cached prefix, is unaffected by the padding, and matches a torch reference. - The existing `test_sparse_mla_q8kv8_prefill_sm90.py` and `test_q8kv8_sparse_prefill_backend.py` are unchanged and pass. ## Future work - **FP8 KV cache.** Our next step is to connect q8 prefill to an fp8 KV cache for this model, so the prefill reads fp8 KV rows directly instead of casting bf16 rows (about half the bytes per row); we expect this to improve end-to-end performance further. ## Checklist - [x] Format your code according to [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit) - [x] Add unit tests according to [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests) - [x] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations) - [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed) - [x] Follow the SGLang [code style guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance) --- ### CI States Latest PR Test (Base): :white_check_mark: [Run #38215276474](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/38215276474) Latest PR Test (Extra): :x: [Run #38215275710](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/38215275710) Latest PR Test (AMD ROCm 10): :x: [Run #38215275905](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/38215275905)

title: [diffusion] kernels: take the Wan VAE decoder's remaining first-decode work off the request path
author: mickqian
body:
Stacked on #41710.

## Motivation

With #41710 and an empty Triton cache, Wan2.2-TI2V-5B's first 720p request still decoded 0.17 s slower than later requests. Two costs remained in the VAE decode, and server warmup cannot absorb either of them:

- **Two DupUp3D-add variants compile during the decode.** #41710 unspecialized the sizes but kept every stride of `_dup_up3d_add_kernel`. In the channels-first arms those strides are products of the resolution (`C*H*W`, `W`, ...), so their divisibility class changes with the shape. Two launches landed in a class warmup had not compiled.
- **The lossless norm+SiLU fusion re-verifies itself at every new resolution.** `FusedWanRMSNormSiLU` keyed its first-sight exactness check on the activation's shape and strides. A new resolution therefore re-ran the eager reference chain plus a `torch.equal` host sync 46 times: 46 `cudaStreamSynchronize` calls in the first decode, none in the second.

Warmup cannot cover either: for TI2V, `InputValidationStage` derives the output size from the condition image's aspect ratio. The 64x64 warmup image gives 928x960, while the nightly's 1024x704 photo gives 1152x768, and no fixed warmup image covers every aspect ratio.

## Modifications

- **`_dup_up3d_add_kernel`.** Plain `do_not_specialize` on these strides would make the kernel up to 98% slower: their divisibility is what lets the compiler emit one 128-bit access per four outputs. The wrapper instead derives a vector width `VEC` from the layout. It passes the non-unit strides of `main` and `out`, and `out_w` when W is innermost, divided by `VEC`; the kernel multiplies them back by the constexpr, which restates the same contiguity without depending on their values. Unit strides stay specialized, but not on alignment.
- **`_cat_pad_cl3d_kernel`.** A second instance with the input strides unspecialized serves channels-first inputs, whose loads gather along the channel stride whatever its value. Channels-last inputs keep the fully specialized kernel; unspecializing it there costs 10-12%. The per-layer `pad`/`cache_t` specialization from #41710 stays.
- **`FusedWanRMSNormSiLU`.** The exactness check is keyed on `(device, dtype, x.is_contiguous(), gamma.dtype)`, which is exactly what selects the kernel template. The per-element ops do not depend on the sizes.

## Accuracy Tests

- `test_shape_specialization.py` adds four launches: `wan_cat_pad_channels_first`, and `wan_dup_up3d` in the cf/cf, cf/cl and cl/cf layouts. All four fail on #41710 and pass with this change.
- New `test_first_sight_check_runs_once_per_layout` in `test_wan_norm_silu_post.py`: #41710 verifies 6 signatures (`6 != 2`), this change verifies 2.
- The bitwise cat/pad and DupUp3D tests in `test_layout.py` now sweep channels-last and channels-first arms (four layout pairs for DupUp3D), plus two widths that exercise vector widths 2 and 1.
- `test_layout.py`, `test_shape_specialization.py`, `test_wan_norm_silu_post.py` and `test_model_fast_paths.py`: 286 passed, 1 skipped.

## Speed Tests

H200, Wan2.2-TI2V-5B at 1280x720, empty `TRITON_CACHE_DIR`:

| | #41710 | This PR |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Decode, first / second / third request (nightly harness) | 5.244 / 5.069 / 5.078 s | 5.061 / 5.067 / 5.062 s |
| First-decode extra | +0.17 s | -0.005 s |
| `DecodingStage` from perf dumps | 5693.7 / 5518.5 / 5532.8 ms | 5514.6 / 5520.7 / 5516.1 ms |
| Compiles during the first request's decode | 2 | 0 |
| Triton layout-kernel variants in the process | 22 (12 cat/pad, 6 DupUp3D) | 15 (7 cat/pad, 4 DupUp3D) |
| Warmup's own decode | 7.30 s | 6.96 s |

- Kernel time was summed over every distinct layout-kernel call site, layout and shape that a real decode passes, with both versions interleaved (ABBA) in one process: lossless fp32 -0.05%, `quality=high` fp32 +0.27%, `quality=high` bf16 +0.11%.
- Every output is identical to #41710's, in both values and strides.
- End-to-end latency of measured requests is unchanged.

title: [Perf] [AMD] Qwen3.8: AITER FlyDSL hc_mix for Qwen3.8 hyper-connections on gfx950
author: amd-nprotaso
body:
**Depends on [ROCm/aiter](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/5993)**. Without that AITER build this PR changes nothing: the path is gated on `aiter.ops.flydsl.hc_mix` being importable.

## Motivation

`GatedResidual`'s input mix is a low-rank gate over the `[M, 4·2560]` hyper-state. It runs in every Qwen3.8 decode step, and at decode sizes (M ≤ 16) it is bound by reading the weights.

On gfx950, AITER's FlyDSL `hc_mix` is 1.7–2.4x faster than the persistent Triton `fused_hc_mix` SGLang uses today.

## Modifications

**`python/sglang/srt/layers/hc_mix_flydsl.py`** (new)

`flydsl_hc_mix_supported(...)` accepts a call only when all of these hold:
- HIP, gfx950, BF16, contiguous inputs;
- 1 ≤ M ≤ 16, hc = 4;
- the shape constraints of the AITER kernel;
- AITER and FlyDSL are importable.

The checks are ordered so NVIDIA and disabled paths never import FlyDSL. `weight_cache_key(...)` gives the packed-weight cache a key from the weights' data pointer and version.

**`python/sglang/srt/layers/hyperconnection.py`**

- `GatedResidual` tries FlyDSL `hc_mix` before `fused_hc_mix`.
- Weights are packed once with `pack_hc_weights`, cached on the layer, and repacked only if the weight key changes.

**Benchmark and tests**

- `benchmark/kernels/bench_hc_mix_flydsl.py` compares FlyDSL, persistent Triton and `torch.compile`. It uses CUDA-graph replay with rotating weights, so the weights are cold in L2.
- `test/registered/kernels/ops/hyperconnection/test_hc_mix_flydsl.py` is registered in the AMD `stage-b-test-1-gpu-small-amd` suite. It checks:
  - the gate rejects inputs when disabled or given unsupported shapes;
  - `GatedResidual` dispatches to FlyDSL and matches the reference (`atol=4e-3`);
  - the packed-weight cache reuses packed weights and repacks after a weight change;
  - inference-tensor weights get a key with no version.

## Accuracy Tests

The FlyDSL output matches the float64 reference within `atol=4e-3, rtol=1e-2`, in both the AITER op test and this PR's dispatch test.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Command: `python benchmark/kernels/bench_hc_mix_flydsl.py --rows 1 2 4 8 16 --weights 64`

Setup: MI355X (gfx950), torch 2.11.0+rocm7.2. Time is the per-call median of CUDA-graph replays.

| M | FlyDSL hc_mix (µs) | persistent Triton `fused_hc_mix` (µs) | torch.compile (µs) | vs Triton |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 18.1 | 36.3 | 34.3 | **2.00x** |
| 2 | 18.8 | 44.9 | 38.1 | **2.38x** |
| 4 | 20.3 | 44.9 | 38.1 | **2.21x** |
| 8 | 22.1 | 45.7 | 38.2 | **2.07x** |
| 16 | 26.3 | 45.5 | 38.6 | **1.73x** |

title: [Perf] [AMD] quark/Qwen3.8: Quantize the BF16 shared expert of Quark MXFP4 checkpoints to MXFP4 while loading for shared-expert fusion
author: amd-oshkarav
body:
## Motivation

This is a ROCm performance change. With `--enforce-shared-experts-fusion` the
BF16 shared expert of a Quark MXFP4 checkpoint is quantized to MXFP4 at load and fused into
the routed grouped GEMM (general matrix multiply), instead of running as a separate BF16
MLP (multi-layer perceptron). On `amd/Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B-Quark-MXFP4` over 8x MI355X at TP8
that is worth **+4.5% output throughput and -4.6% mean ITL (inter-token latency)**, as a
geomean across a 12-point serving sweep.

There is currently no Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B checkpoint in which the shared expert is FP4
quantized, so shared-expert fusion is unavailable for this model family on MXFP4.

`amd/Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B-Quark-MXFP4` quantizes the routed experts to MXFP4 but lists the
shared-expert body in the Quark quantization config's `exclude` list, so
`gate_proj`/`up_proj`/`down_proj` of the shared expert ship in BF16. Shared-expert fusion
works by appending the shared expert as one more routed expert at slot `num_experts`, so
that a single grouped GEMM serves top-k routed experts plus the shared one. That requires
every slot in the fused weight to have the same dtype, so today
`QuarkConfig.can_fuse_shared_expert()` sees the format mismatch and refuses, and the model
falls back to running the shared expert as a separate BF16 MLP alongside the routed grouped
GEMM. Rather than wait for a new checkpoint, this PR quantizes the BF16 shared expert at
load time so the existing checkpoint can use the fused path.

The feature is **off by default** and gated behind the existing
`--enforce-shared-experts-fusion` server argument, which already means "fuse the shared
expert even where the gate would normally refuse". In the fused path the shared expert goes
through the routed experts' W4A4 grouped GEMM, so its weights *and* its input activations
are quantized to MXFP4, where the standalone path it replaces ran BF16 x BF16. That is a
real precision trade and should be an explicit choice rather than something a checkpoint
opts into silently.

### Reproduction

Run inside `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.21-rocm10-mi35x` with this branch reinstalled in full over
the stock SGLang:

```shell
SGLANG_USE_AITER=1 \
AITER_USE_FLYDSL_MOE_SORTING=1 \
ROCM_QUICK_REDUCE_QUANTIZATION=INT4 \
SAFETENSORS_FAST_GPU=1 \
SGLANG_WARMUP_TIMEOUT=10000 \
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
 --model-path amd/Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B-Quark-MXFP4 \
 --tp-size 8 \
 --trust-remote-code \
 --reasoning-parser qwen3 \
 --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder \
 --attention-backend aiter \
 --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 \
 --mamba-ssm-dtype bfloat16 \
 --page-size 64 \
 --chunked-prefill-size 16384 \
 --max-prefill-tokens 16384 \
 --max-running-requests 256 \
 --disable-radix-cache \
 --mem-fraction-static 0.9 \
 --model-loader-extra-config '{"enable_multithread_load": true}' \
 --watchdog-timeout 12000 \
 --enforce-shared-experts-fusion
```

Dropping `--enforce-shared-experts-fusion` gives the baseline: the shared expert stays BF16
and runs unfused.

## Modifications

Nine files, and nothing else in the tree differs from upstream: four under
`python/sglang/srt`, two documentation pages, three test files. No new flag is added, so
`environ.py` and the environment-variable reference are untouched.

| File | Delta | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `python/sglang/srt/arg_groups/fields/exec_.py` | +1 -1 | extends the `--enforce-shared-experts-fusion` help text |
| `python/sglang/srt/layers/quantization/quark/quark.py` | +211 -7 | decides whether the conversion applies |
| `python/sglang/srt/layers/quantization/quark/schemes/quark_w4a4_mxfp4_moe.py` | +52 | performs the MXFP4 quantization, ROCm only |
| `python/sglang/srt/layers/moe/fused_moe_triton/layer.py` | +81 | the weight-loader hook that calls it |
| `docs/docs/advanced_features/server_arguments.mdx` | +1 -1 | documents what the flag additionally does here |
| `docs/cookbook/autoregressive/Qwen/Qwen3.5.mdx` | +1 -1 | mentions it in the Qwen3.5 AMD recipe |
| `test/registered/unit/layers/quantization/test_quark_config.py` | +546 -3 | the gating decision |
| `test/registered/unit/layers/quantization/test_quark_shared_expert_online_mxfp4_loader.py` | +474 | the loader hook (new file) |
| `test/registered/amd/accuracy/mi35x/test_qwen38_mxfp4_eval_mi35x.py` | +103 -6 | the MI35x nightly gate, extended with a fused-shared-expert phase, skiped for now  |

The decision of *whether* to convert lives with the quantization
config, the ROCm-only kernel call lives with the MXFP4 scheme, and the copy into the fused
slot lives with `FusedMoE` alongside the FP8 hook that already solves the same problem.

The change depends on #40754
(`e2f4fed`, merged 2026-09-24), which is in `main`. That PR gave the text-only
`Qwen3_5MoeForCausalLM` the shared-expert fusion weight remapping its multimodal sibling
already had, `mlp.shared_expert.* -> mlp.experts.{num_experts}.*`. Without it those weights
were silently dropped and the fused slot left uninitialized. The remap is what makes the
shared-expert tensors arrive at the fused slot at all, and the loader hook added here
intercepts them at that slot and converts them on the way in. #40754 covered checkpoints
whose shared expert already matches the routed-expert dtype (FP8), so no conversion was
needed; this PR extends the same path to the Quark MXFP4 checkpoint, where the shared expert
is BF16 and the conversion is the missing piece.

## Accuracy Tests

### gsm8k under the nightly e2e test's own parameters, greedy

**This is the headline accuracy result.** It is the only pair measured with the parameter set
`test/registered/amd/accuracy/mi35x/test_qwen38_mxfp4_eval_mi35x.py` uses, and with sampling
switched off, so it is the pair that answers "does this change what CI will report". 

| | fusion ON | fusion OFF | Δ (on − off) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| gsm8k score | **0.9764** | **0.9726** | **+0.38 pp** |
| correct, of 1314 | 1283 | 1278 | +5 questions |
| eval wall time | 215.6 s | 227.2 s | −5.1 % |
| eval output throughput | 841.4 tok/s | 806.1 tok/s | +4.4 % |



**Both arms are one image, one node, one day.** Built from `fse-online-mxfp4` at `747482984`,
this PR's HEAD as submitted, on `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.21-rocm10-mi35x`, run back to back on the
same MI355X host, and every
logged server parameter is identical except `--enforce-shared-experts-fusion`. 



### GPQA, NIAH

The branch at `abddcd87` was re-measured end to end on 2026-10-11, and two further evals ran inside each of those two serving sweeps, against the same server instance that produced the speed numbers below:

| Eval | fusion ON | fusion OFF |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| GPQA via sglang `run_eval`, temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, thinking enabled | 0.9242 | 0.9192 |
| RULER `niah_single_2` at 65536 via `lm_eval` | 1.0 | 1.0 |
| RULER `niah_single_2` at 131072 via `lm_eval` | 1.0 | 1.0 |



## Benchmarking

Measured with `sglang.bench_serve` through a 12-point sweep, twice, changing only
`--enforce-shared-experts-fusion`.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Model | `amd/Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B-Quark-MXFP4` |
| Hardware | 8x MI355X (gfx950), single node, TP8 |
| Base image | `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.21-rocm10-mi35x` |
| Branch commit | `abddcd8701376e29ad460b80a68c1589a9835174`, rebased onto `main` at `11bfd868` |
| aiter | the base image's, ROCm/aiter `acf8fdf93` of 2026-09-12 |
| Server | `--attention-backend aiter --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --mamba-ssm-dtype bfloat16 --page-size 64 --chunked-prefill-size 16384 --max-prefill-tokens 16384 --max-running-requests 256 --mem-fraction-static 0.9 --disable-radix-cache` |
| Env | `SGLANG_USE_AITER=1`, `AITER_USE_FLYDSL_MOE_SORTING=1`, `ROCM_QUICK_REDUCE_QUANTIZATION=INT4`, `SAFETENSORS_FAST_GPU=1` |
| Sweep | ISL 8192 / OSL 1024 at concurrency 4 to 256; ISL 60000 / OSL 600 at 4/16/64; ISL 128000 / OSL 1024 at 4/16. `random_range_ratio` 0.8 and an unbounded request rate throughout |
| Baseline | fusion OFF: no `--enforce-shared-experts-fusion`, shared expert stays BF16 and unfused |
| Candidate | fusion ON: `--enforce-shared-experts-fusion`, shared expert quantized to MXFP4 at load and fused |

Every one of the 12 points improved on throughput, ITL, TPOT (time per output token), end-to-end
latency and median TTFT (time to first token). Across all logged server parameters the two sweeps
differ only in `--enforce-shared-experts-fusion`, verified programmatically.

### Geomean per metric over the 12-point sweep

| Output throughput | tok/s | 409.8 | 428.3 | +4.51% | better | 12 of 12 |
| Request throughput | req/s | 0.5089 | 0.5319 | +4.51% | better | 12 of 12 |
| Mean ITL | ms | 46.2 | 44.1 | −4.57% | better | 12 of 12 |
