title: [Refactor] Translate each KV loc once per iteration
author: ch-wan
body:
This PR is part of a stack (oldest at bottom):

* __->__ #42753
* #40492
* #40491
* #37628
* #37627

## Motivation

On the unified memory pool a KV slot has a virtual id (what the scheduler
allocates and `req_to_token` stores) and a physical id (what kernels index).
The conversion between them was done wherever an id was needed: every
`ForwardBatch` translated its own write window, every attention backend built
its own translated page table (some per forward, some per layer group, some
per captured mode), the multi-step draft kernel translated every id it
gathered, and the speculative KV writers translated the ids they were handed.
Within one speculative iteration the same window was translated three to four
times (draft, verify, draft extend, target-hidden KV writes), and a captured
graph translated its write ids a second time into a private buffer.

Besides the wasted launches, every one of those sites had to agree on which
ids were already physical, and a site that translated twice, or not at all,
silently read or wrote the wrong slot.

**This PR translates an iteration's write window once per sub-pool, in one
place, and gives every read exactly one translation, in one place too: the
translator's read primitives. A read table exists only once a reader that reads
the table form asks for it -- built into that reader's own capture-stable table
when it has one -- and every later reader takes it; every reader before it
translates in its own gather. No table is built that no reader asked for.**

## Modifications

**`KVLocPlan`** (`mem_cache/kv_loc_plan.py`, new) names one iteration's ids,
in every sub-pool of the pool. A sub-pool is an **`IdSpace`**: how it maps the
iteration's virtual token ids (`write`) and the page table its reads go through
(`read_v2p`). A runner's translator holds one per sub-pool its pool has
(`space(IdSpaceKind.FULL / SLIDING_WINDOW)`), keyed so that runners sharing a
sub-pool (a fused draft and its target) share the plan's results; adding a
sub-pool means registering a space, not adding fields. The window itself
stays in allocator-global ids: an NPU DCP target, which writes rank-local
slots, has its own full space mapping the window to them, while the
replicated draft binds the same window global. The plan holds:

- its write window, translated once into the full sub-pool
  (`write_physical`); the virtual window it was built from is never mutated
  (radix tree, accept path and lazy compaction still read it);
- `write_ids(reader, kind=, cols=)`: the window in any sub-pool's ids, derived
  on first use and kept for the iteration -- physical for the target and a
  fused draft, virtual for a static or private draft pool's full sub-pool;
  `cols` selects the part a forward writes (a draft step's columns, a flat
  index for a ragged verify's packed rows, or a run of the window's tokens
  for one half of a two-batch-overlap split, `TokenSpan`, read as a view);
- `read_table(kind=, rows=)`: a sub-pool's page table over
  `[0, seq_lens + read_extent)`, built when a reader that reads the table form
  (a page-table kernel, or a captured graph's table: `copy_page_table`) first
  asks for it, and then shared by every later reader of the iteration; built
  straight into a captured reader's own buffer -- no table of the plan's own,
  no copy; without host lengths (fa3's speculative overlap steps) the build
  stops at that buffer's width. A captured graph's padded lanes are appended by copy, reading the
  sink, and a reader that asks for its batch's rows gets exactly those, a view
  of a wider table a captured reader built. Until a table exists no reader
  waits for one: a CSR stream is gathered and translated straight into the
  reader's buffer, and the multi-step draft kernel gets the virtual rows with
  the sub-pool's page table (`KVIndexTable.v2p`), applied in its own gather.
  Whether to share is local -- does the plan hold a table yet -- so nothing
  predicts which runners will read one;
- `bind(batch, reader, cols)`: the one way a forward gets its write ids. A
  forward carries only the plan and its columns (`ForwardBatch.kv_loc_cols`);
  a backend that writes another sub-pool asks its translator at metadata time
  (`KVIndexTranslator.write_ids(batch, kind)`), padded to the batch's
  `out_cache_loc` with the sink, so padded batches, replay views and the
  halves of a two-batch-overlap split need nothing of their own.

`KVIndexTranslator` keeps what a plan needs: `plan` / `own_plan`, the plan's
table builder (`build_iteration_table`), the readers
(`read_source` for gather kernels, `pack_read_stream` for CSR streams,
`copy_page_table` for captured tables, `read_table`, each by `IdSpaceKind`),
`write_ids` for a backend's sub-pool, the dispositions, and
DCP's read production (`translate_dcp_read_ids`, the one translation that
stays outside a plan: which ids a rank reads is only known where the DCP index
kernels select them). A reader takes a plan's table only when it reads
through it -- same v2p table, same `req_to_token` rows (`is_read_by`).

The commits are layered:

1. **One plan per forward.** `ForwardBatch.init_new` builds a plan and binds
   it; replay views carry it.
2. **Writes.** A captured forward writes through the graph runner's own
   `out_cache_loc` slot, which already holds the batch's physical ids; triton
   and the trtllm_mla family drop the private capture buffers that translated
   them again. Batches a runner builds itself (captures, warmup runs) bind
   their own buffer as it is (`bind_runner_slots`). A forward
   whose lengths do not count the window it writes -- a verify, a speculative
   draft decode, a draft extend -- plans its reads that far
   (`window_read_extent`).
3. **Reads, per backend.** triton, the multi-step draft kernel, fa3, the
   trtllm_mla family, flashmla, trtllm_mha, flashinfer, flashinfer_mla, aiter,
   the speculative inputs' `generate_attn_arg_prefill` and DeepSeek's one-shot
   and chunked-prefix MHA indices read the plan's table instead of
   translating. The plan is passed explicitly through the index updaters (no
   hidden backend state).
4. **One plan per speculative iteration.** EAGLE (single- and multi-layer)
   plans the verify window when the draft gathers it -- in the same launch --
   and the draft decode, verify and draft extend share it. DSPARK and DFLASH
   plan their window where it is allocated; the draft block, the verify
   (including DSPARK's ragged verify, by index) and the target-hidden KV
   writers share it, and a compact DFLASH draft reads its own rows over the
   shared write ids (`reads_from`). At prefill, the target forward hands back
   its plan (`return_kv_loc_plan`), and the draft writes into the same slots
   take their ids from it.
5. **Removal.** The per-forward translate API goes (`index_table_for_batch`,
   `widened_index_table`, `build_index_table`, `fill_read_table`,
   `fill_packed_read_stream`, `translate_full_attn_ids`, `full_flat_v2p`,
   `sliding_window_write_loc_for`); `rebind_write_loc` becomes
   `bind_own_plan`. A padded (DP-attention) batch pads its eager page table
   along with its write ids. DiffusionGemma's FA4 prefill graphs build their
   streams from the batch's plan and take their sliding-window write ids from
   `write_ids`; their private capture buffer of translated write ids goes, as
   triton's did.
6. **Sub-pools as id spaces.** Every sub-pool, the sliding-window one
   included, goes through `IdSpace` (as above): a batch carries no ids of its
   own per sub-pool, a table no per-sub-pool twin, a reader no per-sub-pool
   flag. trtllm_mha's ragged-verify refill takes its sliding-window ids from
   the plan as well, instead of mapping `out_cache_loc`, which on the unified
   pool is already physical.
7. **Tests and comments of the stack.** The stack's tests that duplicate
   another test, pin a development-time detail, or only catch a failure that
   already stops the boot are dropped (about 60); the ones kept check the ids,
   rows, columns and bytes a kernel or captured graph gets. The fused-draft
   bind gate and the speculative aux-state resolver tests run weekly. The
   stack's comments and docstrings are cut to contracts and invariants.

A static pool does no translation work and runs no kernel for it: its plan
is a few host objects over the batch's own write ids, and every read is the
`req_to_token` passthrough, as before.

## Translations per iteration

Counted in the server processes over the 25-prompt greedy run (scheduler
iterations, prefill included), H200, against this PR's previous revision, which
shared a table whenever two runners read the same rows:

| configuration | write translations / iter | reads / iter, previous revision | reads / iter, this head |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.5-4B, MTP (EAGLE), fused draft, flashinfer | 1.00 | 1 table build, read 2.95 times | 2.00 stream gathers + 0.97 in the draft kernel's gather; no table |
| gpt-oss-20b (sliding window), EAGLE3, fused draft, triton | 1.00 | 1 table build, read 2.98 times; 1 sliding-window stream | 3.00 stream gathers + 0.99 in the draft kernel's gather; no table |
| Qwen3.8-27B, DSPARK, fused draft, flashinfer | 1.00 | 1 table and the first stream, read 0.97 times | 1.97 stream gathers; no table |
| gpt-oss-20b (sliding window), EAGLE3, fused draft, fa3 | 1.00 | 2 table builds | 2 table builds (fa3 reads the table) |

A forward that is the only reader of its rows -- every configuration without
speculation -- takes the same path as before. On B200: 1.00 read gather per
iteration for Qwen3.5-4B (flashinfer) and Kimi-Linear-48B (trtllm_mla, its table
built in the captured buffer) without speculation, and 2.00 for gpt-oss-20b (one
stream per sub-pool). Kimi-Linear-48B with DSPARK and a fused flashinfer draft
reads 0.99 stream gathers (the draft's) and 0.99 table builds (in the trtllm_mla
verify's captured buffer) per iteration: the reads it made before this PR,
without the target-hidden write translation it also made per iteration.

## Accuracy Tests

Greedy parity, 24 prompts x 128 tokens (token ids and per-token logprobs),
B200, every configuration against the stack tip (#40492) or `main`:
**identical in every arm, max |dlogprob| 0.0000.**

| target | speculation | attention | pool |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.5-4B | none | flashinfer | unified, static |
| Qwen3.5-4B | MTP (EAGLE) | flashinfer | unified (fused draft), static |
| Qwen3.5-4B | DFLASH | flashinfer | unified (fused; page size 1 / 64; compact window), static |
| gpt-oss-20b (sliding window) | none | triton | unified, static; TP2 DP2 with DP attention |
| gpt-oss-20b (sliding window) | EAGLE3 | triton | unified (fused; page size 1 / 64) |
| gpt-oss-20b (sliding window) | none / EAGLE3 | trtllm_mha | unified (eager: decode graphs are not supported there yet), static |
| Kimi-Linear-48B (TP2) | DSPARK, dummy draft | trtllm_mla target; trtllm_mha (private) / flashinfer (fused) draft | unified; ragged verify on flashinfer |
| Kimi-Linear-48B (TP2) | none; 8 requests over a 6.8k-token cached prefix (chunked-prefix MHA) | trtllm_mla | unified |

The whole stack against `main` (its merge base), H200: greedy parity over
25 prompts x 128 tokens, one at a time -- short prompts, 11k-15k-token
prompts (chunked prefill, past the sliding window), and requests that extend
a cached 6.8k-8.2k-token prefix. **Identical in every arm, max |dlogprob|
0.0000.**

| target | speculation | attention | pool |
|---|---|---|---|
| gpt-oss-20b (sliding window) | none | triton | unified (page size 1 / 64), static |
| gpt-oss-20b (sliding window) | none | fa3 | unified |
| Qwen3.5-4B | none | flashinfer | unified, static |
| Qwen3.5-4B | none | triton, fa3 | unified |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B | none / NGRAM | flashinfer | static |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B | none | fa3 | static |

gpt-oss-20b with EAGLE3 on fa3, H200 (context 4096, so the long prompts are
2.5k tokens): the fused draft against the static pool on the same build and
against `main`, all three identical, accept length 1.204 in every arm.

Qwen3.8-27B with a real DSPARK draft (`RadixArk/Qwen3.8-27B-DSpark`, accept
length about 3.4), H200, fused draft under unified memory: identical to the stack
tip (#40492), accept length 3.396 on both. Qwen3.5-4B MTP (flashinfer), gpt-oss-20b
EAGLE3 (triton, fa3) and Qwen3.8-27B DSPARK, fused, are also identical between
this head and its previous revision, which read through a shared table: the
draft kernel's in-gather translation and the per-reader streams give the same
ids.

This head against the stack tip, B200, rerun: identical for Qwen3.5-4B (no
speculation, MTP, DFLASH), gpt-oss-20b (no speculation, EAGLE3 on triton) and
Kimi-Linear-48B DSPARK; and against its previous revision, H200: identical for
gpt-oss-20b EAGLE3 (fa3, and an fa3 target with a triton draft), Qwen3.8-27B
DSPARK and Qwen3.5-4B MTP.

The draft KV lands where it did: the accept length is identical log line for
log line against the stack tip (DFLASH 3.7465, MTP 2.8355, mean over the
run's decode logs).

Under page relocation: GSM8K, 400 questions 128 at a time, on a small unified
pool (`--mem-fraction-static 0.15`) where lazy compaction moved about 31k pages
of live requests in each run (Qwen3.5-4B, flashinfer; no invalid answers):

| speculation | stack tip | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| MTP (two runs each) | 0.873 / 0.865 | 0.882 / 0.875 |
| DFLASH | 0.887 | 0.890 |
| none | 0.868 | 0.873 |

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Against `main`, DSPARK on the unified pool, servers booted alternately on the
same GPUs, the same `bench_serving` load as below; greedy output identical to
`main` in every row:

| configuration | draft KV, `main` -> this head | c1 mean TPOT | c32 | GPU memory |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Kimi-Linear-48B TP2 (B200), dummy draft on `trtllm_mha` (the default) | private -> private | 4.735 -> 4.710 ms (-0.5%) | median ITL 13.21 -> 13.20 ms | same |
| Kimi-Linear-48B TP2 (B200), dummy draft on flashinfer | private -> fused | 5.297 -> 5.357 ms (+1.1%), 5.377 -> 5.460 ms (+1.6%) on a second GPU pair, 3 runs each | median ITL +0.9% | 127.8 -> 90.7 GiB per rank |
| Qwen3.8-27B (H200), `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-27B-DSpark`, triton target, flashinfer draft, fp8 KV | private -> fused | 5.945 -> 5.967 ms (+0.4%), 4 runs each | 965 tok/s both | 14.1 GiB less after pool allocation |

`main` admits DSPARK on the unified pool only with a triton or MLA-family
target, hence the triton target for Qwen3.8 (its cookbook recipe uses
flashinfer). The fused rows pay for one launch on the host path ahead of the
draft's graph: the plan translates the iteration's write window before the
draft runs, which writes physical ids into it, and at one request in flight
that is idle GPU time. `main`'s private draft writes virtual ids, and `main`
translates the target's window after the draft is launched. A flashinfer
draft that keeps a private pool on this stack pays the same launch.
Translating inside the iteration's first captured graph would remove it; the
plan build carries a FIXME for that.

B200, this head against the stack tip (#40492), the two trees' servers booted
alternately on the same GPUs (A/B/B/A), `bench_serving` random 1024 in / 256
out, 24 prompts at concurrency 1 (mean TPOT, output throughput) and 192 at
concurrency 32 (output throughput). Unified pool, CUDA graphs on. Greedy output
is identical to the tip in every row.

| configuration | runs per tree | c1 TPOT | c1 tok/s | c32 tok/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.5-4B, no speculation, flashinfer | 2 | 2.530 -> 2.530 ms (0.0%) | 0.0% | +0.9% |
| Qwen3.5-4B, MTP, flashinfer | 2 | 1.425 -> 1.425 ms (0.0%) | +0.1% | -2.7% |
| Qwen3.5-4B, DFLASH, flashinfer | 2 | 0.875 -> 0.865 ms (-1.1%) | +1.4% | +2.7% |
| gpt-oss-20b (sliding window), no speculation, triton | 2 | 1.865 -> 1.840 ms (-1.3%) | +1.5% | +10.8% |
| gpt-oss-20b (sliding window), EAGLE3, triton | 2 | 3.380 -> 3.340 ms (-1.2%) | +1.1% | -0.5% |
| Kimi-Linear-48B TP2, DSPARK, fused flashinfer draft | 6, on two GPU pairs | 5.412 -> 5.412 ms (0.0%: +0.3% on one pair, -0.3% on the other) | 0.0% | -0.6% |

At concurrency 32, two runs of the same tree differ by up to 18% on this box (a
gpt-oss tip run read 5,768 tok/s against 7,025), so that column resolves no
direction at two runs per tree; concurrency 1 holds to about 0.3%.

H200, this head against its previous revision, interleaved on one GPU, four
runs each, mean TPOT at concurrency 1 / 32; greedy output and accept length
identical in every pair. The previous revision already translated reads in
each reader's own gather when no reader read a table; this head also stops
building a table before a table reader asks for one:

| configuration | concurrency 1 | concurrency 32 |
|---|---|---|
| gpt-oss-20b, EAGLE3, fa3 target, triton draft (the draft reads first) | 3.767 vs 3.765 ms (+0.1%) | 11.481 vs 11.463 ms (+0.2%) |
| gpt-oss-20b, EAGLE3, fa3 | 3.716 vs 3.713 ms (+0.1%) | 11.076 vs 11.092 ms (-0.1%) |
| Qwen3.8-27B, real DSPARK draft, fused, flashinfer | 5.563 vs 5.562 ms (0.0%) | 11.389 vs 11.372 ms (+0.1%) |
| Qwen3.5-4B, MTP, fused draft, flashinfer (path unchanged; runs overlap) | 1.703 vs 1.697 ms (+0.4%) | 5.411 vs 5.370 ms (+0.8%) |

Qwen3.8-27B DSPARK matches the stack tip: 5.56 ms here, and 5.56 ms for the tip
in an earlier interleaved run against an older revision of this PR that
measured 5.59 ms -- the time its table build spent on the critical path between
the verify and the next draft. The static pool on this stack matches `main`
(H200, gpt-oss-20b EAGLE3 on fa3: 3.69 / 10.48 vs 3.70 / 10.47 ms,
interleaved).

On an earlier revision of this PR, which built at least the tables this head
builds: long, mixed lengths (input 1.6k-16k tokens, 128 out, 64 prompts at
concurrency 16), with the transient peak the CUDA caching allocator reaches
above its warm baseline (worst rank), the same A/B/B/A order:

| configuration | tok/s | median ITL | transient peak allocated |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kimi-Linear-48B TP2, no speculation, trtllm_mla (captured table read first) | +3.7% | 5.29 -> 5.25 ms | -0.3 MiB |
| Kimi-Linear-48B TP2, DSPARK, fused flashinfer draft | -0.4% | 12.50 -> 12.54 ms | +0.1 MiB |
| gpt-oss-20b (sliding window), no speculation, triton, page size 1 | +0.2% | 4.07 -> 4.00 ms | -8.1 MiB |
| Qwen3.5-4B, no speculation, flashinfer, page size 1 | -0.7% | 3.55 -> 3.57 ms | -0.9 MiB |

A captured graph that reads the plan's table first has it built straight into
its own buffer, as the stack tip's capture fill did; a stream read before any
table reader is gathered on its own, as the stack tip did.

## Memory

`max_total_num_tokens` is identical between the stack tip and this PR in
every configuration above (1,381,150 / 1,415,720 / 775,733 / 1,808,890 /
1,620,448 / 970,112 / 2,357,632). gpt-oss-20b TP2 DP2 with DP attention boots
with slightly more (1,933,216 vs 1,913,256, the same in two separate rounds).

At run time the transient peak above the warm baseline matches the stack tip
within 8 MiB in every long-context configuration (the table above). No read
table is built that no reader asked for: a fused target and draft that both
read CSR streams or row gathers (flashinfer, triton) each translate in their own
gather, as before this PR, so no `rows x longest row` table appears (128 MiB at
page size 1 for 256 requests with one 128k-token row); and a stream read before
a captured table reader leaves the table to that reader, built in its own
graph buffer, rather than building one of the plan's own for it to copy. The
caching allocator's reserved peak is not compared: it varied by gigabytes
between two runs of the same tree.

## Notes for reviewers

- **Not validated end to end here:** NPU (its DCP write ids are covered by
  a unit test), fa3 with DFLASH or DSPARK (its draft and verify metadata
  paths are covered by unit tests), multi-layer EAGLE
  (no such model on the test machine), cutedsl_mla / tokenspeed_mla /
  flashmla, `--dcp-size > 1`, and two-batch overlap (the unified pool refuses
  it; a split batch's columns on a static sliding-window pool are covered by
  unit tests).
- **One translation stays outside a plan by design:** DCP's read production
  (`translate_dcp_read_ids`): which ids a rank reads is only known where the
  DCP index kernels select them.
- trtllm_mla's eager block table past a row's live pages now reads the sink
  (0) within the plan's width instead of -1; the kernels bound their reads by
  `seq_lens`, and a draft extend's padded queries (whose outputs are dropped)
  read valid memory.

title: [Perf] deepseek-v4.1: Skip wasted layer 20 work on earlier prompt tokens under decoder bounded replay
author: vincentzed
body:
## Motivation

- DeepSeek-V4.1 has an option called decoder bounded replay (`--enable-decoder-swa-bounded-replay`). When it is on, the last layers of the model only process the last 128 prompt tokens of each request during prefill.
- Today this starts at layer 21. Layer 20 still processes every prompt token.
- Layer 20 does two things. It writes the compressed KV cache that decoding reads later, and that needs every token. It also runs its own indexer, attention and MoE to produce its output, and layer 21 only reads the last 128 tokens of that output.
- So the indexer, attention and MoE work of layer 20 on all the earlier tokens is thrown away. The indexer of layer 20 scans the whole context, so this wasted work grows with the prompt length.

## Modifications

- When decoder bounded replay is on, layer 20 now writes its compressed KV cache for every token first, and then runs the rest of the layer on the last 128 tokens only.
- The compressed KV cache that layer 20 writes is the same as before.
- Layer 20 now writes its indexer results directly for the last 128 tokens. The code that copied those rows out of the full-size buffers is no longer needed, so this PR removes it.
- No flag is added. Nothing changes when decoder bounded replay is off.
- ROCm keeps the old behavior, because its fused layer path runs all of layer 20 in one call.
- This also works with the prefill CUDA graph that #43736 added for decoder bounded replay. Inside the graph, the step that prepares the layer 20 inputs now computes only the part the caller asked for. Before, it always computed the indexer inputs too, and the new full-prompt KV write does not have them.

One behavior change to review:

- For the last 128 tokens, layer 20 now uses the same shortened sliding window as layers 21 to 39. Before this PR, layer 20 saw the full window.
- This matches how the DeepSeek-V4.1 report describes decoder replay: "feed their encoder outputs through the decoder layers under the same SWA truncation".

## Accuracy Tests

- Hardware and model: 4x B300, `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash`, TP4 and EP4.
- "main" is commit `2f6e0ec45d`. The two files this PR changes are the same on current main.

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server --trust-remote-code --model-path deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash --tp 4 --ep-size 4 --mem-fraction-static 0.8 --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 64 --max-running-requests 16 --enable-decoder-swa-bounded-replay
# The DSpark row adds: --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --speculative-dspark-block-size 5
python3 -m sglang.test.few_shot_gsm8k --num-questions 1319 --parallel 32
```

| GSM8K, 1319 questions | main | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No speculative decoding | 0.907 | 0.907 |
| DSpark, block size 5 | 0.902 | 0.914 |

- Each number is one run. Two runs of the same setup can differ by about 0.007.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

- Same launch command as above, without speculative decoding.
- The numbers are time to first token. Requests are sent one at a time, as token ids.
- Each number is the median of 3 to 5 requests. The two numbers in a cell come from two separate server starts.

| Request | main | this PR | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| New prompt, 16K tokens | 139.6 / 139.5 ms | 132.8 / 131.6 ms | 5% faster |
| New prompt, 64K tokens | 577.5 / 564.9 ms | 526.6 / 524.5 ms | 8% faster |
| New prompt, 200K tokens | 2009.6 / 2015.4 ms | 1800.5 / 1811.9 ms | 10% faster |
| New prompt, 500 to 8K tokens | 81.7 to 85.7 ms | 82.5 to 84.4 ms | No change |
| 2K new tokens after 16K cached tokens | 85.8 / 87.2 ms | 84.4 / 85.5 ms | No change |
| 2K new tokens after 64K cached tokens | 93.5 / 89.4 ms | 93.2 / 91.4 ms | No change |
| 2K new tokens after 200K cached tokens | 112.4 / 113.9 ms | 115.2 / 113.3 ms | No change |
| 128 new tokens after 200K cached tokens | 109.3 / 107.8 ms | 114.2 / 113.0 ms | 5 ms slower |

Time spent in layer 20 for one 16K-token prefill chunk, measured with a GPU sync around each layer:

| Prefill chunk | main | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Early in the prompt | 11.9 ms | 3.3 ms |
| Late in a 200K-token prompt | 27.0 ms | 5.2 ms |

- Short requests do not get faster. Prefill without a CUDA graph costs about 80 ms per batch no matter how short the prompt is, and this PR does not change that.
- The last row of the first table is the only one that got slower. In a third pair of server starts it was 109.2 ms on main and 107.3 ms with this PR, so I think it is noise between server starts.

## Rerun after merging main at `684fea8af3`

- Main now runs decoder bounded replay inside the breakable prefill CUDA graph (#43736), so I tested both with and without the graph.
- Same hardware and model as above. The graph rows add `--cuda-graph-backend-prefill breakable --mem-fraction-static 0.7`. Current main ran out of GPU memory with the graph at 0.8, so both sides use 0.7 there.
- Each number is one run from one server start.

| GSM8K, 1319 questions | main | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No prefill graph | 0.906 | 0.911 |
| Prefill graph | 0.898 | 0.908 |
| Prefill graph and DSpark, block size 5 | not run | 0.911 |

| Time to first token, new prompt | main | this PR | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 14,795 tokens, no prefill graph | 152.5 ms | 143.2 ms | 6% faster |
| 14,795 tokens, prefill graph | 172.6 ms | 159.5 ms | 8% faster |
| 6,318 tokens, prefill graph | 97.8 ms | 90.7 ms | 7% faster |
| 590 tokens, prefill graph | 32.5 ms | 32.4 ms | No change |

- No scheduler exceptions in any run.
- Unit tests under `test/registered/unit/layers/test_dsv4*.py`: 70 passed.

## Rerun after merging main at `abf92826ee`

- Main now also allows the TRT-LLM attention backend with decoder bounded replay under the prefill graph (#44326), so this run includes TRT-LLM rows (`--dsv4-attn-backend trtllm`).
- Main also moved the DeepSeek-V4 layer code into separate stage files (#43607). This PR's new layer method and its changes to the model loop carried over without changes.
- Every row uses `--cuda-graph-backend-prefill breakable --mem-fraction-static 0.7`. Each number is one run from one server start.

| GSM8K, 1319 questions | main | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FlashMLA | 0.908 | 0.904 |
| FlashMLA and DSpark, block size 5 | not run | 0.905 |
| TRT-LLM | 0.897 | 0.897 |

| Time to first token, new prompt | main | this PR | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 14,795 tokens, FlashMLA | 165.9 ms | 155.8 ms | 6% faster |
| 14,795 tokens, TRT-LLM | 161.2 ms | 149.1 ms | 8% faster |
| 6,318 tokens, FlashMLA | 97.9 ms | 90.4 ms | 8% faster |
| 6,318 tokens, TRT-LLM | 89.9 ms | 86.3 ms | 4% faster |
| 590 tokens, FlashMLA | 31.6 ms | 32.9 ms | No change |

- Two runs of the same setup can differ by about 0.007 on GSM8K.
- No scheduler exceptions in any run.
- Unit tests under `test/registered/unit/layers/test_dsv4*.py`: 71 passed.

## Not tested

- Prefill context parallelism together with decoder bounded replay.
- ROCm. Its behavior is unchanged.

## Follow-up

- `CandidateMetadata.tail` and its implementations are now only called by their own tests. A later PR can remove them.

title: [DSA] Support TileLang FP8 KV cache on CUDA
author: Jzz1943
body:
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->

## Motivation

<!-- Describe the purpose and goals of this pull request. -->

Enable TileLang DSA with FP8 KV cache on CUDA, removing the backend restriction and reducing KV memory usage for models such as GLM-5.3-Flash.

## Modifications

<!-- Detail the changes made in this pull request. -->

- Dispatch CUDA FP8 KV to the existing TileLang partial/combine kernels.
- Allocate raw FP8 KV rows without the scaled-cache metadata.
- Disable the incompatible one-shot MHA path and validate backend/layout compatibility.
- Extend existing GPU and configuration tests to cover CUDA FP8 KV and CUDA Graph replay.

Requires TileLang for both DSA prefill and decode; DCP and HiSparse are not supported by this path.

## Accuracy Tests

<!-- If this pull request affects model outputs (e.g., changes to the kernel or model forward code), provide accuracy test results. -->

Validated GLM-5.3-Flash on 4 × H200 with BF16 and FP8 KV, with and without MTP.

```bash
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3 sglang serve \
  --model-path /path/to/GLM-5.3-Flash \
  --served-model-name llm \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --tp-size 4 \
  --ep-size 4 \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.75 \
  --max-mamba-cache-size 240 \
  --max-running-requests 48 \
  --chunked-prefill-size 8192 \
  --cuda-graph-backend-prefill breakable \
  --cuda-graph-max-bs-prefill 8192 \
  --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 48 \
  --dsa-prefill-backend tilelang \
  --dsa-decode-backend tilelang \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 \
  --moe-runner-backend deep_gemm \
  --moe-a2a-backend none \
  --reasoning-parser glm45 \
  --tool-call-parser glm47 \
  --random-seed 42 \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 30000
```

Configuration/GPU tests (13 tests, 4 subtests) and pool-configurator tests (51 tests, 11 subtests) passed.

GSM8K: 1,314 scored questions per run, 5-shot, temperature 0, two runs with Prefill BCG enabled.

| KV dtype | MTP | Run 1 (rounded) | Run 2 (rounded) | Mean |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BF16 | Off | 95.8% | 95.9% | 95.852% |
| FP8 E4M3 | Off | 95.7% | 95.7% | 95.738% |
| BF16 | 5/1/6 | 95.4% | 95.6% | 95.472% |
| FP8 E4M3 | 5/1/6 | 95.2% | 95.2% | 95.205% |

Tested both KV dtypes with EAGLE/MTP516 by adding:

```bash
  --speculative-algorithm EAGLE \
  --speculative-num-steps 5 \
  --speculative-eagle-topk 1 \
  --speculative-num-draft-tokens 6
```

Target and draft KV use the selected dtype. Mean acceptance length was 4.15 for BF16 and 4.16 for FP8; prefill and speculative CUDA Graphs passed.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

<!-- If this pull request impacts inference speed, provide benchmarking and profiling results. -->

4 × H200, TP4/EP4, TileLang DSA, DeepGEMM MoE, EAGLE 5/1/6 and Prefill BCG. Only `--kv-cache-dtype` changes between cases.

Workload: 32,768 input / 1,024 output tokens, concurrency 8, 64 requests. Values are medians of three warmed-up runs, using mean TTFT/TPOT per run and the final KV token capacity reported at startup.

| KV dtype | KV capacity (tokens) | TTFT (ms) | TPOT (ms) | Output throughput (tok/s) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| BF16 | 607,232 | 2,664.34 | 12.76 | 518.63 |
| FP8 E4M3 | 1,177,856 | 2,804.25 | 13.35 | 495.48 |

FP8 provides **1.94× KV token capacity**. At this fixed concurrency, TTFT increases by 5.3%, TPOT by 4.6%, and output throughput decreases by 4.5%.

title: [Speculative] Support block verification for the DFlash family
author: maocheng23
body:
## Motivation

https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/42297 added `--speculative-use-block-verification` ([Block Verification Accelerates Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.10444), Algorithm 2) for linear EAGLE / EAGLE3 / NEXTN only. The DFlash family (`DFLASH`, `DSPARK`) already verifies sampled drafts through the same Triton chain sampler, but the flag was rejected for these algorithms at startup.

## Modifications

- **Startup gate** (`speculative_hook.py`): accept `DFLASH` and `DSPARK` with `--speculative-use-block-verification` on CUDA/ROCm. NPU stays rejected because `sgl_kernel_npu`'s chain sampler has no block mode. Only EAGLE/EAGLE3 still auto-enable `--speculative-use-rejection-sampling`. DFlash-family sampled paths always pass their proposal distribution and never read that flag.
- **Shared accept path** (`dspark_accept.py`): `AcceptSampling` / `accept_sampling` / `_accept_sampling_core` take an explicit `block_verification` keyword and call `chain_speculative_sampling_triton(..., block_verification=True)` when it is set. The kernel is unchanged from #42297.
- **Callers**:
  - DSpark: `DSparkWorkerV2` passes the flag to `TargetVerifyExecutor`, which forwards it through `accept_draft_tokens` to both the all-sampling branch and the mixed greedy/sampling branch.
  - DFlash: `DFlashWorkerV2._selector_sampling_accept` forwards it. This method serves the candidate-selector drafts and the sampled LiLiCorr drafts (`SGLANG_ENABLE_LILICORR_SAMPLING=1`).
- **Greedy DFlash drafts**: plain DFlash, Domino, and LiLiCorr without sampling propose argmax tokens. The proposal is a point mass, so `q(x_i) = 1`, `r_i = prod p(x_j)`, and token-wise verification already reaches the per-prefix upper bound `P(accept >= i) = r_i`. Block verification therefore accepts the same prefixes, so these paths keep the existing target-only verifier. The worker logs a warning that the flag has no effect.
- Ragged/cutoff verify (`cutoff_verify_lens`) still truncates the sampler's result afterward, as it does in token-wise mode. A prefix of a target-distributed sample is still target-distributed, so the cutoff does not affect correctness.
- Updated the docs and the CLI help.

## Accuracy Tests

- `test_block_verification_args.py`:
  - DFLASH/DSPARK are accepted, and block verification does not switch on rejection sampling for them. The per-algorithm handlers are patched out because they need a real draft checkpoint.
  - DFLASH/DSPARK on NPU are rejected.
  - The rejected-algorithm case moves from DFLASH to NGRAM.
- `test_block_verification.py::test_dflash_family_accept_uses_block_verification` (GPU): calls DSpark's real `accept_draft_tokens`, in both the all-sampling and the mixed-greedy branches. The proposal uses `q(x1) = 1, p(x1) = 1/2` and `q(x2) = 1/2, p(x2) = 1`, so `r_1 = 1/2` and `r_2 = 1`.
  - With block verification, every sampled row accepts both drafts and the bonus token from the target.
  - Without it, each row rejects the first draft with probability 1/2, so the test asserts that at least one of 63 rows does.

Local (macOS, CPU, Torch 2.14.1):

```bash
PYTHONPATH=python python -m pytest -q \
  test/registered/unit/spec/test_block_verification_args.py \
  test/registered/unit/spec/test_spec_registry.py \
  test/registered/unit/spec/test_eagle_gate_routing.py \
  test/registered/unit/spec/test_spec_cpu_overlap_constraint.py
# 45 passed, 21 subtests passed
```

GPU (one NVIDIA GB300; Torch 2.14.1+cu130, sglang-kernel 0.4.9, FlashInfer 0.7.0.post1, Triton 3.8.0, Transformers 5.17.0; source snapshot of `c8699a8046`):

```bash
python -m pytest -q \
  test/registered/kernels/ops/speculative/test_block_verification.py \
  test/registered/unit/spec/test_block_verification_args.py \
  test/registered/spec/dspark/test_dspark_kernel_parity.py
# 30 passed, 43 subtests passed
```

Pre-commit passed on all changed files.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

### Qwen3.8-27B + DFlash2 / AIME25 end-to-end

Block verification increased acceptance length on all three seed pairs, by +3.31% pooled. That is larger than the +0.88% that #42297 measured for MTP with three proposed tokens. DFlash2 proposes seven tokens per step, so there are more prefixes for block verification to rescue after an early rejection. The pooled throughput gain of +1.76% was not consistent: per seed it was +2.75%, +2.67%, and -0.29%. The accuracy and cap-hit differences are within run-to-run noise for three sampled runs.

| Metric | Token-wise | Block | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Acceptance length (includes bonus) | 4.0091 | 4.1416 | +3.31% |
| Correct drafts per verify step | 3.0091 | 3.1417 | +4.40% |
| Output throughput (tokens/s) | 1260.93 | 1283.17 | +1.76% |
| Boxed score over entire response | 76/90 | 76/90 | |
| Responses hitting the 32,768-token cap | 18/90 | 21/90 | |

| Seed | Token AL | Block AL | Token tok/s | Block tok/s | Token correct | Block correct |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 980406 | 4.0106 | 4.1573 | 1219.29 | 1252.76 | 25/30 | 24/30 |
| 981406 | 3.9919 | 4.1371 | 1260.97 | 1294.64 | 24/30 | 27/30 |
| 982406 | 4.0256 | 4.1306 | 1306.96 | 1303.13 | 27/30 | 25/30 |

**Setup**:
- **Hardware and models**: one NVIDIA GB300, TP1. Target `Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B` BF16, revision `1d4bf0f2ff`. Draft `incoai/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2`, revision `015e795645` (`DFlash2DraftModel`: candidate selector with top-k 16, block size 8).
- **Speculative settings**: `--speculative-algorithm DFLASH --speculative-num-draft-tokens 8`.
- **Server settings**: BF16 KV cache, FP32 recurrent state, FlashInfer attention, CUDA graphs on, radix cache off, concurrency 8.
- **The two arms**: they run identical commands, except that the block arm adds `--speculative-use-block-verification`. The server log confirms that selector sampling is folded into the draft CUDA graph (`sampling_enabled=True`), and neither arm logged the no-effect warning.

**Protocol**: same as #42297.
- **Workload**: all 30 MathArena/aime_2025 questions, with the same frozen dataset (SHA256 `b4bdeba5...`). Thinking is enabled at xhigh. Sampling uses temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, and top-k 20, with at most 32,768 new tokens.
- **Seeds and arm order**: three base seeds, offset by problem ID. Arm order alternates by seed.
- **Warmup**: each run warms up eight slots and flushes the cache before timing.
- **Metrics**: acceptance length is total completion tokens divided by total verification steps. Throughput is total output tokens divided by measured wall time. An independent pass over the raw per-request records reproduced every aggregate and checked request coverage, the sampling seeds, and that the commands match.

### Qwen3.8-27B + DSpark / AIME25 end-to-end

DSpark shows the same effect. Block verification increased acceptance length on all three seed pairs, by +3.13% pooled (+3.02%, +2.42%, +3.96% per seed). Throughput was flat at +0.54% pooled, and per seed it was +1.51%, +0.42%, and -0.45%. Other jobs were running on the same node's other GPUs during this run, so its throughput is noisier than the DFlash2 run's. The differences in score and cap hits are within run-to-run noise for three sampled runs.

| Metric | Token-wise | Block | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Acceptance length (includes bonus) | 4.0134 | 4.1390 | +3.13% |
| Correct drafts per verify step | 3.0135 | 3.1393 | +4.17% |
| Output throughput (tokens/s) | 1296.61 | 1303.58 | +0.54% |
| Boxed score over entire response | 77/90 | 82/90 | |
| Responses hitting the 32,768-token cap | 19/90 | 17/90 | |

| Seed | Token AL | Block AL | Token tok/s | Block tok/s | Token correct | Block correct |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 980406 | 4.0068 | 4.1278 | 1269.98 | 1289.17 | 25/30 | 27/30 |
| 981406 | 4.0597 | 4.1582 | 1283.60 | 1288.97 | 26/30 | 27/30 |
| 982406 | 3.9731 | 4.1306 | 1337.45 | 1331.40 | 26/30 | 28/30 |

**Setup**: same code, image, target model, server settings, and protocol as the DFlash2 run above. The differences are:
- **Speculative settings**: `--speculative-algorithm DSPARK` with draft `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-27B-DSpark`, revision `b9a5dbdf03` (`DSparkDraftModel` with a vanilla Markov head and a confidence head). Gamma 7 is read from the checkpoint, so the verify window is 8. `SGLANG_RAGGED_VERIFY_MODE` is left at its default, `static`.
- **The two arms**: they run identical commands, except that the block arm adds `--speculative-use-block-verification`. Every server logged `DSpark draft proposal (greedy + sampling) folded into the draft cuda graph`, so the sampling batches drafted from `softmax(corrected_logits / T)` and verified on the eager accept path, where the flag is wired. The folded in-graph accept serves all-greedy batches only.
- **Audit**: an independent pass over the raw per-request records reproduced every aggregate.

### Sampler

No kernel change. The sampler cost is the block-mode cost measured in #42297. Paths that do not opt in are unchanged: the flag defaults to off, and greedy DFlash drafts never reach the block sampler.

## Checklist

- [x] Format code with pre-commit.
- [x] Add registered unit tests.
- [x] Update documentation.
- [x] End-to-end acceptance-length and throughput comparison for DFlash2 and DSpark.
- [x] Follow SGLang code style.

title: [Diffusion] Add ModelOpt FP8 checkpoint quantization for Pi0.5
author: trebladev
body:
## Motivation

Add Pi0.5 checkpoint calibration and native FP8 inference using SGLang’s existing ModelOpt FP8 linear backend.

The quantization coverage and synthetic calibration recipe follow https://jetson-ai-lab.com/tutorials/openpi\_on\_thor/.

## Modifications

- Add a calibration/export tool supporting observation datasets and explicitly selected synthetic inputs.
- Quantize PaliGemma and action-expert fused projections, SigLIP encoder projections, the multimodal projector, and action input/output heads using per-tensor E4M3 weights and static activation scales.
- Preserve existing tensor/tuple interfaces and output dtypes. Keep embeddings, convolutions, norms, AdaRMS dense layers, and time MLPs unquantized.
- Add checkpoint validation, projection replacement, and FP8 weight finalization.
- Support resident BF16 inference on a single SM89+ NVIDIA GPU; reject TP/SP and component offload.
- Add CPU contract tests and a CUDA calibration, checkpoint-loading, and graph-replay test.

## Accuracy Tests

Validated on RTX 4090 D with PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130, ModelOpt 0.47.0, and Transformers 5.12.1.

- Full Pi0.5 Libero checkpoint: calibrated all five supported components using one synthetic observation, then validated on four separate synthetic observations.

Consistency metrics use only the **10 predicted steps and 7 returned action dimensions**:

| Comparison | Mean absolute difference | Maximum absolute difference | Cosine similarity |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| BF16 vs native FP8 | 0\.008364 | 0\.100873 | 0\.999526 |
| Fake quant vs native FP8 | 0\.006177 | 0\.059110 | — |

Cosine similarity flattens the four observations into one vector. Per-observation BF16/FP8 cosine similarities range from **0\.999384 to 0.999659**.

All returned actions were finite. Eager and CUDA Graph outputs matched exactly for both BF16 and FP8 across the four observations, including changed inputs.

These results validate numerical behavior on synthetic observations. Real robot task accuracy and success rates have not been evaluated.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Measured full Pi0.5 Libero model inference on one RTX 4090 D, batch size 1, three 224×224 camera inputs, 200 tokens, and 10 denoising steps, using `torch_sdpa`.

Each mode uses 5 warmup runs and 30 timed runs with CUDA synchronization. Timing includes prefix encoding and action sampling from preprocessed inputs, without prefix-cache reuse. It excludes preprocessing, network overhead, checkpoint loading, and initial graph capture.

| Mode | BF16 median latency | FP8 median latency | BF16/FP8 speedup | BF16 peak allocated memory | FP8 peak allocated memory |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Eager | 248\.44 ms | 360\.67 ms | 0\.69× | 6\.71 GiB | 4\.22 GiB |
| CUDA Graph | 70\.97 ms | 55\.53 ms | 1\.28× | 6\.72 GiB | 4\.22 GiB |

CUDA Graph latency decreased by **21\.8%**, with **37\.2% lower peak allocated memory**. Eager latency increased by **45\.2%**; the measured speed improvement applies to CUDA Graph execution.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit (https://docs.sglang.io/developer\_guide/contribution\_guide.html\#format-code-with-pre-commit)](<https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit>). All applicable hooks passed.
- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests (https://docs.sglang.io/developer\_guide/contribution\_guide.html\#run-and-add-unit-tests)](<https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests>).
- [ ] Update documentation according to [Write documentations (https://docs.sglang.io/developer\_guide/contribution\_guide.html\#write-documentations)](<https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations>).
- [ ] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy (https://docs.sglang.io/developer\_guide/contribution\_guide.html\#test-the-accuracy)](<https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy>) and [Benchmark the speed (https://docs.sglang.io/developer\_guide/contribution\_guide.html\#benchmark-the-speed)](<https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed>). Synthetic consistency and latency results are included; real-task accuracy remains unverified.
- [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance (https://docs.sglang.io/developer\_guide/contribution\_guide.html\#code-style-guidance)](<https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance>).

title: [Perf] gdn: Select FlashInfer prefill for page-major pools
author: caihuali95
body:
This PR is part of a stack (oldest at bottom):

* #44973
* #44972
* #44971
* #44970
* #44969
* #43326
* #43325
* __->__ #43171
* #43170
* #43168

Current head `7006d22143`, based on main `ba50ea3d77`. Stack predecessor: #43170. This PR targets `main` after its stack predecessor merged.

## Motivation

`flashinfer_gdn_prefill_default` declined whenever `enable_page_major_kv_layout` was set. `--enable-unified-memory` runs page-major, so Qwen3.5 GDN prefill stayed on the Triton chunk kernels there while the default pool on the same GPU auto-selected FlashInfer. On SM90 (Qwen3.5-9B, page size 256, no speculative decoding) unified prefill cycles ran +1.24..+1.41% longer than the default pool's at matched batch size, all of it GPU time: the Triton chunk kernels cost +17.8 ms per cycle where the FlashInfer GDN kernels cost 10.7 ms. End to end that was -1.1..-1.5% throughput on every attention backend.

## Modifications

Explicit `--linear-attn-prefill-backend flashinfer` is accepted by the page-major gate, matching automatic GDN selection. The test covers this explicit configuration.

`layers/attention/linear/gdn_backend.py`: page-major no longer disqualifies the FlashInfer prefill. For prefill the layout does not matter: `forward_extend` gathers a non-contiguous pool's conv and SSM state into contiguous per-sequence copies before any prefill kernel runs and scatters them back after (`needs_state_gather`), so FlashInfer's extend sees the same contiguous, identity-indexed state as on the default pool. Decode and verify are unaffected; their backends resolve separately (verify follows decode, Triton by default).

Test (`test_gdn_prefill_backend_policy.py`): `test_selects_flashinfer_for_a_page_major_pool` (SM100 with a bf16 state, SM90 with an fp32 state) fails before (the policy returns None) and passes after; page-major leaves `test_rejects_unvalidated_runtime_modes`.

## Accuracy Tests

Earlier combined stack `b550cacde6` adds a test-fixture correction in #43326: the Gemma4 read-stream fixture declares its FULL address space, and the HiSparse registry test uses real `CacheInitParams` for the retained-window calculation. Both complete test files pass locally with GPUs hidden: 4 Gemma4 tests and 26 registry tests. Pre-commit passed. The five descendant patches are unchanged (`git range-diff`); this follow-up changes no production code. The earlier 455-test run did not cover these two files; GitHub CI has not yet been revalidated for this head.

Validation before the test-fixture follow-up, on combined stack `4cf27a551c`: 455 tests and 921 subtests passed on B300, plus the two widened-history regressions against Rust TreeCore. The new FULL-fallback metadata cases cover eager execution and CUDA graph replay. New allocation-reclaim, explicit-prefill and JIT-reuse regressions fail on the previous code and pass with the fixes. These are combined-stack checks, not independent model reruns of each PR.

The measurements in this section are historical results from before this rebase, at the revisions/configurations stated below. Current combined-stack validation is linked above.

SM90, TP1, Qwen3.5-9B, no speculation, page size 256, radix cache, overlap scheduler, CUDA graphs on, `--mem-fraction-static 0.8`. Baseline: the default pool. Unified: `--enable-unified-memory`. Every unified server now logs `Linear attention kernel backend: decode=triton, prefill=flashinfer, verify=triton`, as the default pool's does (on main its unified servers log `prefill=triton`). These ran on this commit over main 7224fce1b5. GSM8K, all 1314 test questions, 5-shot, greedy:

| attention backend | baseline | unified |
|---|---|---|
| fa3 | 0.896 | 0.898 |
| flashinfer | 0.899 | 0.895 |
| triton | 0.896 | 0.893 |

GPU unit tests for unified memory: 4102 passed, 0 failed.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

title: [Perf] Enable fast-math for JIT activations on Blackwell
author: zcnrex
body:
## Motivation

On Blackwell the JIT activation kernels are built without fast-math. For SiLU, `x / (1 + expf(-x))` then compiles to an IEEE division. In the SASS (sm_103a, default 16-element vector), every element gets its own `BSSY`/`BSYNC` region: `MUFU.EX2` → `MUFU.RCP` → Newton `FFMA`s → `FCHK` → conditional `CALL` to the division slow path. That is 16 `FCHK`s and 16 `CALL`s per thread, so the elements run back to back instead of interleaving (~46 ns per element on B300). At decode sizes there are too few warps to hide this, and SiLU-and-mul costs 1.7–1.8 µs/layer even for a single token.

The precise-math choice was not specific to activation. The AOT sgl-kernel stopped using `-use_fast_math` for SM100 builds when Blackwell FP8 blockwise GEMM landed (#4278, #4376), and #10701 later split AOT `common_ops` into an SM90 fast-math build and an SM100+ precise build. The JIT activation (#22094) mirrored that policy. Hopper has always run these kernels with fast-math.

## Modifications

`get_activation_cuda_cflags()` now returns `["--use_fast_math"]` whenever `is_cuda()`, and `[]` otherwise. That drops the SM100+ exception. Fast-math turns the IEEE division into a branch-free approximate one, uses the approximate `expf`, and flushes subnormals to zero.

**Affected kernels:** everything built with these flags.
- The gated activations (`silu_and_mul`, `gelu_and_mul`, `gelu_tanh_and_mul`).
- `relu2` when called with its default `fast_math=True`. Callers that need BF16 subnormals already pass `fast_math=False` (e.g. Cosmos3).
- `situ_and_mul`.

The rounding variants (`*_with_activation_rounding`) still build the precise `rounded_activation` module. HIP still gets no fast-math. MUSA previously received `--use_fast_math`; it now follows whatever `is_cuda()` returns under `torchada`, which I have not tested.

## Accuracy Tests

**Kernel numerics.** Outputs on Blackwell are **not** bitwise identical to main. The difference is almost entirely flush-to-zero of BF16 subnormal results: BF16 shares fp32's exponent range, so BF16 subnormals are fp32 subnormals.

Exhaustive check of SiLU-and-mul on B300 over all 65,536 gate bit patterns, fast-math against precise, with 7 `up` cases (±1, 0.5, 3, randn ×2, randn×100):

| dtype | outputs that differ | what they are |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BF16 | 0.78–1.22% | Precise gives a subnormal and fast-math gives 0, at \|g\| < 1e-36 or g < −80. Over the 47,819 gates in −80 ≤ g, \|g\| ≥ 1e-36 there are 0 differences at `up=1` and one 1-ulp rounding flip with random `up`. |
| FP16 | 1–3 values | 1-ulp rounding flips (FP16 subnormals are normal in fp32, so there is no FTZ effect) |

Against an fp64 reference rounded to BF16 (`up=1`), precise is correctly rounded on 65,263 / 65,280 finite outputs and fast-math on 64,752. The gap is the flushed subnormals. GELU, GELU-tanh, ReLU² and SiTU were covered by the unit tests below, not by an exhaustive sweep.

**End-to-end.** `test_inkling_small_nvfp4.py` (Inkling-Small-NVFP4, TP4, DSpark speculative decoding, `--enable-deterministic-inference`) asserts bitwise prefill/decode logprob consistency. In this server the JIT SiLU runs in the DSpark draft model. On 4× B300, with #43447 applied:

| build | three KL checks (`avg_kl_div`) | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| this PR (fast-math) | 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 | 3 passed |
| main policy (precise) | 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 | 3 passed |

The earlier CI failure of this test (KL 0.0015) was the main regression from #41887, fixed in #43447 after this branch's last merge of main. On the unfixed base, fast-math and precise both gave the identical KL (0.00013463538375007566 on B300) across four sequential runs.

**Unit tests on B300:**

| test | result |
| --- | --- |
| `kernels/ops/activation/test_activation.py` | 452 passed, 6 skipped |
| `kernels/ops/activation/test_situ_and_mul.py` | 1 passed |
| `kernels/ops/moe/test_situ_and_mul_quant.py` | 1 passed |
| `kernels/ops/diffusion/test_activation.py` | 10 passed |
| `kernels/ops/diffusion/test_cosmos3_edge_fusions.py` | 4 passed, 3 skipped |
| `unit/kernels/test_kernels_namespace.py` | 71 passed |

## Speed Tests and Profiling

**Setup:** one B300 (sm_103, 148 SMs), BF16 SiLU-and-mul, activation only: 36 disjoint layer buffers captured in one CUDA graph, 20 replays, median of 11 runs. Main and this PR alternated 3× on the same GPU.

| hidden × tokens | main µs/layer | this PR µs/layer | speedup |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2432 × 8 | 1.77 | 1.14 | 1.55x |
| 3584 × 32 | 1.94 | 1.31 | 1.48x |
| 9728 × 8 | 1.94 | 1.31 | 1.48x |
| 9728 × 128 | 3.52 | 2.64 | 1.33x |
| 13824 × 512 | 9.01 | 7.62 | 1.18x |
| 9728 × 2048 | 21.10 | 18.73 | 1.13x |
| 13824 × 2048 | 28.73 | 25.97 | 1.11x |

Over 28 shapes (hidden 2432/3584/9728/13824 × tokens 1–2048), the total drops from 134.6 to 108.8 µs. Every shape is at least 1.11x faster.

These are kernel timings, not serving-throughput gains. Only B300 was measured; Hopper already built with fast-math and is unchanged.

## Checklist

- [x] Repository pre-commit checks pass.
- [x] B300 unit tests, exhaustive numerics comparison, and Inkling-Small-NVFP4 determinism test.
- [ ] Upstream CI and review.

title: [Perf] [XPU] server_args: Enable fused QK-norm + RoPE by default
author: mehersai07
body:
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->

## Motivation

[#40190](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40190) wired the fused QK-norm + RoPE kernel (`sgl_kernel.fused_inplace_qknorm_rope`) into Qwen3-MoE on XPU behind the existing opt-in `--enable-fused-qk-norm-rope`. Its A/B on Qwen3-30B-A3B (TP=4, 4x Arc Pro B60) showed +4.7-7.0% output throughput, -60% q/k-norm + RoPE stage device time, and no accuracy change (GSM8K 0.9414 vs 0.9460).
The flag is opt-in on CUDA for a reason that does not apply to XPU: on CUDA the unfused path already fuses RoPE with the KV-cache write (`fused_set_kv_buffer`), and the fused QK-norm path gives that up. `enable_fused_set_kv_buffer` is CUDA/HIP-only, so the XPU unfused path has nothing to lose. This PR makes the fused path the XPU default; everything else is unchanged.

## Modifications

- `arg_groups/fields/exec_.py`: `enable_fused_qk_norm_rope` becomes a tri-state (`Optional[bool] = None`, `BooleanOptionalAction`, `resolvable=True`), the same shape as `enable_dsa_fused_indexer`. `--enable-fused-qk-norm-rope` keeps working; `--no-enable-fused-qk-norm-rope` is the new opt-out.
- `arg_groups/platform_hook.py`: `handle_xpu_backends` declares `enable_fused_qk_norm_rope=True` when the device is XPU and the user did not choose, next to the existing XPU `sampling_backend` default.
- Docs: the flag's rows in `server_arguments.mdx` and the Ascend support table.

On every other platform the field stays `None`. Its two readers (`qwen3_moe.py`, `mellum.py`) use it only in `and` chains and truthiness checks, so `None` behaves exactly like the old `False`. No model code changes.

One visible difference: off XPU, `/get_server_info` now reports `enable_fused_qk_norm_rope: null` instead of `false`, matching how `enable_dsa_fused_indexer` reports.

## Accuracy Tests

No new numerics: the kernel and call site are the ones #40190 measured (GSM8K above). The nightly `test/registered/xpu/llm_models/test_xpu_qwen3_30b_a3b.py` (TP=4 GSM8K, threshold 0.90) now runs the fused path by default.

Resolution, checked through `prepare_server_args` + `resolve_once()`:

| device | flag | resolved |
|---|---|---|
| xpu | none | `True` |
| xpu | `--enable-fused-qk-norm-rope` | `True` |
| xpu | `--no-enable-fused-qk-norm-rope` | `False` |
| non-XPU | none | `None` (off) |
| non-XPU | `--enable-fused-qk-norm-rope` / `--no-enable-fused-qk-norm-rope` | `True` / `False` |

title: [Perf] moe: Extend FlashInfer CUTLASS MoE autotune coverage to prefill chunks
author: JackChuang
body:
## Summary

**TL;DR: This PR enables sglang's startup autotune to tune FlashInfer's CUTLASS MoE kernel for prefill sizes too, not only for decode sizes.** sglang already autotunes this kernel (`cutlass_fused_moe`, FlashInfer's MoE kernel, not its attention backend) at startup, but each call tells FlashInfer to tune only up to its own token count. The startup run is one decode-sized batch, so only decode sizes get a tuned kernel configuration (tactic), and prefill chunks above that size run FlashInfer's untuned fallback tactic (its default kernel configuration). This PR gives FlashInfer one tuning range per server instead: the largest prefill batch the MoE layer sees (chunk size × attention data-parallel size, capped at 8192, FlashInfer's own default range for this call), so the same startup autotune also covers prefill. No new flag, kernel or extra pass. It applies on every GPU this kernel runs on (SM90, SM100, SM110, SM120), where it is the default MoE kernel of DeepSeek-V4.1/V4, Ling-3.0, Nemotron-H, gpt-oss and ModelOpt NVFP4 MoE models (which GPU for which model: Design notes), and to any other MoE model that runs on it. Other MoE kernels and the decode servers of prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation are unchanged. Measured on H200 (SM90).

- **Performance** (H200): faster prefill on all seven MoE models measured (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Nemotron-3.5, Ling-3.0, gpt-oss-20b, GLM-5.3-Flash, MiniMax-M3, Gemma-4): TTFT (time to first token) for 8k-token prompts **30.3–57.8% lower** (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: 573.9 → 400.0 ms, **30.3%**), for 32k-token prompts **23.0–52.8% lower**, prefill throughput **43.4–143.4% higher**; decode ITL (inter-token latency) unchanged on the three models measured for it. It complements open PR #42736 (an extra startup tuning pass): with both, 8k-token TTFT on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is **24.7% lower** than with #42736 alone.
- **Accuracy:** unchanged by design (only the tile configuration, or tactic, of the same GEMM changes); GSM8K on all seven models and the DeepSeek-V4-Flash CI GSM8K test stays within the 95% noise range (−0.83 to +0.15 points on the seven models).
- **Cost:** a longer startup autotune when no saved results exist: 41–42 → 176–177 s on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 8×H200 (server ready 153–154 → 288–289 s), 116 → 604 s on Ling-3.0-flash, and 4–26 s more on the other five models. Saved results are reused on one GPU, but multi-GPU servers currently re-tune at every start; `--disable-flashinfer-autotune` turns the startup autotune off. Each GPU has 0.4–1.2 GiB (0.3–0.9% of an H200) less free memory while the server runs, mostly the buffer FlashInfer keeps for timing tactics at startup, now sized for the prefill chunk instead of the decode batch; the KV cache size is unchanged. PD decode servers pay nothing.

## Motivation

sglang runs FlashInfer's autotune at startup (#12306, on by default since #14357). For `cutlass_fused_moe`, FlashInfer keeps one tactic per token-count bucket (powers of two up to 256, then larger steps up to 8192: 21 buckets) and tunes every bucket up to the caller's `tune_max_num_tokens`; the same value also decides which bucket a call uses. Both sglang call sites (the `flashinfer_cutlass` runner, used for BF16, FP8 and NVFP4 experts, and the CUTLASS path of `flashinfer_mxfp4`, used for MXFP4 experts) pass `next_power_of_2(x.shape[0])`, which dates from #7327, before the startup autotune existed. This has two effects:

1. **Prefill runs an untuned tactic.** The startup batch is decode-sized, one token per request up to the request limit (256 tokens on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, 138 on Nemotron-3.5-Lightning, 4096 on gpt-oss-20b), so nothing above that size is tuned: an 8k-token chunk maps to bucket 8192 and gets FlashInfer's fallback tactic. The server log shows nothing, because sglang sets FlashInfer's logger to ERROR.
2. **The tactic depends on earlier requests.** Every `cutlass_fused_moe` call that runs Python code (the startup autotune, CUDA graph capture, and every serving forward that is not a CUDA graph replay) first calls `MoERunner.refine_tuning_config(tune_max_num_tokens)`. That method is wrapped in `functools.lru_cache` and rebuilds FlashInfer's class-wide bucket list only the first time it sees a value, so a call with a value seen before keeps the list built for the latest new value. On DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with `--cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 64`, the first decode batch of 65–128 requests while serving runs without a CUDA graph and rebuilds the list for 128 tokens (a short prompt of a new size likewise rebuilds it, for its own size); later prefill chunks of an already-seen size, such as every 8k-token chunk after the first, then run the 128-token bucket's tactic, because a list built for 128 tokens ends at bucket 128 and every larger call falls into that last bucket.

flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#5625 was filed by an sglang user who hit both effects serving DeepSeek-V4-Flash on 4×H100 with `flashinfer_mxfp4`. One value for the whole server, computed from its configuration and used by every call, as large as the largest prefill batch (up to 8192 tokens), removes both.

## Modifications

- **`python/sglang/srt/layers/moe/moe_runner/flashinfer_cutlass.py`** -- the new `_cutlass_moe_tune_max_num_tokens(num_tokens)` gives both `cutlass_fused_moe` calls their `tune_max_num_tokens`: `min(prefill chunk size × attention DP size, 8192)`, with the chunk size (`--chunked-prefill-size`, or `--max-prefill-tokens` when chunked prefill is off) read the way `flashinfer_autotune.py` already does (`max_prefill_buffer_tokens() or get_schedule().max_prefill_tokens`). PD decode servers keep `next_power_of_2(num_tokens)`.
- **`test/registered/unit/layers/moe/test_flashinfer_cutlass_swiglu_params.py`** (CPU suite) -- new `TestCutlassMoeTuneMaxNumTokens`. With the kernel stubbed, it checks at both calls that token counts 1, 257, 777, 2048, 4097, 8192 and 16384 map to a bucket the startup autotune tunes, in five server configurations, and that PD decode servers keep the per-call value. 60 of its 80 sub-cases fail on main.
- **`test/registered/unit/layers/quantization/test_mxfp4_sm{90,120}_cutlass.py`, `test/registered/unit/layers/moe/test_moe_runner_config_placement.py`** -- their fused-MoE calls now run inside `get_context().override_server_args()`, because the helper reads the server configuration.

Design notes:

- Where this kernel is the default MoE path: on SM90 and SM120, DeepSeek-V4.1/V4 and Ling-3.0 (MXFP4 experts, through `flashinfer_mxfp4`) and BF16/FP8 Nemotron-H (`flashinfer_cutlass`); on SM120 also gpt-oss and ModelOpt NVFP4 MoE models, the latter on SM110 too since #41765. On SM100 no model uses it by default (`flashinfer_mxfp4` runs a TRT-LLM kernel there). Any other MoE model reaches it with `--moe-runner-backend flashinfer_cutlass` (BF16, ModelOpt FP8/NVFP4) or `flashinfer_mxfp4` (MXFP4).
- DP attention: sglang splits `--chunked-prefill-size` across the DP ranks, and the MoE layer runs on the tokens gathered from all of them, so the largest batch the MoE layer sees is each rank's chunk × the DP size, which is the `--chunked-prefill-size` the user set.
- The 8192 cap is a choice, not a limit on chunk size: it is FlashInfer's own default range for this call, and chunks larger than 8192 tokens still run, using bucket 8192's tactic, which in a one-layer test with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash's MoE shape is as fast as a tactic tuned for each larger size (One MoE call, under Experimental Results); tuning beyond 8192 would only lengthen startup. Omitting the argument would also give one value, but PD decode servers and servers with smaller chunks would then tune sizes they never use.
- Servers whose startup decode batch is above 8192 tokens (for example attention DP 8 with the default request limit) tune fewer buckets than main and start faster, at no MoE run-time cost: main cannot use those larger buckets at run time either (item 2), and in a one-layer test bucket 8192's tactic is about as fast as each size's own tactic at 12288–32768 tokens (One MoE call, under Experimental Results).

## Experimental Results

### Performance

Setup: **in every prefill row below, every server with this PR beats every server without it** (main, or #42736 alone). Every number in this section was measured with this PR's code at head `a4c96d4080f` on main `c7f3ae1dd59` (H200, CUDA 13.0, torch 2.14.1, FlashInfer 0.7.0.post1). Every measurement starts a new server for each version, alternating which goes first; each value is the median over server starts (for TTFT, of each server's median over the 8 prompts). TTFT rows send 8 random prompts one at a time (2k, 8k and 32k mean 2,000, 8,000 and 32,000 tokens; percentages are computed from unrounded medians). Prompts are prefilled in chunks of 8192 tokens (`--chunked-prefill-size 8192`, set on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and the default on the other models here), so a 32k prompt runs as four chunks and every MoE call has at most 8192 tokens. With this chunk size this PR's tuning range is also 8192 (it follows the chunk size; the 8192 cap is FlashInfer's default range for this call, see Design notes); throughput rows send 64 prompts at 8 concurrent requests with 1 output token, so they measure prefill throughput (`bench_serving` total token throughput). Launch commands are under Commands below; settings not listed there are the defaults.

This table measures the main claim: on a newly started main server, prefill chunks larger than the startup decode batch run FlashInfer's untuned fallback tactic (Motivation, item 1), and with this PR a tuned one. Result: **on all seven models, TTFT is 30.3–57.8% lower (8k-token prompts) and 23.0–52.8% lower (32k), and prefill throughput 43.4–143.4% higher.**

**Prefill speed, all models** (each server newly started; main → this PR, improvement; +% = this PR better)

| Model (expert weights), GPUs, MoE runner | TTFT, 8k-token prompts (ms) | TTFT, 32k-token prompts (ms) | Prefill throughput, 8k-token prompts (tok/s) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (MXFP4 experts), 8×H200, `flashinfer_mxfp4` (default) | 573.9 → 400.0 (**+30.3%**) | 2,685.0 → 1,994.3 (**+25.7%**) | 14,755 → 21,154 (**+43.4%**) |
| Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B (BF16), 1×H200, `flashinfer_cutlass` (default) | 309.1 → 136.6 (**+55.8%**) | 1,227.5 → 599.9 (**+51.1%**) | 27,320 → 63,131 (**+131.1%**) |
| Ling-3.0-flash (MXFP4 experts), 1×H200, `flashinfer_mxfp4` (default) | 430.4 → 254.7 (**+40.8%**) | 1,761.0 → 1,073.3 (**+39.1%**) | 18,961 → 31,557 (**+66.4%**) |
| gpt-oss-20b (MXFP4 experts), 1×H200, `flashinfer_mxfp4` ¹ | 422.0 → 177.9 (**+57.8%**) | 1,790.9 → 846.2 (**+52.8%**) | 20,301 → 49,408 (**+143.4%**) |
| GLM-5.3-Flash (BF16), 8×H200, `flashinfer_cutlass` | 495.1 → 250.3 (**+49.5%**) | 1,896.4 → 1,019.3 (**+46.3%**) | 17,160 → 34,122 (**+98.8%**) |
| MiniMax-M3 (BF16), 8×H200, `flashinfer_cutlass` ² | 631.2 → 294.4 (**+53.4%**) | 2,547.0 → 1,224.8 (**+51.9%**) | 13,657 → 30,302 (**+121.9%**) |
| Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it (BF16), 1×H200, `flashinfer_cutlass` | 408.3 → 244.3 (**+40.2%**) | 2,798.8 → 2,156.1 (**+23.0%**) | 19,978 → 34,302 (**+71.7%**) |

Runners not marked "(default)" are set with `--moe-runner-backend`. ¹ With gpt-oss's default request limit of 4096, main already tunes buckets up to 4096; this PR adds bucket 8192. ² Both versions also run `--disable-prefill-cuda-graph`: capturing MiniMax-M3's prefill CUDA graph fails at startup on main too.

**DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on a server that has already served traffic** (+% = this PR better)

On main, the tactic a prefill chunk gets depends on what the server has served before (Motivation, item 2). On a newly started server (the table above), an 8k chunk gets FlashInfer's untuned fallback tactic. After one decode batch larger than the CUDA graph limit (here 65–128 requests, above `--cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 64`), later 8k chunks get the tactic tuned for 128 tokens instead: faster than the fallback, but not tuned for 8k. This PR uses the tactic tuned for its 8192-token chunks in both cases. A long-running main server stays in whichever state its last new batch size left it: a busy server whose decode batches often exceed the CUDA graph limit tends to end in the second state, a lightly loaded one in the first. This test measures the second case. Both servers first get the same requests (listed under Commands), and every main server's log shows such a batch.

Result: **this PR is faster in both cases.** main's 8k-token TTFT is 573.9 ms on a new server and 496.5 ms after this traffic; this PR's is 400.0 ms and 398.2 ms:

| Benchmark | main | this PR | improvement |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| TTFT, 8k-token prompts (ms) | 496.5 | 398.2 | **+19.8%** |
| TTFT, 32k-token prompts (ms) | 2,383.5 | 1,991.9 | **+16.4%** |
| Prefill throughput, 8k-token prompts (tok/s) | 17,152 | 21,152 | **+23.3%** |

This table measures the two costs of tuning more buckets, a longer startup autotune and a larger buffer for timing tactics, and checks the KV cache size. Result: **the KV cache size is unchanged, and each GPU gives up 0.4–1.2 GiB (0.3–0.9% of an H200)**; with no saved results, the startup autotune takes 4–26 s more on five models, about 135 s more on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (8×H200, paid at every start) and 488 s more on Ling-3.0-flash (1×H200, paid once).

**Cost of this PR: startup time and GPU memory** (main → this PR, from the server logs of the servers above)

| Model | Tuned buckets per MoE GEMM | FlashInfer autotune at startup, no saved results (s) ³ | Free memory per GPU after startup, lowest GPU (GiB; in parentheses, the extra memory this PR uses as a share of the H200's 140.4 GiB, so here + is a cost) | KV cache size (tokens), unchanged |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, 8×H200 | 9 → 21 | 41–42 → 176–177 | 20.72 → 19.64 (+0.77%) | 21,542,656 |
| Nemotron-3.5-Lightning, 1×H200 | 9 → 21 | 6–7 → 21–22 | 12.46 → 11.88 (+0.41%) | 6,137,490 |
| Ling-3.0-flash, 1×H200 | 8 → 21 | 116 → 604 | 11.80 → 11.37 (+0.31%) | 4,239,637 |
| gpt-oss-20b, 1×H200 | 20 → 21 | 132 → 157–158 | 5.78 → 5.28 (+0.36%) | 2,641,507 |
| GLM-5.3-Flash, 8×H200 | 9 → 21 | 7–8 → 17 | 16.28–16.48 → 15.27 (+0.72–0.86%) | 2,118,400 |
| MiniMax-M3, 8×H200 | 16 → 21 | 16–17 → 21 | 9.88 → 9.15 (+0.52%) | 407,296 |
| Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, 1×H200 | 16 → 21 | 11 → 18–19 | 20.88 → 20.38 (+0.36%) | 382,802 |

³ This column leaves out each model's first start after download, whose autotune window also JIT-compiled other kernels (main: Ling-3.0 170 s, GLM-5.3-Flash 61 s, Gemma-4 33 s); that start's other values are included.

The extra memory is mostly the buffer FlashInfer uses at startup to time each candidate tactic. It is sized for the largest token count being tuned: the prefill chunk size with this PR (capped at 8192, so 8192 tokens in these measurements) instead of the decode batch size on main, and FlashInfer keeps it while the server runs. The KV cache is sized before the startup autotune runs, so its size is unchanged and the buffer comes out of the memory left outside it.

**Together with open PR #42736** (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, same setup; **baseline: main with #42736 applied**). This shows what this PR adds when both land: #42736 adds a startup pass that tunes the same 21 prefill-sized buckets, and this PR makes the prefill calls use them, so the two work well together, and **the improvements are what this PR adds on top of #42736's own gain** (#42736's own gain over main, from a separate set of server starts: 8k-token TTFT 574.8 → 522.7 ms, 9.1% lower): with both, 8k-token TTFT is **24.7% lower** than with #42736 alone (527.1 → 396.8 ms), and **19.8% lower** on a server that has already served the traffic above (497.0 → 398.7 ms). For this kernel's prefill, both together match this PR alone (396.8 vs 400.0 ms; 398.7 vs 398.2 ms after the traffic), as this PR already tunes the same buckets; #42736 also tunes other FlashInfer operations. This combination was measured on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash; since both PRs act on the same buckets in the same way, the other models above should also gain on top of #42736 (expected from the mechanism; not measured here).

<details>
<summary>Together with #42736: table and mechanism (baseline: main + #42736; +% = with both better)</summary>

#42736 at its head `ef17b191caf0` (2026-10-06), on the same main. Startup is the same for #42736 alone, this PR alone and both (autotune 176–179 s, 21 buckets).

| Benchmark | #42736 alone | #42736 + this PR | improvement |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| TTFT, 8k-token prompts (ms) | 527.1 | 396.8 | **+24.7%** |
| TTFT, 32k-token prompts (ms) | 2,511.8 | 1,996.8 | **+20.5%** |
| Prefill throughput, 8k-token prompts (tok/s) | 16,006 | 21,152 | **+32.2%** |
| After the traffic above: TTFT, 8k-token prompts (ms) | 497.0 | 398.7 | **+19.8%** |
| Same: TTFT, 32k-token prompts (ms) | 2,376.5 | 2,003.6 | **+15.7%** |
| Same: prefill throughput, 8k-token prompts (tok/s) | 17,157 | 21,190 | **+23.5%** |

With #42736 alone, CUDA graph capture runs after its extra pass and captures from the largest batch down to 1 (`decode_cuda_graph_runner.py`), so FlashInfer's cached bucket list ends as the 1-token list (item 2) and the prefill calls look up small buckets even though the large ones are tuned; this PR's fixed range makes them find the tuned large bucket. A profile agrees (TP rank 0, three 8k-token prefills): every MoE GEMM runs a 64×16 or 128×16 tile with #42736 alone and a 128×64 tile with both; per prefill both MoE GEMMs together take 123 → 58 ms, the all-reduce that waits for them 119 → 75 ms, and the GPU time 480 → 370 ms (22.9% less). FlashInfer does not log the bucket, so the list state is inferred from the code and the tile shapes. #42736 also tunes other FlashInfer operations; this PR does not overlap with that part.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Decode (+% = this PR better)</summary>

This PR targets prefill, but it also changes the tuning range that decode calls pass, so this checks that decode does not get slower. Result: **decode ITL is unchanged on all three models**, and TTFT and throughput improve, mostly at 8 and 32 concurrent requests, where several 2k-token prompts are prefilled together in batches of up to 8192 tokens, sizes main leaves untuned.

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, newly started servers running 1, then 8, then 32 concurrent requests; 2k-token prompts, 256 output tokens.

| Concurrent requests | median ITL (ms) | throughput (tok/s) | TTFT (ms) |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1 | 7.48 → 7.24 (+3.2%) | 1,085 → 1,121 (+3.3%) | 168.0 → 162.0 (+3.6%) |
| 8 | 9.68 → 9.67 (+0.1%) | 5,186 → 5,615 (+8.3%) | 978.9 → 725.4 (+25.9%) |
| 32 | 13.96 → 13.95 (+0.1%) | 9,779 → 11,558 (+18.2%) | 2,520.3 → 1,785.4 (+29.2%) |

GLM-5.3-Flash and MiniMax-M3 (8×H200, `flashinfer_cutlass`), the same requests:

| Model | Concurrent requests | median ITL (ms) | throughput (tok/s) | TTFT (ms) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| GLM-5.3-Flash | 1 | 6.62 → 6.63 (−0.2%) | 1,189 → 1,217 (+2.4%) | 198.4 → 153.2 (+22.8%) |
| GLM-5.3-Flash | 8 | 10.24 → 10.25 (0.0%) | 5,068 → 5,707 (+12.6%) | 781.0 → 480.7 (+38.5%) |
| GLM-5.3-Flash | 32 | 15.83 → 15.82 (0.0%) | 10,035 → 12,870 (+28.3%) | 1,909.6 → 1,007.6 (+47.2%) |
| MiniMax-M3 | 1 | 8.61 → 8.61 (0.0%) | 964.5 → 964.8 (0.0%) | 138.4 → 137.3 (+0.9%) |
| MiniMax-M3 | 8 | 15.16 → 15.17 (−0.1%) | 3,616 → 4,069 (+12.5%) | 878.2 → 501.7 (+42.9%) |
| MiniMax-M3 | 32 | 23.77 → 23.76 (0.0%) | 6,922 → 8,958 (+29.4%) | 2,589.1 → 1,212.2 (+53.2%) |

On all three models, decode batches use buckets 1–256, which main already tunes, so ITL is unchanged (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash's 1-request difference is smaller than main's own spread between restarts, 3.4%); the throughput and TTFT gains at 8 and 32 requests come from these batched prefills (MiniMax-M3's main already tunes up to 2048 tokens, so a single 2k-token prompt gains only 0.9% there).

</details>

<details>
<summary>One MoE call</summary>

The tables above time whole requests; this test times one MoE call alone to answer two questions. (1) Does the gain come from the tactic, that is, from replacing FlashInfer's fallback tactic with a tuned one? (2) This PR tunes up to 8192 tokens, so a chunk larger than 8192 tokens reuses bucket 8192's tactic: is that slower than a tactic tuned for the chunk's own size? Result: **(1) yes: at 8192 tokens the tuned tactic is 2.6× faster than the fallback; (2) no: above 8192 tokens, bucket 8192's tactic is never slower than each size's own tactic.** It even measured 1.5–3.4% faster, but that is within the measurement spread: at 8192 tokens, where the last two columns run the very same tactic, the last column also measured 2.3% slower (1.549 vs 1.514 ms). `cutlass_fused_moe` on one H200, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash's per-GPU shape under EP8 (48 of 384 experts, hidden size 5120, intermediate size 2304, top-6, uniform random routing; median time per call), tuned once up to 8192 tokens (this PR's range with 8192-token chunks) and once up to 32768 tokens. Time per call (ms):

| Tokens | fallback tactic | bucket 8192's tactic (this PR) | tactic tuned for the call's own bucket |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 8192 | 3.990 | 1.514 | 1.549 (the same tactic) |
| 12288 | 5.900 | 2.138 | 2.194 |
| 16384 | 7.744 | 2.733 | 2.825 |
| 24576 | 11.482 | 3.976 | 4.035 |
| 32768 | 14.998 | 5.137 | 5.222 |

Tuning this layer's two GEMMs up to 8192 tokens takes 185 s, about as long as the server's whole startup autotune (176–177 s), because FlashInfer tunes each input shape once and every MoE layer has this shape; up to 32768 tokens it takes 232 s. The three tactics give bit-identical output at every size in the table.

</details>

$B --random-input-len 8000  --random-output-len 1 --num-prompts 8  --max-concurrency 1
