released FlashInfer 0.7.1 / 0.7.1+cu130 packages. No package install/change or
FlashInfer source build. All 373 Python distributions and six SGLang native
libraries stayed unchanged. Only the source-matched SGLang Rust TreeCore
binding was built into an isolated cache; tests load it with build mode `never`.

**Fixtures:** Qwen3 FP8 online checkpoint revision
`5a5a776300a41aaa681dd7ff0106608ef2bc90db`; NVIDIA Qwen3 NVFP4 serialized checkpoint
revision `2538ded2a4edb247b4d2b4a8ba24e44bd4c017c3`. Cached snapshots were checked
against config/index hashes and four shard sizes each; full weight payloads
were not hashed.

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Local CPU adapter | 29 passed; real Torch tensors, native/serving imports stubbed |
| C2 registered units | 65 passed, 35 subtests passed; no failures/errors/skips |
| Native W4A16 SiLU/SiTU | Cold and fresh-process warm passed on all four ranks; 192 graph replays |
| Dummy W4A16 / W4A4 | Each: 4 routed requests, 32 output tokens, finite logprobs |
| Online W4A16 GSM8K | 191/200 correct (95.5%), unchanged threshold >90% |
| Registered serialized W4A16 reload | Both cache-flush modes passed; 1 test, zero failures/errors/skips (port-separated retry) |
| Local serialized W4A4 reload control | Both cache-flush modes passed; 1 test, zero failures/errors/skips |

- **Online settings:** TP4/attention-DP4/EP4, BF16 compute and KV, online 4over6
  MSE recipe with fast math and E4M3-256, all routed experts converted, memory
  fraction 0.7, no MTP. The unchanged registered test uses decode graph max 128,
  disabled prefill graphs, 200 examples, 128 evaluation threads and a 512-token
  output cap. Effective per-worker prefill is 4096, running cap 3839, KV capacity
  1,965,696 and context limit 262144. The earlier example command is a separate
  configuration, not the measured accuracy setup.
- **Native settings:** H=I=256, E=8, top-k=4, EP4; capacities 1/2/4/8/16 and
  DP counts `[0,1,1,2]`, `[0,1,2,7]`, `[8,8,8,8]`, `[0,4,9,16]`. Two owners/
  startup contexts; five cold AUTO calls per rank, zero warm calls; pooled refs
  2→1→0. Borrowed outputs are cloned immediately. Eager/captured outputs are
  finite and bit-exact against a separate fixed-default native session before
  and after a visible FC1-scale update. This is not an independent BF16 oracle.
- **Dummy settings:** two-layer full-geometry fixture, BF16 compute, FP8 E4M3 KV,
  context 2048, per-rank prefill 64, running cap 4, memory fraction 0.4, decode
  graphs 1/2/4 and native profiles 1/2/4/64; no MTP. This checks finite output,
  not model accuracy.
The measured model configurations resolve as follows (all use TP4/attention-DP4/EP4 and no MTP):

| Case | Compute / KV dtype | Per-rank prefill | Running cap per worker | Context | KV tokens per worker | Memory fraction | Decode graph max |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Online W4A16 | BF16 / BF16 | 4096 | 3839 | 262144 | 1,965,696 | 0.70 | 128 |
| Serialized W4A16 reload | BF16 / FP8 E4M3 | 4096 | 4096 | 40960 | 4,930,816 | 0.87 | 512 |
| Serialized W4A4 reload | BF16 / FP8 E4M3 | 4096 | 4096 | 40960 | 4,932,224 | 0.87 | 512 |

- **Reload contract:** same-checkpoint reload, both cache-flush modes, weights/
  KV/graph release-resume, exact text/token IDs and logprobs within 1e-4. The
  output comparison routes to DP0; it does not prove equality across all DP
  workers. W4A4 is a local control reusing the registered W4A16 class with its
  opt-in set to 0; no additional upstream class.
- **Boundaries:** no full Kimi K3/GLM-5.2 E2E, online RL reload, MTP validation,
  or speedup claim. Server cases leave the three NVSHMEM variables unset to
  exercise production defaults; synthetic native cases set them explicitly.

title: [Perf] [AMD] batch-invariant: Tune the bf16 matmul for gfx950
author: aarnetalman
body:
## Motivation

This PR speeds up deterministic inference on MI350X/MI355X (gfx950): about 6% more throughput with 1k-token inputs and about 1.5% with 8k-token inputs. It gives the batch-invariant bf16 matmul a launch configuration tuned for gfx950.

With `--enable-deterministic-inference`, every linear layer goes through the persistent batch-invariant Triton matmul (`_matmul_persistent_triton`). That kernel uses one bf16 configuration on every GPU (128x128x64 tiles, 3 stages, 8 warps), with no AMD-specific options. On gfx950, a 128x64x128 tile with 16-wide MFMA instructions is up to 2x faster at decode batch sizes.

The configuration is still fixed for every M, so each output element keeps the same reduction order whatever the batch: batch invariance is unchanged.

## Modifications

- `batch_invariant_ops.py`: on gfx950 only, the bf16 entry becomes `BLOCK_SIZE_M=128, BLOCK_SIZE_N=64, BLOCK_SIZE_K=128, GROUP_SIZE_M=8, num_stages=3, num_warps=8, matrix_instr_nonkdim=16`.
  - It needs about 147 KB of LDS, so it is limited to gfx950 (160 KB).
  - Other GPUs, fp16/fp32 and the non-deterministic path are unchanged.
  - In deterministic mode every unquantized bf16 linear layer (`aten::mm`/`addmm`) runs this kernel on ROCm, so the change applies to any bf16 model. Quantized layers, MoE experts (Triton MoE runner) and attention don't use it.
- Chosen from a sweep of about 2,900 configurations on MI350X, each checked bitwise for batch invariance.
- The launch configurations are now built by a small helper, `_matmul_persistent_configs()`, and a new CPU test (`test/registered/unit/batch_invariant_ops/test_matmul_persistent_configs.py`, `base-a-test-cpu`) guards the preset: on gfx950 the bf16 entry must be exactly this configuration and fit gfx950's 160 KB of LDS, and on other GPUs it must stay the original one.

## Accuracy Tests

MI350X, `rocm/sgl-dev:v0.5.21-rocm724-mi35x-20261012` with this change applied, Qwen3-8B BF16, TP1, `--attention-backend triton --enable-deterministic-inference`, `SGLANG_USE_AITER=0`:
- `python3 -m sglang.test.test_deterministic --test-mode prefix --return-logprob` and `--test-mode radix_cache` (50 trials): pass.
- Bitwise comparison of 1,275 responses (batch sizes 1-50) against batch size 1: 1275/1275 token IDs and log-probabilities identical.
- `test/registered/unit/batch_invariant_ops/test_batch_invariant_ops.py`: 6 passed, 54 subtests, before and after (also with the helper refactor).
- `test_matmul_persistent_configs.py`: 2 passed (2 failed on the code before this PR, which has no helper).

## Speed Tests and Profiling

**End to end**, deterministic mode as above, `python3 -m sglang.benchmark.serving --backend sglang --dataset-name random --random-range-ratio 1.0 --request-rate inf --seed 1`, median of 3 runs each:

| Workload | | Output tok/s | ITL p50 | TTFT p50 | Request latency p50 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ISL/OSL 1024/1024, 256 prompts, concurrency 256 | main | 3,370 | 66.79 ms | 5.03 s | 77.7 s |
| | this PR | 3,585 (**1.064x**) | 61.98 ms (**-7.2%**) | 5.28 s (+4.8%) | 73.0 s (**-6.0%**) |
| ISL/OSL 8192/1024, 256 prompts, concurrency 128, GPU A | main | 686.9 | 121.61 ms | 34.5 s | 190.8 s |
| | this PR, GPU B | 695.4 (1.012x) | 118.34 ms (-2.7%) | 35.1 s (+1.7%) | 188.4 s (-1.3%) |
| same, GPUs swapped | main, GPU B | 686.0 | 121.36 ms | 34.8 s | 191.0 s |
| | this PR, GPU A | 697.6 (1.017x) | 118.27 ms (-2.5%) | 34.8 s (0.0%) | 187.9 s (-1.6%) |

- 1k/1k: same GPU, before and after; an earlier run with the GPUs swapped gave the same gain (1.059x on both GPUs).
- With 8k inputs most of the time goes to prefill, where the new tile is about 5% slower at the GEMM level (table below), so the gain is smaller. Decode is still faster, and request latency still improves.

**Kernel**, speed-up over the current configuration (`triton.testing.do_bench`, weights passed transposed as `F.linear` does):

| N x K | M=1 | M=16 | M=64 | M=256 | M=1024 | M=4096 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6144 x 4096 | 1.77x | 1.92x | 1.84x | 1.60x | 1.16x | 0.96x |
| 4096 x 4096 | 1.98x | 1.94x | 1.85x | 1.57x | 0.95x | 0.96x |
| 24576 x 4096 | 1.02x | 1.01x | 1.00x | 1.14x | 0.95x | 0.96x |
| 4096 x 12288 | 2.05x | 2.02x | 1.87x | 1.56x | 0.96x | 0.95x |
| 16384 x 5120 | 1.16x | 1.15x | 1.15x | 0.88x | 0.94x | 0.94x |
| 5120 x 6144 | 2.03x | 1.99x | 1.87x | 1.58x | 1.15x | 0.98x |
| 34816 x 5120 | 1.21x | 1.20x | 1.21x | 1.04x | 0.99x | 0.96x |
| 5120 x 17408 | 2.13x | 2.11x | 1.96x | 1.57x | 1.11x | 0.95x |

The shapes are the linear layers of Qwen3-8B and Qwen3.8-27B. The geomean is 1.59x at M <= 64 and 0.99x at M >= 1024. A per-(N, K) configuration could recover the prefill shapes later; the configuration must never depend on M.

title: [Perf] [NVIDIA] qsa: Keep sparse decode scratch in FP8 for FP8 KV pools
author: YAMY1234
body:
## Motivation

#38851 fixed QSA sparse-decode corruption with three changes:

- zero-filling the scratch tail;
- int64 pool offsets;
- dequantizing FP8 pool rows into a BF16 scratch.

The first two fix the bug. The third was a conservative choice: it makes TRTLLM-gen decode always run BF16-q + BF16-KV.

FlashInfer's `trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache` supports BF16-q + FP8-E4M3-KV. With an FP8 pool, keeping the packed scratch in FP8 halves gather and attention KV traffic and removes the dequant from `fused_kv_prepare`.

## Modifications

- `_forward_trtllm_sparse` allocates the packed K/V scratch in FP8 when the KV pool is `float8_e4m3fn` and the device is SM10x. Otherwise it uses the query dtype, as before.
  - The query stays BF16.
  - The scratch cache is already keyed by dtype.
- Unchanged:
  - the zero-fill, int64 offsets and scale-free handling from #38851;
  - BF16 pools;
  - the FA2/FA4 fallback;
  - prefill;
  - SM120.
- `test_qsa_fused_kv_prepare` and `test_qsa_strided_zero_fill` now cover FP8 pool → FP8 scratch.

## Accuracy Tests

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 on VR200: TP1, FP8 KV, FP8 QSA indexer, NEXTN MTP (3 steps, 4 draft tokens).

Sampling: temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95, top_k 20, `max_new_tokens` 131072. No sample reached the length limit.

| Eval | Main (BF16 scratch) | This PR (FP8 scratch) | Paired diff |
|---|---|---|---|
| AIME24+25, 60 × 16 samples | 90.52% | 92.08% | +1.56 pp, 95% CI [−0.47, +3.59] |
| GPQA, 100 × 8 samples | 87.25% | 88.62% | +1.38 pp, SE 1.09 |
| GSM8K, 200 | 198 | 198 | 0 |

- Output length is unchanged (+0.15%).
- Attention output error against an FP32 reference is the same on both paths, about 2.1e-3. It does not grow with KV length up to 64K and beyond.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Same model and configuration on VR200, C64 with MTP.

**Per decode step:**

| | Main | This PR |
|---|---|---|
| `fused_kv_prepare` | 135.19 µs | 86.69 µs |
| FMHA | 97.61 µs | 89.42 µs |
| Step time | 20.686 ms | 19.908 ms (−3.76%) |

**Agentic multi-turn serving, 3 paired 1-hour runs:** median per-user throughput (P90) +1.49%, median total throughput per GPU +2.29%.

This matches the expected gain: decode is about 68% of wall time, so −3.76% per step gives about +2.6% end to end.

title: [Feat] watermark: Add DSPARK speculative decoding support
author: JustinTong0323
body:
> Note: the first commit on this branch is the EAGLE verify-append hotfix from #44199 (watermarked EAGLE/EAGLE3 output is undetectable on main without it). This branch will be rebased to a single commit once #44199 lands.

DSPARK verifies a linear draft chain. Each verify row's context is the committed watermark tail followed by the earlier draft tokens, so the existing speculative selector applies with a lower-triangular chain mask. The DSPARK worker forces those rows before acceptance. After acceptance it records the accepted rows' contexts and appends the committed tokens to the ring.

**Design: verify-side forcing.**
- A forced row's target distribution is one-hot, so DSPARK's rejection-sampling accept — with or without block verification — emits exactly the watermarked token.
- Detection therefore follows the unchanged contract: no DSPARK-specific detector logic, single and dual key alike.
- Draft-side keyed sampling would raise acceptance, but it needs the selector inside DSPARK's folded draft graph and a cropped-vocabulary hash contract. It is left as follow-up given the measured cost below.

**Evidence** (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, 8×H200, TP8/EP8, DSPARK block size 5):
- Detection: 40 essays × 512 tokens, temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95. DSPARK median request z is 2.73 (16/40 at p < 1e-3) against 3.06 (18/40) without speculation on the same prompts; wrong key z 0.91. OFF: median z 0.21, 0/40.
- GSM8K-100 (temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95): 99% with 100% stop rate, both watermarked and not, 0 truncated, 0 errors.
- Throughput: bench_serving random 1024/512, c8, 100 prompts, temperature 0.8, top-p 0.95, top-k 20, six reps over two launches: TPOT +3.73%, output throughput −2.25%, accept length −3.27%.

**Also fixes** an EAGLE/NEXTN regression (#44199): the fused verify-commit path (#41175) skipped the watermark ring append, so watermarked EAGLE3 output on main is undetectable. On Qwen3-8B with EAGLE3 3/1/4, 0/40 requests reach p < 1e-3 before the fix and 40/40 after; tree 5/8/32 is also 40/40.

**Tests:**
- CUDA watermark selector/state suites, plus a DSPARK chain case. The case checks that rejection-sampling accept, with and without block verification, emits the forced tokens, and that the committed ring and context history equal those of non-speculative decode (22 passed total).
- Endpoint e2e `test_watermark.py` (5 passed).

Not covered: DSPARK with DP attention or PD disaggregation (PD stays rejected by validation). DFLASH stays rejected; its chain can reuse `force_speculative_chain` in a later PR.

title: [Perf] distributed: Skip the DLPack re-wrap of custom all-reduce results
author: mickqian
body:
## Motivation

`custom_all_reduce` in `sglang/kernels/ops/communication/all_reduce.py` ends with `torch.from_dlpack(result)`. With apache-tvm-ffi 0.1.11 and torch's DLPack exchange API loaded (`torch_c_dlpack_ext`, present in the `lmsysorg/sglang` image), the tvm-ffi call already returns a `torch.Tensor`. So `torch.from_dlpack` does a pure torch → DLPack → torch round trip. Along the way it also builds a current-stream object from a device string and makes a `__dlpack__` call that may be retried.

On a Grace host (GB300) this round trip costs about 20 µs per call. That is about half of the ~42 µs host time of an eager TP all-reduce, and twice the cost of the tvm-ffi call itself. Diffusion DiTs run several all-reduces per block in eager mode, so on GB300 with TP the step is host-bound and this cost shows up directly in end-to-end latency.

## Modifications

Return `result` as is when it is already a `torch.Tensor`. Otherwise, e.g. with `TVM_FFI_DISABLE_TORCH_C_DLPACK=1`, keep `torch.from_dlpack`.

The returned tensor aliases the same memory as before. `torch.from_dlpack` passed the current stream, so the round trip never added a cross-stream wait, and dropping it changes no ordering. No memory is involved, and CUDA-graph capture and the compiled path (`diffusion_all_reduce`) are unchanged.

## Accuracy Tests

- `test/registered/kernels/ops/communication/test_custom_all_reduce.py --num-gpu 2` on GB300 ×2:
  - 180 passed with the exchange API loaded;
  - 180 passed with `TVM_FFI_DISABLE_TORCH_C_DLPACK=1`, which covers the `from_dlpack` branch.
- End to end: every configuration below produced the same output image md5 as main.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Base `c54ba66cd4`, torch 2.13, apache-tvm-ffi 0.1.11, GB300 ×2 (Grace host). Processes were pinned to the GPUs' NUMA node.

**Host time per call** (µs, eager, inference mode; the GPU is kept busy so only submission is timed):

| | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `GroupCoordinator.all_reduce` (diffusion TP group), 0.4 MiB | 42.0 | 20.7 |
| same, 4.5 MiB | 39.2 | 18.2 |
| same, 27 MiB | 43.7 | 20.6 |
| for reference: the tvm-ffi call alone | ~10 | ~10 |

**End to end.** Client wall clock, median, TP2 eager. Servers for main and this PR were resident together and requests alternated over 10 pairs.

| | main | this PR | | this PR faster in |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen-Image-2.1 512² | 1462.4 ms | 1298.3 ms | −11.2% | 10/10 |
| Qwen-Image-2.1 1024² | 1548.4 ms | 1391.3 ms | −10.1% | 10/10 |
| FLUX.1-dev 512² | 3794.0 ms | 3559.2 ms | −6.2% | 10/10 |
| FLUX.1-dev 1024² | 4019.0 ms | 3696.4 ms | −8.0% | 10/10 |

The same applies to srt's eager TP all-reduces through `CustomAllReduceV2`, e.g. extend/prefill outside CUDA graphs. Those were not measured here. This change is independent of #43859 and #44158, which cut host time elsewhere.

**H200 (x86 host), added 2026-10-16.** Base `c15edf314d`, 2xH200 (Xeon 8558P), TP2 eager.

- Host time per call of `custom_all_reduce` in `kernels/ops/communication/all_reduce.py` (bf16 [1, 4096, 3072]): 22.39 µs on main, 6.42 µs with this PR. The round trip costs about 16 µs on x86 too.
- End to end, client wall-clock median at 512². The second column is from #44642's in-process A/B, which bypasses this wrapper and so also drops the re-wrap; it measured −0.2% (Qwen-Image-2.1) and −2.4% (FLUX.1) on top of this PR.

| | main | this PR (different server instance) | in-process A/B: main vs main + #44642 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen-Image-2.1 TP2 512² | 797.0 ms | 686.6 ms | −14.4% (10/10) |
| FLUX.1-dev TP2 512² | 2196.0 ms | 1856.9 ms | −15.2% (8/8) |

Two identical co-resident servers differed by up to 3.5% on this box, so the cross-instance column is indicative only; the gap here is far larger.

title: [Fix] moe: Fix --enable-fused-moe-sum-all-reduce outside CUDA and with LoRA hooks
author: ZhengGong-amd
body:
## Motivation

With `--enable-fused-moe-sum-all-reduce` (#19672) the Triton down GEMM sums the experts into `out_hidden_states` and leaves `intermediate_cache3` unwritten, but `_fused_moe_kernel_sequence` honours that only under `_is_cuda or _is_musa` and ignores LoRA's `after_down` hook; this PR handles the fused case before the platform dispatch and disables the fusion when `hooks.after_down` is set.

On HIP, XPU and the fallback, the combine reduces the unwritten `intermediate_cache3` over the result. On every platform the LoRA down delta, added to `intermediate_cache3`, is dropped. On ROCm every Triton-runner MoE layer with `topk > 2` breaks; GSM8K is 0 % for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Kimi-Linear-48B with `--moe-runner-backend triton`, and for GLM-5.3, MiniMax-M2.7 and Qwen3-Next/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next FP8 with `SGLANG_USE_AITER=0`. gemma-4-26B-A4B (I=704) runs Triton by default, so the flag alone breaks it.

## Modifications

- In the fused case, apply `routed_scaling_factor` as the platform's unfused combine does: everywhere except the aiter path, whose `moe_sum` skips it too. The CUDA/MUSA code is moved, not changed.
- An empty `LoRAHooks()` (LoRA enabled, no active adapter) keeps the fusion on.
- Add `TestFusedMoeSumAllReduce`: flag-on output must match flag-off and the fused kernel launch is asserted, for routed scale None/2.5 with no hooks, empty hooks or an `after_down` hook. Without the LoRA guard the 6 `after_down` cases fail with ~20 % relative error.

## Accuracy Tests

On MI355X at main `b960aa903a`, `TestFusedMoeSumAllReduce` passes with `SGLANG_USE_AITER=0` and `=1` (main fails 18/18 in both), as does the rest of `test_fused_moe.py`.

`sgl-eval` gsm8k, temperature 0, MI355X. First two rows: 1319 items, Triton runner, main flag-off run twice as noise control. Rest: 200 items, `SGLANG_USE_AITER=0`, `auto` resolves to Triton:

| model | main off | main on | this PR, on |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | 94.09 / 94.16 | 0.00 | 94.31 |
| Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B (routed scale 2.45) | 91.28 / 91.96 | 0.00 | 92.42 |
| GLM-5.3 FP8, TP4 | 51.5¹ | 0.0 | 49.0 |
| MiniMax-M2.7, TP2 | 96.0 | 0.0 | 96.0 |
| Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8 | 96.5 | 0.0 | 96.0 |
| Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-FP8 | 96.0 | 0.0 | 96.0 |

¹ GLM-5.3 loops on most answers in this aiter-off config regardless of the flag; the gap is within n=200 noise.

Block-FP8 MoE with `SGLANG_USE_AITER=1` and `--moe-runner-backend triton` is broken on main even flag-off; #41636 fixes that separately.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

No speed change is intended. gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, cookbook command, flag off, TP1, `sglang.benchmark.serving` random 1937/389, 307 prompts, concurrency 61, median of runs 2–4 of 4: total 13870.9 → 13935.4 tok/s (+0.5 %), TTFT and TPOT flat. With the flag on, gemma-4 runs ~60 % below its flag-off throughput on gfx950 (`acq_rel` atomics), so the flag should stay off on ROCm.

- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).

title: [Perf] detokenizer: Group return IPC sends by tokenizer worker
author: hope1262946533
body:
# Summary

Fixes #43096.

Add opt-in grouping for the **Detokenizer → TokenizerWorker** return path. Requests from one already-produced output are grouped by their original `http_worker_ipc` and sent once per destination instead of once per request.

**Measured benefit: +2.1% whole-machine client output throughput**, from a trace-free, single-variable, 16-round comparison on DeepSeek-V4-Pro (see "Benchmark evidence" below). The same change cuts return-hop IPC sends by ~94% and roughly halves return-worker CPU.

1. Register `SGLANG_OPT_DETOK_TOKENIZER_GROUP_SEND` as `EnvBool(False)` and read it once when the multi-HTTP-worker detokenizer event loop starts.
1. Reuse `_handle_output_by_indices()` from the merged Router grouped-send change (#42238); do not duplicate, downgrade, or modify the current message-field slicing logic.
1. Group only when at least two requests share a destination; when every request has a distinct owner, keep the original per-request path unchanged.
1. Construct every destination payload before sending the first one. If the splitter raises `_CannotSplitBatch`, fall back for the entire output to the original per-request path.
1. Keep send failures outside the fallback handler so an earlier successful send is never duplicated by a fallback/retry.

Enable before launching the service:

```bash
export SGLANG_OPT_DETOK_TOKENIZER_GROUP_SEND=1
```

Unset or `0` preserves the existing per-request path. The benchmark prototype used `SGLANG_DETOK_TOKENIZER_GROUP_SEND`; this upstream extraction uses the canonical `SGLANG_OPT_*` name and the typed `Envs` API. The prototype name is not an alias in this patch.

# Dependency and scope

The Router hop is addressed by #42238 (`[Perf] Reduce multi-detokenizer router IPC sends`), which is **merged into main** (merge commit `cb9bd1d`, 2026-10-09). This commit is its follow-up: it reuses the merged `_handle_output_by_indices()` helper and does not modify it, so the Router path is unchanged.

The incremental commit changes only:

1. `python/sglang/srt/environ.py` — default-off optimization switch.
1. `python/sglang/srt/managers/multi_tokenizer_mixin.py` — owner-grouped return sends and event-loop wiring.
1. `test/registered/unit/managers/test_multi_tokenizer_mixin.py` — actual message-class regression coverage.
1. `docs/docs/references/environment_variables.mdx` — environment-variable documentation.

Excluded: HTTP listener/reuse-port changes, Scheduler diagnostics or admission changes, output-chain trace/profiling, changes to the Router routing rule, and deployment-specific code.

Preserved: per-request owner, intra-destination order, first-destination order, current single/control request handling, watchdog behavior, and default-disabled behavior. No cross-message merge, delay window, or new output protocol is introduced.

# Benchmark evidence

Measurements use SGLang 0.5.17 at `29481685462732237d80d86076d6563e1f658102`: DeepSeek-V4-Pro, TP8/DP8, no MTP, 32 tokenizer and 32 detokenizer workers, decode graph maximum 310, maximum running requests 2480, memory fraction 0.96859, server seed 81095743. Upstream Router grouping was enabled for every run.

Client settings were identical: aiakperf streaming generate API, random dataset, concurrency 4960, 79,360 requests, input/output 60,000/1,000, 16 client processes, seed 0, temperature 0, top-p 1, fake bootstrap and ignore EOS enabled.

## Measured end-to-end benefit

1. **Trace-free whole-machine client output throughput (clean net gain).** Default shared-listener configuration, no tracing and no in-process probes, three runs each, only this switch changed (2026-10-11): disabled `42,297.97 / 42,564.88 / 42,306.00 token/s`; enabled `43,740.88 / 43,106.29 / 43,025.66 token/s`. Derived from the three-run means, **+2.13%**. Total duration moved from `1876.21 / 1864.45 / 1875.86 s` to `1814.32 / 1841.03 / 1844.48 s`.
1. **Instrumented A/B six-run** (all runs with output-chain tracing enabled; three disabled followed by three enabled): disabled `42,463.52 / 42,350.61 / 42,426.76 token/s`; enabled `43,547.89 / 42,816.95 / 43,280.41 token/s`. Derived from the three-run means, **+1.89%**. Reported separately from item 1 because reducing sends also reduces instrumentation work.
1. **Return-hop IPC calls:** disabled `79,376,257 / 79,376,257 / 79,376,257`; enabled `4,790,103 / 4,325,743 / 5,063,191`. The same `79,376,257` output events were carried in each run, so the enabled condition reduced actual return-hop send calls by approximately 93.62%-94.55%. Send counters include warmup/non-formal output events.
1. **Return-worker CPU:** detokenizer p50 decreased from `288.56% / 276.91% / 289.95%` to `107.51% / 99.74% / 105.75%`; TokenizerWorker p50 decreased from `731.38% / 732.34% / 730.86%` to `373.87% / 384.82% / 364.64%`. Percentages use single-core process-group CPU units.
1. **Batchsize and preallocation:** per-rank Batchsize p50 was `309 / 309 / 309` disabled and `310 / 310 / 310` enabled; p10 was `235 / 209 / 178` disabled and `307 / 215 / 307` enabled. The preallocation-queue p50 was `151 / 176 / 168` disabled and `282 / 293 / 284` enabled; `#transfer-req` was zero in all six runs.
1. **Correctness and completion:** all formal requests succeeded in all runs; output-stage request IDs were conserved and output lengths were 1,000. Text/token-ID bitwise equivalence was not measured.

## Qualification

1. The benefit is **conditional on the default HTTP listener topology**. When new connections are spread across HTTP workers per-worker (SO_REUSEPORT or an equivalent multi-listener server), grouping stops paying off: a same-workload comparison measured grouping enabled versus disabled at `42,733` versus `42,764 token/s` (means of three runs each) under per-worker listeners, compared with `43,291` versus `42,390` under the default shared listener. Grouping helps when one output batch concentrates in few HTTP workers, which is what the default listener produces; it does not itself fix connection imbalance.
1. This does not claim uniform latency improvement: median TTFT was `33.12 / 39.85 / 37.33 s` disabled versus `52.06 / 52.44 / 52.53 s` enabled; median E2EL was `86.02 / 92.89 / 89.93 s` versus `104.96 / 105.27 / 105.31 s`. Remaining HTTP-worker ownership imbalance and long tails are outside this patch.

# Validation and unit-test benefit

The unit tests demonstrate send-count reduction at the component level, not a timed performance speedup: the noncontiguous three-request/two-owner case produces two sends instead of three; the two-request/same-owner case produces one send instead of two. When every request has a different owner, the send count and per-request payloads remain unchanged. No standalone CPU microbenchmark or unit-test throughput gain was measured.

They also provide regression protection for the correctness and failure-boundary properties that make the optimization safe to enable:

1. They verify noncontiguous owner grouping preserves first-destination order, per-destination request order, and the original `http_worker_ipc` ownership.
1. They verify current string and token-ID message classes are grouped correctly, and that an embedding batch falls back to the per-request path (the shared splitter only covers `BatchTokenIDOutput`/`BatchStrOutput`), including optional wire fields through both pickle and msgpack round trips.
1. They verify the input output object is not mutated, unique-owner batches preserve the original per-request payload behavior, and outputs from separate messages are never accumulated together.
1. They verify `_CannotSplitBatch` falls back for the whole output before any grouped send, while a send error propagates without resending an earlier successful payload.
1. They verify the default-off behavior and the event-loop switch behavior.

Tests run separately in their own CPU Python processes:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=python python -m pytest test/registered/unit/managers/test_multi_tokenizer_mixin.py -q
PYTHONPATH=python python -m pytest test/registered/unit/managers/test_msgpack_ipc_roundtrip.py -q
```

1. The return-path component tests and the existing IPC serialization tests pass, run separately in their own CPU Python processes. (The local CPU environment is Python 3.10 / torch 2.5.1, which cannot import current `main`; the suite is re-run in CI.)
1. Repository-selected Ruff checks (`F401,F821,F823,UP037`) plus `F811`, Ruff formatting, isort and `git diff --check` passed.

Added coverage checks noncontiguous owner grouping and ordering, unique-owner equivalence with the original per-request path, no input mutation, no cross-message accumulation, latest optional fields through both pickle and msgpack, token-ID grouping with embedding fallback, default-off and enabled event-loop behavior, fallback after an earlier group has been constructed but before any send, and send errors without resending earlier results.

# Submission note

The Router dependency (#42238) is merged into main, so this commit rebases directly onto current `main`. The comparison base is `main` and the diff contains only the files listed under "Dependency and scope".

title: [Feat] [AMD] dsa: Enable DCP on the triton sparse-MLA backend
author: EricKing626
body: ## Motivation This PR enables `--dcp-size > 1` for the RoPE DSA models on the `triton` DSA backends, which is the path ROCm runs. Previous work [#43735](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/43735) brought DCP to these models on the `trtllm` backends; this builds on that work and supplies the pieces the triton path additionally needs: - The triton sparse-MLA kernel now returns its LSE(Log-Sum-Exp), so the per-rank partials can be merged. - The HIP FP8 KV cache now works under DCP: writes land on the row the reader looks up. - Fixes the GPU memory access fault the ROCm DSA MTP draft hit under DCP, by putting the draft on the target's sharding and addressing rule. ## Correctness MI355X, `amd/GLM-5.2-MXFP4`, TP4/EP4, FP8 KV, MTP (EAGLE, 5 steps, 6 draft tokens), real draft acceptance. | check | no DCP | PR after; DCP=4 | |---|---|---| | passkey 8K / 34K / 96K | 3/3 | 3/3 | | GSM8K (400 questions, few-shot) | 0.953 | 0.953 | | MTP accept length (4 prompts x 400 tokens, greedy) | 3.11 | 3.47 | | KV capacity (tokens) | 2.83M | 8.81M (2.20M rows per rank x 4) | The FP8 write kernel test passes with 4 simulated ranks, and the triton LSE matches at the kernel level. ## Performance InferenceX agentic replay on this head, TP4/EP4 + DCP4 with MTP (simulated AL 3.61), 1 h per point. All four points finish with no GPU fault. The TP4 rows without DCP but with HiCache are for reference only. Table baseline: 10/19/2026 commit: 33dd8f6a2e TP4 + DCP4: 10/28/2026 commit: b8a0a1ac70 | Conc | Config | P90 Interactivity (tok/s/user) | TPUT per Chip (tok/s/GPU) | Chip Cache Hit Rate | CPU Cache Hit Rate | Theoretical Cache Hit Rate | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | 16 | TP4 | **53.07** | **17,396** | 71.1% | 22.7% | 97.0% | | 16 | TP4 + DCP4 | 41.19 | 17,196 | 96.7% | — | 97.0% | | 24 | TP4 | 14.07 | 10,872 | 18.6% | 57.5% | 96.2% | | 24 | TP4 + DCP4 | **31.32** | **23,416** | 96.8% | — | 97.3% | | 40 | TP4 | 7.19 | 5,144 | 31.2% | 0.9% | — | | 40 | TP4 + DCP4 | **16.79** | **24,740** | 95.5% | — | 97.0% | | 48 | TP4 | **6.30** | 4,781 | 27.3% | 0.9% | — | | 48 | TP4 + DCP4 | 2.56 | **10,774** | 82.6% | — | 96.1% | - At c24 and c40, DCP4 keeps almost the whole working set in HBM (chip hit rate 95–97%): throughput per GPU is 2.2x and 4.8x the baseline, and P90 interactivity is 2.2x and 2.3x. - At c16 the baseline still fits most of its working set in HBM plus host memory, so DCP4 brings no gain: throughput per GPU is on par (0.99x), and P90 interactivity is 0.78x. - At c48 the DCP4 pool fills up (chip hit rate 83%) and DCP rejects HiCache, so evicted prefixes are recomputed: throughput per GPU stays 2.3x the baseline, but P90 interactivity falls to 0.41x of it. ## Modifications Correctness: - **`DSA DCP on the triton sparse-MLA backend`** 811248c80b - The triton sparse-MLA decode now returns an LSE, which DCP needs to merge each rank's partial result — letting decode, target verify and paged extend reuse upstream's DCP path. - **`Shard the DSA FP8 latent KV write under DCP`** fa4f2fc48f - The FP8 quant write only writes `slot % dcp_size == dcp_rank`, at row `slot // dcp_size`, the same rule as the BF16 write. - **`Shard the DSA MTP draft KV like the target under DCP`** 20107f85b8 - Fixed GPU memory access fault on DSA EAGLE/NEXTN draft. Puts the ROCm DSA draft on the target's allocator page and owner rule, with extend on the owned-slot path. Performance: - **`Bound the triton DCP sparse-MLA scan by the owned top-k count`** 171e960082 - `localize_dcp_page_table` already returns the per-row owned count, but the triton path dropped it and scanned all top-k slots, masking about (W-1)/W of them. The kernels now stop after the owned tiles. - **`Split DSA prefill indexer rows across the DCP group`** d7f9605feb - DCP now splits the rows evenly across ranks instead of computing the same top-k `W` times. The results are all-gathered directly into the destination buffer when possible. - **`Gather the DSA DCP Q in the FP8 KV dtype`** b8a0a1ac70 - Halves the Q traffic between DCP ranks with no change in results, because the kernel converted Q to that same format on arrival anyway. Scope: Without DCP nothing changes: the new arguments default to the old behavior. CUDA is untouched; the draft sharding is gated on `is_hip()`. On ROCm, pass `--dsa-prefill-backend triton --dsa-decode-backend triton`, because #43735 defaults to `trtllm` when they are unset. ## Known issues - DCP rejects HiCache, so once the DCP pool is full (c48 above), evicted prefixes are recomputed rather than reloaded from host. HiCache under DCP is a #43735 fast follow. - Add feature to enable DCP+HiCache at #45205 ## Checklist - [x] `pre-commit` - [x] Kernel tests (FP8 write, triton LSE) - [x] GLM-5.2 DCP4 end-to-end sanity (math, passkey up to 379K) - [x] GSM8K, DCP4 vs. no DCP - [x] Agentic replay at c16 / c24 / c40 / c48 - [x] Unit tests in repo --- ### CI States Latest PR Test (Base): :white_check_mark: [Run #40516763996](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/40516763996) Latest PR Test (Extra): :x: [Run #40516763980](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/40516763980) Latest PR Test (AMD ROCm 10): :hourglass_flowing_sand: [Run #40516764530](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/40516764530)

title: [Feat] [CPU] cpu-graph: Add prefill torch compile graph and dynamic graph support
author: CaoE
body:
## Motivation

Ported from the internal implementation.

Add CPU torch.compile graph support for both prefill and decode on Intel AMX systems, including static bucket graphs and optional dynamic-shape fallback graphs.

The implementation supports:

- Static prefill graphs using total-token buckets.
- Optional dynamic fallback graphs through `SGLANG_TORCH_DYNAMIC_SHAPE=true`.
- Exact buckets first, padded buckets second, and dynamic fallback last.

CPU prefill graphs are experimental and remain disabled by default; they must be explicitly enabled with the `full` backend.

## Modifications

- Extend `CPUGraphRunner` with CPU prefill graph capture and replay.
- Add static and dynamic graph support for both decode and prefill.
- Add prefill padding and hidden-state trimming.
- Define CPU decode configuration precedence:
  `decode.bs` > `decode.max_bs` > `--torch-compile-max-bs`.
- Generate prefill buckets from `prefill.max_bs` when needed.
- Reject unsupported CPU graph backends such as `breakable` and `tc_piecewise`.
- Add a stable prefill forward dispatcher to avoid unnecessary recompilation.
- Make layer-boundary objects compatible with TorchDynamo during CPU graph capture and replay.
- Fix graph breaks, runtime recompiles, and `InternalTorchDynamoError` failures related to `msgspec.Struct` objects and
  Python-side CPU capability checks.
- Update required CPU custom-op schemas, fake registrations, rotary embedding handling, and related kernels.
- Update CPU graph documentation and tests.

## Tests

- Cover backend gating, bucket generation, option precedence, padding, dispatcher stability, dynamic fallback, and encoder-decoder decode graph reuse.
- Reuse the existing real-model benchmark and MMLU test while enabling explicit CPU prefill graphs and dynamic-shape fallback.
- Verify graph and eager accuracy and graph execution without graph breaks or runtime recompiles.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Qwen3.5-35B (BF16, TP4) Prefill graph:  ~6% TTFT Speedup (BS=1, Input=1024).

title: [Perf] [AMD] deterministic: Allow AITER decode attention on gfx950
author: aarnetalman
body:
## Motivation

This PR lets deterministic inference on MI350X/MI355X (gfx950) use AITER for decode attention: `--decode-attention-backend aiter`, with prefill attention still on a deterministic backend such as Triton. Decode attention is a large part of the cost of deterministic mode on these GPUs, and with AITER decode, deterministic throughput is 1.27-1.91x higher for Qwen3-8B, 1.53-1.61x for Qwen3-30B-A3B and 1.09-1.13x for Qwen3.8-27B, with every determinism check still passing and unchanged GSM8K.

AITER's paged decode attention (`paged_attention_ragged`) splits each request's KV cache into fixed 256-token partitions and reduces them per request. The split depends only on the request's own context length, never on the batch, so a request gets the same result whatever it is batched with.

This builds on #44438, which makes deterministic mode check `--prefill-attention-backend` and `--decode-attention-backend`. Decode has to be set explicitly: `--attention-backend aiter --prefill-attention-backend triton` stays refused, because `--attention-backend` itself must be a deterministic backend.

### Refused in deterministic mode, and why

| Configuration | Why |
| --- | --- |
| AITER as `--attention-backend` or `--prefill-attention-backend` | AITER prefill attention is not batch-invariant (in our tests its results changed with the batch from about 480 tokens, and with mixed batches) |
| AITER decode for MLA models | MLA decode sizes its KV splits by the batch size |
| AITER decode on other GPUs than gfx950 | not tested |
| AITER decode with speculative decoding | target verify (`--speculative-attention-mode decode`) and some draft workers would run AITER's verify and extend kernels, which are not verified |
| AITER decode with sliding-window models, `SGLANG_USE_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN` or the vectorized 5D KV-cache layout | these run AITER's unified-attention or 5D-pool decode kernels instead of `paged_attention_ragged`; not verified. Refused when the AITER backend starts |
| `--enable-mixed-chunk` (any backend) | a mixed batch runs its decode tokens through the prefill kernels; handled separately in #44701, which switches it off in deterministic mode |

## Modifications

- `arg_groups/overrides.py` (`_deterministic_attention_backend`): the allowed backends are built per phase first; `aiter` is added for decode on gfx950, for non-MLA models and without speculative decoding. Both phases are then checked in one loop. When AITER decode is refused, the error says why. The per-phase fields are read directly.
- `layers/attention/aiter_backend.py`: in deterministic mode, the AITER backend refuses to start when decode would not run `paged_attention_ragged` (unified attention or the vectorized 5D KV-cache layout), so an accepted configuration always runs the kernel that was verified.
- `test_model_overrides.py`: a table test (gfx950 or not, MLA or not, AITER prefill or not, speculative decoding or not) for which configurations are accepted. #44438's refusal test pins `is_gfx95_supported` to `False` and sets both per-phase fields, so it does not depend on the machine it runs on.
- Unchanged: deterministic mode off; every configuration that does not set `--decode-attention-backend aiter`; the radix cache (it follows `--attention-backend`, which stays a deterministic backend).

## Accuracy Tests

Environment: 8x MI350X, `rocm/sgl-dev:v0.5.21-rocm724-mi35x-20261013` (SGLang `27b68303d0`, AITER `e7d2453f2`), `SGLANG_USE_AITER=1` (the image default); `aiter_backend.py` is identical to upstream main. Deterministic mode on MI350X also needs the open fixes #43788 (AITER GEMM and MoE bypass; not merged yet) and #34543 (all-reduce for oversized inputs), which were applied in all runs, together with our other open PRs. These runs used the image without #44438, where `--decode-attention-backend aiter` was not checked yet; the server arguments are the ones this PR accepts:

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-8B --tp $TP \
  --attention-backend triton --prefill-attention-backend triton --decode-attention-backend aiter \
  --enable-deterministic-inference
# Qwen3.8-27B additionally: --linear-attn-prefill-backend triton --linear-attn-decode-backend triton
```

Checks, each on a fresh server:
- `python3 -m sglang.test.test_deterministic --test-mode {single,prefix,radix_cache} --n-trials 50`, and `--test-mode prefix --return-logprob`;
- a bitwise batch-size check: `single`'s batches (the same prompt repeated 1 to 50 times, 1,275 responses), requesting logprobs and comparing every response's token IDs and selected-token logprobs with the batch-size-1 response, exact equality.

| Model | TP | single | prefix | prefix logprobs | radix_cache | bitwise (token IDs and logprobs) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen3-8B | 1 | 1 output | 1 per prompt | identical | pass | 1,275 / 1,275 |
| Qwen3-8B | 2 | 1 output | 1 per prompt | identical | pass | 1,275 / 1,275 |
| Qwen3-8B | 4 | 1 output | 1 per prompt | identical | pass | 1,275 / 1,275 |
| Qwen3-8B | 8 | 1 output | 1 per prompt | identical | pass | 1,275 / 1,275 |
| Qwen3.8-27B | 1 | 1 output | 1 per prompt | identical | pass | 1,275 / 1,275 |
| Qwen3.8-27B | 2 | 1 output | 1 per prompt | identical | pass | 1,275 / 1,275 |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B (MoE) | 1 | 1 output | 1 per prompt | identical | pass | 1,275 / 1,275 |
| Qwen3-8B, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3` | 1 | 1 output | 1 per prompt | identical | pass | 1,275 / 1,275 |
| Qwen3.8-27B, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3` | 1 | 1 output | 1 per prompt | identical | pass | 1,275 / 1,275 |

The TP1 Qwen3-8B row was repeated on two more fresh servers with this PR's final code, with the same result.

Long contexts: `test_deterministic`'s prompts stay near 1k tokens (at most about 4 KV partitions per request). So we also sent 8k, 12k and 16k-token prompts (token IDs), each alone twice and in one batch with 12 other requests of 64-4,096 tokens, with 4 different sets of batchmates, and compared the generated token IDs and logprobs exactly with the first batch-of-1 result: identical in 15 / 15 comparisons for Qwen3-8B at TP1 and TP2 and for Qwen3.8-27B at TP1.

GSM8K (`sgl-eval`, all 1,319 questions, temperature 0, thinking off), Triton decode / AITER decode: Qwen3-8B 93.56% / 93.48%; Qwen3-30B-A3B 94.77% / 94.39%; Qwen3.8-27B 96.06% / 95.83%.

A per-layer check at TP1 and TP2 (Qwen3-8B; batch sizes 2-50 and mixed batches; forward hooks hashing each op's inputs and outputs) found no op whose output changed while its input was bitwise equal; attention was compared 5,940 times in decode per rank.

`--test-mode p_vs_d` (prefill vs decode logprobs of the same tokens) differs, as it does with Triton for both phases; it is not part of the AMD deterministic CI.

Unit tests, `python3 -m pytest test/registered/unit/test_model_overrides.py -k deterministic` (MI350X, same image): with #44438 only, the new test fails (1 failed, 6 passed); with this PR, 6 passed.

With this PR applied, a Qwen3-8B server with the command above starts with AITER decode and Triton prefill (radix cache on) and passes a short bitwise batch check; with `SGLANG_USE_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN=1` it refuses to start with the new error; with `--speculative-algorithm NGRAM` it is refused: "... but --decode-attention-backend is 'aiter' (aiter decode is accepted only on gfx950, for non-MLA models and without speculative decoding)". With only `--prefill-attention-backend triton --decode-attention-backend aiter` (no `--attention-backend`) the server starts with AITER decode and Triton prefill; `--attention-backend` itself then resolves to the existing deterministic default (`fa3`), which only the per-phase backends override.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Deterministic mode with AITER decode (this PR) vs Triton for both phases, same server otherwise, MI350X, same image and fixes as above. `python3 -m sglang.benchmark.serving --backend sglang --dataset-name random --random-input-len {1024,8192} --random-output-len 1024 --random-range-ratio 1.0 --num-prompts 256 --max-concurrency {256 for 1k/1k, 128 for 8k/1k} --request-rate inf --seed 1 --warmup-requests 8 --flush-cache`; fresh server per run, 3 rounds interleaved, medians (rounds within 0.5%):

| Model | TP | Workload | Triton decode, tok/s | AITER decode, tok/s | Throughput | ITL p50 (Triton / AITER) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen3-8B | 1 | 1k/1k | 3,691 | 7,064 | **1.91x** | 60.6 / 27.1 ms |
| Qwen3-8B | 1 | 8k/1k | 737 | 1,284 | **1.74x** | 116.2 / 42.2 ms |
| Qwen3-8B | 2 | 1k/1k | 5,783.6 | 9,269.9 | **1.60x** | 37.0 / 20.3 ms |
| Qwen3-8B | 2 | 8k/1k | 1,224 | 1,933 | **1.58x** | 63.5 / 25.0 ms |
| Qwen3-8B | 8 | 1k/1k | 12,356.0 | 15,627.0 | **1.27x** | 16.0 / 11.6 ms |
| Qwen3-8B | 8 | 8k/1k | 2,907.8 | 3,795.3 | **1.31x** | 22.3 / 12.0 ms |
| Qwen3.8-27B | 1 | 1k/1k | 1,811 | 2,032 | **1.12x** | 46.6 / 39.2 ms |
| Qwen3.8-27B | 2 | 1k/1k | 3,833 | 4,332 | **1.13x** | 49.7 / 42.0 ms |
| Qwen3.8-27B | 1 | 8k/1k | 653 | 726 | **1.11x** | 72.0 / 52.8 ms |
| Qwen3.8-27B | 2 | 8k/1k | 1,085 | 1,186 | **1.09x** | 46.1 / 36.0 ms |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B | 1 | 1k/1k | 4,159 | 6,700 | **1.61x** | 55.4 / 31.7 ms |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B | 1 | 8k/1k | 851 | 1,303 | **1.53x** | 91.4 / 39.1 ms |

Qwen3.8-27B gains less because only a quarter of its layers use attention (the rest are Gated DeltaNet). TTFT p50 is unchanged where measured (prefill still uses Triton), except 12% lower for Qwen3.8-27B at TP1 1k/1k, from faster decode steps under load. The Qwen3-8B TP1, Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.8-27B 8k/1k rows were measured with this PR's final code; the others with its first version (same decode path). Each row compares both configurations on one node.

For scale, against normal mode with AITER attention on the same node: Qwen3-8B TP1 deterministic mode goes from 0.382x to **0.731x** (1k/1k) and from 0.329x to 0.572x (8k/1k); at TP8 from 0.377x to 0.476x (1k/1k) and from 0.301x to 0.393x (8k/1k); Qwen3.8-27B TP2 8k/1k from 0.587x to 0.641x.

No change with deterministic mode off.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).

- [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance).

title: [Perf] [AMD] monokernels: Let a plugin skip per-step attention metadata
author: kevin-mii
body:
## Motivation

A monokernel forward may never read some of the attention metadata a backend builds every step. sgl-amd-mono's DeepSeek-V4.1 forward scores every index source with K2i, so on each step it runs, the HIP radix backend builds the aiter decode schedule of each low ratio and nothing reads it. The build is recorded in the decode CUDA graph, so it runs on every replay.

Co-authored with @kkHuang-amd: this is kevin-mii/sglang#19 with the plugin contract stated as data.

## Modifications

- `monokernels/spec.py`: a `StepMetadata` enum and `MonoSpec.unread_metadata`, the per-step metadata a spec's forward never reads. It defaults to empty, so existing plugins are unchanged and the API version stays 1.
- `monokernels/runtime.py`: `is_metadata_unread(model, forward_batch, metadata)`, true only on a step the forward switch routes, for metadata the spec lists.
- `deepseek_v4_backend_hip_radix.py`: the low-ratio decode schedule build skips a ratio when `is_metadata_unread`, next to the identity-rows filter. Without `--monokernel-backend`, every schedule is built as before.
- CPU test `test_only_routed_steps_skip_the_metadata_a_spec_never_reads`.

- `pyproject_other.toml`: the plugin pin moves into one `monokernels_hip` extra that `srt_hip` and `srt_hip_rocm724` both include, at sgl-amd-mono e07665c (sgl-project/sgl-amd-mono#5), whose DeepSeek-V4.1 spec declares the schedule unread. A bump is one line, and the two extras cannot disagree. #5 merged first; until this PR merges, plugin main's DeepSeek-V4.1 spec needs it (it imports `StepMetadata`).
- `docker/rocm.Dockerfile`: the plugin install step from #44621 checks out the commit pip installed through `monokernels_hip`, read from the plugin's `direct_url.json`, instead of its own pin; `SGL_AMD_MONO_COMMIT` stays as an optional override, and the step skips SGLang versions that do not install the plugin. The image and pip then install the same commit. The step's text, run with git and `pip install` stubbed but the real `pip show` and metadata read, covers the installed, not-installed, override, gfx942 and opt-out cases; the image itself was not built.

## Accuracy Tests

MI350X, TP4, sgl-amd-mono's `test/e2e` (9 tests) on DSpark (verify steps) and decode servers. KL is against the standard path's prefill (limits 0.03, long prompts 0.06):

|---|---|---|---|
| DSpark GSM8K / KL / long-prompt KL | 0.915 / 0.0139 / 0.0273 | 0.910 / 0.0101 / 0.0284 | 0.905 / 0.0139 / 0.0244 |
| decode GSM8K / KL | 0.905 / 0.0103 | 0.905 / 0.0101 | 0.905 / 0.0115 |
| tests | 9 passed | 9 passed | 9 passed |

`test/registered/unit/monokernels`: 18 passed. The measurements ran at 9fd4430dd3; 212f36daa1 after it changes only a docstring, a comment and a test variable name, and a3a83ffc88 pins sgl-amd-mono e07665c, the same plugin code as ae2f020. 31e3031b74 merges main (with #44405 and #44630), and 958d06d3e9 pins the plugin once and has the image check out what pip installed; 29 CPU tests (`test/registered/unit/monokernels` and the CUDA graph config tests) pass on it. The e2e on b3e0ba62aa with sgl-amd-mono e07665c: 9 passed (DSpark GSM8K 0.910, KL 0.0123, long-prompt KL 0.0319; decode GSM8K 0.910, KL 0.0103).

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Decode time per output token (ms), MI350X, TP4, DSpark with simulated acceptance 3.51, median of 3 rounds of 1024 tokens, one server per arm. Main is ec7ab9d0c2 with sgl-amd-mono 3970534; kevin-mii/sglang#19 is ec43db1bff with 3970534; this PR is 9fd4430dd3 with sgl-amd-mono#5 (ae2f020):

title: [Perf] diffusion: Defer full GC collections while importing the runtime
author: rwang5203
body:
## Motivation

A diffusion scheduler process imports about ten thousand modules before it builds its pipeline. Imports create long-lived modules, classes and functions and very little garbage, yet CPython runs a full collection every time the surviving heap has grown by a quarter, and each one traces every tracked object again. A scheduler process runs 12 of them during startup, which together take about 1.6 seconds of CPU, with or without compiled bytecode.

Where those collections fall also depends on the import order rather than on the work done. Moving an import, for example to load a module on first use, can add or remove a whole-heap collection inside a given span of startup, which makes import time changes hard to judge.

## Modifications

- `runtime/utils/process.py` gains `defer_full_gc_for_imports()`, a context manager that raises the third GC threshold so that no automatic full collection runs inside the block. Young collections keep running, so short-lived cyclic garbage is freed as usual. Restoring the original thresholds lets automatic full collections resume after the block. On CPython 3.14.0–3.14.4, which uses incremental GC and ignores the third threshold, the context manager is a no-op.
- On exit it restores the thresholds it found, also when the block raises. Nested and concurrent blocks restore them when the last one exits, a child forked inside a block restores them at fork, and the collector's enabled state is never changed, so a process that disabled the collector keeps it disabled.
- It is used where diffusion processes import their runtime in bulk, in the activation phase of `bootstrap_scheduler_process` (platform initialization through the `gpu_worker` import), the activation phase of `bootstrap_http_server_process`, and pipeline and config discovery in the registry. Pipeline discovery enters the block only on its first run, so the registry lookups that return early touch nothing.
- No new option, and nothing changes for srt.

Two simpler forms were measured first and not used. `gc.disable()` over the same blocks saved the same CPU, but it also stops young collections, so about 7 MB of short-lived cyclic garbage (frames of caught exceptions, closures, package metadata structures) stayed alive until the block ended, which showed up as 8 MiB more anonymous memory in the HTTP server child. `gc.freeze()` after the imports would keep import-time objects out of every later collection, but frozen objects are never collected again, so it changes steady-state serving memory, and freezing after warmup is the existing pattern for that.

## Accuracy Tests

No output path changes. Only the timing of garbage collections during startup imports changes.

`test_process.py` checks that full collection is deferred where the collector supports threshold2, that incremental GC is left unchanged on CPython 3.14.0–3.14.4, and that nesting, exception exits with GC disabled, and forked children restore the correct state. The file passes on CPython 3.11.16, 3.12.15, 3.13.15, 3.14.0, 3.14.4, and 3.14.5; only the threshold2-specific collection assertion is skipped on 3.14.0–3.14.4. The earlier CPU diffusion-unit comparison had the same per-test outcomes as the base, apart from the added GC coverage.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Measured on a CPU-only host with scripts that start each process the way it starts in a server, without touching a device. A scheduler child runs through `bootstrap_scheduler_process` up to the point where `build_pipeline` would construct the pipeline, and the `--webui` HTTP child runs through `bootstrap_http_server_process` up to `create_app`. After each run, the same process allocates 100,000 objects so that any collection this change postpones is paid inside the measurement. Each process ran once with compiled bytecode present, as in an installed package, and once with every module compiled from source.

The comparison ran as eight counterbalanced pairs with a local Cosmos3 Nano checkpoint, then eight fresh pairs with a local Wan2.1 T2V 1.3B checkpoint as an independent confirmation, each beside an A/A control that compared two separate copies of the base. A gain is listed only where both sets established it at 1 percent or more and the A/A control showed no difference. The table gives the mean change with this PR and its 95 percent interval over the pairs, for the Cosmos3 Nano and the Wan2.1 pairs.

| Process | Backend | Bytecode | CPU time | Wall time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| scheduler child | auto | compiled | -2.9 % [-3.3, -2.6] and -2.8 % [-3.5, -2.2] | -5.8 % [-6.5, -5.0] and -5.2 % [-6.4, -4.0] |
| scheduler child | auto | from source | -2.5 % [-2.6, -2.3] and -2.5 % [-2.9, -2.2] | -4.5 % [-5.1, -3.9] and -4.5 % [-5.5, -3.6] |
| scheduler child | sglang | compiled | -2.8 % [-3.5, -2.0] and -3.0 % [-3.2, -2.8] | -5.2 % [-6.6, -3.7] and -5.5 % [-6.2, -4.8] |
| scheduler child | sglang | from source | -2.7 % [-3.2, -2.2] and -2.8 % [-3.2, -2.4] | -4.8 % [-6.0, -3.6] and -5.2 % [-6.3, -4.1] |
| HTTP child (`--webui`) | auto | compiled | -2.2 % [-2.7, -1.6] and -2.9 % [-3.4, -2.4] | -4.7 % [-6.0, -3.5] and -5.6 % [-6.7, -4.6] |
| HTTP child (`--webui`) | auto | from source | -2.8 % [-3.2, -2.3] and -2.6 % [-3.0, -2.2] | no claim |

In absolute terms the scheduler child uses about 0.7 s less CPU, out of about 26 to 28 s, and reaches the point where it would build its pipeline 0.7 to 0.8 s sooner. It runs 8 full collections instead of 12 in every run, and spends about 0.8 s less in garbage collection. The HTTP child wall time from source has no claim because the A/A control of the Wan2.1 pairs read a difference of -0.53 % [-1.05, -0.02] on that metric.

No performance claim for the launcher and HTTP frontend process, where no full collection falls inside the blocks this change covers. In every process measured, including the launcher, anonymous memory (`Pss_Anon`), peak RSS (`VmHWM`), minor page faults and the number of full collections read no worse than without this change.

### Additional real-server check

Compared base `b234b5c32e0d` with `04c42400522d` on one H200 (143771 MiB), Xeon Platinum 8558P, driver 595.71.05, Python 3.12.15, PyTorch 2.14.1+cu130, Transformers 5.19.0, and Diffusers 0.37.0. The native SGLang backend used FA3, speed mode, GPU-resident components, and no torch.compile or CUDA graphs.

Model: `Wan-AI/Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B-Diffusers`, revision `0fad780a534b6463e45facd96134c9f345acfa5b`. Server warmup: 256×256, 9 frames, one step. First API request: the same shape, two steps, seed 42, CFG 5, prompt “A small red boat floating on a calm lake.” We timed readiness via `/health` and the first completed `/v1/videos` job, polling every 100 ms. Checkpoint download and kernel priming were excluded. A/B/B/A order, two measured starts per revision; means below:

| Measurement | Base | This PR |
|---|---:|---:|
| Process start → server ready | 41.97 s | 41.47 s |
| Process start → first request completed | 42.28 s | 41.78 s |
| First request after readiness | 0.309 s | 0.309 s |

All four output MP4s were byte-identical. This small sample observed about 0.50 s (1.2%) lower complete startup latency, not a general speedup guarantee. It does not establish a steady-state inference speedup. The scheduler and HTTP bootstrap ordering tests also passed.

title: [Perf] deepseek_v4: size the masked silu-mul-quant grid to the GPU, not the padded capacity
author: Monishver11
body:
## Motivation In short: the DeepSeek-V4 masked SiLU-mul-quant kernel runs on every MoE layer of DeepEP low-latency decode, and it launches one CTA for every row the padded DeepEP buffer could hold. At decode almost none of those rows are real, so most CTAs only scan the per-expert counts and exit. On the Flash TP4 shape that is 24,576 CTAs for about 400 real rows, and on H100 the kernel takes 15.9 us even with zero real rows. This PR sizes the grid to the GPU instead: 17.1 -> 3.3 us at 64 decode tokens per GPU, with bit-identical output. Details: `silu_and_mul_masked_post_quant` (`python/sglang/kernels/jit/csrc/deepseek_v4/silu_and_mul_masked_post_quant.cuh`) runs the SiLU-mul + FP8 quant between the two masked DeepGEMM GEMMs on the DeepEP low-latency path. DeepSeek-V4 takes it on every decode MoE layer because of its `swiglu_limit` (10.0 in the Flash config), through `_varlen_deep_gemm_silu_mul_quant` in `moe_runner/deep_gemm.py`. That covers the DeepEP balanced and high-throughput recipes in the DSV4 cookbook (B200/B300/GB200/GB300 FP4 with `--moe-a2a-backend deepep`, and the H200 FP8 ones). The input is the DeepEP buffer `[E_local, T, 2D]`, where T is the padded per-expert capacity (`SGLANG_DEEPEP_NUM_MAX_DISPATCH_TOKENS_PER_RANK` x ranks) and `masked_m[e]` (on the GPU) says how many rows of expert e are real. The host can't read `masked_m` without a sync, so the kernel launched `T * topk` CTAs, one per possible real row. Every CTA loads `masked_m`, does a block prefix scan with 2 `__syncthreads`, and then all but the CTAs that own a real row exit. On the Flash B200 TP4 recipe that is `4096 * 6 = 24,576` CTAs per call, for about 400 real rows at 64 decode tokens per GPU. On H100 the kernel costs 15.9 us with zero real rows and 17.1 us at 64 tokens per GPU; almost all of it is empty CTAs going through the scheduler. ## Modifications In short: launch only as many CTAs as the GPU can hold at once, instead of one per possible row, and let each CTA loop over the real rows. The output is bit-identical to main. On H100 the kernel goes from 15.9 to 1.6 us with no real rows and from 17.1 to 3.3 us at 64 decode tokens per GPU (Flash TP4 shape), and every decode point up to the dispatch cap is faster (1.09x-16.25x). The one slower case is when every one of the `T * topk` rows is real, 2-4%, which uniform routing doesn't get near (details in Speed Tests). How it works: the host still can't read `masked_m`, so the grid stays fixed, but it is now one resident wave (1,056 CTAs on H100) instead of `T * topk` (24,576 on the Flash TP4 shape). Each CTA prefix-scans `masked_m` once, keeps the result in shared memory, and then takes rows `b, b + grid, b + 2 * grid, ...` of the flattened real-row list. At decode there are fewer real rows than CTAs, so each CTA handles at most one row, exactly like before, just without the other ~23,500 CTAs (24,576 - 1,056) that found no row. Changes, in simple terms: - Smaller grid: sized to the GPU, not to the padded capacity. - One `masked_m` scan per CTA, kept in shared memory, instead of one scan per possible row. - A loop over real rows in each CTA; the per-row math is the same code as before. - A new test that checks every real row matches the contig kernel and no padded row is written. Details: - Launch `min(SMs x resident CTAs, T * topk)` CTAs instead of `T * topk` (1,056 on H100 at 256 threads; about 1,184 on B200, not measured). Occupancy comes from `cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor`, cached per block size. - Each CTA scans `masked_m` once into shared memory (`s_row_end`, inclusive prefix, 1 KB), exits before the PDL wait if it has no row, then walks the flattened real rows with a grid stride. A row's expert comes from a binary search over `s_row_end`. - The per-row body moved verbatim into `silu_mul_quant_varlen_row`, so the math and the output bytes don't change. The PDL wait now runs once before the loop; the trigger stays where it was in the row body. - `max_rows = T * topk` keeps the old implicit cap (rows past it were never processed before and still aren't). - New test `test_masked_post_quant_writes_exactly_the_real_rows`: masked vs contig kernel byte-equal on real rows, sentinel untouched on padded rows, for both scale layouts and all-zero / one hot expert / uneven / full `masked_m`. Capacity is 4x the resident CTAs so "full" makes each CTA loop over several rows. Same idea as vLLM's Silu v2 `persistent_masked_m_silu_mul_quant` ([vllm-project/vllm#25074](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/25074)): fixed grid, one scan of the counts per CTA into shared memory, then each CTA walks the real rows. Not a duplicate: no open PR touches this kernel's grid (searched `silu_and_mul_masked_post_quant`, `masked silu quant`, `silu_mul_quant_varlen`). [sgl-project/sglang#32066](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/32066) adds a launch guard on the same launcher lines, so whichever lands second needs a small rebase. ## Accuracy Tests The output is bit-identical to main, so model accuracy can't change. I checked it at the kernel level instead of with an e2e eval: - Bitwise vs main, in one process (main's kernel built from the base file under its own namespace), CPU-seeded inputs, outputs pre-filled with a sentinel and compared as whole buffers including padded rows: **464 identical, 0 mismatched**. Matrix: 5 shapes (up to 256 experts, and a `full` case where `sum(masked_m) > T * topk` to check the cap), group size 32 and 128, 3 scale layouts (fp32, UE8M0, transposed packed UE8M0), swizzle on/off, swiglu_limit on/off, 4 `masked_m` patterns. - `test_per_token_group_quant.py`: 121 passed (8 new). `test_humming_fp8_dispatch.py` (the other caller): 2 passed. - The new test fails on each of 3 broken mappings (wrong loop stride, `>=` in the binary search, wrong row offset). - Registers: 32/thread before and after (`__launch_bounds__(1024, 2)` cap), 0 spills. ## Speed Tests and Profiling H100 80GB HBM3, driver 595.71.05, nvcc 13.2, torch 2.14.1+cu130, triton 3.8.0. Validated on main 97d3150a6a; the branch is rebased onto ed8c3139f1 and neither the kernel nor the test file changed upstream in between. `triton.testing.do_bench_cudagraph` on the op, 2 interleaved rounds (main, PR, main, PR) in one process. Shapes from the DSV4 cookbook DeepEP recipes, group 128, swiglu_limit 10. Real rows come from uniform top-6 routing at the given decode tokens per GPU, up to the dispatch cap; "all real" sets every one of the `T * topk` rows real. On H100 the kernel takes the fp32-scale layout; I didn't have a B200 for the transposed UE8M0 layout. All numbers are from one H100. The GPU in brackets is the cookbook recipe the shape comes from, not where it ran. | shape (cookbook recipe it comes from) | 0 rows | 64 tok/GPU | dispatch cap | all real | |---|---|---|---|---| | Flash EP4, T=4096 (B200/B300/GB200 TP4) | 15.92 -> 1.63 us (9.74x) | 17.10 -> 3.26 us (5.25x) | 1024 tok: 49.89 -> 45.89 us (1.09x) | 176.07 -> 180.88 us (0.97x) | | Flash EP8, T=8192 (B200 TP8) | 31.27 -> 1.92 us (16.25x) | 32.19 -> 3.32 us (9.70x) | 1024 tok: 61.68 -> 44.85 us (1.38x) | 350.95 -> 356.45 us (0.98x) | | Pro EP4, T=1024 (GB300 TP4) | 6.52 -> 1.57 us (4.15x) | 8.64 -> 4.32 us (2.00x) | 256 tok: 15.31 -> 11.50 us (1.33x) | 65.92 -> 68.74 us (0.96x) | | Flash EP4, T=1024 (H200 FP8 TP4) | 4.92 -> 1.96 us (2.52x) | 5.84 -> 3.17 us (1.84x) | 256 tok: 10.15 -> 8.24 us (1.23x) | 43.34 -> 44.38 us (0.98x) | | Pro EP16, T=2048 (H200 FP8 TP16) | 12.01 -> 1.66 us (7.25x) | 14.33 -> 4.29 us (3.34x) | 128 tok: 16.35 -> 6.01 us (2.72x) | 130.82 -> 132.89 us (0.98x) | Every decode point up to the dispatch cap is faster (1.09x-16.25x). The one slower regime is "all real", 2-4%: every token on every rank routing all 6 experts to the same rank, which uniform routing doesn't get near. There each CTA loops over about 9-47 rows and pays a binary search per row. A contiguous per-CTA split (search once, then step forward) brings it to 1.00-1.03x but is 2-5% slower at decode and more code, so I kept the stride loop; happy to switch if you'd rather have no regime below 1.0x. For the Flash B200 TP4 recipe at 64 decode tokens per GPU, the H100 number is 13.8 us saved per call, so about 0.6 ms per decode step over 43 MoE layers. That's arithmetic from the microbench, not an e2e measurement; e2e needs 4x B200 with DeepEP, which I haven't run.

title: [Perf] DeepSeek-V4.1: Raise the SM100 swap-AB decode cap to 40 rows
author: weireweire
body:
## Motivation

SM100 swap-AB decode attention for DeepSeek-V4.1 admits at most 8 query rows. DSpark verify sends 5 rows per request (block size 5), so only batch size 1 takes swap-AB; batch size 2 and up fall back to FlashMLA. FlashMLA pads q to 64 heads and runs split-KV, so its time is flat at about 24 µs across 5–40 rows, while swap-AB is 2.7x faster at 5 rows and grows with the row count.

## Modifications

- `decode_attention_sm100.py`: admit up to 40 rows (`MAX_ROWS`) on SM100, so TP4 verify up to batch size 8 takes swap-AB. The kernel grid is (rows, KV tiles) and no program depends on the row count, so the cap is only a dispatch choice. The gfx950 path keeps its 8-row `MAX_BATCH`.
- `test_swapab_attention.py`: add 20- and 40-row cases and a 40-row CUDA graph replay; the per-row lengths now repeat so they cover any batch.

## Kernel timing

GB300, 16 heads (TP4), one decode layer shape (SWA 128 + extra KV 512), CUDA graph timing, µs per call:

| rows | batch size (verify) | swap-AB | FlashMLA | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 1 | 8.8 | 23.7 | 0.37 |
| 10 | 2 | 9.3 | 23.9 | 0.39 |
| 20 | 4 | 12.5 | 23.9 | 0.52 |
| 24 | — | 13.1 | 23.8 | 0.55 |
| 40 | 8 | 20.1 | 24.2 | 0.83 |

Break-even is near 48 rows; 40 leaves a margin.

## Benchmark

AgentX, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash FP4 on GB300, TP4/EP1, one hour per run, DSpark with simulated acceptance length 3.51. Both arms use `lmsysorg/sglang:nightly-dev-cu13-20261012-e6072935`; "this PR" overlays the changed attention files onto the same image. Server flags: `--tensor-parallel-size 4 --expert-parallel-size 1 --mem-fraction-static 0.8 --chunked-prefill-size 16384 --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 128 --max-running-requests 128 --swa-prefix-tails 4096 --tokenizer-worker-num 4`, with `--prefill-decode-interval` 0 at c8 and 192 at c16.

| conc | main: P90 tok/s/user @ tok/s/GPU | this PR | P90 | median tok/s/user |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | 413.3 @ 16,089 | 411.3 @ 16,184 | −0.5% | 577 → 610 (+5.7%) |
| 16 | 422.0 @ 28,885 | 442.4 @ 29,108 | +4.8% | 538 → 559 (+4.0%) |

## Accuracy Tests

GSM8K, all 1319 questions, 5-shot, real MTP verification (no simulated acceptance), 64 concurrent requests, TP4 on GB300:

| main | this PR |
|---|---|
| 0.9696 | 0.9711 |

## Unit tests

`test/registered/kernels/ops/attention/dsv4/test_swapab_attention.py` passes on GB300.

title: [Perf] [AMD] dsv4: Add a separate MegaMoE decode instance
author: RolaoDenthu
body:
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->

<!-- PR title: [Type] scope: title, or [Type] [Hardware] scope: title.

Hardware: optional single tag without spaces. Use uppercase hardware tags (AMD, NVIDIA, NPU, MI300X), except for exactly these four spellings: Intel, Apple, Huawei, Ascend.
Title: no letter-case restriction.
Reverts: use GitHub's default title, Revert "original title".
Examples: [Fix] attention: Fix KV cache indexing; [Perf] [AMD] flash-attn: Optimize decode performance. -->

## Motivation

Decode currently shares a MegaMoEV2 instance sized for prefill. Even with a small decode batch, the large MTPR keeps it on the large-instance dispatch/combine path, preventing it from benefiting from kernel configurations optimized for small token counts.

Introduce a separate, smaller decode instance to enable the small-MTPR execution path while retaining the main instance for prefill.

## Modification

Add `SGLANG_AMD_FLYDSL_MEGA_MOE_DECODE_MTPR` (default: `0`, disabled). When enabled, maintain two cached `MegaMoEV2` instances:

- **Main instance:** uses `SGLANG_AMD_FLYDSL_MEGA_MOE_MTPR` for steps containing prefill.
- **Decode instance:** uses the smaller MTPR `SGLANG_AMD_FLYDSL_MEGA_MOE_DECODE_MTPR` for decode, target verify, and draft extend in decode-only steps. 

Both instances are constructed together in a fixed order across EP ranks before graph capture. They own separate communication buffers and synchronization state while sharing model weights through per-layer rebinding.

Instance selection follows the globally synchronized step type, ensuring all EP ranks use the same instance regardless of local batch size or graph/eager execution. Startup validation checks that the decode MTPR covers the maximum per-rank workload.

## Accuracy Tests
gsm8k 1319: 0.939

MegaMoEV2 per-layer time in µs, max across the 8 ranks (MI355X, EP8, DeepSeek-V4-Pro shapes, a8w4, uniform routing, CUDA-graph):

| 112 | 362 (1.30x faster) | 472 | 469 |
| 224 | 449 (1.28x faster) | 566 | 573 |
| 448 | 647 (2% slower) | 632 | 633 |
| 672 | does not fit | 797 | 790 |

The speedups are relative to the 16384 column.

title: [Perf] deepseek_v4: fold the MegaAttention query layout into wq_b for block-FP8-as-MXFP8 checkpoints
author: kpham-sgl
body:
## Motivation

`setup_mega_attention` folds the MegaAttention query head layout into `wq_b`'s rows (`interleave_query_rows`) only when `wq_b` is a native MXFP8 linear. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash ships a `[32, 32]` block-FP8 checkpoint whose dense linears run through the same FlashInfer MXFP8 GEMM via the block-FP8-as-MXFP8 view (`block_fp8_mxfp8_ready`), so `mega_wq_b_permuted` stays false and every layer packs the query at forward time with `pack_query`: a `new_zeros` of the `[tokens, 64, 512]` bf16 query and a strided transpose copy into it.

Measured on GB300, DEP2 (TP2 + DP attention, EP2, MegaMoE, decoder bounded replay, Mega-mHC on), one cold 16,384-token prefill chunk per rank, torch profiler:

| per 16K step, rank 0 | count | per launch | total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `aten::new_zeros` (vectorized fill) | 40 | 141 µs | 5.7 ms |
| `aten::copy_` (strided `direct_copy` elementwise) | 40 | 691 µs | 27.6 ms |

That is 33 ms of a 322 ms step (10%) and 80 launches on an eager step that is dispatch-bound (median inter-kernel gap 41 µs). Per layer it writes ~1.2 GB of zeros and moves ~2.4 GB through a non-contiguous copy.

## Modifications

- `_wq_b_uses_flashinfer_mxfp8` also accepts a block-FP8 `wq_b` served as MXFP8 (`block_fp8_as_mxfp8` on the FlashInfer CUTLASS / CuTe-DSL backend), so `mega_wq_b_permuted` is set for this checkpoint.
- In `setup_mega_attention`, for that case: `interleave_query_rows` moves 16-row groups, so the `[32, 32]` block scale is refined to 16 rows, permuted the same way as the weight, and rebound as `weight_scale_inv` with `weight_block_size = [16, 32]`. The existing post-load pass then builds the swizzled MXFP8 scale from it as for any block-FP8-as-MXFP8 layer. The native MXFP8 path is unchanged.

After this `pack_query` is skipped for the block-FP8 checkpoint exactly as for native MXFP8 ones.

Numerics: the same FP8 bytes and the same e8m0 scales reach the GEMM, only in the row order the attention kernel already consumes; refining a 32-row block scale to 16-row blocks is exact.

## Measured

GB300, DEP2 (TP2 + DP attention, EP2), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, MegaMoE, Mega-mHC, decoder bounded replay, eager prefill, 16K-token prefill budget per rank, rank 0. Main (job 3470, `2d3dd3168d`) against this branch (job 3476). Startup log on the branch: `MegaAttention wq_b query-layout permute: applied=True (block-fp8 served as mxfp8)`.

| Unprofiled, median of 3 | main | this PR |
|---|---:|---:|
| One 16K-token cold chunk per rank (ms) | 247 | 235 |
| 128K-token prompt in eight 16K chunks (ms) | 1,906 | 1,764 |

| Profiled 16K step | main | this PR |
|---|---:|---:|
| `new_zeros` fill and strided `copy_` launches per step | 80 (33.9 ms) | 0 |
| Kernel launches per step | 1,847 | 1,756 |
| Attention section per layer (mHC kernel to the MoE block's mHC kernel), median over layers (ms) | 5.03 | 3.39 |

The cached-prefix cells of the same run moved both ways by up to 15% between runs and are not reported.

Before: main, layer 6, 5.00 ms and 17 launches between the two mHC kernels; the fill (264 µs) and the strided copy (1.30 ms) sit between `k_norm_rope` and the attention kernel.

![main, layer 6 attention section](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kpham-sgl/sglang/assets-prefill-h2h-2026-10-16/prefill-h2h-2026-10-16/main-job3470-layer6-attention-section.jpg)

After: this branch, same layer, 3.36 ms and 15 launches.

![this PR, layer 6 attention section](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kpham-sgl/sglang/assets-prefill-h2h-2026-10-16/prefill-h2h-2026-10-16/pr44838-job3476-layer6-attention-section.jpg)

Not run yet: the GSM8K native-acceptance gate.
