title: [Feat] ComfyUI: Add online INT8 quantization for BF16 Qwen-Image-2.1 single files
author: OnePunchMonk
body:
## Motivation

Users on 24 to 32 GB GPUs often already have the BF16 ComfyUI file for Qwen-Image-2.1 but cannot use online quantization with it. Today they have to find and download a separate pre-quantized file.

Two things blocked this:

1. The plugin preflight rejected `quantization` for any ComfyUI single file.
2. The worker's single-file loader (`comfyui_checkpoints/spec.py`) only built a quant config from per-layer markers in the file. A BF16 file has none, so `--quantization` was silently ignored and the DiT stayed in BF16.

## Modifications

- `runtime/loader/comfyui_checkpoints/spec.py`: when a single file has no quant markers and `quantization` is set, resolve it through the existing `resolve_transformer_quant_load_spec` (same path native directories use), build the matching `WeightLoadPlan`, and run the quant post-load hooks. Methods that need serialized weights (e.g. `mxfp8`) raise a clear error instead of being ignored.
- Plugin `core/preflight.py`: allow `convrot_int8` on BF16 Qwen-Image-2.1 single files. Other models and other methods stay rejected with a clear message.
- Options tooltip and README updated.
- Tests: worker regression test (quant config, param dtype, load device and hooks reach the loader) and preflight accept/reject cases.

Scope is Qwen-Image-2.1 + INT8 ConvRot only. FP8 was tested and left out (results below). Other single-file models can be added once validated.

## Accuracy and speed (Modal, L40S)

ComfyUI v0.41.0, headless API graph through `SGLDUNETLoader` + `SGLDOptions`. `Comfy-Org/Qwen-Image-2.1` turbo file, 1024x1024, 8 steps, euler/simple, cfg 1, seed 42. Time is the second (warm) run. Peak GPU is whole-process `nvidia-smi` (includes ComfyUI's text encoder and VAE). PSNR/SSIM are against SGLD BF16 on the same seed.

| Run | Sampling time | Peak GPU | PSNR / SSIM vs SGLD BF16 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Native ComfyUI BF16 | 3.43 s | 22.9 GB | 28.19 dB / 0.969 |
| SGLD BF16 | 3.29 s | 26.9 GB | reference |
| **SGLD online INT8 (this PR)** | **2.35 s** | 23.5 GB | **28.55 dB / 0.966** |
| SGLD online FP8 (not enabled) | 4.49 s | 23.5 GB | 21.74 dB / 0.855 |

Worker log for the INT8 run:

```
convrot_int8: quantized 224 linear layers (13.00 GiB of BF16 weights -> 6.50 GiB INT8; jit 0, comfy_kitchen 224), left 0 in BF16
```

INT8 is about 1.4x faster than BF16 and halves DiT weight memory, and its distance from BF16 is in line with native ComfyUI vs SGLD BF16. On L40S (CC 8.9) the JIT INT8 kernels are unavailable, so this ran on the comfy_kitchen backend.

### Why FP8 is not enabled

Online FP8 quantizes the same 224 layers but drifts from BF16 and is slower than BF16 on L40S. Keeping some layers in BF16 (`--quantization-ignored-layers`) did not fix it consistently (2 seeds each):

| FP8 variant | Time | SSIM (seed 42 / 1234) | PSNR dB (seed 42 / 1234) |
|---|---|---|---|
| BF16 reference | 3.17 s | | |
| FP8, all layers | 4.36 s | 0.855 / 0.854 | 21.7 / 20.8 |
| keep `img_mlp.out` in BF16 | 3.75 s | 0.814 / 0.866 | 20.6 / 21.7 |
| keep `attn.to_out` in BF16 | 4.18 s | 0.915 / 0.876 | 24.0 / 21.4 |
| keep both | 3.55 s | 0.879 / 0.884 | 22.6 / 21.8 |
| keep blocks 0 and 31 in BF16 | 4.23 s | 0.955 / 0.881 | 27.2 / 22.0 |

So the plugin rejects `fp8` for single files for now.

### Pre-quantized file note

Loading Comfy-Org's own `qwen_image_2.1_turbo_int8_convrot.safetensors` through `SGLDUNETLoader` fails on current main with `Parameter transformer_blocks.1.attn.comfy_attention.config not found in custom model state dict`. That is the serialized-marker path, which this PR does not touch; I can open a separate issue.

## Testing

- Unit tests on Modal (`test_comfyui_checkpoint_spec.py`, `test_comfyui_options.py`, `test_comfyui_generator.py`, `test_comfyui_qwen_image21.py`): 64 passed, 3 skipped.
- Same new tests against unmodified main: 5 failed (the 3 worker regression tests and 2 preflight cases), confirming they guard the change.
- End-to-end ComfyUI runs on L40S as above.

## Limitations

- Only Qwen-Image-2.1 single files are allowed in the plugin; Flux, Qwen-Image, Z-Image and MiniMax-H3 keep the existing rejection until validated.
- FSDP inference with online ConvRot INT8 on single files was not tested.

title: [Perf] [AMD] deterministic: Faster extend attention launch on gfx950
author: aarnetalman
body:
## Motivation

Deterministic inference (`--enable-deterministic-inference`) runs prefill with the unified extend-attention kernel (`extend_attention_fwd_unified`), whose reduction order does not depend on the batch. On gfx950 it launches every head_dim <= 128 with a 64-row query tile and 4 warps. Each workgroup streams the whole prefix for its query rows, so with long prompts the kernel is bound by KV reads: at 64k-token inputs it takes 82% of deterministic mode's GPU time (Qwen3-8B on MI350X), and deterministic throughput falls to about 0.2x of normal mode.

A 256-row tile with 8 warps reads each KV block once for 4x as many query rows. The KV block size (`BLOCK_N`), and so the order in which each row's softmax and sums are accumulated, is unchanged, so the output is bitwise identical to today's.

## Modifications

- `extend_attention.py` (`extend_attention_fwd_unified`): on gfx950, for head_dim <= 128 with the default `BLOCK_N` of 64, launch with `BLOCK_M = 256` and 8 warps. Other GPUs, head dims, the shared block-size table and the non-deterministic extend kernels are unchanged.
- `test_triton_attention_kernels.py`: on gfx950, the unified kernel's output with the new tile equals the default tile's output bit for bit (head_dim 128 and 64, three sequences with 0-4k prefixes).

A pipelined variant (128-row tile, 2 stages) was faster in isolation but aborted in ROCm Triton's compiler (LLVM `iota_range` assertion) for the server's kernel specialisation, so it is not used.

## Accuracy Tests

The output is bitwise identical to the current launch, so accuracy cannot change. Checked three ways on MI350X (`rocm/sgl-dev:v0.5.22-rocm724-mi35x-20261018`, `SGLANG_USE_AITER=1`, our open deterministic-mode fixes for MI350X applied):

- Kernel level: 500 launch configurations timed on 8k-token chunks after 0-56k-token prefixes and a 4-sequence mixed batch, head_dim 128 (Qwen3-8B: 32/8 heads) and 64 (gpt-oss: 64/8 heads, sinks). Every configuration with `BLOCK_N = 64` gives output equal to the current launch (`torch.equal`); the new one is 2.0-2.6x faster.
- New unit test `test_extend_attention_unified_gfx950_tile_bitwise` passes on MI350X. Two existing tests in the same file fail on gfx950 with and without this change (same results on the unchanged image): `test_extend_attention_block_sizes` (expects the tile #34461 added, which #35770 narrowed) and the head_dim-80 case of `test_extend_attention_unified_vs_regular` (max diff 0.167, tolerance 0.15/0.17). Both are pre-existing; the first is fixed by #45099, which restores that tile and is independent of this PR (the two apply together cleanly and were tested together).
- End to end, deterministic mode with the change, `python3 -m sglang.test.test_deterministic --test-mode {single,prefix,radix_cache} --n-trials 50`, `--test-mode prefix --return-logprob`, and a bitwise batch-size check (the same prompt in batches of 1 to 50, 1,275 responses, token IDs and logprobs compared exactly): all pass for Qwen3-8B (TP1, TP2, TP8), Qwen3-30B-A3B, Phi-4, gpt-oss-20b (TP1, TP2) and gpt-oss-120b. Long prompts (16k-120k tokens alone vs with other requests in the batch, and with chunked-prefill boundaries moved by other requests) give identical token IDs and logprobs. Rechecked on the 2026-10-19 nightly (`v0.5.22-rocm724-mi35x-20261019`): Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30B-A3B pass every check.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

`python3 -m sglang.benchmark.serving --backend sglang --dataset-name random --random-range-ratio 1.0 --request-rate inf`, deterministic mode, before and after alternating twice on the same GPU (every pair within 0.5%), output throughput:

| Model, attention | 1k in / 1k out (256 prompts, conc. 256) | 8k / 1k (256, conc. 128) | 15k-32k / 256 (64, conc. 16) | 64k / 256 (32, conc. 8) | 120k-126k / 256 (16, conc. 4) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen3-8B, Triton prefill + AITER decode | 7,070 -> 7,234 (+2.3%) | 1,211 -> 1,469 (+21%) | 47.9 -> 86.2 (+80%, 32k) | 17.8 -> 35.2 (+98%)* | 5.9 -> 13.7 (+130%)* |

title: [Perf] [AMD] Kimi-K3: prepare the attention interface for mono fusion
author: billishyahao
body: This PR co-work with mono patch: https://github.com/sgl-project/sgl-amd-mono/pull/13 ## Motivation The AMD monokernel backend runs a Kimi-K3 decode or DSpark verify step as two persistent launches a layer. They run in this order. - **K1, the KDA front launch**, covers the attention side of a KDA layer: the attention-side residual seam, `input_layernorm`, the in-projection, `f_b`, the conv, the recurrence and the gated output norm. It covers the 69 KDA layers. The 24 full-attention layers keep stock SGLang's attention instead. - **K2, the layer launch**, takes the TP-local attention output from there and runs o_proj, the attention-TP all-reduce, the MLP attention-residual seam and the MoE. It covers all 92 MoE layers, whichever attention produced its input. That backend is sgl-project/sgl-amd-mono. It loads through the `sglang.srt.plugins` entry point and is selected with `--monokernel-backend amd`. SGLang needs nothing else for it: `install_monokernel_forward` swaps the whole model forward (`srt/monokernels/runtime.py`), so the kernels, the spec and its registration all live in the plugin. This method is the one thing the plugin cannot reach from outside, which is why it is the only change here. In short, this change follows the sgl mono kernel RFC https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/43949 ## Modifications **1. The KDA in-projection gate**, which K1 reads. Take the merge when `do_fuse_qkvbfg` allows it, as before, or when a monokernel backend is selected: ```python if not self.use_full_rank_gate: return False if not (self.do_fuse_qkvbfg or get_exec().kernel.monokernel_backend): return False ``` With no backend selected this reduces to `use_full_rank_gate and do_fuse_qkvbfg`, which is what the predicate tested before. That identity is deliberate. The fused GEMM is a different kernel from the split pair. A wider gate on its own would move decode output by one bf16 rounding step for every ROCm Kimi-K3 user. The file's own docstring records that the two paths agree to bf16 rounding and not bitwise. The weight checks below the gate do not change, and they still decide. The backend changes the policy. It does not remove the safety checks. `_is_unquantized_mergeable` requires the three weights to share one dtype, and that dtype to be bf16 or fp16. A per-channel FP8 weight or a packed MXFP4 weight still refuses, because `_merge_weights_as_views` concatenates `.weight` alone. Nothing else changes. `do_fuse_qkvbfg` also gates a weight-loader branch and the low-rank gate's projection layout. This commit touches neither. **2. `forward_pre_o_proj()` on `KimiK3DeltaAttention` and `KimiK3MLAAttention`**, where K2 starts. It returns the TP-local attention output after the output gate and before o_proj. The caller owns o_proj and the attention-TP reduction that o_proj carries, so `o_proj(forward_pre_o_proj(x)) == forward(x)`. - `KimiK3DeltaAttention`: a plain extract. `forward()` now calls the new method and keeps the o_proj tail. The moved body does not change. - `KimiK3MLAAttention`: the MLA cores reach o_proj from several places. The split therefore uses the instance-level wrapper that already applies the output gate. `forward_pre_o_proj()` sets `_return_pre_o_proj`, runs `forward()`, and takes the tensor that the wrapper puts in `_pre_o_proj_out` instead of running o_proj. Four guards hold the MLA path together. It has no in-tree caller to exercise it, and a fault on it gives wrong numbers rather than an error. - `use_output_gate` must be on. Without it the wrapper does not exist. - The method is not re-entrant. A second entry while the flag is set raises. - `_pre_o_proj_out` holds one tensor. If o_proj is reached twice in one attention forward, the second call raises instead of overwriting the first. The message names the layer. - A quantized o_proj input raises. On ROCm the MLA core quantizes what it hands to o_proj when o_proj's weights are MXFP4 or block-scale fp8 (`forward_mla_rocm.py:325,351`). The output gate is skipped with it, so there is no gated bf16 tensor to hand back. Every rank quantizes alike, so this raises on all of them. It does not split the TP group. The standard path remains no change. `forward()` produces what it produced before if no mono kernel server args are specified. ## Accuracy Tests 8 x MI355X, TP8 / DCP1, FP8 KV cache, DSpark block size 7. `/data-models/Kimi-K3`, GSM8K 200 questions, `--parallel 2`: | | Accuracy | |---|---:| | This branch, no monokernel backend | 0.990 | | This branch, `--monokernel-backend amd` | 0.985 | ## Speed Tests and Profiling `--monokernel-backend amd` against the standard path, both launches on. Two server instances an arm, four probe runs each, the first run of each server dropped. Decode steps/s rather than tok/s, because the speculative accept length swamps tok/s on this recipe. | | decode steps/s | sd | range | |---|---:|---:|---| | Monokernels off | 41.63 | 0.62 | 40.28 - 42.10 | | Monokernels on | **55.26 (+32.8%)** | 0.38 | 54.72 - 55.94 | The ranges do not overlap. The win is on 8-row verify steps; wider steps and all prefill take the standard path. #### Fixed-length decode latency at long context The table above is short prompts at the draft's real acceptance. This one is the interactive shape the backend is for: a cached long prefix, a small new turn, and a short answer. It also reports the inter-token latency the backend moves, rather than a step rate that a reader has to convert. | ISL | ITL P50 off | ITL P50 on | Δ | ITL P90 off | ITL P90 on | Δ | steps/s off | steps/s on | Δ | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 64k | 6.17 ms | **4.62 ms** | **−25.2%** | 8.11 ms | **6.17 ms** | **−24.0%** | 40.4 | **52.7** | +30.5% | | 128k | 6.67 ms | **5.29 ms** | **−20.6%** | 8.56 ms | **6.88 ms** | **−19.7%** | 37.3 | **47.1** | +26.3% | | 256k | 7.70 ms | **6.19 ms** | **−19.6%** | 9.86 ms | **8.10 ms** | **−17.9%** | 32.2 | **40.3** | +24.9% | `off` / `on` is `--monokernel-backend amd`. Lower ITL is better, so Δ is the reduction; as a speedup the same numbers are +33.7% / +25.9% / +24.3% at P50. **P90 moves with P50** (−24.0% against −25.2% at 64k) and the P90/P50 ratio is unchanged (1.31 off, 1.33 on). The launch shifts the whole distribution rather than clipping a tail. The three columns agree because acceptance is pinned: `ITL ~= 1000 / (steps/s * accept)`. **The gain falls as ISL grows** (−25.2% to −19.6%). Attention over a longer KV takes a larger share of the step, and that part is outside the launch. **TTFT is unchanged** -- 0.24/0.25 s, 0.30/0.29 s and 0.41/0.41 s at 64k/128k/256k. The launch covers decode only. #### End-to-end agentic replay The two tables above are synthetic prompts at a pinned acceptance. This one is a full AgentX agentic-coding replay, one hour per arm. It therefore carries real session content, real prefix-cache behaviour and the batching of the scheduler itself. | conc 1, 8 rows a step | off | `--monokernel-backend amd` | Δ | |---|---:|---:|---:| | **TPOT mean** | 6.28 ms | **4.94 ms** | **−21.3%** | | TPOT P50 | 6.23 ms | **4.91 ms** | −21.2% | | TPOT P75 | 6.60 ms | **5.26 ms** | −20.3% | | **TPOT P90** | 6.74 ms | **5.37 ms** | **−20.3%** | | TPOT P95 | 6.77 ms | **5.43 ms** | −19.8% | | interactivity P50 | 160.4 tok/s | **203.7 tok/s** | +27.0% | | interactivity P90 | 148.5 tok/s | **186.1 tok/s** | +25.3% | | TTFT mean | 2.70 s | **2.10 s** | −22.4% | | e2e P90 | 37.3 s | **30.0 s** | −19.5% | | output | 97.5 tok/s | **112.0 tok/s** | +14.9% | | requests completed | 205 | **222** | +8.3% | **Every percentile moves by the same amount**, −19.8% to −21.3%, as in the fixed-length table. Throughput rises less than latency falls, +14.9% against −21.3%. AgentX replays a closed loop, so a faster answer shortens only the part of each session's cycle that the engine owns. **The number of steps the backend can take bounds the gain.** An earlier pair of the same runs admitted two requests instead of one. That pair held the SSM state in bf16, so read its percentages against its own baseline and not against the table above. There 6 to 7% of decode windows held two running requests. That is 2 x 8 = 16 rows, which is outside the spec, and the result split: P50 −16.5%, but **P90 −2.6%** and P95 −2.1%, with the mean diluted to −9.4%. The server log shows it directly when read by `#running-req`: the one-request steps ran 9.8% faster and the two-request steps 2.2%. Admitting one request removes the steps that are not covered, and the whole distribution then moves together. A caller that wants the full gain must keep every verify step inside the supported width. ## Checklist - [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit). - [ ] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests). - [ ] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations). - [ ] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed). - [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance). ## Review and Merge Process 1. Ping Merge Oncalls to start the process. See the [PR Merge Process](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/.github/MAINTAINER.md#pull-request-merge-process). 2. title: [Perf] qknorm: run head_dim-128 rows two per warp with 16B lanes, bit-identical
author: Monishver11
body:
## Motivation

In short: `fused_qknorm_warp` is the default QK-norm for Qwen3 dense and Qwen3-MoE on CUDA. At head_dim 128 it gives each warp one (token, head) row, so a lane moves only 8 B per row. This PR runs two rows per warp with 16 B lanes, the same scheme mickqian merged for the diffusion QK-norm + RoPE kernel. The output is bit-identical. On an H100 NVL the kernel is 1.09-1.45x faster from 32 tokens up, and 1.29x inside a Qwen3-8B prefill trace; serving throughput is flat because the kernel is under 1% of GPU time.

Details:

`fused_qknorm_warp` (`python/sglang/kernels/jit/csrc/elementwise/qknorm.cuh`) runs through `apply_qk_norm` in `python/sglang/srt/models/utils.py`. Per row it does a load, a 5-step xor reduce, an rsqrt and a store, then moves to the next row. With 8 B per lane that is at most 64 warps x 32 lanes x 8 B = 16 KB in flight per SM, and out of L2 the kernel reaches 2.8-2.9 TB/s on an H100 NVL.

## Modifications

In short: a new `fused_qknorm_half_warp` kernel for head_dim 128, picked at compile time. Each row gets 16 lanes and each lane moves 16 B. Every other head_dim, the CTA path and ROCm keep their current kernels.

How it stays bit-identical: each lane covers two lanes of the warp kernel. It keeps their two partial sums, accumulated in the same order, and replays that kernel's xor butterfly with `warp::reduce_sum<16>` (the same `Trait::reduce` as before). Offsets 16..2 become 8..1 on each partial, and the final xor-1 step becomes `part0 + part1`. The rsqrt and the per-element output are the same expressions.

Changes:

- `fused_qknorm_half_warp`: two rows per warp; a missing second row recomputes the last one and skips its store.
- The new kernel needs 16 B alignment where the warp kernel needed 8 B. If a q/k or weight pointer, or a q/k row stride, is not 16 B aligned, the launcher keeps the one-row-per-warp kernel, so every input that ran before still runs.
- `_jit_qknorm_module(half_warp=False)` builds the one-row-per-warp kernel, for the new test.
- New test `test_two_rows_per_warp_match_one_row_per_warp`: byte-compares the two kernels with q and k sliced from one qkv row as Qwen3 passes them, BF16 and FP16, 5 q heads so a q/k boundary falls inside a row pair, an odd row count, 4099 tokens so the persistent grid loops, and rows padded by 8 B so odd-token rows are only 8 B aligned and the launcher falls back.

Same scheme as [#43337](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/43337) and [#43508](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/43508), which changed only the diffusion `qknorm_rope.cuh`.

Not a duplicate: no PR runs `fused_qknorm_warp` two rows per warp. The open [#43425](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/43425) refactors `fused_qknorm_warp` into a per-row helper with an epilogue hook for Qwen3-VL MRoPE fusion on Blackwell; it keeps the 8 B lane layout, but the two PRs will conflict in `qknorm.cuh`, so whichever lands second needs a rebase. [#39071](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39071) and [#40585](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40585) touch this file only for ROCm `#include` lines.

## Accuracy Tests

The output is bit-identical to main, so model accuracy can't change. I checked it at the kernel level:

- Bitwise vs main 97d3150a6a, CPU-seeded inputs, whole qkv buffer compared: 384 cases, each run with both branch kernels, **768 of 768 identical**. The two-rows kernel runs in 192 of them (head_dim 128: Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, TP2 and ragged head counts, 1 to 16384 tokens, qkv-slice and contiguous layouts, BF16 and FP16, with and without PDL). The rest cover the 8 B-aligned fallback and head_dim 64 and 256, which are unchanged.
- `test_qknorm.py` and `test_rope.py`: 1827 passed. `test_rope.py` uses `fused_inplace_qknorm` as its `torch.equal` reference.
- Registers: 28 -> 40 per thread, 0 spills.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

H100 NVL (PCIe, 400 W), driver 595.91, CUDA 13.0, torch 2.14.1+cu130. Validated on main 97d3150a6a; the branch is rebased onto 5ed306bd69, and upstream only removed unused helpers from `norm.py` and `test_qknorm.py` in between. `triton.testing.do_bench_cudagraph`, median of 5 rounds that interleave the two kernels in one process. q and k are slices of one qkv row (Qwen3 layout), BF16, in place.

| tokens | Qwen3-8B (32 + 8 heads) | Qwen3-30B-A3B (32 + 4 heads) |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | 1.03 -> 1.06 us (0.97x) | 1.16 -> 1.22 us (0.95x) |
| 8 | 1.39 -> 1.32 us (1.05x) | 1.45 -> 1.53 us (0.95x) |
| 32 | 1.65 -> 1.48 us (1.12x) | 1.76 -> 1.69 us (1.04x) |
| 128 | 3.11 -> 2.26 us (1.38x) | 3.04 -> 2.38 us (1.28x) |
| 256 | 4.31 -> 3.19 us (1.35x) | 4.38 -> 3.02 us (1.45x) |
| 1024 | 6.31 -> 5.32 us (1.19x) | 6.11 -> 4.98 us (1.23x) |
| 2048 | 11.13 -> 8.39 us (1.33x) | 10.33 -> 7.84 us (1.32x) |
| 4096 | 25.96 -> 22.18 us (1.17x) | 22.13 -> 17.86 us (1.24x) |
| 8192 | 58.65 -> 53.83 us (1.09x) | 53.20 -> 48.59 us (1.09x) |
| 16384 | 116.16 -> 105.23 us (1.10x) | 104.23 -> 94.73 us (1.10x) |
| 65536 | 459.86 -> 414.60 us (1.11x) | 417.29 -> 374.92 us (1.11x) |

Over BF16 and FP16, both models and 1-65536 tokens: geomean 1.14x up to 256 tokens (0.95-1.45x) and 1.17x from 512 tokens (1.09-1.36x). From 8192 tokens q and k no longer fit in L2, and the kernel goes from 2.8-2.9 TB/s to 3.1-3.3 TB/s. At 1-8 tokens the difference is 0.03-0.08 us, the same spread as two runs of the same kernel.

In a model: torch profiler, Qwen3-8B TP1, 32 requests of 4096 input tokens. The QK-norm kernel goes from 43.82 to 34.09 ms over 720 launches (1.29x), from 0.94% to 0.73% of GPU time. `sglang.benchmark.serving` on the same model, 3 interleaved rounds, is flat: random 4096/1 input throughput 26597 -> 26567 tok/s (-0.11%) and random 1024/128 19.94 -> 19.93 req/s (-0.07%), while main alone moves 0.6-0.7% between rounds.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).
- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).
- [ ] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations). (no user-facing change)
- [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed). (bitwise, microbench, profile and serving)
- [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance).

I used Claude Code for this change. I reviewed every line and ran the tests and benchmarks above myself.

title: [Perf] mlp: Fuse dense SwiGLU with block-FP8 quantization on decode
author: JiaFengYu
body:
## Motivation

Dense block-FP8 MLPs normally launch SwiGLU to materialize a BF16 activation, then launch activation quantization before the down-projection GEMM. This PR fuses those two operations for eligible decode calls, removing one launch and the intermediate BF16 write/read per MLP.

The latest controlled comparison measured **1.92% lower single-request decode TPOT** on Qwen3-8B-FP8 on a B200. This is activation/MLP fusion, independent of KV-cache dtype. Concurrent decode and the full-patch prefill non-regression claim have the limitations documented below; this is not an unconditional performance clearance.

## Modifications

- Extend the existing JIT `per_token_group_quant` kernel with an explicit dense SwiGLU mode. Match the dense CUDA activation's compiler math and round the product to source precision before quantization, without materializing it in HBM. Reuse the existing quantizer and UE8M0 packing machinery; the default/legacy mode is unchanged.
- Allow the DeepGEMM block-FP8 wrapper to consume validated prequantized FP8 activations and column-major packed UE8M0 scales. Reject incompatible packed layouts instead of passing them to a fallback that cannot consume them.
- Add a shared `DenseSiluAndMulQuant` helper and small Llama/Qwen2 MLP integrations; Qwen3 uses the Qwen2 implementation. The runtime fast path is limited to SM100-family CUDA, TP1, ordinary decode, BF16 activations, and dynamic block-128 FP8 with DeepGEMM/UE8M0.
- Call the helper only for decode. Prefill/extend, speculative verification, other non-decode modes, and calls without a forward batch invoke the original activation directly. Keep the helper's own eligibility checks and preserve fallbacks for unsupported layouts/dtypes/backends, LoRA, deterministic execution, compilation, and overrides. Preserve DualGemm unchanged. The model-level phase check remains; this is not a claim of literally zero host overhead.
- Use the current fused-op `_resolve_forward_method()` API when the activation's cached method is unset. This resolves the callable without launching activation; it preserves the check that the dense CUDA activation implementation is selected.
- Keep operator tests with the quantizer and real-MLP dispatch/graph tests under `test/registered/unit/layers/quantization/`, registered for the B200 runtime-test stage. Cover cold dispatch and require every non-decode mode to bypass the helper. Include the kernel benchmark extension and standalone numerical-sweep/MLP microbenchmark; keep server A/B automation local and outside this PR.


Checks on B200 with PyTorch 2.14.1+cu130 and CUDA toolkit 13.0:

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Full per-token-group quantizer suite | 167 passed |
| Kernel namespace and fused-op dispatch suites | 119 passed, 1 skipped |
| Real Llama/Qwen MLP integration, fallback gates, CUDA graph replay | 3 passed, 13 subtests passed |
| Packed DeepGEMM input regression | 1 passed, 3 subtests passed |
| Existing DualGemm regressions | 6 passed, 2 subtests passed |
| Llama parallel regressions | 2 passed, 32 subtests passed |
| Total unique registered tests | 298 passed, 1 skipped, plus 50 subtests |
| Extended numerical sweep | 240 cases; 184,023,040 FP8 bytes checked; exact FP8/scales parity |
| Compute Sanitizer memcheck | 46 repeated subset cases; zero memory errors |
| Full pinned pre-commit suite and diff whitespace checks | Passed |

The dense quantizer tests compare FP8 bytes and scale bits against the real CUDA SwiGLU followed by the existing quantizer, including BF16/FP16 sources, multiple shapes and scale layouts, special values, non-mutation, and graph replay. Runtime integration is narrower than the standalone operator: BF16 only. Real-MLP and packed-DeepGEMM comparisons use zero tolerance. The non-decode bypass regression failed before the dispatch changes and passed afterward. Repeated test runs and the memcheck subset are not added to the unique-test total.

In the latest full A/B, all 174,720 measured client requests completed without reported request errors. All 81,920 paired prefill texts and 320/320 concurrency-1 decode responses matched. Concurrency-32 decode matched 5,084/5,120 paired responses: those differences are disclosed, and their cause was not isolated. A separate 192-output-token probe had identical token IDs and zero corresponding logprob difference. Both variants scored 19/20 on the GSM8K sanity sample. These focused checks are not a comprehensive model-quality evaluation or a claim of bit-identical concurrent generation.


## Speed tests and profiling

### Full fusion versus direct unfused activation

Ten paired fresh-server comparisons on one B200, TP1, `Qwen/Qwen3-8B-FP8`, DeepGEMM, BF16 activations, TRTLLM MHA, KV dtype `auto` resolving to BF16, full decode CUDA graphs, breakable prefill CUDA graphs, and torch.compile disabled. Runtime dependencies included Python 3.12.15, PyTorch 2.14.1+cu130, CUDA toolkit 13.0, sgl-deep-gemm 0.2.3, sglang-kernel 0.4.10, and FlashInfer 0.7.2.

Five pairs were baseline-first and five fused-first, with matched requests and alternating phase/concurrency order. There were no result-dependent retries, exclusions, or added pairs. All 80 timed windows were unprofiled and excluded server startup:

- Prefill: exact 1,024 input token IDs and one output token; 1,024 warmups and 4,096 measured requests per window. Every response reported zero cached tokens. TTFT uses the first token-bearing SSE event, including blank rendered output.
- Decode: nominal 1,024 inputs and 512 outputs using the stock serving benchmark, random-ids, seed 42, temperature zero. Concurrency 1 used 16 warmups and 32 measured requests; concurrency 32 used 128 warmups and 512 measured requests. Actual input lengths after text round-trip were 992-1,325 and 867-1,360 respectively, with identical vectors across variants. These are client concurrency limits, not fixed GPU batch sizes.

Changes are geometric means of ten paired per-window median ratios. Negative means lower latency. Intervals are paired log-ratio Student-t **97.5% two-sided confidence intervals**, df=9. The absolute columns are medians of ten run medians; their ratio is not the paired estimator.

| Workload | Metric | Baseline | Fused | Paired change | 97.5% interval | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Decode, concurrency 1 | Median TPOT | 3.02064 ms | 2.96433 ms | -1.921% | [-2.082, -1.759]% | Faster in 10/10 pairs |
| Decode, concurrency 32 | Stock median TPOT | 4.35948 ms | 4.30988 ms | -0.919% | [-1.643, -0.188]% | Provisional: client timing defect |
| Prefill, concurrency 1 | Median TTFT | 13.199 ms | 13.363 ms | +0.662% | [-0.464, +1.800]% | Inconclusive against the +1% non-regression bound |
| Prefill, concurrency 32 | Median TTFT | 314.701 ms | 314.469 ms | +0.062% | [-0.132, +0.256]% | Passes the +1% bound; not a speedup claim |

Secondary whole-request latency decreased 1.901% at concurrency 1 (interval [-2.077, -1.724]%) and 0.837% at concurrency 32 ([-1.083, -0.590]%), with 10/10 paired wins each. These are secondary metrics, not substitutes for an invalid primary endpoint.

**Limitations:** the stock decode client records timing only when rendered text is nonempty. One response per concurrency-32 window had empty text, TTFT zero, no inter-token timings, and a defaulted completion length. All 20 affected responses were retained; no statistics were silently corrected. That TPOT result remains provisional. Prefill concurrency 1 also remains inconclusive against the +1% bound and showed execution-order sensitivity. The full experiment therefore does not establish unconditional prefill neutrality or an all-workload performance clearance.

### Incremental prefill effect of bypassing the helper

A separate, predeclared ten-pair experiment compared the **previous fused implementation** (always enters the helper; helper falls back on prefill) against **the new decode-only call sites**. Both retain decode fusion and the callable-resolution fix; only the two MLP dispatch sites differ. It used the same model/runtime, exact 1,024-input/one-output uncached requests, and concurrency 1/32, with 1,024 warmups and 4,096 measured requests per window.

All 163,840 measured requests and 40,960 warmups succeeded, and all 81,920 paired texts matched. No pairs were retried, excluded, or added. The paired estimator and 97.5% Student-t intervals are reported separately from the full-fusion experiment.

| Client concurrency | Previous fused TTFT | New bypass TTFT | Paired change | 97.5% interval | +1% non-regression bound |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| 1 | 13.353 ms | 13.326 ms | -0.155% | [-0.979, +0.676]% | Pass |
| 32 | 315.272 ms | 314.586 ms | -0.158% | [-0.470, +0.156]% | Pass |

This supports keeping the bypass for explicit non-decode isolation. Neither a prefill speedup nor a slowdown is statistically established. It bounds the incremental change relative to the previous fused implementation.
### Engagement and scope

Post-timing first-pair profiles from the full A/B recorded 5,667 GPU kernels in the baseline and 5,343 with fusion, including 324 dense-fused launches only in the fused variant. Separate activation launches decreased from 360 to 36. This is 324 net launches removed in a mixed ten-step capture (one prefill plus nine decode steps), not a per-token count. Profiler durations were not used for end-to-end latency claims.

Both experiments retained frozen source manifests, plans, raw measurements, and ownership/telemetry checks. No foreign compute process was observed on the selected GPU in sampled checks; its 750 W power cap was unchanged and no thermal-slowdown samples were recorded. Clocks were not locked and the host was shared. Results apply to this model/configuration, not all workloads. H100, TP greater than one, and MoE are outside the runtime fast path.

### Reproduction and retained evidence

With this checkout and matching dependencies installed on a B200:

```bash
python test/manual/kernels/bench_dense_swiglu_quant.py --check-only
```

Representative server command used in the full A/B and direct bypass comparison:

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-8B-FP8 \
  --revision 220b46e3b2180893580a4454f21f22d3ebb187d3 \
  --dtype bfloat16 --tp-size 1 --fp8-gemm-backend deep_gemm \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.6 --random-seed 42 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 30000
```

Variant selection used frozen Python source snapshots; all other server settings were identical. The local-only `full_run.py`/`runner.py` and direct-comparison `run.py` retain the orchestration, preregistered plans, and raw results. Evidence identifiers are `sglang-swiglu-prefill-bypass.dCzr2o` (focused checks), `sglang-swiglu-prefill-bypass-run.4j38zT` (full A/B), and `sglang-swiglu-direct-bypass.9mmC3I` (incremental bypass comparison). These artifacts are retained locally and are not publicly attached. Independent reproduction of the exact server tables requires supplying those harnesses/manifests; the included microbenchmark and server command alone do not reproduce them.

## Checklist

- [x] Add focused operator and runtime integration tests.
- [x] Run local correctness, graph-replay, fallback, and memory-safety checks.
- [x] Provide controlled live A/B measurements and disclose their limitations.
- [x] Complete the full pinned pre-commit hook suite.
- [ ] Obtain passing required PR CI on the submitted commit.

title: [Feat] kernels: Beam model support
author: Jiminator
body:
## Motivation

Split #44747 into reviewable parts. This is the kernels part, position 3 of 7 in the merge order below.

## Modifications

- **Beam fused ops**, listed by class method as in Muse Spark's kernels part:
  - `elementwise.beam_attention_gate`: the per-head gate, with Beam's activation-dtype bias and sigmoid rounding.
  - `layernorm.beam_sandwich_residual_rmsnorm`: the post-norm, depth-scaled residual and next RMSNorm in one launch.
- **`communication.beam_all_reduce_norm`**: Beam's BF16 TP all-reduce fused with that norm and residual, on CustomAllReduceV2's push plane. Each row runs on one CTA, or on a 5-CTA cluster at TP8 for up to 16 rows. It needs a new `CustomAllReduceV2.supports_push` capacity check.
- **FP32 router gates:**
  - FP32 weights in main's `tiny_gemm` (N variant) and `router_gemv` (CUDA, up to 8 rows);
  - `gemm.router_gemm_bf16x3_cublas` for larger batches, with the weight split per call by `quantization.split_fp32_to_bf16x3`.

Main's existing callers are unchanged:
- BF16 tiny GEMM builds the same kernel with the same split as on main (its JIT build key gains the weight type, so it recompiles once on first use);
- the gfx950 BF16 router GEMV path is unchanged.

`gemm.router_gemv` is registered for Triton CUDA/HIP; its existing predicate retains CUDA FP32 and gfx950 BF16 gating. `split_fp32_to_bf16x3` lives in `ops.quantization.bf16x3_split`, which #45361 now imports directly. The cuBLAS wrapper keeps its internal import.

Committed coverage adds 18 representative numerical cases, reusing the existing tiny GEMM and fused-op parity suites plus a focused CUDA router test. The collective test covers both native unicast and multicast, changing-input graph replay, interleaved regular all-reduce, and both TP8 launch shapes. These checks complement the model E2E test from #45257.

The optional SM103 single-token BF16 MoE GEMV and shared SiLU helper moved to draft #46401, with their own correctness test and performance benchmark. They are outside Day-0 kernel support; performance measurements for that follow-up remain pending.

This part changes 21 files (+1,364 / -34).

## Validation

The following focused results belong to the tested review changes preserved in `851658f9b8`. The branch subsequently merged main at `d360915f64`; verification has not been rerun after that merge.

On GB300/SM103, with torch 2.14.1+cu130 and Triton 3.8.0:

- Numerical tests: **196 tiny GEMM, 5 router and 13 fused-op parity cases passed**. The added cases check FP32 router results against FP64, exact gate rounding, BF16 norm output within one ULP, and fixed FP16 cancellation bounds. FP16 has no universal one-ULP guarantee.
- The registered collective test passed at TP2, TP4 and cross-node TP8 over MNNVL, in native unicast and multicast modes. It covers rows 1/8/16/32/64/128, top-k 1/8, optional next norm, changing payloads during graph replay, and interleaved regular all-reduce. TP8 covers one-CTA and five-CTA launches. Native pointer inspection confirmed the selected modes.
- The existing 42-tensor-per-rank probes found zero byte differences between unicast and multicast, and between multicast and the saved original baseline. Those probes cover rows through 64.
- Beam-kernel memcheck passed at TP2/TP4 through 64 rows; TP8 racecheck and synccheck passed the full registered matrix in both modes. These runs used `--report-api-errors no` after a setup-only control reproduced 41 `cuGetProcAddress_v2` API errors per rank without calling either all-reduce. Device-memory/race/sync checks remained enabled. The setup/API issue remains unresolved; this is not clean CUDA API validation. No TP8 or row-128 memcheck claim.
- Namespace tests passed 101 cases. Existing MoE suites passed. The generic custom-all-reduce TP4 suite retained **309 passes and one failure**, `test_custom_all_reduce_eager_plan_follows_config`, reproduced on the unchanged baseline.
- No physically multicast-incapable hardware, H200, ROCm or SM120 rerun was added for these review changes.

An earlier NVFP4 integration with the model/parser stack passed the original Beam verifier at `dfa85fe771`: **133/133 required chat cases and 5/5 optional raw-completion cases**. Temperature 0 applied only to recall; `no_stop_trim` applied only to raw completions. That integration included a separate parser compatibility fix and predates the final unicast restoration; it is not a fresh model run on this head or a matched reference comparison.

<details>
<summary>Historical validation and performance from earlier revisions</summary>

The original results below are retained as historical evidence. They were not rerun for the latest review commits or main merge; references to pending work describe the state at those earlier runs.

On GB300 (SM103), with torch 2.14.1+cu130 and Triton 3.8.0:

- **Main's tests for the touched code pass:**
  - tiny GEMM;
  - fused MoE (SwiGLU epilogue, padding, TMA cache, `test_fused_moe`);
  - collectives;
  - the kernel registry and fused-op CPU tests.

  `test_custom_all_reduce.py` has one failure, `test_custom_all_reduce_eager_plan_follows_config`, which main also fails on the same machine.
- **Each new op checked against an independent reference:**
  - The attention gate is bitwise equal to eager over every finite FP16 and BF16 gate value (two bias and two attention settings), including through the `torch_compile` backend.
  - The sandwich norm matches eager in BF16 within one ULP. In FP16, 3 of 327,680 elements at a residual-cancellation point differ by 2^-11. As its docstring states, cancellation can amplify reduction-order differences, so there is no one-ULP guarantee.
  - The all-reduce boundary matches an all-gather reference at TP2, TP4 and TP8 within BF16 tolerance, and its CUDA-graph replays are bitwise reproducible across payload changes. TP8 ran across two 4×GB300 nodes over MNNVL, where the outputs are bitwise equal between the one-CTA and cluster launches.
  - The FP32 router tiny GEMM and GEMV show errors comparable to SGEMM against FP64 references over the tested shapes.
  - The BF16x3 split is exact for 2^-110 <= |w| < 2^128 - 2^119.
  - The decode GEMV matches an FP64 reference with BF16 rounding points to within 7.6e-6 across 20 graph replays.
- **End to end:** this part with #45256, #45257 and #43216, on 4×GB300, with the cookbook GB300 NVFP4 low-latency recipe and the public `reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-NVFP4` checkpoint:
  - GSM8K 96.59% (sgl-eval, 1,319 questions, temperature 0, 0 errors);
  - the [Beam Verifier](https://github.com/reflection-oss/beam-verifier) at `dfa85fe771` passes its required suites 133/133: 131 cases at its defaults and the 2 recall cases at temperature 0. The optional suites did not run;
  - chat reasoning, streaming, chat tool calls, Responses text, function and shell, and `/tokenize` all pass.
- Merges into main without conflicts. pre-commit passes.

On 8×H200 (SM90), with the same torch and Triton and FlashInfer 0.7.2:

- **Main's tests pass:** tiny GEMM, fused MoE (SwiGLU epilogue, padding, TMA cache, `test_fused_moe`), and the kernel registry and fused-op CPU tests.
- **Numerical checks:**
  - The attention gate is bitwise equal to eager over every finite FP16 and BF16 gate value.
  - The all-reduce boundary matches an all-gather reference at TP2, TP4 and TP8 within BF16 tolerance, and its outputs are bitwise equal between the one-CTA and cluster launches.
  - compute-sanitizer racecheck and synccheck are clean on the all-reduce boundary at TP8, covering both launch shapes.
- **FP32 router:** the boundary norm followed by the FP32 tiny GEMM is 0.02–1.26 µs per layer faster than with this PR's earlier PDL ordering and split selection, at 1–16 tokens, with bitwise-identical outputs.
- **End to end:** with the same parts as above, at FP8 TP8 (`fa3`, DFlash), with the public `reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-FP8` checkpoint:
  - GSM8K 96.21% (sgl-eval, 1,319 questions, temperature 0, 0 errors);
  - the Beam Verifier required suites pass 133/133, with the recall cases at temperature 0;
  - chat reasoning, streaming, chat tool calls, Responses text and function calls, and `/tokenize` pass. The Responses shell round trip fails with the current public chat template; the fix goes in #45257.

**TP8 cluster launch.** At TP8 with up to 16 rows, each row runs as a 5-CTA cluster. Per call, compared with one CTA per row:
- on 8×H200, it is 4–10% faster with top-k 1 and 8–16% faster with top-k 8 (6.76 vs 5.68 µs at one row);
- on 8×GB300 across two nodes (MNNVL), it is 3–11% faster with top-k 8. With top-k 1 it ranges from 2.2% faster to 0.9% slower, inside run-to-run noise (median of five sweeps).

One CTA per row stays at TP2 and TP4, where it is as fast or faster on GB300 and H200. It also stays for TP8 batches above 16 rows. At 32 rows with top-k 8, a cluster would be 1.4% faster on H200 but is 3.4% slower on GB300.

Not measured here:
- end-to-end serving and compute-sanitizer at TP8 on Blackwell (TP8 there covers the all-reduce boundary only);
- ROCm (the gfx950 BF16 path is unchanged and was checked statically);
- the unicast publish path.

</details>

## Merge order

Each part is based on the one before it, so its diff shows only its own changes. Merge bottom-up; after each part merges, the next part is retargeted to `main` and `main` is merged into it. #44747 stays open, unchanged, as the full reference. Merge in this order:

1. #45253: Beam CUDA Docker image (merged)
2. #45291: OpenAI SDK 2.8.0, needed by the Responses shell tools in #45257 (merged)
3. #45254: Kernels
4. #45256: Attention, memory and DFlash DP support, and the Beam model (#45255 folded in; also after #43216)
5. #45257: Beam reasoning, tool calls, response templates and the Beam E2E test (merged into #45256)
6. #45290: `nvidia-cuda-tileiras`, needed by #45361
7. #45361: cuTile BF16x3 router GEMM (optional: without it Beam uses the cuBLAS router)

#45292 (Dynamo and `grpcio-tools` pins for the Beam image) is not in the merge order for now.

title: [Fix] [AMD] diffusion: Enable `--quantization fp8` on gfx1250 (torch.compile lowering + per-channel weight scales)
author: yichiche
body:
## Motivation

`--quantization fp8` does not work on gfx1250. With `--enable-torch-compile` it dies in Inductor lowering on the first warmup request, before a single image:

```
LoweringException: AssertionError: target: aten._scaled_mm.default
  args[3]: ... FixedLayout('cuda:0', torch.float32, size=[], stride=[])
```

`args[3]` is the weight scale, and it is a **rank-0 scalar**. Inductor's `_scaled_mm` template loads it with two index symbols against a zero-length stride, so the `len(index) == len(stride)` assert at `ir.py:2034` fires.

The scalar comes from the missing-CUTLASS fallback: `cutlass_fp8_supported()` is `False` for every ROCm device (`fp8_utils.py:398` is `if not _is_cuda: return False`, before it looks at compute capability), so `process_weights_after_loading` falls to `input_to_float8`, whose single `aminmax()` yields a 0-dim `weight_scale` instead of a per-channel `[N]` vector. **The crash and the quality loss are therefore one bug**: a per-tensor scale that Inductor cannot lower *and* that throws away the range a BF16 checkpoint needs to survive FP8. NVIDIA takes the per-channel CUTLASS branch and sees neither symptom, which is why this is gfx1250/ROCm-only.

Avoiding the lowering is not enough on its own: hipBLASLt ships no tuned gfx1250 kernels, so at the FLUX.2-dev 720p shapes `torch._scaled_mm` FP8 reaches 471-506 TFLOPS while the BF16 torch.compile templates it replaces already reach 645-710.

**The scheme here is A8W8** -- a fully FP8 GEMM. Both operands are `e4m3`: per-token dynamic scales on the activations, per-channel scales on the weights, FP32 accumulate. It is explicitly *not* weight-only (A16W8); the activations are quantized too, so the matrix cores actually issue FP8 MFMA, which is where the speedup comes from.

**The fix** is two changes for two different reasons, either of which alone stops the crash:

* `process_weights_after_loading` takes the per-channel branch (`per_token_group_quant_fp8`), giving a real `[N]` scale. This is the *accuracy* fix; the ranks line up as a side effect.
* `apply` quantizes the activations per token and routes both operands to an A8W8 Triton tile, so `aten._scaled_mm` is never reached. This is the *performance* fix: 1150-1255 TFLOPS instead of 471-506.

This affects any gfx1250 run passing `--quantization fp8` with a BF16 checkpoint. Nothing in the fix is model-specific -- it is the shared `Fp8LinearMethod` in the diffusion stack -- though the reproduction here is FLUX.2-dev at 720p, where linears are 83% of GPU kernel time. MI300X, MI355X and NVIDIA are unaffected: `is_gfx1250_supported()` is false there, and `cutlass_fp8_supported` already routes NVIDIA to a per-channel CUTLASS GEMM.

## Modifications

* New `python/sglang/kernels/ops/gemm/fp8_gfx1250.py`: an A8W8 (per-token activation / per-channel weight) FP8 `[M, K] @ [K, N]` Triton tile plus the per-token activation quantizer that feeds it. The tile indexes its operands modulo M and N rather than masking the loads (masked loads cost ~10% on this target and the tail is at most one tile), and masks only the store. `_select_config` carries the tile sizes an offline sweep picked for the served shapes.
* `multimodal_gen/runtime/layers/quantization/fp8.py`: `Fp8LinearMethod.__init__` computes `use_gfx1250_triton_fp8` once; when set, `process_weights_after_loading` takes the **per-channel** branch for a non-FP8-serialized checkpoint -- replacing the rank-0 `input_to_float8` scale that both breaks the lowering and drops the checkpoint's range -- and `apply` tries `_apply_gfx1250_triton_fp8` first, returning `None` to the existing path for any shape the tile does not cover.
* `srt/environ.py`: `SGLANG_DISABLE_GFX1250_FP8_GEMM`, a diagnostic kill switch.
* The quantized weight is stored **row-major** `[K, N]` rather than as the transposed view of `[N, K]` that this method has always produced. A BLOCK_N slice of one k-row otherwise reads N single bytes strided by K instead of BLOCK_N contiguous ones; making it contiguous once at load is worth 1.05-1.33x per GEMM and 1.06x end to end. The tile's config table is tuned for that layout, and a unit test pins it, since a refactor that drops the transpose would be a silent regression.
* `test/registered/amd/test_fp8_gemm_gfx1250.py`: tile correctness against a dequantized reference, and the dispatch seam itself.

**BLOCK_SIZE_K is capped at 64 on purpose.** On gfx1250 with triton 3.8.0, an FP8 `tl.dot` miscompiles for `BLOCK_SIZE_K >= 128`: it silently returns NaN for every `num_warps` x `num_stages` combination tested (16 of 16), and the broken kernel *times about 40% faster than a correct one*. An autotune sweep without a correctness gate will therefore select it and report a phantom ~1730 TFLOPS. This also means 1150-1255 TFLOPS is the ceiling for correct Triton FP8 on this target today, not the hardware's ceiling. Note that `triton_scaled_mm`'s own heuristic picks `(128, 128, 128)` for M 128, so callers must not route gfx1250 FP8 there until the compiler is fixed.

## Accuracy Tests

No accuracy harness applies -- this is a diffusion image model, so there is no gsm8k-style score. The gate is instead split into the two questions that can actually be answered separately: is the kernel numerically correct, and did the image get worse.

Measured on one gfx1250 (DPX half-package), FLUX.2-dev 720p, 50 steps, seed 42, `--enable-torch-compile true`, aiter attention, all offload off. The "before" arm is BF16 at this PR's merge base. There is no "FP8 without this PR" arm, because that configuration does not run at all -- it is the lowering crash described in Motivation.

### 1. Trajectory divergence -- is the kernel correct

Comparing the per-step denoise latents of the two arms (`[1, 50, 3600, 128]`) separates the error the GEMM introduces from the amplification the sampler applies to it afterwards. One seed is sufficient here: this measures numerics, not a sample distribution.

| step | relative L2 | cosine | mean bias | growth vs prev |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.00149 | 0.999956 | +5.75e-05 | -- |
| 2 | 0.00224 | 0.999954 | +1.71e-04 | x1.51 |
| 3 | 0.00288 | 0.999952 | +2.47e-04 | x1.28 |
| 5 | 0.00407 | 0.999949 | +2.01e-04 | x1.18 |
| 10 | 0.00778 | 0.999926 | -7.04e-05 | x1.14 |
| 20 | 0.03700 | 0.999273 | +1.41e-03 | x1.13 |
| 30 | 0.11282 | 0.993576 | -6.01e-04 | x1.10 |
| 50 | 0.31035 | 0.951731 | +3.72e-04 | x1.00 |

**Mean bias stays within +-1e-3 at every step and changes sign.**

### 2. Image quality -- did it get worse

| Prompt | CLIP BF16 | CLIP FP8 | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cat and dog baking in a kitchen (many small props) | 36.31 | 35.96 | -0.35 |
| Watchmaker's hands close-up (skin and metal micro-detail) | 24.66 | 24.91 | +0.25 |
| **mean** | **30.49** | **30.44** | **-0.05** |

All deltas are within +-0.5 CLIP points and go both ways (mean -0.05), i.e. no quality change. n=2 at a single seed.

### 3. Pixel similarity to BF16 -- reported, not the gate

| Prompt | PSNR (not a gate) | SSIM (fine: > 0.8) | LPIPS (fine: < 0.1) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cat and dog baking | 18.30 | 0.8413 | 0.0959 |
| Watchmaker's hands | 18.79 | 0.8530 | 0.0843 |
| **mean** | **18.55** | **0.8472** | **0.0901** |

## Benchmarking and Profiling

### End to end, on the tracked MI450 dashboard configuration

Both rows are from the same dashboard harness, same image (`rocm/sgl-dev:v0.5.22-rocm10-mi45x-20261020`), same day, same arm (**MI450-MC Hammer: DPX TP1 (A0), `--enable-torch-compile true`**). The baseline row is the arm as it ships today -- BF16, because `--quantization fp8` cannot be passed on this target without the crash above. The second row is this PR *plus* the flag it enables:

| Arm | Text encode (s) | **Denoise (s)** | VAE decode (s) | **Total (s)** |
|-----|-----------------|-----------------|----------------|---------------|
| DPX TP1 (A0) + torch-compile (BF16, today) | 0.0034 | 48.7215 | 3.0623 | 51.787 |
| + PR 45304 + `--quantization fp8` | 0.0031 | 36.0457 | 2.9947 | **39.044** |
| **Delta** | -- | **-26.0% (1.35x)** | -2.2% | **-24.6% (1.33x)** |

The entire win is in denoise, which is what the change touches; text encode and VAE decode are unchanged, and they are what keeps the e2e ratio (1.33x) below the denoise ratio (1.35x).

> Note for anyone reproducing: the `+ PR45304` row **must** carry `--quantization fp8`. Every line of this PR sits behind `Fp8LinearMethod.use_gfx1250_triton_fp8`, and that class is only constructed when the flag is passed -- so a "+PR45304" arm without it measures plain BF16 and shows no change. Also discard the first run after a cold start; cold Inductor/aiter JIT costs roughly 8 s of denoise.

### Isolated A/B on one gfx1250

FLUX.2-dev, 720p, 100 denoise steps, seed 42, one gfx1250, `--enable-torch-compile true --attention-backend aiter`, all offload off. Runs serialized on an otherwise idle box, two repetitions each, no profiler attached.

| Metric | BF16 s/step | FP8 s/step | BF16 e2e | FP8 e2e |
|--------|-------------|-----------|----------|---------|
| rep 1 | 0.7553 | 0.5553 | 87.77 s | 64.13 s |
| rep 2 | 0.7569 | 0.5592 | 87.93 s | 64.45 s |
| mean | **0.7561** | **0.5573** | **87.85 s** | **64.29 s** |

**-26.3% per denoise step (1.357x), -26.8% end to end (1.367x).** Spread across repetitions is under 0.5%.

The row-major weight layout is a further **-5.3%** on top of that, measured the same way (3 reps each, same GPU, serialized, warm compile cache):

| s/step | rep 1 | rep 2 | rep 3 | mean |
|--------|-------|-------|-------|------|
| column-major weights | 0.5522 | 0.5523 | 0.5565 | **0.5537** |
| row-major weights | 0.5234 | 0.5288 | 0.5211 | **0.5244** |

A matched pair of profiles (same step count, same GPU) attributes -174 ms of GPU time over three steps to the GEMMs, against a total of -108 ms; GPU-busy time falls 1791.5 -> 1683.6 ms, which tracks the wall-clock change. Cumulative against BF16: **0.7561 -> 0.5244 s/step, 1.44x.**

These per-step figures are the host loop average (`[DenoisingStage] average time per step`), while the dashboard's Denoise column is `[DenoisingStage] finished in`, which includes the GPU tail drain and runs ~20% higher on the same run. Compare within a table, not across the two.

title: [Perf] [AMD] dsv41: Skip unneeded layer 20 computation under decoder-bounded-replay
author: 1am9trash
body:
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->

Examples: [Fix] attention: Fix KV cache indexing; [Perf] [AMD] flash-attn: Optimize decode performance. -->

## Motivation

<!-- Describe the purpose and goals of this pull request. -->

With `--enable-decoder-swa-bounded-replay`, DeepSeek-V4.1's decoder layers only process the last 128 prompt tokens of each request during prefill. Layer 20 (the first decoder layer) still has to write the KV cache for every token, but it does not need to run the indexer, attention, and MoE on all of them. Currently, The amd code path still runs all of layer 20 on every token.

Nv enabled the skip in #42901. Amd was left out because its fused layer path runs the whole layer 20 in one call, so the KV write could not be split from the rest of the layer.

This PR enables it on amd. Layer 20 writes the KV cache for every token first, then runs the rest of the layer on the last 128 tokens only.

## Modifications

<!-- Detail the changes made in this pull request. -->

No change on nv. All changes are in `deepseek_v4_backend_hip_radix.py` or under `_is_hip`.

- **`deepseek_v4.py`**
  - Set `tail_writes_source_kv` to `True` on amd, so the tail starts at layer 20 instead of layer 21.
  - Get layer 20's input for the KV write from `fused_boundary_attn_input`.
- **`deepseek_v4_platform_stage.py`**
  - The fused boundary delays each layer's mHC post to the start of the next layer, so it has not run yet when layer 20 starts.
  - Add `fused_boundary_attn_input`, which runs that pending mHC post and builds layer 20's attention input for every token.
- **`deepseek_v4_backend_hip_radix.py`**
  - Reuse `DeepseekV4AttnBackend.write_tail_source_kv` to write layer 20's KV cache for every token.
  - Layer 20 now runs its indexer on the last 128 tokens only, and writes data straight into the tail buffers.
  - Remove the code that copied these results out of the full-token buffers, since it is no longer needed.

## Accuracy Tests

<!-- If this pull request affects model outputs (e.g., changes to the kernel or model forward code), provide accuracy test results. -->

Server cmd:

SGLANG_ENABLE_DSV41_ENGRAM_HOST_TABLE=1 SGLANG_DSV41_ENGRAM_HOST_TABLE_LAYOUT=per_rank \
ROCM_QUICK_REDUCE_QUANTIZATION=INT8 \
python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash --trust-remote-code \
  --tp 2 --enforce-shared-experts-fusion --fp8-gemm-backend aiter --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 64 \
  --enable-decoder-swa-bounded-replay --cuda-graph-backend-prefill disabled \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.8 --chunked-prefill-size 16384 --prefill-decode-interval 32 \
  --swa-prefix-tails 2048 --max-running-requests 64
# DSpark rows add: --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --speculative-dspark-block-size 5
# The radix-cache-off row adds: --disable-radix-cache
python3 -m sglang.test.few_shot_gsm8k --num-questions 1319 --parallel 32

title: [Perf] glm-5.3: Encode GLM-5.3 Python chat template prompts segment by segment
author: Dovis01
body:
## Motivation

Follow-up to #45154. The GLM-5.3 Python chat template still renders the prompt to one string, which `parallel_prompt_encode` then has to take apart again. It scans the text for added tokens to find cut points, only engages at `SGLANG_PARALLEL_PROMPT_ENCODE_MIN_CHARS` (32,768 characters) and above, and probes once whether `encode_batch` really runs in parallel. Shorter prompts are encoded with a single tokenizer call, and every request re-encodes its whole prompt, even though in function-calling and agent workloads most of it (system prompt, tool list, earlier turns) repeats from request to request.

The renderer already knows where each turn's special tokens go. This PR hands those positions to the encoder: the text between them is encoded in one `encode_batch` call at any prompt length without scanning the prompt, and its token ids are cached, so the parts that recur are encoded once.

## Modifications

- **`parser/glm53_chat_template.py`**: `render_glm53_segments` / `render_glm53_flash_segments` return the prompt as the list of strings it concatenates, with `[gMASK]`, `<sop>`, `<|system|>`, `<|user|>`, `<|assistant|>`, `<|observation|>` and the generation prompt's `<think>` as items of their own. `render_glm53` / `render_glm53_flash` join them, so the rendered prompt is unchanged byte for byte.
- **`parser/python_chat_template.py`**: `PythonChatTemplate.render_segments`. The installed `apply_chat_template` and the new `render_chat_segments` share one render path. `render_chat_segments` returns `None` when `chat_template_kwargs` holds an argument of `apply_chat_template` itself (`chat_template`, `continue_final_message`, `documents`, ...), so those requests keep the original path, errors included.
- **`entrypoints/openai/parallel_prompt_encode.py`**: `encode_prompt_segments(tokenizer, segments, encode_kwargs)`, a drop-in for `parallel_prompt_encode(tokenizer, "".join(segments), encode_kwargs)`.
  - A segment that is a whole added token is a cut point if no added token can match across it (`_cuts_at`, checked once per token). The text between cut points goes through one `encode_batch` call, whatever the prompt length, and the prompt itself is not scanned.
  - The ids of that text are kept in a per-tokenizer LRU (up to 1M tokens, entries up to 128K tokens), so a recurring system prompt, tool list or earlier turn is encoded once.
  - Uncached text of at least `SGLANG_PARALLEL_PROMPT_ENCODE_MIN_CHARS` is still split with `split_prompt`, so a long document stays parallel on its first request.
  - It uses the same one-time tokenizer validation (the per-tokenizer plan) and per-call checks as `parallel_prompt_encode`, and falls back to it for everything else: no plan, post-processor specials, truncation / padding / `encode_special_tokens` left on the backend, `SGLANG_PARALLEL_PROMPT_ENCODE=0`, other encode kwargs.
- **`entrypoints/openai/serving_chat.py`**: `_render_and_encode_chat_template` takes the segment path when a Python chat template is active. Jinja templates, and every model without a Python template, keep `apply_chat_template` + `parallel_prompt_encode` unchanged.

## Accuracy Tests

- **Token-id identity on the real tokenizers** (GLM-5.3 and GLM-5.3-Flash): 6,608 comparisons, 0 mismatches. Segment-path ids equal `tokenizer.encode(rendered_prompt)` for randomized conversations whose content contains special-token spellings, partial spellings next to the cut points, and unicode, plus a 150K-character document and the 128-tool prompt below, each encoded a second time from the cache. 600 of them are also compared with Jinja `apply_chat_template` ids.
- **Online A/B** (this PR vs. `main`, GLM-5.3-Flash, greedy decoding): identical `prompt_token_ids`, status and outputs for 24 cases. They cover chat, `reasoning_effort`, multi-turn reasoning, `clear_thinking`, tools (`auto` / `required` / named / `none`), out-of-order tool results, inline system messages, `continue_final_message`, images, streaming, `/v1/responses`, `/v1/messages`, and the 400 error cases.
- **Unit tests**:
  - `test_parallel_prompt_encode.py::TestPromptSegments`: id identity on fuzzed segment lists, text encoded once with no length threshold, long text split, tokens another added token can overlap are not cut points, fallbacks, cache budget.
  - `test_glm53_chat_template.py`: segments join to what `apply_chat_template` renders, turn tokens are segments of their own, routing back to `apply_chat_template`. With `SGLANG_TEST_GLM53_CHECKPOINT` / `SGLANG_TEST_GLM53_FLASH_CHECKPOINT` set, segment-encoded ids are also compared with the checkpoints' tokenizers.
  - `test_serving_chat.py`: the serving wiring.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

**Render + encode per request** (what `_render_and_encode_chat_template` does), median ms with the GLM-5.3-Flash tokenizer. The last message differs on every request. *Cold* has nothing cached: the first request with a given tool list and history. *Warm* has the tool list and earlier turns cached: the next request of a conversation, or another request with the same tools.

| Scenario | Prompt chars / tokens | `main` | This PR, cold | This PR, warm |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| chat, 1 turn | 103 / 23 | 0.050 | 0.065 | 0.038 (1.3x) |
| 8 tools, 1 turn | 2,312 / 596 | 0.730 | 0.601 (1.2x) | 0.083 (8.8x) |
| 128 tools, 1 turn | 82,925 / 20,238 | 2.835 | 2.918 | 1.003 (2.8x) |
| agent: 8 tools, 18 tool-call rounds | 38,262 / 7,997 | 1.559 | 1.447 (1.1x) | 0.357 (4.4x) |
| agent: 8 tools, 8 rounds × 3 parallel calls | 25,053 / 5,276 | 7.596 | 1.160 (6.5x) | 0.233 (32.6x) |

- The 8 × 3 agent prompt is below 32,768 characters, so `main` encodes it with a single tokenizer call. The segment path batches it at any length, so it is 6.5x faster even with nothing cached.
- The 128-tool prompt is above the threshold, so `main` already encodes it in parallel, and cold the two paths are on par. Warm, the remaining ~1 ms is the Python render.
- A cold request whose new text is two or more tiny segments pays rayon's dispatch (+15 µs in the first row), once per conversation.

**End to end**, client-side TTFT p50 in ms. Setup: GLM-5.3-Flash FP8, TP4 / EP4 on 4×B200, EAGLE MTP (5 / 1 / 6, adaptive), `--reasoning-parser glm45 --tool-call-parser glm47`. `main` and this PR ran side by side with the same checkpoint and flags. Requests are streamed with `max_tokens` 512 and temperature 1.0, with no cache flush and a unique nonce in the last message of every request: the radix prefix cache is warm, and the whole-request render cache misses. 20 requests at concurrency 1, 64 at concurrency 16.

| Scenario | Prompt tokens | c=1: `main` → this PR | c=16: `main` → this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| 128 tools, 1 turn | 20,247 | 185.3 → 159.1 (−14.1%) | 550.3 → 422.9 (−23.1%) |
| agent: 8 tools, 18 tool-call rounds | 8,006 | 77.6 → 65.7 (−15.3%) | 142.4 → 122.0 (−14.3%) |
| agent: 8 tools, 8 rounds × 3 parallel calls | 5,285 | 73.6 → 66.1 (−10.2%) | 103.0 → 108.4 (mean 136.3 → 123.6) |
| 8 tools, 1 turn | 606 | 54.5 → 55.0 | 129.4 → 127.5 |

- With this PR, the 128-tool request comes within 3 ms of the ~156 ms measured when the render cache returns the whole prompt for a repeated request.
- The 8-tool prompt has under 1 ms of preprocessing to save, so its TTFT is unchanged.
- Environment: Intel Xeon 6960P (144 threads), Python 3.12.15, transformers 5.19.0, tokenizers 0.23.2.

title: [Perf] dsv4: Compute request-window history rows once per batch
author: hnyls2002
body:
- `window_layout` now computes each history slot's source row (`history_src`: `row_loc` of the slot's request and position, or the zero row when invalid) once per batch and stores it in `WindowLayout`, instead of `RequestWindow.buffer` recomputing it in every layer through `_history_src`. It takes the window's `zero_row` to do so.
- `WindowLayout.copy_` copies the new field, so a captured layout refreshed in place for graph replay carries the current batch's rows.
- The two `window_layout` callers (the CUDA and HIP DeepSeek V4 backends) and the tests that build a layout pass `zero_row`.
- DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on GB300, DEP4: `row_loc` and `_history_src` take 4.1-4.8% and up to 2.9% of the scheduler thread at 4K tokens per rank, and 3.2% and 1.7% in a multi-turn prefill workload at 640 concurrent sessions, all per layer under `get_swa_raw_buffer`. With this change and the V4.1 index-K slot snapshot (#45577) together, the 4K step goes from 106-110 to 98.7 ms (one run per arm); this change alone was not measured.

No behavior change; only applies with encoder SWA bounded replay.

title: [Perf] [AMD] kda: Use a HIP fused decode kernel by default for KDA (Kimi-K3) on gfx950
author: Monstertail
body:
## Motivation On MI350X / MI355X (gfx950), Kimi-K3 KDA decode runs the unfused chain by default (`f_b` tiny GEMM, causal Conv1D update, Triton recurrent decode, gated RMSNorm), or the AITER FlyDSL fused boundary with `SGLANG_ROCM_K3_KDA_FUSED_BACKEND=aiter`. This PR adds a HIP kernel for the same fused boundary and makes it the default on gfx950. It is the decode companion of #45710 (KDA prefill); the two PRs change disjoint runtime files. **Note: This kernel is generated by [KDAgent](https://nvlabs.github.io/kda/blog/2026-09-27-kda-for-kda/) in AMD ecosystems. Cost around 5k dollars in humanize2 flow to get this.** ## Modifications The kernel follows the `sglang.kernels` layout of RFC #29630: it was produced with the Kernel Design Agents workflow, so the implementation lives in `kernels/kda_kernels`, it is registered with `KernelBackend.KDA`, and runtime code reaches it only through the `sglang.kernels.ops` facade. - `kernels/kda_kernels/csrc/attention/kda_decode_gfx950.cu` and its loader `kernels/kda_kernels/kda_decode_gfx950.py`, JIT-compiled on first use. One 256-thread workgroup per (token, head), for 12 heads of 128 per rank (Kimi-K3 TP8), runs the `f_b` projection, the depthwise Conv1D update with SiLU, the q/k L2 norms and gate decay, the delta-rule update of the 128 x 128 fp32 state, and the gated RMSNorm. State and Conv1D slot strides are read from the tensors, so padded hybrid cache layouts work. Slot 0, the mamba pool's padding slot, returns zeros without touching either cache. - `kernels/kda_kernels/README.md`: provenance entry. - `kernels/ops/attention/__init__.py`: registers `attention.kda_decode_gfx950` (`KernelBackend.KDA`, HIP). - `kernels/ops/attention/kda_fused_decode_gfx950.py` (facade): the same fail-closed `available` / `covered` / `warmup` / `run` interface as `kda_fused_decode_aiter_hip`; `run` calls the kernel through `get_kernel`. - `srt/models/kimi_k3.py` (ROCm branch of `_prepare_fused_decode`): maps `SGLANG_ROCM_K3_KDA_FUSED_BACKEND` to a facade, `gfx950` (the new default) or `aiter`; any other value keeps the unfused chain. The chosen facade is stored on the layer. - `srt/layers/attention/linear/kda_backend.py` (gfx950 fused-decode branch): calls the facade stored on the layer instead of the hard-coded AITER adapter. - `test/registered/kernels/ops/attention/test_kda_fused_decode_gfx950.py` (MI35x suite): matches the Triton chain over 4 steps under the default backend, skips slots <= 0, and CUDA graph replay equals eager. Behavior change: on gfx950 the fused decode is now on by default. `SGLANG_ROCM_K3_KDA_FUSED_BACKEND=aiter` selects FlyDSL, and any other value (for example `none`) selects the unfused chain. Both edits in `srt/` are inside the existing ROCm-only branches. ## Accuracy Tests MI355X, `lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:v0.5.22-rocm10-mi35x-20261020`. - Against a per-token fp32 PyTorch reference (batch 1, 2, 8 and 37 with padded rows, and batch 16 over 64 steps): output relative RMSE at most 7.1e-6 (the Triton chain reaches 1.2e-5 and FlyDSL 2.7e-5 in the same checks). The Conv1D state is bit-identical; padded rows return zeros and slot 0 is untouched. - Pass: the new test, `unit/kernels/test_kernels_namespace.py` (includes the KDA directory/backend pairing check), `kernels/ops/attention/kda_flydsl/test_kimi_k3_kda_decode.py`, `attention/unittests/kda/test_triton.py`, `attention/test_kda_kernels.py`, `kernels/ops/attention/test_fused_kda_conv_recurrent_verify.py` and `amd/test_kimi_k3_kda_inproj_fusion.py`. - Kimi-K3 TP8 GSM8K (8-shot, 1319 questions): 0.960 with both HIP kernels off, 0.961 with this PR and #45710 on. ## Speed Tests and Profiling **Kernel.** Per-layer time inside a 69-layer CUDA graph with a separate cache per layer (median of 11 trials): | Batch | Triton chain | FlyDSL | HIP | vs Triton chain | vs FlyDSL | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | 11.51 us | 8.54 us | 5.96 us | 1.93x | 1.43x | | 2 | 11.60 us | 8.45 us | 6.09 us | 1.90x | 1.39x | | 4 | 13.45 us | 10.44 us | 7.15 us | 1.88x | 1.46x | | 8 | 27.42 us | 11.82 us | 7.93 us | 3.46x | 1.49x | | 16 | 29.87 us | 13.92 us | 9.91 us | 3.02x | 1.41x | | 32 | 33.60 us | 19.65 us | 16.21 us | 2.07x | 1.21x | | 64 | 38.26 us | 31.50 us | 26.28 us | 1.46x | 1.20x | | 128 | 61.11 us | 56.29 us | 46.68 us | 1.31x | 1.21x | | 256 | 108.86 us | 100.83 us | 86.48 us | 1.26x | 1.17x | For reference, AITER's Triton/Gluon packed KDA decode (not a SGLang backend) is 1.10x-1.30x slower than HIP up to batch 32 and 3%-6% faster from batch 64. **The model runs the kernel.** Kimi-K3 TP8, rank-0 GPU profile (`/start_profile`) of one 10,244-token request with 8 output tokens (7 decode steps x 69 KDA layers = 483 layer steps): | Kernels (calls) | Baseline | This PR + #45710 | |---|---|---| | KDA decode | `_causal_conv1d_update_kernel` (483), `fused_sigmoid_gating_delta_rule_update_kernel` (483), `layer_norm_gated_fwd_kernel` (483 of 552) | `kda_decode_gfx950_kernel` (483); none of the three | **Kimi-K3 TP8 E2E.** Measured with this PR and #45710 applied; the baseline sets `SGLANG_ROCM_KDA_HIP_PREFILL=0 SGLANG_ROCM_K3_KDA_FUSED_BACKEND=none`, which is the current `main` behavior. Baseline and candidate servers were launched alternately, two rounds each; the table shows the mean of the two rounds. ```bash SGLANG_USE_AITER=1 SGLANG_AITER_K3_OPT=1 AITER_FLYDSL_FORCE=1 AITER_SITUV2_A8W4=1 \ python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path moonshotai/Kimi-K3 --tp-size 8 \ --attention-backend triton --dtype bfloat16 --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \ --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 64 --max-running-requests 64 \ --reasoning-parser kimi_k3 --tool-call-parser kimi_k3 --trust-remote-code python3 -m sglang.bench_serving --backend sglang --dataset-name random-ids \ --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 512 --random-range-ratio 1 \ --num-prompts 80 --max-concurrency 16 --warmup-requests 16 --flush-cache --seed 42 # also: --num-prompts 320 --max-concurrency 64; and --random-input-len 8192 # --random-output-len 64 --num-prompts 40 --max-concurrency 8 --warmup-requests 8 python3 -m sglang.test.few_shot_gsm8k --num-shots 8 --num-questions 1319 \ --max-new-tokens 512 --parallel 64 ``` | Workload | Metric | Baseline | Both PRs | Change | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1024 in / 512 out, concurrency 16 | median TPOT | 23.7 ms | 22.9 ms | -3.6% | | | median ITL | 23.8 ms | 22.9 ms | -3.8% | | | output throughput | 617.7 tok/s | 642.7 tok/s | +4.1% | | 1024 in / 512 out, concurrency 64 | median TPOT | 33.5 ms | 32.4 ms | -3.2% | | | median ITL | 33.5 ms | 32.5 ms | -2.9% | | | output throughput | 1536.7 tok/s | 1590.1 tok/s | +3.5% | | 8192 in / 64 out, concurrency 8 | median TPOT | 20.2 ms | 19.5 ms | -3.8% | | | median ITL | 20.6 ms | 19.8 ms | -3.8% | | | output throughput | 99.5 tok/s | 102.4 tok/s | +3.0% | The two rounds of each server differed by at most 0.6% in output throughput.
Decode throughput with bench_one_batch_server `steady_state_output_throughput` of `python3 -m sglang.bench_one_batch_server --model None --base-url http://127.0.0.1:30000 --batch-size 1 8 32 64 --input-len 1024 --output-len 512 --dataset-name random-ids`, median of 2 runs; the steady-state window excludes prefill: | Batch | Baseline | This PR | Change | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | 69.2 tok/s | 72.4 tok/s | +4.6% | | 8 | 378.1 tok/s | 385.4 tok/s | +1.9% | | 32 | 1137.2 tok/s | 1174.1 tok/s | +3.2% | | 64 | 1779.7 tok/s | 1866.6 tok/s | +4.9% |
The Kimi-K3 cookbook's MI355X recipe (DCP8, AITER attention, fp8 KV cache) failed to allocate the KDA state cache on this image for both variants, so these runs use Triton attention without DCP. ## Checklist - [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit). title: [Perf] [AMD] Qwen3-Next: fused QK Gemma RMSNorm + partial RoPE on gfx950
author: karverma-amd
body:
## Summary

Route the Qwen3-Next full-attention prologue — the per-head `[Q||gate]` split, Q/K Gemma RMSNorm (`x*(1+w)`), and partial NeoX RoPE (rotary_dim 64) — through the fused aiter op `fused_attention_qk_norm_rope` on gfx950, replacing three small launches with one.

## Gating 

- Gated on `SGLANG_USE_AITER` + `is_hip()` — no bespoke per-kernel flag.
- The aiter import is lazy and only reached on HIP, so the NVIDIA common path never imports or touches the AMD-only code.
- Support is probed (`fused_attention_qk_norm_rope_supported`), not asserted, so any uncovered shape (dtype/width/arch) falls back to the native split + GemmaRMSNorm + RoPE. The attention backend still writes the KV cache.

## Dependencies

- **aiter op**: `fused_attention_qk_norm_rope` in ROCm/aiter — https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/compare/main...karverma-amd:aiter:karverma/qwen3-next-fused-prologue?expand=1
- **Stacked on #45738** (the `smallm_fp8_blockscale_gfx950` import fix), which Qwen3-Next FP8 needs to serve on gfx950. The first commit in this PR is that fix; the second commit is the wiring under review here.

## Test results

E2E on Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-FP8, MI355X 2×TP4, latest nightly (`v0.5.22-rocm724-mi35x-20261021`) with **Triton 3.8.0**:

- Median TPOT **−2.3 to −3.0%** at concurrency 1/8/32 (throughput +2.3 to +7.9%); stable through cuda-graph capture and sustained conc-8/32/64 load.
- GSM8K 1319-question 5-shot: parity (fused 0.941 / native 0.948, 0 invalid).
- Engagement confirmed on the fused arm; fail-closed to native verified on the control arm.
- The same nightly on stock Triton 3.7 and v0.5.21 + Triton 3.8 reproduce the same −2.5 to −3.0% TPOT and GSM8K parity.
