title: [Perf] fp8: Hopper small-M GEMV, fused KDA output quant, CUDA grouped top-k, partial-block tails
author: JustinTong0323
body:
## Motivation

Split out from the Ling-3.1-flash day-0 support effort.

Block-FP8 decode on Hopper spends small-M linear work in GEMM kernels that are built for large batches, the KDA output normalization and FP8 quantization run as separate kernels, the 512-expert sigmoid router goes through a generic Triton top-k, and weights whose K dimension is not a multiple of the 128-wide quantization block cannot use the native Triton/DeepGEMM paths at all. This PR adds opt-in fast paths for each, with explicit dispatch contracts and no change to default behavior.

Measured on H200 with Ling-3.1-flash (FP8, TP8+EP8+NEXTN, fp32 router as on current main): batch-size-1 decode output throughput **+7.3%** (218.6 → 234.6 tok/s), median TPOT **−8.5%**, both environment flags on vs current main; throughput at concurrency 16 is unchanged. Accuracy on full GSM8K is unchanged (see below).

## Modifications

- **Hopper small-M GEMV** (`SGLANG_ENABLE_FP8_BLOCK_GEMV`, default off): CUDA block-FP8 GEMV for M≤8 with optional fused side projection, and a BF16 tiny GEMV (N≤64, M≤4, SM90 only) under `--bf16-gemm-backend gemv`. Dispatch checks device, dtype, layout, scale grid, and shape; anything else keeps the existing path. Also a CUDA router gate matvec (fp32/bf16 weight) for the Bailing-class gate shape, gated the same way.
- **Fused KDA output quant** (`SGLANG_ENABLE_FUSED_KDA_OUTPUT_QUANT`, default off): the gated RMSNorm at the KDA output fuses with FP8 quantization, emitting the `(q, scale)` tuple the FP8 o_proj consumes; requires target-verify batches and BF16, falls back otherwise.
- **CUDA grouped top-k** for the 512-expert / 8-group / group-top-4 / topk≤8 sigmoid routing shape. Dispatch is shape-driven (no model check): any model with the matching shape uses it, everything else keeps the Triton path. Shared-slot weighting follows the same contract as `moe_fused_gate` (incl. `renormalize=False` and zero-score semantics).
- **Partial-block FP8 support** (opt-in per layer): serialized block-FP8 weights whose K crosses a quantization block boundary — partial-block quant/GEMM in the native Triton MoE, a `prequant_k_tail` dispatcher for pre-quantized inputs (DeepGEMM only when the TMA alignment contract holds: contiguous operands, base pointer and K divisible by 16), and fused SwiGLU+quant for two-group K-tails. All admission is opt-in and default-off; no in-tree model enables it yet (the Ling3 model PR follows separately).

Traces on H200 (bs=1 decode, flags on): the 510 dense FP8 GEMM calls move from DeepGEMM `sm90_fp8_gemm_1d2d` to the GEMV kernel, the 189 KDA norm+quant pairs collapse into the fused kernel, and the router matvec runs its CUDA path. On GB300 (SM103) every SM90-gated path is a no-op — OFF/ON kernel sequences are identical — while the shape-driven top-k runs normally.

## Accuracy Tests

- H200 8x, Ling-3.1-flash FP8, TP8+EP8+NEXTN, full GSM8K (1319 questions, temp 1.0, top_p 0.95, 2 rounds per mode): OFF 96.89% / stop 99.92% vs ON 97.04% / stop 99.89% (within ±0.5pp run noise). GB300 4x TP4+EP4: OFF 96.82% vs ON 96.97%, stop 99.92% both.
- Kernel numerics (H200 + GB300): new GEMV/side-projection, router matvec, fused KDA quant, grouped top-k (incl. `renormalize=False` shared-slot and zero-score cases), block quant tail, Triton K-tail (incl. aligned-K non-fusion and explicit zero clamp vs `None`) suites all pass; partial-K linear matches a dequant-fp32 reference on both the DeepGEMM route (K=160, descriptor built) and the Triton fallback (K=161). On GB300 the SM90-only suites skip cleanly and the K160 selector rejects with bitwise-generic output.
- Kimi-Linear-48B BF16 smoke (KDA fallback path): 100-question GSM8K 93.0%, stop 100%.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

H200, Ling-3.1-flash TP8+EP8+NEXTN, 3 rounds bs=1 (2048/512) + 2 rounds conc16 (8192/1024), `--flush-cache`, seed 11:

| workload | main | this PR (env off) | this PR (flags on) |
|---|---|---|---|
| bs=1 output tok/s | 218.6 | 221.6 (+1.4%) | 234.6 (+7.3%) |
| bs=1 median TPOT (ms) | 4.351 | 4.191 (−3.7%) | 3.981 (−8.5%) |
| conc16 output tok/s | 1087.6 | 1087.8 | 1094.9 (+0.7%, within run noise) |

The +1.4% with flags off comes from the shape-driven grouped top-k; the flags-on gain comes from the GEMV and fused KDA quant. The CUDA router matvec is neutral at fp32/M=4 (1.41 vs 1.30 ms in trace) and is not claimed as a speedup. Concurrency-16 gains are diluted by MoE/attention compute; low-batch decode is where these kernels pay.

Note: the K160 large-M specialization (H20-3e) is intentionally **not** in this PR — it needs qualifying-hardware evidence and will follow separately.

title: [Perf] DFLASH: route draft bf16 GEMMs through tuned dispatch on GB300
author: wookjeHan
body:
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->

<!-- PR title: [Type] scope: title, or [Type] [Hardware] scope: title.
Type: Feat, Fix, Refactor, Perf, Doc, Test, CI, or Chore.
Scope: any module or model name (no fixed list or letter-case restriction), e.g. attention, qwen3, or flash-attn.
Hardware: optional single tag without spaces. Use uppercase hardware tags (AMD, NVIDIA, NPU, MI300X), except for exactly these four spellings: Intel, Apple, Huawei, Ascend.
Title: no letter-case restriction.
Reverts: use GitHub's default title, Revert "original title".
Examples: [Fix] attention: Fix KV cache indexing; [Perf] [AMD] flash-attn: Optimize decode performance. -->

## Motivation

<!-- Describe the purpose and goals of this pull request. -->

At low concurrency the DFLASH draft model runs its bf16 linears at small M: one block of `num_draft_tokens` tokens per request. 
Two of its paths bypass SGLang's tuned bf16 GEMM dispatch and always use cuBLAS:

- `DFlashGroupedConv.kernel_projection` is a plain `nn.Linear`;
- the candidate head in `_project_candidate_logits` calls `torch.matmul` directly.

Most of the draft's other GEMM shapes have no GB300 tuned entry and fall back to cuBLAS, which is well below the memory bandwidth
limit at these M sizes. The exception is TP4 qkv at M = 8 and 16, which already used the split-K tactics of the "GB300 TP16" block.

## Modifications

<!-- Detail the changes made in this pull request. -->
- `models/dflash.py`
  - `kernel_projection` becomes `ReplicatedLinear`, so it goes through `UnquantizedLinearMethod.apply` and the tuned dispatch.
  - The candidate head calls `bf16_gemm_dispatch` when the backend is cutedsl/gemv and the weight is bf16 on CUDA; otherwise it
    keeps `torch.matmul`.
- `layers/quantization/unquant.py`: GB300 split-K / warp split-K entries at M <= 32, TP4 and TP8.
- `kernels/ops/gemm/cutedsl_bf16_gemm.py`: TGV M ranges for three shapes at M = 17..32.

Each entry was kept only if it beats the current kernel in all three timings of the micro-benchmark below.

The tables are keyed by (M, N, K) only, so the entries are not draft-specific:

- The qkv / gate_up / down shapes (hidden 8192, intermediate 28672, 64 q / 8 kv heads) are also those of Llama-3-70B-class dense
  models at TP4 and TP8. With the default `auto` backend on SM10x those models switch kernels at M <= 32 as well. Only GB300 was
  measured; GB200 was not.
- For TP4 qkv at M = 8 and 16, the new warp split-K entries replace the existing GB300 TP16 split-K tactics (warp split-K takes
  precedence). They are faster in all three timings; see the micro-benchmark.
- `precompile_splitk_tactics()` (only Qwen4-Exp calls it) compiles every table entry, so it now builds 19 more tactics at startup.

## Accuracy Tests

<!-- If this pull request affects model outputs (e.g., changes to the kernel or model forward code), provide accuracy test results. -->
| Model | GSM8K (x1, 65K max tokens) | AIME26 pass@1 (30 x 16, 131K) | AIME26 pass@16 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Muse Spark Open (NVFP4, TP4, DFLASH) + this PR | 97.50% | 95.83% ± 3.33% (std over 16 runs; SEM 0.83%) | 100% |

## Speed Tests and Profiling

<!-- If this pull request impacts inference speed, provide benchmarking and profiling results. -->
### Micro-benchmark (GB300, CUDA graphs, cold L2; us per call, after-PDL timing)


| GEMM (N, K) | M | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| kernel_projection (2048, 8192) | 8 | 9.66 (cuBLAS) | 5.95 (-38%) |
| TP4 gate_up (14336, 8192) | 16 | 42.28 (cuBLAS) | 35.59 (-16%) |
| TP4 qkv (2560, 8192) | 8 | 8.70 (split-K) | 7.41 (warp split-K, -15%) |
| TP4 qkv (2560, 8192) | 16 | 9.04 (split-K) | 8.12 (warp split-K, -10%) |
| TP4 candidate head (50512, 8192) | 7 | 136.21 (cuBLAS) | 113.74 (-16%) |
| TP8 qkv (1280, 8192) | 8 | 9.82 (cuBLAS) | 4.82 (-51%) |
| TP8 candidate head (25256, 8192) | 7 | 67.35 (cuBLAS) | 60.64 (-10%) |
### End-to-end (Muse Spark Open NVFP4, GB300, DFLASH 8 drafts, FlashInfer autotune off on both sides)


Mean decode cycle (target verify + draft step) from nsys, main -> this PR; FlashInfer autotune off on both sides.

| | c=1 | c=2 | c=4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| TP4 | 9354.9 -> 9252.9 us (**-1.09%**) | 10946.2 -> 10862.4 us (**-0.77%**) | 13219.6 -> 13048.4 us (-1.30%\*) |
| TP8 | 7573.1 -> 7465.7 us (**-1.42%**) | 8495.7 -> 8390.4 us (**-1.24%**) | 9820.0 -> 9769.0 us (**-0.52%**) |

\*Includes about ±1% MoE routing variation between runs; the GEMMs this PR changes account for -52.6 us/cycle (**-0.40%**).

No change at c >= 5 (draft GEMM M > 32, no new entries).


Decode throughput scales with 1 / cycle, so the gain is about +1.1% (TP4) and +1.4% (TP8) at c=1.

title: [Perf] diffusion: Turn on breakable CUDA graphs by default for LTX-2/LTX-2.3 two-stage serving
author: mickqian
body:
## Motivation

LTX-2 two-stage stage 1 runs at half resolution (~1.5k video tokens), so its step is launch-bound: on 4xB300, TRT-LLM's CUDA-graph configuration runs a stage-1 step in 0.044 s against 0.192 s for sglang eager. Breakable CUDA graphs (BCG) close most of that gap, and the graphs replay the same kernels, so the output is bitwise equal to eager. Today BCG is opt-in, so every flagless LTX deployment leaves this on the table.

BCG stays opt-in everywhere else. The validated-model list records correctness, not speed: FLUX.3 won 1 of 10 cells, Qwen-Image-2.1 on 1 GPU is 0.5% slower, and MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA showed no speedup.

| HW (2 GPUs, CFG parallel) | Model | Eager (s) | BCG (s) | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| B300 | LTX-2 T2V 768x512x121, 40 steps | 6.693 / 6.882 | 3.797 / 3.785 | −44% |
| B300 | LTX-2.3 T2V 768x512x121, 30 steps | 6.294 / 6.202 | 4.735 / 4.726 | −24% |
| H200 | LTX-2 T2V 768x512x121, 40 steps | 7.398 / 7.593 | 5.969 / 5.970 | −20% |

B300 rows: two interleaved rounds, fresh server per arm. H200 rows: see Speed Tests.

## Modifications

- `ModelDeploymentConfig.bcg_default_pipeline_class_names`: the pipeline classes measured faster with BCG. `LTX2PipelineConfig` lists `LTX2TwoStagePipeline`; LTX-2.3 inherits it. The field names the pipeline class because one config serves the one-stage, two-stage and HQ pipelines, and only two-stage was measured.
- `--enable-breakable-cuda-graph` defaults to unset. `_adjust_breakable_cuda_graph_support` resolves an unset flag to on only when all of these hold, and to off otherwise:
  - the pipeline class is opted in and the checkpoint is on the validated BCG list;
  - `--performance-mode` is `auto` or `speed`;
  - the platform is CUDA (`current_platform.is_cuda()`, so ROCm, NPU and MPS stay off) with separate host and device memory (GB10 stays off);
  - the server warms up at startup (`sglang serve`); `sglang generate` and request warmup would pay a full extra generation;
  - monolithic role, ComfyUI mode off;
  - no torch.compile, Cache-DiT, dynamic batching or `--lora-path`;
  - both stage DiTs stay resident: no DiT component, snapshot or layerwise offload, no FSDP, a GPU with at least 130 GiB (the threshold LTX already uses to pick `resident` mode), and LTX-2.3 in `resident` mode.
  An explicit `--enable-breakable-cuda-graph true|false` always wins. When the default turns BCG on, the server logs `[Diffusion BCG] enabled by default for LTX2TwoStagePipeline; pass --enable-breakable-cuda-graph false to run eager.`
- Video BCG warmup now captures the model's full default resolution. It used the server-warmup resolution, which caps video at 832x480: LTX's 768x512 fits under the cap, but Wan (1280x720), MiniMax-H3 (1344x768) or LTX-2.5 (1920x1088) would capture a shape no request uses. Frame counts already used the full default under BCG.
- Graphs replay the weights and LoRA branches they were captured with, and serving never re-captures. So an external LoRA change (`/v1/set_lora`, merge, unmerge) or `resume_memory_occupation` now drops the captured graphs, and later requests run eager with a warning. The two-stage pipeline's own per-request distilled-LoRA switch is part of the capture and is unaffected.
- Docs: CLI reference and the LTX cookbook describe the default, its gates and the captured shape.

Behavior to know about (one-shot `MISSED` warning, then eager; no regression against today's eager path):
- Only the captured shape replays: 768x512, 121 frames, the warmup's quality level, text-to-video. The OpenAI video API defaults to 4 seconds, which LTX rounds to 89 frames, so those requests run eager unless the server passes `--warmup-num-frames 89`. Image-conditioned requests run eager.
- A request at another quality level (for example `quality="exact"`) runs eager; the runners are already keyed per level.
- Per-request attention-backend overrides are rejected under BCG, as before.

Tests:
- `test_server_args.py::TestBreakableCudaGraphDefault`: flagless LTX-2 two-stage serving on a mocked 141 GiB CUDA GPU resolves BCG on and captures 768x512; LTX-2.3 needs `resident`; explicit off, offline runs, request warmup, memory/manual modes, compile, batching, `--lora-path`, ComfyUI, one-stage and HQ pipelines, unvalidated checkpoints, every DiT offload form, low free memory and an 80 GB card resolve it off; ROCm (`is_cuda()` false) and shared-memory devices stay off; explicit on elsewhere is unchanged.
- `test_cfg_parallel_warmup.py::test_bcg_capture_keeps_the_full_default_video_resolution`.
- `test_diffusion_bcg_padding.py::TestBCGWeightChangeAfterCapture`: `set_lora`, merge, unmerge and `resume_memory_occupation` drop the graphs, and the runner then runs eager.

On main the default-on, platform-gate, capture-shape and graph-drop tests fail; the gate-off cases pass there by construction and guard the gates from here on.

## Accuracy Tests

LTX-2 two-stage on 2xH200, CFG parallel, the benchmark-default command (`--performance-mode speed`), seed 42, 768x512x121. Same MP4 bytes and same decoded-frame md5 for every arm:

| Server | Request | Path | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| this PR, no BCG flag | default quality | BCG replay | `742a1862…` |
| this PR, `--enable-breakable-cuda-graph false` | default quality | eager | `742a1862…` |
| main | default quality | eager | `742a1862…` |
| this PR, no BCG flag | `quality="exact"` | eager (no graph at that level) | same as eager server |
| this PR, no BCG flag | API default, 89 frames | eager (`MISSED`) | same as eager server |
| this PR, no BCG flag | after `/v1/set_lora` | eager (graphs dropped) | same as eager server after the same call |

With the CI-shaped request (1 second = 25 frames, `quality="exact"`, `--warmup-num-frames 25 --warmup-sampling-params '{"quality": "exact"}'`), BCG, eager and main also produce identical outputs.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

LTX-2 two-stage, 2xH200, CFG parallel, the benchmark-default command (`--performance-mode speed --dit-layerwise-offload false --enable-torch-compile false`, no BCG flag), 768x512x121, 40 steps. [diffusion-bench-framework](https://github.com/mickqian/diffusion-bench-framework) `single_e2e` (median of 2 measured requests after warmup), fresh server per run, rounds interleaved main / PR / main / PR:

| | round 1 | round 2 |
|---|---|---|
| main (eager) | 7.398 s | 7.593 s |
| this PR (BCG by default) | 5.969 s | 5.970 s |

Stage breakdown (round 2): `LTX2AVDenoisingStage` 5.368 → 3.702 s, `LTX2RefinementStage` 1.187 → 1.096 s, decode unchanged (0.67 s). On Hopper the FA attention calls stay eager, so each forward captures 289 segments; on B300 LTX attention is captured as well (1 segment per forward), which is why the gain there is about twice as large.

Cost on 2xH200, this PR with and without `--enable-breakable-cuda-graph false`, two alternating rounds:

| | BCG default | `--enable-breakable-cuda-graph false` |
|---|---|---|
| Startup to healthy (round 1 / round 2) | 104.1 / 84.1 s | 86.1 / 78.0 s |
| Server warmup | 121 frames, 40 steps: 52.1 / 32.2 s | 25 frames, 2 steps: 31.6 / 26.5 s |
| Peak memory per request (rank 0) | 82,654 MB | 75,690–75,704 MB |

Startup grows by about 6 s once caches are warm (about 20 s on a cold first start), and peak memory by 6.9 GB. On B300 the same comparison was +2 s and +0.95 GB (LTX-2) / +1.1 GB (LTX-2.3).

## CI and baselines

No perf or memory baseline should move:
- The H100 suite's LTX cases run on 80 GB cards, below the 130 GiB gate, so they stay eager. The B200, 5090 and XPU suites have no LTX two-stage case, and AMD is not CUDA.
- The explicit-BCG CI tests (`test_diffusion_bcg_*zimage_turbo.py`) are image models; the warmup-resolution change only affects video.
- If an H200/B200-class LTX two-stage case is added later, its runtime peak will include the capture (+~7 GB on Hopper), and its warmup runs one full generation; seed its baseline with the usual two-step flow.

## Risks

- Startup grows by one full-shape generation plus capture: +6 s on 2xH200 with warm caches, about +20 s on a cold first start, +2 s on B300.
- Peak memory grows by ~7 GB on Hopper, where attention stays eager (289 segments per signature), against ~1 GB on Blackwell, where LTX attention is captured too (1 segment). The 130 GiB gate keeps 80 GB cards, whose speed-mode headroom is smaller than that, on eager.
- LTX-2.3 is validated on B300 only (above). The H200 runs here cover LTX-2.
- #45943 changes the dynamic-LoRA linear path that stage 2 runs; BCG captures whatever eager runs, so outputs stay equal to eager, but its speed should be re-checked once both land.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).
- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).
- [x] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations).
- [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed).
- [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance).

title: [Perf] diffusion: Keep every component resident in auto mode when memory allows
author: mickqian
body:
## Motivation

`--performance-mode auto` places components from a static per-model allowlist. Above `keep_resident_min_available_gb` (the model's value, else 45 GB for image and 120 GB for video models) only `keep_resident_components` stay resident: the VAE by default, plus the DiT for image models. Everything else streams layer by layer at any memory size:
- Z-Image, Ideogram-4, FLUX, Qwen-Image and LTX-2 stream their text encoder even on a 288 GB GPU. A B300 server log reads `267.1 GiB of free device memory selects layerwise offload for text_encoder` and then `resident=0/36`; Z-Image-Turbo spends 0.066 s of a 0.354 s request moving 3.4 GB over PCIe.
- Wan2.2-T2V/I2V-A14B list `auto` in `dit_layerwise_offload_modes` and set no threshold, so both 14B experts stream layer by layer on every GPU, including H200/B200/B300. That also pins ~54 GB of host memory per rank.

On H100, Z-Image-Turbo with every component resident was 12% faster than auto (0.701/0.699 vs 0.793/0.799 s). The memory-aware fix was meant to come from the warmup-calibrated planner (#37917/#37918), which is not merged. This PR adds a conservative interim rule.

## Modifications

- Memory-rich tier in auto mode (`ServerArgsAutoTuner._fits_all_components_resident`): when the least-free selected GPU has at least twice the per-GPU weight bytes free, every component without an explicit placement stays resident. That means no default layerwise list, no DiT layerwise and component offload cleared, which is the placement `speed` mode gives. Explicit placement flags still win per component.
  - Weights are sized before load from the cached checkpoint's safetensors headers (`checkpoint_component_sizes` in `loader/utils.py`): every `model_index.json` component, counted in its serving precision (`resolve_component_precision`, else as stored), with DiT folders divided by `tp_size`. Text encoders count as full copies even when TP-folded, which is conservative.
  - The tier does not apply, and the per-model policy runs as before, when the checkpoint is not fully cached yet, holds non-safetensors or quantized weights, or is overridden (`--quantization`, `--transformer-weights-path`, SVDQuant, component paths, weights or quantizations, model overlays). It also does not apply with dynamic batching (the factor of two assumes one request's activations), on shared host/device memory (GB10) or on MPS.
  - The rule is platform-agnostic. On ROCm, where auto has no layerwise defaults and offloads the text encoder whole, a GPU that fits the rule now keeps it resident too.
- Wan2.2-T2V/I2V-A14B set `keep_resident_min_available_gb=120` with the DiT and VAE resident. Both experts stay on the GPU on H200-class cards and above; 80 GB cards keep streaming (the two bf16 experts alone are 53 GiB). This holds even when the tier cannot size the checkpoint.

What changes on common GPUs (single GPU unless noted; per-GPU weights at serving precision):

| Model | Weights per GPU | Tier at 2x | H100 80 GB (~79 GiB free) | H200 (~139 GiB free) | 32 GB RTX 5090 (~31 GiB free) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Z-Image-Turbo | 19.1 GiB | 38 GiB | all resident (text encoder was layerwise) | all resident | unchanged |
| FLUX.1-dev | 31.4 GiB | 63 GiB | all resident (T5 was layerwise) | all resident | unchanged |
| Qwen-Image-2.1 | 30.2 GiB | 60 GiB | all resident | all resident | unchanged |
| Qwen-Image | 53.7 GiB (TP2: 34.7) | 107 GiB (TP2: 69) | unchanged (TP2: all resident) | all resident | unchanged |
| Cosmos3-Nano | 32.5 GiB | 65 GiB | all resident | all resident | unchanged |
| Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B | 24.3 GiB (fp32 T5) | 49 GiB | all resident | all resident | unchanged |
| LTX-2 | 65.7 GiB | 131 GiB | unchanged | all resident | unchanged |
| Wan2.2-T2V-A14B | 74.9 GiB (fp32 T5) | 150 GiB | unchanged | both experts and VAE resident (threshold), T5 layerwise | unchanged |
| Ideogram-4 FP8, ModelOpt FP8/NVFP4 | not sized (quantized or `--transformer-path`) | | unchanged | unchanged | unchanged |

B200 (178 GiB free) and B300 (288 GiB) fit every bf16 row, Wan2.2-A14B included. Rows other than Z-Image-Turbo and Wan2.2-A14B follow from the sizing rule; they were not run.

Tests:
- `test_server_args.py`: Z-Image-Turbo keeps every component resident at 139 GiB free and at 45 GiB free (the bf16 serving size fits twice there, the fp32-stored bytes would not). 31 and 23 GiB free resolve exactly as an unsized checkpoint does. Batching, shared host/device memory and an unsized checkpoint keep the text encoder layerwise. Off CUDA, the tier replaces the whole-component text-encoder offload. Wan2.2-A14B keeps both experts and the VAE resident at 139 GiB free while T5 streams, and keeps everything resident at 280 GiB free with sizes.
- `test_weight_utils.py::TestCheckpointComponentSizes`: per-component sizes from a local layout and from a cached hub snapshot without network access; a partially downloaded snapshot (only `model_index.json`, as before the worker downloads), a missing shard, `.bin` weights or FP8 weights stay unsized.
- `conftest.mock_cuda_platform` and the server-args helper stub the sizing, so tests that construct `ServerArgs` for a real repo id never read the runner's HF cache.
- Docs: the `auto` row of the performance-mode table in the deployment cookbook describes the tier.

The new tests fail on main: the sizing helper does not exist there, and the all-resident, serving-precision, off-CUDA and Wan2.2 assertions fail on their own.

## Accuracy Tests

Placement only: the same modules run on the same device, so outputs do not change. On 1xH200, Z-Image-Turbo outputs for five distinct prompts have the same md5s on main and this PR.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Z-Image-Turbo on 1xH200, flagless `sglang serve` (auto mode), 1024x1024, 9 steps. Each run: fresh server, 2 warmup requests, then 5 measured requests, each with a distinct prompt so the conditioning cache never answers the text encoder's work. Rounds interleaved main / PR / main / PR:

| | e2e median (round 1 / round 2) | `TextEncodingStage` | Peak memory per request |
|---|---|---|---|
| main (text encoder layerwise) | 0.952 / 0.954 s | 0.130 s | 15,456 MB |
| this PR (all resident) | 0.867 / 0.863 s | 0.031 s | 22,170 MB |

That is −9% end to end. Every PR sample is below every main sample (0.860–0.872 vs 0.950–1.008 s). The server logs `Auto memory policy for ZImagePipelineConfig: 139.3 GiB free on the least-free selected GPU holds the 19.1 GiB of weights per GPU at least 2x, so every component without an explicit placement stays resident.`

The same PR with all but 30 GiB of the GPU held by another process (the inputs of a 32 GB card) keeps main's placement: text encoder and VAE layerwise, DiT component-offloaded, `TextEncodingStage` 0.130 s.

Earlier evidence for the same gap: H100 Z-Image-Turbo, all resident 0.701/0.699 s vs auto 0.793/0.799 s (−12%).

Wan2.2-T2V-A14B, flagless on 1xH200 (startup only; no timed request): main streams both experts (`transformer` and `transformer_2`: 1.74 GB on the GPU, 26.18 GB pinned on the host each) and the text encoder. This PR loads both experts on the GPU (26.62 GB each) and keeps the VAE resident and the fp32 T5 layerwise, so 52 GB less pinned host memory per rank; the tier itself does not apply (150 GiB needed, 139 free). The end-to-end gain was not measured here.

## CI and baselines

The tier changes placement on the 80 GB H100 lanes wherever the checkpoint is cached and fits twice, so these scenarios will report higher `load_peak_vram_mb` / `runtime_peak_vram_mb` and fail the up-only 1%/2% memory checks by design. Their latency baselines may become stale-high (not a failure). Re-seed them with the usual two-step flow (first run prints the blocks to add to `perf_baselines/h100.json`):
- 1 GPU: `flux_image_t2i`, `zimage_image_t2i`, `zimage_image_t2i_multi_lora`, `cosmos3_nano_t2i`, `cosmos3_nano_t2v` (transformer already pinned resident; the small components join it), `sana_video_2b_t2v`, `longlive2_t2v`, `longlive2_i2v`, `fast_hunyuan_video` (38.5 GiB, 77 of ~79 GiB: closest to the line), `wan2_2_ti2v_5b`, `fastwan2_2_ti2v_5b`, `turbo_wan2_1_t2v_1.3b`, and the Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B family (`wan2_1_t2v_1.3b`, `_teacache_enabled`, `_frame_interp_2x`, `_upscaling_4x`, `_frame_interp_2x_upscaling_4x`, `wan2_1_t2v_1_3b_lora_1gpu`).
- 2 GPUs: `flux_image_t2i_2_gpus`, `zimage_image_t2i_2_gpus`, `zimage_image_t2i_2_gpus_non_square`, `qwen_image21_t2i_tp2`, `wan2_1_t2v_1.3b_cfg_parallel`, `wan2_1_t2v_1_3b_cache_dit_sp_only_2gpu`, `fsdp-inference`.
- `wan2_1_t2v_1.3b_encoder_permanent_residents` exists to test a permanent layerwise resident set on the text encoder, so it now pins the encoder layerwise with `--component-residency text_encoder=layerwise-offload`.
- Unchanged: the 5090 lane (nothing fits twice in ~31 GiB), every quantized or `--transformer-path` case, cases with explicit placement of the components that would move, Wan2.2-A14B, Qwen-Image 1-GPU, LTX and MiniMax-H3 on H100. The B200 lane runs only ModelOpt cases with `--transformer-path`/quantized weights.

The list comes from sizing each case's checkpoint at its serving precision against ~79 GiB free; a runner whose HF cache misses a model keeps main's placement for it.

## Risks

- Steady VRAM grows by the components that used to stream (Z-Image-Turbo +6.7 GB peak, the LTX-2 text encoder on H200, ~53 GiB of Wan2.2-A14B experts on H200). The factor of two leaves at least the weights' size free for activations, assuming one request at a time.
- A checkpoint that is not cached at startup is not sized, so a first start can place components differently from later ones. That is the same placement as main, never more resident.
- `ServerArgs` now reads safetensors headers of a cached checkpoint at startup (local files only, no network).

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).
- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).
- [x] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations).
- [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed).

title: [Perf] mhc: Split hc_combine_norm_mxfp8 rows by batch size and zero padding scales in the kernel
author: akhilg-nv
body:
[by Claude Code]

## Motivation

`hc_combine_norm_mxfp8` is the DeepSeek-V4.1 mHC kernel that builds the attention input on Blackwell: it combines the
four residual streams weighted by `pre` (the per-row weights of the four streams), applies RMSNorm, and writes the
result in BF16 and in MXFP8 for `wqkv_a`. It runs when the batch has at most 128 rows, and only where the previous
mHC post has not already built that input (the fused MoE all-reduce epilogue at TP2/TP4 and Mega-mHC do), so with DP
attention and Mega-mHC off, as in every published DEP recipe, it runs before 39 of the 40 attention layers of each
decode step of up to 128 tokens per rank. It had two fixed costs. It always ran 4 CTAs per row, and each of them
recomputed the whole row (the combine and the RMS statistic) to store a quarter of it; that split was chosen when the
kernel took at most 8 rows, and #42245 raised the limit to 128 rows without revisiting it. And its MXFP8 scale buffer
came from `torch.zeros`, a separate fill kernel before every call (the scales of the rows past the batch are padding
of a 128-row scale tile and must be zero). This PR picks the split by row count, as `hc_combine_norm` in the same
file already does, and zeroes the padding scales inside the kernel. The outputs are bitwise identical: every CTA still
computes the whole row in the same order, and the split only decides which CTA stores which columns.

- **Accuracy:** bitwise identical to the previous kernel on B200, B300 and VR200 (3,082-3,850 cases per GPU, 0
  mismatches). GSM8K under AgentX load on B200: 97.67% without this PR, 96.33% with it (exact McNemar p = 0.29).
- **Kernel:** 41-46% faster on average at 49-128 rows (B200 6.24 → 3.40 us, B300 5.63 → 3.20 us, VR200 4.56 →
  2.68 us) and 20-26% faster at 1-32 rows, measured alone; the fill kernel before every call is gone.
- **End to end: no measurable change.** DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on 4x B200, the published InferenceX AgentX DEP4 c192
  cell (where this kernel runs on the most decode steps at the most rows), real speculative acceptance, 2 ABBA pairs on
  one node: per-request decode time per token −0.32% (95% interval −0.56% to +0.02%), inside the run-to-run noise of
  the same configuration (0.6-1.1%); output throughput per GPU −0.01% and −0.12%.
- **Why the kernel saving does not reach the step on B200:** in decode the combine runs at the same time as the mHC
  statistics of the same residual on a side stream (on SM100, two DeepGEMM TF32 GEMMs from 32 rows up, a Triton kernel
  below). Next to them the new kernel is not faster: with the DeepGEMM statistics beside it, a combine + GEMM
  iteration takes 19.82 us before and 21.89 us after this PR (mean over 48-120 rows, microbenchmark), and in the
  serving profile the next GEMM did not start earlier.
- **End to end (estimate, not measured):** counting the per-call saving as if the combine were on the critical path,
  a B200 DEP4 c64 profile (decode at 24-30 rows) gives 39 calls x 2.45 us = 96 us per 11.5 ms decode step, about
  0.8%. The measurement above and the side-stream overlap show that this upper bound is not reached.

## Modifications

**+41 / −25 runtime code (1 file), +74 / −1 tests (1 file).** A Triton kernel change; no new flags, no default
changes.

In `python/sglang/kernels/ops/layernorm/hc_combine_norm.py`:

- `_parts_for(m, k)` uses the same split as `hc_combine_norm`: 4 CTAs per row up to 8 rows, 2 up to 48 rows, and 1
  above that. Up to 8 rows the split is unchanged.
- The scale buffer is allocated with `torch.empty`. Extra programs after the last row zero the padding, as
  `rmsnorm_mxfp8` already does: each takes one 512-byte block of the scale buffer and zeroes the bytes of the rows
  past the batch. At hidden 5120 that is 40 extra programs; at 128 rows there is no padding and none run.
- The kernel takes the row count `M` as an argument. The per-row body is unchanged, now under `if row < M`.

**Related:** draft #41628 by @harmya contains the same row split inside a larger change (it raises the fusion batch
limits and keeps `torch.zeros`). This PR carries the split on its own, plus the in-kernel zeroing.

Tests, in `test/registered/kernels/ops/layernorm/test_mxfp8_epilogue.py`:

- The existing bitwise test against `hc_combine_norm` followed by FlashInfer `mxfp8_quantize` (cuda and cute-dsl
  backends) adds rows 48 and 49 (either side of a split threshold), 84 and 120.
- New `test_combine_norm_mxfp8_split_invariant`: with the split forced to 1, 2 and 4, the outputs equal the default
  split byte for byte, both eagerly and on a CUDA-graph replay whose outputs were first filled with `0xFF`.
- New `test_combine_norm_mxfp8_padding_disjoint_from_live_rows`: on the GPU, a padding program that also overwrote a
  live row's scales would go unnoticed, because the live row stores its scales last (on B200 even the largest grid,
  520 CTAs, runs in one wave). The test runs the kernel in Triton's interpreter (`TRITON_INTERPRET=1`, in a
  subprocess, on CPU), which runs the programs one at a time in grid order, over a scale buffer filled with `0xFF`,
  for 1, 49 and 127 rows and splits 1, 2 and 4. It checks that every byte gets written and that exactly 160 bytes per
  live row are non-zero. It takes about 20 s.

## Accuracy Tests

**The kernel's outputs are bitwise identical to the previous kernel's:**

| Check | B200 | B300 | VR200 (SM107) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `test_mxfp8_epilogue.py` | 107 passed, 0 skipped (this branch) | 106 passed, 0 skipped (before the interpreter test) | 106 passed, 0 skipped (before the interpreter test) |
| Byte-for-byte against the previous kernel (BF16 output, FP8 values, scales) | 3,850 cases, 0 mismatches (re-run: 3,082 / 0) | 3,082 cases, 0 mismatches | 3,850 cases, 0 mismatches |

- The byte-for-byte check covers every row count from 1 to 128, input scales 1e-3 / 1 / 1e3, BF16 and FP32 `pre`,
  the split forced to 1 / 2 / 4, and 10 CUDA-graph replays over `0xFF`-filled outputs. The 3,850-case runs add 768
  cases for a benchmark-only variant that is not part of this PR.
- CI runs this file on B200 (`base-b-kernel-unit`). Hopper and ROCm never reach this kernel: the caller takes it only
  on Blackwell with MXFP8 output and hidden size 5120.

**Do the tests catch a broken padding program?** Each row is this PR's kernel with one deliberate change, on one B200:

| Kernel change | GPU tests (before the interpreter test) | Interpreter test |
|---|---|---|
| Drop the padding branch, keep `torch.empty` | 76 of 106 fail | fails: "scale bytes unwritten" |
| Padding mask `pad_row >= M - 1` (also zeroes the last live row) | **all 106 pass**; 0 bad calls in 480 poisoned-buffer GPU calls | fails: "160 live bytes zeroed" |
| Padding block index without `* tl.num_programs(1)` | 49 of 106 fail | fails: "scale bytes unwritten" |
| The previous kernel (scales zeroed by `torch.zeros`), default split | - | fails: "scale bytes unwritten" |

**GSM8K under load**, on the end-to-end setup below (runs B2 and A2): 60 s into a second AgentX run on the same
server (concurrency 192, 300 s window), `sgl-eval run gsm8k` (sgl-eval 0.1.3, 300 questions, 16 threads, temperature
1.0, top_p 0.95, max tokens 16384, seed 0; thinking on through the server's `SGLANG_DEFAULT_THINKING=1`):

| | GSM8K-300 | Errors | AgentX load during the eval |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Without this PR | 97.67% (293/300) | 0 | 1,300 requests, 0 errors |
| With this PR | 96.33% (289/300) | 0 | 1,301 requests, 0 errors |

- The arms answered 8 questions differently: 6 right only without this PR, 2 only with it (exact McNemar p = 0.29).
  The kernel's outputs are bitwise identical, so the difference is sampling at temperature 1.0 in batches whose
  composition differs between runs.
- One answer with this PR hit the 16,384-token limit: a coherent, long deliberation over an ambiguous question that
  the run without this PR also answered wrongly, after 7,441 tokens.
- Speculative accept length (real acceptance, rank 0, profiling window): 3.464 and 3.355 without this PR, 3.386 and
  3.396 with it.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

**Microbenchmark**, one GPU, CUDA graphs. Inputs: BF16 `x` of shape [m, 4 x 5120] and FP32 `pre`. Times are per call
in us: the median of 7 repetitions, each 100 replays of a graph of 20 calls (hot L2 on purpose: the inputs are at most
5.2 MB, and in serving the kernel reads residual streams that the previous sublayer wrote just before).

| rows | B200 | B300 | VR200 (SM107) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3.89 -> 2.87 | 3.38 -> 2.67 | 3.20 -> 2.46 |
| 32 | 4.01 -> 3.08 | 3.59 -> 2.87 | 3.45 -> 2.59 |
| 64 | 5.12 -> 3.28 | 4.51 -> 3.17 | 4.28 -> 2.65 |
| 96 | 6.18 -> 3.38 | 5.63 -> 3.18 | 4.32 -> 2.68 |
| 128 | 7.08 -> 3.48 | 6.46 -> 3.28 | 5.21 -> 2.71 |
| mean of 49, 64, 84, 96, 100, 112, 120, 128 rows | 6.24 -> 3.40 (-46%) | 5.63 -> 3.20 (-43%) | 4.56 -> 2.68 (-41%) |

- Every timed row count got faster: 17 row counts from 1 to 128 (14 on B300). At 1-32 rows each is 20-26% faster.
- Above 48 rows, the two parts of the change save, per call (means over 49-128 rows): the new split alone (the old
  kernel with only the split changed) 1.90 / 1.74 / 1.13 us on B200 / B300 / VR200, and removing the fill alone (the
  new kernel forced to 4 CTAs per row) 1.02 / 0.65 / 0.53 us. Up to 8 rows the split is unchanged; the 0.7-1.0 us
  saved there is the fill.

**Next to the side stream (B200).** In decode, `deepseek_v4_mhc` forks the mHC statistics of the same residual onto
a side stream right before the combine. On SM100 with at least 32 rows they are `hc_mix_stats_sinkhorn_deepgemm` (two
DeepGEMM `tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm` calls and a Sinkhorn kernel); below 32 rows, and where DeepGEMM's prenorm is off, the
Triton `hc_mix_stats_sinkhorn`. Per iteration: fork; side stream the statistics; main stream the combine, then a
stand-in for `wqkv_a` (BF16 GEMM [m, 5120] x [5120, 2048]); join. Mean us per iteration over 48, 60, 72, 84, 96, 108
and 120 rows (each the median of 7 repetitions), outputs checked byte for byte:

| Layout | Before | This PR | This PR, split forced to 4 | This PR, split forced to 2 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Combine alone | 5.48 | 3.24 | 5.03 | 3.73 |
| Combine + GEMM, no side stream | 13.90 | 11.67 | 13.48 | 12.19 |
| + DeepGEMM statistics on the side stream (the SM100 serving path) | 19.82 | 21.89 | 21.20 | 22.09 |
| + Triton statistics on the side stream | 27.04 | 22.66 | 25.84 | 23.80 |

- With the DeepGEMM statistics beside it, this PR is about equal at 48 and 60 rows (18.86 → 18.42, 19.14 → 18.79 us)
  and slower from 72 rows, by 1.3 to 4.0 us per iteration. Without the fill kernel, the combine starts as soon as the
  statistics do and competes with them for SMs; the variant that keeps 4 CTAs per row and drops only the fill is
  slower than before as well.

**In the server (B200 DEP4 c192, GPU profile of 80 steps on all ranks, one run per arm, profiler on):**

- Every target-verify decode graph holds 39 calls of this kernel in both arms. Before this PR every call (12,168 of
  12,168) directly follows the fill kernel; with it, none do.
- At 60 rows, at 37 of the 39 layers both kernels run entirely beside the side-stream DeepGEMM GEMMs. The old path
  takes 1.31 us (fill) + 0.48 us (gap) + 4.38 us (kernel), medians over all calls and ranks; the new kernel takes
  7.0 us (median; 3.2 us alone in the microbenchmark, and 4.1 us at the other two layers, where the GEMMs overlap it
  for only about 2 us). At 18-30 rows (Triton statistics) the new kernel takes 3.8 us, and the old path 6.2 us from
  the start of the fill to the end of the kernel (4.6 us of it the kernel): 2.45 us more per call, the figure the
  estimate above uses.
- The time from the end of the mHC post to the start of the `wqkv_a` GEMM was not shorter with this PR: 6.85 → 7.68
  us at 60 rows, 6.9-7.4 → 8.6-10.7 us at 18-30 rows. In both cases the GEMM waits for SMs held by the side-stream
  statistics, which start later relative to the combine once the fill is gone.

**End to end on B200.**

- Setup: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, 4x B200 on one node, the published InferenceX AgentX DEP4 c192 cell (command below),
  image `lmsysorg/sglang:nightly-dev-cu13-20261021-c1c287a4`, whose `hc_combine_norm.py` is byte-identical to this
  PR's base and to current main. "With this PR" is the same image with this PR's `hc_combine_norm.py` mounted over it;
  each run checks the md5 of the file Python imports before any traffic. One change from the published cell: real
  speculative acceptance (the published runs set a simulated acceptance length).
- Why c192: the kernel runs only when a rank's decode batch is at most 120 rows (a CUDA-graph batch of at most 20
  requests x 6 verify tokens with DSpark block size 5; the next graph size, 22, is 132 rows). In the published B200
  DEP4 runs (InferenceX run 39606211010, server logs) the busiest rank decodes a median of 5 requests at c64, 10 at
  c128, 16 at c192 and 26 at c256. In our c192 windows 62% of the decode log samples ran the kernel, 41% at 49-120
  rows.
- Runs: without, with, with, without this PR, fresh server per run; AgentX (agentx-harness 1.0.12, the published
  trace set, concurrency 192, 900 s profiling window after its warm-up).
- Rule, fixed before the runs: a change counts only if the 95% interval of the pooled per-request ratio excludes 0,
  both pairs agree in sign, and the pooled change is larger than both same-arm repeat differences.

| | Without (A1) | With (B1) | With (B2) | Without (A2) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Output tok/s/GPU (InferenceX scorer) | 1,808.7 | 1,808.6 | 1,806.0 | 1,808.1 |
| p90 interactivity (1000 / p90 ITL) | 104.19 | 103.04 | 103.60 | 102.35 |
| TTFT p50 / p90 (s) | 1.10 / 2.31 | 1.10 / 2.39 | 1.09 / 2.31 | 1.10 / 2.39 |
| Requests / errors | 6,936 / 0 | 6,912 / 0 | 6,924 / 0 | 6,902 / 0 |
| Accept length (rank 0) | 3.464 | 3.386 | 3.396 | 3.355 |

Per-request decode time per token ((latency − TTFT) / (output tokens − 1)), median of the per-request ratio over the
6,648 requests present in all four runs (AgentX replays the trace set in a fixed order; output lengths are equal):

| | B1 / A1 | B2 / A2 | Pooled with / without | A2 / A1 (same arm) | B2 / B1 (same arm) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Change (95% bootstrap interval) | +0.26% (−0.07, +0.66) | −0.89% (−1.29, −0.51) | −0.32% (−0.56, +0.02) | +0.59% | −1.10% |

**Result: no measurable change.** The pooled interval includes 0, the two pairs disagree in sign, and the pooled
change is smaller than the same-arm differences. Output tok/s/GPU changes by −0.01% and −0.12% (same-arm: −0.04%,
−0.14%), p90 interactivity by −1.11% and +1.22% (same-arm: −1.76%, +0.55%).

title: [Perf] diffusion/registry: Reduce model discovery work at startup
author: mickqian
body:
## Summary

Model discovery parses every component file and walks every expression in each model's forward implementation, although registration only needs class and assignment statements.

- Skip parsing helper files without `EntryClass`.
- Skip expression subtrees while preserving breadth-first declaration and alias ordering, including nested statements.
- Flatten the registration branches without changing the supported entry formats.

No new runtime flag, persistent cache, production file, or model import. Pipeline discovery and external-package registration keep their existing behavior. This is separate from the CLI backend-detection work in #43317.

## Validation

Compared main `4b273537dec5` with `41558c352e38` on a dedicated two-H200 environment: Xeon Platinum 8558P, approximately 2 TiB host RAM, Python 3.12.15, PyTorch 2.14.1+cu130, Diffusers 0.37.0, Transformers 5.19.0.

| Measurement | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Registry discovery, 20 interleaved samples, median | 664 ms | 377 ms |
| Single-GPU process start to HTTP readiness, 3 paired samples, median | 30.26 s | 29.39 s |
| Ulysses2 process start to HTTP readiness, 3 paired samples, median | 30.02 s | 29.61 s |

The complete mapping of **110 models and 18 aliases** is unchanged. Discovery is faster by about 43%; that is not a 43% server-startup improvement.

The 12 real server launches use `Wan-AI/Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B-Diffusers`, cached checkpoint revision `0fad780a534b6463e45facd96134c9f345acfa5b`, offline Hub access, `--warmup-mode off`, and otherwise unchanged defaults. Each launch completes 4-step and 24-step requests at 512x320, 17 frames, seed 42; all 24 outputs were downloaded and decoded. Decoded-frame hashes match before/after within each GPU configuration. No live child processes remain after shutdown.

Startup measurements exclude model download and warmup. They are bounded measurements of this configuration, not a general speedup guarantee; first-request JIT time is not included or claimed as an improvement.

24 tests passed across `test_registry.py`, `test_external_model_package.py`, and `test_plain_component_loader.py`. Added coverage preserves nested declarations, aliases, and single/list/tuple entry formats without importing optional model dependencies. Pre-commit passed.

Production diff: one existing file, +50/-52; tests: +27 lines. No user-facing API or command changes, so no documentation update is needed.

title: [Perf] diffusion: Route dense attention with a sub-tile side to FA4 on Blackwell
author: mickqian
body:
Branch: mick/blackwell-sub-tile-attention-fa4 (on main 02b983603d), commit cfecddc185

## Motivation

`DYNAMIC_CUDNN_SDPA` sends every dense non-causal attention on sm_10x to cuDNN. When one side is shorter than one 128-row tile and the other is not, cuDNN falls back to `cudnn_generated_fort_native_sdpa_sm80_flash_fprop_wmma`. FA4 is 2-3x faster on those shapes. LTX-2's audio stream has 126 tokens, so audio-prompt, audio-to-video and video-to-audio attention hit this in every block (4 of the 6 attention calls per block in the LTX-2 stage-1 profile).

B300, bf16, no mask, B=1 (B=2 behaves the same):

| q x kv (heads x dim) | cuDNN | FA4 |
|---|---|---|
| 126 x 1024 (32x64) | 17.6 us | 9.5 us |
| 1536 x 126 (32x64) | 13.2 us | 7.5 us |
| 126 x 1536 (32x64) | 24.4 us | 11.6 us |
| 6144 x 126 (16x128) | 35.6 us | 11.7 us |
| 126 x 6144 (16x128) | 84.9 us | 35.3 us |
| 192 x 6144 (32x64) | 32.0 us | 55.6 us |
| 1536 x 1536 (32x128) | 34.7 us | 35.5 us |
| 126 x 126 (32x64) | 6.0 us | 5.6 us |

At 192 tokens and above cuDNN is already on its sm_100 kernels and equal or faster, and with both sides short the two tie.

## Modifications

`layers/attention/backends/sdpa.py`: on sm_10x, `DynamicCudnnSDPAImpl` keeps cuDNN unless exactly one side is shorter than 128 tokens. Those calls go to the FA4 path the backend already holds as its fallback.

Both kernels compute exact softmax attention; only the rounding order changes.

## Tests

`test_dynamic_cudnn_sdpa_routing.py`: both sides at or above a tile, including 192 x 6144, keep cuDNN; one side under a tile routes to FA4; both short keeps cuDNN.

## Accuracy Tests

4xB300 (2 GPUs), LTX-2 two-stage 768x512x121, CFG parallel + BCG, 4 prompts: PSNR against the cuDNN run 16.0 / 19.5 / 23.1 / 14.9 dB.

Reference band for a rounding-only change on this workload: the same server with `quality="exact"` against the default `lossless` (which already mounts other rounding-moving fusions) gives LTX-2 PSNR 17.0 / 20.6 / 23.1 / 20.8 dB and LTX-2.3 18.1 / 19.3 / 17.6 / 20.4 dB over the same four prompts. The 40-step CFG trajectory amplifies any rounding difference to that level, so the e2e number shows only that the change stays inside the band every rounding change lands in.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

LTX-2 stage-1 attention per block drops from 180 us to about 100 us together with the prompt-mask PR. Stage-1 steps go from 51.5 ms to 48.5 ms for the two PRs together (synced stage timing). LTX-2.3 uses the same audio attention shapes at batch 2.

title: [Perf] diffusion: Prefer FA4 over cuDNN SDPA for long self-attention on B300
author: mickqian
body:
Branch: mick/diffusion-sm103-fa4-long-self-attn (on main efd2ce8a9d), commit 638be52100

## Motivation

`DYNAMIC_CUDNN_SDPA` sends every dense non-causal call on sm_10x to cuDNN SDPA, a choice measured on B200 ("cuDNN SDPA measured 1.25-1.5x faster than FA4 CuTe"). On B300 (sm_103) FA4 uses the hardware exp2 path and the `tcgen05.ld.red` row max, and long video self-attention is where diffusion models spend most of their step (Wan2.2 A14B 720p: ~67% of a denoising step).

A video DiT on B300 runs at the 1100 W power cap for the whole denoise, so kernels were timed under sustained load (2 s warm-up to the cap, then 2-6 s of back-to-back calls), bf16, B=1 unless noted:

| q x kv, heads x dim | cuDNN | FA4 | FA4/cuDNN |
|---|---|---|---|
| 75600 x 75600, 4 x 128 | 7.411 ms | 7.259 ms | 0.979 |
| 75600 x 75600, 20 x 128 | 36.901 ms | 36.360 ms | 0.985 |
| 37800 x 37800, 10 x 128 | 4.635 ms | 4.549 ms | 0.981 |
| 32760 x 32760, 12 x 128 | 4.281 ms | 4.214 ms | 0.984 |
| 16384 x 16384, 24 x 128 | 2.155 ms | 2.139 ms | 0.993 |
| 8192 x 8192, 24 x 128 | 0.575 ms | 0.577 ms | 1.003 |
| 4608 x 4608, 24 x 128 | 0.185 ms | 0.186 ms | 1.006 |
| 4352 x 4352, 24 x 128, B=2 | 0.338 ms | 0.338 ms | 1.000 |
| 37800 x 512, 40 x 128 | 0.350 ms | 0.338 ms | 0.964 |
| 18900 x 18900, 24 x 64 | 1.928 ms | 2.076 ms | 1.077 |
| 4096 x 4096, 24 x 64 | 0.108 ms | 0.120 ms | 1.114 |

FA4's sm_103 tuning knobs (softmax/correction registers, exp2 emulation, row-max reduction, 2-CTA) were swept at the Wan shape; the defaults are the best of them.

## Modifications

`layers/attention/backends/sdpa.py`: on sm_103, `DynamicCudnnSDPAImpl` takes FA4 for self-attention (`Sq == Skv`) with head_dim 128 and at least 16384 tokens. B200 (sm_100), cross-attention, shorter sequences and head_dim 64 keep cuDNN.

Both are exact softmax attention in bf16 with fp32 accumulation; only the rounding order changes (max |diff| 2.4e-4 on unit-scale inputs).

This touches the same function as "Route dense attention with a sub-tile side to FA4 on Blackwell"; the two conditions are independent and rebase trivially.

## Accuracy Tests

- `test_dynamic_cudnn_sdpa_selection.py`: sm_103 routes 16K and 75.6K self-attention to FA4; 8K, 512-key cross-attention and head_dim 64 stay on cuDNN; sm_100 stays on cuDNN at 75.6K.
- Wan2.2 T2V A14B 720p, 4xB300, same prompts and seeds, video at x264 crf 0, against cuDNN (with the other, bit-identical B300 Wan changes and a 63 dB VAE change in the build): PSNR 27.5 / 22.4 dB, SSIM 0.989 / 0.965 on two prompts. Same scene and composition; the 40-step trajectories drift apart as with any change of rounding order (the subject's pose differs by the last frame).

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Wan2.2 T2V A14B 720p, 81 frames, 40 steps, 4xB300, CFG 2 x Ulysses 2, eager. Attention per block (5 head groups of 4 heads): 38.1 -> 36.8 ms. E2E with the Ulysses pipeline fix: main 92.83 / 92.61 s -> 91.23-91.44 s (6 requests, median 91.34 s). On an older main with NCCL all-to-all, `--attention-backend fa` measured 95.75 s against 97.08 s for the default selection.

title: [Perf] diffusion: Speed up Wan's spatial-parallel VAE decode
author: mickqian
body:
Branch: mick/wan-vae-parallel-decode-fast-path (on main efd2ce8a9d), commits 6e09543c4f, 93ccc5dc4f

## Motivation

Multi-GPU Wan decode shards the frame height across ranks (`WanDistResidualBlock`, `SpatialParallelCausalConv3d` with halo exchange). That decoder never got the CUDA fast path ("Wan VAE: spatial-parallel decode; skipping fast path."), and its Conv3d weights stayed NCDHW because the channels_last_3d policy only covers `num_gpus == 1`. In the decode profile of Wan2.2 T2V A14B 720p on 4xB300 (fp32 decode, 1.32 s): cuDNN's own `nchwToNhwc` / `nhwcToNchw` conversions around every conv took 111 ms, the unfused RMSNorm + SiLU chains (`BinaryFunctor`, `silu`, `norm`, adds) ~250 ms, and 4114 `direct_copy` kernels 149 ms.

The spatial-parallel blocks only swap in halo-exchanging convs; the halo exchange slices and concatenates along height, which works in either memory layout.

The mid-block attention gathers the full frame height on every rank and attended every query row of it (21 fp32 `fmha_cutlassF` calls, 143 ms per decode), then kept only its own rows.

## Modifications

- `models/vaes/wan_vae_cuda_opt.py`: the installer accepts the spatial-parallel residual block, resample and attention block classes (`residual_block_cls` is now a tuple of classes) and no longer skips parallel decode.
- `loader/component_loaders/vae_loader.py`: Wan configs convert the VAE's Conv3d weights to channels_last_3d at any GPU count (LTX-2 and Cosmos3 keep the one-GPU rule). On more than one GPU the automatic policy converts the decoder only: cuDNN's TF32 convs round differently in channels_last, and an I2V condition latent that differs by ~3e-3 sends a 40-step 14B trajectory elsewhere (the 2-GPU Wan I2V consistency cases fell to 14-24 dB on the last frame). An explicit `SGLANG_DIFFUSION_VAE_CHANNELS_LAST_3D=1` still converts the whole VAE, as before.
- `models/vaes/wanvae.py`: under spatial-parallel decode each rank attends only its own height shard's query rows (the `tensor_split` chunk the output was cut to) against the whole frame's keys and values.

The fast path is the existing "lossless" quality tier (fp32 ops re-associated, nothing lowered); `quality="exact"` requests still run the reference ops.

## Accuracy Tests

- Wan2.2 T2V A14B 720p, 4xB300, same latents, video saved at x264 crf 0: PSNR 63.2 dB, SSIM 0.99999, max |diff| 4/255, mean |diff| 0.02 against the decode without this change (three requests). No seams at the shard boundaries (rows 180/360/540).
- Row-sharded attention: decoded video byte-identical (mp4 md5 at crf 0, three requests).
- Encoder: with the decoder-only rule, Wan2.1-I2V-14B on 2 GPUs encodes bit-identically to main; with `quality="exact"` (and the decoder's channels_last off) the output mp4 md5 equals main's. The 2-GPU Wan I2V consistency cases pass again (wan2_1_i2v_14b_480P 34.6/37.9/37.5 dB, wan2_1_i2v_14b_720P 36.2/35.9/35.3 dB, wan2_2_i2v_a14b 38.4/36.7/35.5 dB); the Animate cfg-parallel case is bitwise to its GT. Decode on 2 GPUs: main 372 ms, decoder-only 277-283 ms (the encoder no longer gets channels_last's ~8% encode speedup).
- `test_vae_loader.py`: the channels_last_3d policy covers multi-GPU Wan; `test_model_fast_paths.py` passes with the tuple form (33 Wan/Qwen cases); `test_wan_vae_attention_rows.py`: a row range equals those rows of the full-frame block output.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Decode stage with synchronized stage timers, Wan2.2 T2V A14B 720p, 4xB300, fp32 decode (three requests each): 1.284 / 1.266 / 1.269 s -> fast path 1.042 / 1.000 / 1.000 s -> + row-sharded attention 0.972 / 0.942 / 0.938 s (same build without it in the same session: 1.038 / 1.004 / 1.005 s).

title: [Perf] batch-invariant: Fused residual add + RMSNorm kernel
author: aarnetalman
body:
## Motivation

In deterministic mode, RMSNorm with a residual add (both norms in every decoder layer) falls back to eager PyTorch, which takes about ten kernel launches instead of a single fused kernel. This PR adds a fused, batch-invariant add+RMSNorm kernel for that path. It applies to any model whose decoder layers use `RMSNorm` with a residual (Llama, Mistral, Qwen2/3, Qwen3-MoE, Phi, DeepSeek, gpt-oss and most others). Tested on MI350X with Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-30B-A3B and Phi-4: single-request decode throughput with the fused kernel is 56-73% higher and 12-22% higher at concurrency 16, and every determinism check passes on Qwen3-8B (TP1, TP2) and Qwen3-30B-A3B.

The fallback is a large share of deterministic decode time. Profile of a single-request decode (1k-token prompt, 256 output tokens, CUDA graphs off) in deterministic mode on MI350X:

| model | GPU time, deterministic | GPU time, normal mode | eager add+RMSNorm fallback |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen3-8B | 603 ms | 323 ms | about 205 ms (34%) |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B | 678 ms | 298 ms | about 215 ms (32%) |
| Phi-4 | 902 ms | 474 ms | about 205 ms (22%) |

In normal mode the same norms take 12.6 ms on Qwen3-8B as one fused kernel.

Scope: deterministic mode only, on every platform that runs the batch-invariant Triton kernels. The new kernel uses the same float32 math as `forward_native`. Models that use `GemmaRMSNorm` (Gemma, Qwen3-Next/3.5/3.8) take a different path and are not affected. Normal mode is unchanged.

## Modifications

- `batch_invariant_ops.py`: new `_fused_add_rms_norm_kernel` and `fused_add_rms_norm_batch_invariant`, next to the existing `rms_norm` kernel and in the same style. One program per row:
  - adds the residual (and the optional post-residual addend) to the input in float32;
  - stores the sum as the new residual, in the input's dtype or float32 (`fp32_residual`);
  - RMS-normalizes the float32 sum and applies the weight.

  The reduction runs over one row with a fixed block size, so a row's result does not depend on the batch.
- `layernorm.py`: in the batch-invariant branches of `RMSNorm.forward_cuda`, `forward_aiter`, `forward_hip` and `forward_xpu`, calls with a residual use the new kernel where `forward_native`'s math applies. These cases keep falling back to `forward_native` as before:
  - `cast_x_before_out_mul`;
  - a variance-size override;
  - a padded output;
  - the FSDP RL target.
- New `test/registered/unit/batch_invariant_ops/test_fused_add_rms_norm_batch_invariant.py` (per-PR, CUDA and MI35x):
  - every row's output and new residual are bit-identical (`torch.equal`) when computed in batches of 1, 3, 17 and 64;
  - the new residual equals the eager float32 sum exactly, and the output matches the eager path within rounding;
  - covered: hidden sizes 2048/4096/5120/2880, bf16 and fp16, with and without the addend, `fp32_residual` on and off.
- Unchanged: normal mode; batch-invariant calls without a residual; the fallback cases above.

## Accuracy Tests

MI350X, ROCm 7.2.4, `rocm/sgl-dev:v0.5.22-rocm724-mi35x-20261021`.

Unit tests:

```bash
python3 -m pytest -q test/registered/unit/batch_invariant_ops/test_fused_add_rms_norm_batch_invariant.py test/registered/unit/batch_invariant_ops/test_batch_invariant_ops.py
```

```
7 passed, 1 skipped, 86 subtests passed in 16.00s
```

End to end, Qwen3-8B TP1, deterministic mode with AITER prefill and decode attention. These runs use the open MI350X deterministic-mode PRs (#43788, #44045, #44438, #44489, #45599, #45601, #34543), which is the configuration that deterministic mode runs in on MI350X today; "before" is the same tree without this change:

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-8B --enable-deterministic-inference \
  --attention-backend triton --prefill-attention-backend aiter --decode-attention-backend aiter
python3 -m sglang.test.test_deterministic --test-mode {single,prefix,radix_cache} --n-trials 50
```

With this change, Qwen3-8B: `single` 1 output, `prefix` 1/1/1/1 (twice), `prefix --return-logprob` identical, `radix_cache` pass, and a bitwise batch-size check (the same prompt in batches of 1 to 50, 1,275 responses, token IDs and logprobs compared exactly with the batch-size-1 response) 1,275 / 1,275. Qwen3-30B-A3B (same setup): `single` 1, `prefix` 1/1/1/1, bitwise 1,275 / 1,275. Qwen3-8B at TP2: `single` 1, `prefix` 1/1/1/1, bitwise 1,275 / 1,275.

GSM8K (sgl-eval 0.1.2, `--temperature 0 --max-tokens 2048`, all 1,319 questions, Qwen3-8B, deterministic): 93.18% with this change (before: 93.25% deterministic, 93.48% normal mode, same image).

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Deterministic mode (setup above, CUDA graphs on), before vs after on the same node and image, `python3 -m sglang.benchmark.serving --backend sglang --dataset-name random --random-range-ratio 1.0 --request-rate inf --max-concurrency C` (output throughput, median inter-token latency):

| model | workload | before | after | change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen3-8B | 1k in / 256 out, concurrency 1 | 105 tok/s, 9.42 ms | 173 tok/s, 5.64 ms | +65%, ITL -40% |
| Qwen3-8B | 1k / 256, concurrency 16 | 1,663 tok/s, 7.70 ms | 2,033 tok/s, 6.14 ms | +22%, ITL -20% |
| Qwen3-8B | 8k / 256, concurrency 16 | 582 tok/s, 10.71 ms | 653 tok/s, 9.11 ms | +12%, ITL -15% |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B | 1k / 256, concurrency 1 | 94 tok/s, 10.5 ms | 163 tok/s, 6.0 ms | +73%, ITL -43% |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B | 1k / 256, concurrency 16 | 1,070 tok/s, 13.55 ms | 1,282 tok/s, 11.18 ms | +20%, ITL -17% |
| Phi-4 | 1k / 256, concurrency 1 | 72 tok/s, 13.74 ms | 112 tok/s, 8.70 ms | +56%, ITL -37% |

A second alternating round for Qwen3-8B gives the same numbers within 1% (before 105 tok/s / 9.40 ms and 1,655 tok/s / 7.75 ms; after 174 tok/s / 5.64 ms and 2,036 tok/s / 6.11 ms).

For reference, normal mode on the same setup has an inter-token latency of 4.8 ms (Qwen3-8B) and 4.4 ms (Qwen3-30B-A3B) at concurrency 1, so this closes most of the deterministic-mode gap for single-request decode. No change outside deterministic mode.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).
- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).
- [ ] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations).

title: [Perf] mamba: write the deduplicated conv verify window as one tile
author: jianc99
body:
This is component 1 of the DFlash adaptive-verification series. Original implementation and component-only review: https://github.com/jianc99/sglang/pull/1. Integration and full-system results: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/46182.

Updated onto upstream `main` (6a319e7b). All applicable pre-commit checks passed on this branch. The GPU tests and benchmark results below were run previously on the original source branch; they have not been rerun after this upstream update. Submission preparation used AI assistance.

---

## Motivation

On hybrid models, linear-chain speculative verify (EAGLE chain, MTP, DFLASH, DSPARK, standalone) calls `causal_conv1d_update` with an intermediate conv window. The window lets the conv state of the accepted prefix be restored after verify.

On CUDA and ROCm, `MambaPool` stores this window deduplicated. Each slot holds one `[dim, T + K - 2]` row, exposed as an overlapping `[T, dim, K - 1]` view whose step stride equals its window stride.

The kernel still writes the window per token, with three lane-strided element stores per draft token. Each column is therefore written up to three times by narrow scattered stores. On GB300 (dim 10240, bf16, T = 8, bs 128), the verify conv takes 106 us with the deduplicated window, against 39 us with a dense window.

## Modifications

- **`_causal_conv1d_update_kernel`**: adds a `DEDUP_CONV_WINDOW` path.
  - Step t's window is columns t..t+2 of the row `[state[1], state[2], x_0, ..., x_{T-1}]`.
  - The kernel writes that row once, as a `[BLOCK_N, next_pow2(T + 2)]` tile before the token loop, and skips the per-token window stores.
  - The tile mask covers exactly the T + 2 columns the per-token path writes.
  - Padded rows still exit before any store.
  - Two `tl.static_assert`s keep the branch from being compiled for a conv width other than 4 or together with a tree mask, so the kernel is safe without relying on its caller.
- **`causal_conv1d_update`**: takes the tile path only when all three hold:
  - the window view's step stride equals its window stride;
  - the verify is a chain (no tree mask);
  - the conv width is 4.

  With step stride == window stride == s, the per-token stores write column t + w of the row at (t + w) * s, and the tile writes column c at c * s: the same addresses and the same values, for any layout with those strides. MambaPool's deduplicated view is one such layout. There are no new arguments, and callers are unchanged. Kernels that do not take the tile get `NP2_WINDOW_COLS=1`, so no extra variants are compiled.
- **Test**: `test_causal_conv1d_update_dedup_window_matches_per_token`.
  - It runs the kernel on a dense window (per-token path) and on the deduplicated view (tile path).
  - It checks bitwise that the shared rows, the windows read through the view and the conv state match a reference row built in torch.
  - It checks that slots of padded rows are untouched.
  - It compares the conv output with the file's update tolerances.
  - Coverage: T in {2, 3, 8, 16} (T + 2 pads to tiles of 4, 8, 16 and 32), a `num_accept_tokens` state offset, MambaPool's axis-0 window layout seen transposed, fp32 and bf16, a dim that leaves a partial channel block, with and without padded rows.
- A comment in `MambaPool` is updated to describe the new write.

## Scope

This path is used by every chain verify (topk <= 1) whose conv window uses `MambaPool`'s deduplicated layout. Examples are GDN models (Qwen3.5/3.8) and Mamba2, on CUDA and ROCm.

These are unchanged and keep the per-token stores:
- dense windows: `UnifiedMambaPool`, KDA / Kimi-Linear, tree verify;
- deduplicated windows of a conv width other than 4 (for example LFM2, width 3).

## Accuracy Tests

- The new test passes, and so does the full test file (270 tests at 8eb01f2c9, which adds the tree-mask assert and the accept-offset, axis-0 and odd-T cases).
- The test is sensitive: a tile that ignores `num_accept_tokens` fails exactly the accept-offset cases, and forcing the tile together with a tree mask fails at compile time on the new assert.
- compute-sanitizer memcheck, racecheck and initcheck are clean on the tile test as of 8177311a1 (T in {2, 4, 8, 16}); besides comments and tests, 8eb01f2c9 adds only a compile-time assert and `NP2_WINDOW_COLS=1` for launches without the tile. The extra 72-case check below, which covers accepted-token offsets, transposed views and odd T, is also memcheck-clean.
- An extra 72-case check also passes, comparing the tile path bitwise with the per-token path. It covers T in {1, 3, 9}, mixed input and state dtypes, transposed views and accepted-token offsets.
- End to end, greedy, c1: acceptance length and output tokens are identical to main.

## Benchmarking and Profiling

Kernel time per call in microseconds (GB300, dim 10240, K 4, bf16, CUDA graph):

| bs | T | before | after | dense window |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 8 | 5.35 | 2.49 | 3.71 |
| 64 | 8 | 57.39 | 9.96 | 21.08 |
| 128 | 8 | 106.45 | 17.55 | 38.58 |
| 128 | 16 | 322.63 | 39.10 | 74.12 |

End-to-end setup:
- Qwen3.8-27B + DFlash2 (block 8), TP1, one GB300;
- chain verify, bf16 mamba state, overlap scheduling on, `--max-running-requests 128`;
- SPEED-Bench first turns, T = 1, top_p 0.95, top_k 20, up to 4096 output tokens;
- mean of 3 interleaved runs.

Decode tok/s = per-request decode rate (output tokens after the first / time after the first token), times concurrency; c1 is the single-request decode rate.

| concurrency | main | this PR | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| 64 | 6048 | 6361 | +5.2% |
| 128 | 6992 | 7329 | +4.8% |

Acceptance length is 3.59-3.63 in all six runs.

At c128 the running cap equals the concurrency, so about one request waits in the queue. https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/46182 shows that this setup reads 7-15% higher at that level than a larger cap, on both sides, so compare c128 only within this table.

Single runs at lower concurrency: c8 2031 -> 2104 (+3.6%), c32 4723 -> 4973 (+5.3%). At c1 the change is within noise: 332 -> 321, with acceptance length 3.70 vs 3.60 from sampling; per accepted token the rate differs by under 0.5%. Greedy (single runs): c1 357.0 -> 357.1 with identical acceptance length and output tokens, c64 6746 -> 7145 (+5.9%).

The end-to-end runs used the first commit; the two later commits add compile-time asserts, comments and tests, and pass `NP2_WINDOW_COLS=1` to kernels that skip the tile, with no runtime change on the tile path.

## Related upstream work

- sgl-project/sglang#38897 adds a separate packed variable-length kernel, `causal_conv1d_update_varlen`, to the same file. It writes the intermediate window per token with three stores per step, the pattern this PR replaces. There is no textual conflict (it is a new function), but if both land, packed verify through that kernel does not get the tile store. https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/46189 takes the other route: it adds packed rows to this kernel, so the tile store covers them too.
- This PR does not depend on any open PR.

## Notes

- The tile store is SubSir's work from the dynamic-verify branch. This PR ports it to the current kernel, gates it on the view's strides and adds the tests.
- Only GB300 was tested; ROCm takes the same path but has not been run.
- Commits: 7526326d8 (tile store and stride gate), 8177311a1 (width assert, test trim, `MambaPool` comment), 8eb01f2c9 (tree-mask assert, stride-based wrapper comment, `NP2_WINDOW_COLS=1` when the tile is off, more test layouts). Squash them when merging upstream.
